Plot the two sets of costs as curves, and the condition for replacement is their intersection,

\begin{equation}
C_{\text{human}}=w,
\qquad
C_{\text{machine}}=\frac{K}{L}+m
\end{equation}

Here $w$ is the annualized cost assigned to the human option, $K$ is the investment in machine purchase and installation, $L$ is the depreciation period, and $m$ is annual operating and maintenance expenditure. Given comparable output, quality, availability, and risk, the lower annualized cost drives replacement. Financing, utilization, switching costs, and the allocation of responsibility must be accounted for separately. Once the numbers favor the machine, procurement, installation, certification, and staff transfers still have to happen one by one.

This defense has clear limits. The scissors gap protects labor's relative price, rather than labor itself. An order-of-magnitude fall in electricity costs, through commercially realized controlled fusion, for example, would change the comparison between 100 and 3,000 watts; higher robot production would spread capital costs further; sufficiently structuring a setting would also eliminate the premium for error tolerance. The relative positions of two cost curves protect human jobs, rather than an inviolable physical law. This distinction must be clear, or physical protection will be mistaken for permanent exemption.

\subhead{Psychological Collapse: From the Pinnacle of Creation to a Cheap Interface}

Physical security has brought no peace of mind, instead creating a new problem. This explains a common perplexity. Many people still have jobs, yet have begun questioning the meaning of their work. Their positions survive because the high viscosity of their systems protects them; the way their skills are priced, however, has already been rewritten by generative capabilities in low-viscosity domains. The danger lies in the premature failure of the interface through which people establish their value, rather than in immediate replacement.

A distinction is easily lost here. Uneven timing means that cognitive labor's way of demonstrating its value fails first, rather than that cognitive labor disappears first. The work remains, but its pricing changes; the position remains, but the training needed to enter it no longer automatically secures a place. Separating these two processes explains why unemployment data can miss a transformation that workers experience intensely. The statistics count whether jobs exist; the experience concerns whether one's place is still recognized.

Understanding this failure requires returning to the old equation of value. Since the Enlightenment and the Industrial Revolution, modern civilization's values have rested on an equation: a person's value equals their social function, which equals the skills they command. Education emphasizes mathematics, physics, and chemistry, workplaces encourage greater professional expertise, and social standing is allocated according to productive efficiency. This hierarchy assumes that work demanding complex thought ranks higher, while purely physical labor ranks lower. Large models strike at the foundation of this hierarchy. Logical reasoning, programming, writing, painting, and legal advice, abilities once treated as the province of intelligence, become cheap commodities purchased by volume. A generative model can supply in a second the lighting effects an artist has spent ten years learning; a completion tool can produce in an instant what once rested on a programmer's five years of architectural experience.

The consequences of skill depreciation are independent of income. The fear this depreciation brings is not “I cannot feed myself,” because one can still make a living delivering for DoorDash, but “I am no use.” For middle-class and knowledge workers, being stripped of intellectual self-respect is harder to bear than a fall in income. In the past, being able to write, calculate, and summarize showed that a person had been trained, had engaged with the subject, and occupied a place in a community; now, these abilities are copied, amplified, and automated by external systems, and ability no longer automatically proves value. What technology externalizes is not some isolated capability but the interfaces through which the old society recognized training, experience, qualifications, and responsibility; once those interfaces are taken over, people must migrate to other interfaces to establish their value.

A new form of work has emerged in the gap between physical employment and psychological disempowerment. Platforms can join algorithmic planning and dispatch to actions still needing human hands. DoorDash couriers and Uber drivers offer early examples: platforms organize tasks through dispatch, prices, route suggestions, timing, rewards, and penalties, while people drive, climb stairs, deliver, and absorb customers’ emotions. People handle the final stretch of friction in the physical world. The work can provide an income, sometimes a good one; the question is how much control workers retain over objectives, conditions, and assessment. As decisions move to the platform, operators can become components called by an algorithm, temporarily cheaper than robotic arms; their actual labor still creates value, while their standing depends on usable refusal, negotiation, organization, and accountability.

Yuval Harari has proposed the idea of a “useless class.” Within this framework, the idea needs one amendment: people remain economically useful, indeed highly useful; it is the narrative that has no use for them. Civilization's central story has always been one of human-led exploration, creation, and conquest; when systems make frontier scientific discoveries and decide the most complex schedules, people become spectators. If the system has read every book I have read and remembers it better, can imitate every poem I write with surer rhythm, and can optimize every decision I make with greater stability, then who am I, and why do I need to exist? This fear is less acute than hunger, but persistent and penetrating. Its practical consequence is often an entire generation withdrawing from the climb up the skill tree, rather than unemployment.

The picture this section presents has two faces. On the physical side, entropy increase and high viscosity keep people temporarily safe in the high-entropy labor of moving atoms, fighting friction, and tending bodies. On the psychological side, the bit world's light-speed iterations remove the old explanation of their place. Two phrases sum it up: you keep your job, but lose your soul. The body remains fixed at the old world's worksite while the mind drifts through territory taken over by algorithms. This is harder to address than a problem of livelihood alone, because no directly corresponding compensation exists and because it takes place within a larger systemic change: efficiency gains themselves are producing new scarcities.

\subsection{Efficiency Inflation and Structural Bottlenecks in Development}

New demand can soon fill the space that greater efficiency releases. Cheaper generation brings a flood of proposals, code, and drafts; if review and maintenance cannot keep up, people move from drafting to processing candidates in a review queue. Work has no conservation law that requires it to return; the arrival rate has exceeded the capacity to receive it. The real question is how much extra work a saving at one step creates at the next.

 Technological progress often begins with a local reduction in resistance. A route becomes shorter, a device more efficient, a model cheaper, a process automated, a metric clearer, or a risk reduced by a safety device. Intuition says that lower local resistance should improve the whole system. Costs fall, efficiency rises, choices expand, risks shrink, and control strengthens. Yet complex systems often deliver the opposite. An extra road may worsen congestion; greater efficiency may raise total consumption; stronger safety may encourage riskier behavior; clearer metrics may corrode the actual objective; greater faith in a model may change what it predicts; automation may reduce routine work while leaving people with rarer, harder exceptions carrying greater responsibility. These phenomena have different names. 

\subhead{ Local Resistance Reduction and Actor Response }

 These phenomena have different names and are scattered across six unrelated fields: energy, transport, management, prediction, safety, and automation. Set them alongside one another, and their shared structure becomes visible. 

\begin{table}[ht]
\centering
\caption{ A shared structure across six paradoxes: local resistance reduction, actor response, global reorganization }
\label{tab:ch1-paradox}
{\small
\begin{tabularx}{\textwidth}{@{}l >{\RaggedRight\arraybackslash}p{2.7cm} >{\RaggedRight\arraybackslash}p{3.4cm} >{\RaggedRight\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
 Paradox  &  Local resistance reduction  &  Actor response  &  Global outcome  \\
\midrule
 Jevons  &  Cost per use falls  &  More applications and more uses  &  Total consumption rises instead of falling  \\
 Braess  &  A new route becomes available  &  Travelers reroute according to local optima  &  A worse equilibrium increases total network travel time  \\
 Goodhart and Campbell  &  A clear, measurable metric  &  Measured parties reorganize behavior around the metric  &  The metric detaches from its original objective; measurement fails  \\
 Lucas and reflexivity  &  A model predicts more accurately  &  Those being predicted adjust in response to the model  &  The old relationship fails; the system changes trajectory  \\
 Peltzman  &  Failure probability per exposure falls  &  Actors increase speed, frequency, or leverage  &  Total risk exposure expands, offsetting net benefits  \\
 Automation paradox  &  Routine operations are automated  &  People are left with rare exceptions  &  Remaining tasks grow harder; responsibility concentrates  \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}}
\end{table}

 Table  \ref{tab:ch1-paradox}  lists six different entries in its second column. Its fourth column points to the same class of consequence. This is no coincidence. Every row follows three steps: a local condition changes, actors within the system choose again according to their interests, and aggregate quantities reorganize at a new equilibrium. We will examine all six rows below; first, remember the third column: technology changes actors' field of choice, and even if their behavioral rules remain unchanged, their choices may change with it. This also explains why reports of these paradoxes find local indicators improving while overall conditions deteriorate: they measure quantities at different levels, and conflating those levels leaves only a contradiction. 

 Technology does more than subtract a patch of resistance from a system. It is more like a change in the system's cost landscape. Lower a local barrier, and actors choose new paths rather than stand still. Once actors choose again, the fields of flows, risks, and metrics, and the distributions of tasks and responsibility, all reorganize. Instead of staying in its original state and enjoying a local benefit, the system reaches a new equilibrium under changed boundary conditions. The paradox arises here: a local barrier falls, yet total viscosity is higher at the new equilibrium. 

 Technological effects therefore cannot be judged by local parameters alone. Faster, cheaper, more accurate, or safer performance at one point does not automatically make the whole faster, cheaper, more accurate, or safer. The global cost of a complex system is generated jointly by flows, bottlenecks, risk, verification, and responsibility after actors respond, rather than by a linear sum of local gains. The common framework can be stated as follows: local resistance reduction changes the cost landscape, actor response redistributes the system, a new equilibrium forms, and hidden bottlenecks emerge at new locations. 

 Following this framework, the six kinds of paradox fall into three groups. The first type is Jevons's paradox: expansion through lower resistance. Jevons's paradox originally concerned energy efficiency. Equipment that uses less coal, oil, or electricity should intuitively reduce total consumption. Yet when efficiency lowers the cost per use, more people use it, more applications become viable, and more demand is released, so total consumption may end up rising rather than falling \cite{jevons1865coal,allwood2012sustainable}. This is a throughput rebound, rather than an isolated counterintuitive feature of energy history. Lowering resistance in a channel attracts more flow from the system. Activities once too expensive become common; capabilities once used sparingly because they were slow become routine calls; resources once constrained by scarcity find their way into more applications. 

Efficiency lowers resistance per unit; total throughput may expand. In the AI era, Jevons's paradox becomes more conspicuous. Cheaper generation produces more content; easier code production increases software complexity and maintenance burdens; easier proposal generation raises verification pressure; easier access to computation drives further growth in total demand for it. Technology lowers resistance per operation while sending more operations through the system. Efficiency therefore does not automatically mean lower total cost. Whether a system is truly relieved depends on whether energy, cooling, verification, maintenance, responsibility, and absorptive capacity can still bear the expanded throughput, rather than simply on cheaper individual operations. In the framework of technological viscosity, Jevons's paradox shows how lower local viscosity may induce greater global throughput. The relationship between unit cost and total use can be expressed through elasticity,

\begin{equation}
E=q\,N(p),\qquad p=\alpha q,
\qquad
\varepsilon\equiv-\frac{d\ln N}{d\ln p},
\qquad
\frac{d\ln E}{d\ln q}=1-\varepsilon
\end{equation}

Here $q$ is physical consumption per operation, $p$ is unit price, and $N(p)$ is the number of operations per unit time; a fixed $α$ links the two, and $E$ is total consumption per unit time. When elasticity $ε<1$, efficiency improvements reduce total consumption; when $ε>1$, additional demand outweighs per-operation savings. In April 2026, the International Energy Agency recorded substantial gains in energy efficiency for individual AI tasks alongside a 17\% increase in total data-center electricity use in 2025 \cite{iea2026questions}. Savings per operation and rising totals can coexist; the size of the rebound must still be identified from demand data.

 The second type is Braess's paradox: a new route, a worse equilibrium. Braess's paradox shows that, in some traffic networks, adding a road increases everyone's travel time. The problem is not that the road itself is harmful, but that it changes the choices available to each driver. Everyone selects a new route according to a local optimum, traffic redistributes, and the system settles into a worse equilibrium \cite{braess1968}. This is a general problem of topological coupling rather than something peculiar to traffic. A path's cost is a property produced by the traffic loaded onto it, rather than a static attribute of the path. A road may offer low resistance to a few users and become a new bottleneck when everyone enters. We can place each traveler's minimization alongside minimization for the whole system, 

\begin{equation}
f_i>0\ \Longrightarrow\ c_i(\mathbf f)=\min_{j\in\mathcal P}c_j(\mathbf f);
\qquad
\min_{\mathbf f}\sum_{e\in E}f_{e}\,c_{e}(f_{e})
\end{equation}

 Here $f_e$ is flow on a road segment, $c_e(f_e)$ is the corresponding travel time, $\mathcal P$ is the set of routes between the same origin and destination, with route costs obtained by adding the costs of their segments. With fixed demand, user equilibrium requires every used route to have the current minimum cost, while the system optimum minimizes total network travel time. Adding a road expands the feasible set, so the system optimum cannot worsen when the new road need not be used; the new equilibrium reached through independent choices, however, may be worse. Braess's paradox occurs in this gap: more options do not themselves deliver coordination. 

 A tool can confer an advantage on a few users and become a bottleneck once everyone copies its use. A new road enlarges the set of physically reachable options, while the flow that users collectively create is a separate matter. Technology supplies paths, actors choose them, and pressure redistributes after those choices. The same question deserves asking in software and organizational systems, where the outcome depends on the particular mechanisms. 

\subhead{ Measurement and Models }

 Flows and paths reorganize at the level of material movement, but for actors to perceive, compare, and choose among those changes, they must pass through an information layer, which the same reorganization also rewrites. The third type comprises Goodhart's law and Campbell's law: metric corruption. Goodhart's law is commonly summarized as follows: once a measure becomes a target, it ceases to be a good measure \cite{goodhart1975problems}. Campbell's law likewise observes that the more a social indicator is used for decision-making, the more vulnerable it becomes to corruption and the more it distorts the process it was meant to monitor \cite{campbell1979assessing}. The root of these paradoxes is measurement's entry into the system. A metric begins as an observable, approximating a complex reality. Once it enters systems of rewards, penalties, resource allocation, and organizational control, however, it ceases to be merely an observable and becomes a control variable. Those being measured learn the metric, cater to it, game it, and may even sacrifice the real objective to optimize it. Behavioral feedback thus rewrites the relationship between metric and objective. Schools adapt teaching to rankings, hospitals adapt services to performance measures, platform creators adapt content to recommendation algorithms, and businesses adapt their actions to KPIs. The more consequential a metric becomes, the more behavior reorganizes around it; the more behavior reorganizes around it, the further the metric may drift from the real objective it was meant to measure.

 In terms of physical mechanism, a metric is no disturbance-free measurement. Once connected to an incentive structure, it changes the distribution of the system's degrees of freedom. It compresses a complex reality into a few optimizable variables while inducing actors to concentrate their actions on those variables. The stronger the metric, the more likely reality is to be reshaped by it. 

 Verification systems therefore generate viscosity of their own. Mature verification must improve measurement accuracy while also preventing behavior from taking over the measurement channel in reverse. Otherwise, the clearer the metric, the more likely the system is to develop new paths of low resistance around it, while obscuring the actual objective. Goodhart's law and Campbell's law arise on this side of measurement: clarity in local measurement can induce erosion of the global objective. 

 The fourth type is the Lucas critique and reflexivity: a model changes its object on entering the system. The Lucas critique observes that once a model built from past behavioral relationships is used in policy, actors adjust their behavior and the old relationships may fail \cite{lucas1976econometric}. Reflexivity emphasizes that, in markets, organizations, and social systems, participants' perceptions and actions change the very object they perceive \cite{soros1987alchemy}. The root of this problem is the model's entry into the action loop. A model initially describes a system, but once it is used for decisions, actors within the system change their behavior in response to it. Market forecasts influence traders' behavior, risk models influence financial institutions' strategies, policy models influence the expectations of firms and the public, and organizational diagnoses influence members' responses. Once a model enters the system, it ceases to be merely an external representation and becomes an internal variable. 

 This differs from a physical object. A cup does not deliberately change itself because you have modeled it; markets, organizations, public opinion, and negotiating counterparts do. They understand, adapt to, counteract, and exploit models. The more a model is believed, the more likely it is to change what it predicts; the more widely predictions enter action, the less the system follows its original trajectory. The difficulty in these systems is that model output changes boundary conditions, rather than that the model is insufficiently accurate. The model initially faced a system in a particular state; after the model is used, the system is no longer the same system. 

 A prediction becomes a new source of disturbance once it enters the action loop. It may fulfill itself or defeat itself. A model in a highly coupled system therefore needs more than static accuracy. It must also ask: how will its use change the system itself? The model enters the flow and changes the next round of movement, beyond drawing the system from outside. The Lucas critique and reflexivity carry the issue into prediction: improved local predictive capability may induce reconstruction of the object being predicted. 

\subhead{ Risk and Task Distribution }

 Once measurements and models are rewritten, actors' judgments about the world change, and with changed judgments come changed ways of acting. The fifth type is the Peltzman effect: risk compensation. The Peltzman effect describes how, after safety technology lowers a local risk, actors may take greater risks and offset part of the safety benefit. Safer roads may bring faster driving; stronger driving assistance may invite more distraction; finer financial risk controls may encourage more aggressive institutions; more automated platform moderation may prompt users to test boundaries more frequently \cite{peltzman1975effects}. This means that risk is no static substance, rather than that safety is useless. Risk is a distribution jointly produced by technology, actors, and the environment. A safety device lowers a local failure probability, but actors adjust their exposure, frequency, and intensity of risk-taking to the new safety boundary. Lower risk per exposure does not guarantee a proportional fall in total risk. 

 The key is expansion of the boundary. After a system gains a greater safety margin, actors may turn that margin into higher speeds, greater frequency, more leverage, less attention, or more aggressive behavior. Safety lowers a local barrier while also changing the space of action. Whether total risk ultimately falls depends on whether the local risk reduction exceeds the additional exposure created by expanding behavioral boundaries. Risk governance must therefore count total exposure after actors respond, as well as failure probability per exposure. Otherwise, safety systems will overestimate their net benefits. Reducing risk does not eliminate it; it can change how risk is used. The Peltzman effect is the risk-domain version of this logic: greater local safety may induce greater global exposure. The comparison can be written directly, 

\begin{equation}
R=p\,n\,d,
\qquad
\Delta R\approx n\,d\,\Delta p+p\,d\,\Delta n,
\qquad
\Delta R<0\ \Longleftrightarrow\ \frac{|\Delta p|}{p}>\frac{\Delta n}{n}
\end{equation}

$R$ is expected loss per unit time, measured in loss per unit time, such as accidents per year; $p$ is the probability of failure per exposure, a dimensionless quantity; $n$ is the number of exposures per unit time, measured in exposures per year; and $d$ is the mean loss per failure, measured in loss per failure. A safety device lowers $p$ ($\Delta p<0$), while actors respond by increasing exposure ($\Delta n>0$); to first order, the two effects on $R$ have opposite signs, and total risk falls if the relative decrease exceeds the relative increase. The “magnitude of the local risk reduction” in the text corresponds to $|\Delta p|/p$, and the “additional exposure created by expanding behavioral boundaries” corresponds to $\Delta n/n$: safety produces a net benefit only if the reduction exceeds the expansion, which is also why risk governance cannot count failure probability per exposure alone. The limits of applicability are these: the first-order approximation holds only when both relative changes are small; if actors respond discretely, by switching the safety device off altogether or withdrawing from the activity, or if mean loss $d$ itself varies with exposure intensity, this linear decomposition fails. The equation also addresses only whether total risk rises or falls, rather than how risk is distributed across a population. A safety device often protects only part of the population, while another part bears the expanded exposure.

The sixth type is the automation paradox: the concentration of residual burdens. Also known as the ironies of automation, it describes how automation reduces routine operations yet may make it harder for people to take over when something goes wrong. Machines handle routine processes while people lose contact with their details; when an exception occurs, people lack continuous involvement yet must judge quickly. Routine burdens fall, but what remains becomes more concentrated, harder to formalize, and harder to assign responsibility for \cite{bainbridge1983ironies}. The burden changes distribution rather than disappearing. Automation usually absorbs the frequent, regular, repeatable parts first, leaving people with the rare, marginal, ambiguous, and consequential ones. People therefore cease to bear the burden of continuous operation and instead bear the burden of residual tasks in the tail. Task numbers fall while task density rises; everyday burdens decline while responsibility for exceptions grows. The system looks more automated, yet the human role moves into harder territory.

Stronger AI makes this problem more pronounced. Models can handle many routine judgments, but the questions left behind are often harder to verify, explain, and take responsibility for. Automation reduces viscosity in front-line operations while concentrating residual burdens in exceptions, verification, and accountability. It rearranges people's place in a system rather than freeing them from it altogether. In the framework of technological viscosity, the automation paradox shows how automating local tasks can concentrate residual burdens in the tail.

\subhead{Redistributing the Field of Resistance}

These paradoxes differ in name and setting but share an underlying structure. Jevons's paradox concerns throughput response. Braess's paradox concerns route response. Goodhart's and Campbell's laws concern metric response. The Lucas critique and reflexivity concern model response. The Peltzman effect concerns risk response. The automation paradox concerns the response of task distributions.

Together they form a paradigm of technological paradox: technology first lowers a local barrier; actors act again in response to the new barriers; their actions change the fields of flows, risks, and measurements, and the distributions of tasks and responsibility; the system forms a new equilibrium under changed boundary conditions. The paradox arises when the total cost at the new equilibrium exceeds the benefit of the local reduction in resistance. This places existing paradoxes within one mechanistic framework, rather than inventing another name for a paradox.

To judge whether a technology has truly reduced system viscosity, we cannot look only at local efficiency, cost, speed, safety, or accuracy. We must examine whether, after entering the system, it changes total throughput, equilibrium, behavior around metrics, model reflexivity, risk exposure, verification pressure, and structures of responsibility. Technological paradox is no argument against technology. It simply reminds us that \key{Local optimization is not system optimization.} An open system responds to benefits, amplifies them, exploits them, and turns them into new pressures, rather than receiving them passively. The more effective a technology, the more likely it is to redistribute behavior; the better a path of low resistance, the more flow it attracts; the more useful a metric, the more it invites optimization around itself; the more a model is trusted, the more the object of its predictions changes through being predicted. Here, too, lies the deeper significance of technological viscosity.

Viscosity is a field of resistance that redistributes in response to technological inputs, rather than a fixed wall. When technology lowers resistance in one place, the system may develop new resistance elsewhere. Resistance can move from energy to cooling, generation to verification, paths to equilibrium, safety to behavior, automation to residual burdens, and models to responsibility.

Mature technological judgment asks not “Is this local improvement faster, cheaper, more accurate, or safer?” but: after local resistance falls, how does the cost landscape change? How will actors act again? Where will flows be directed? Where will bottlenecks reappear? Who will bear the risks and responsibility? What new equilibrium will the system enter? Has total viscosity actually fallen, or merely changed location?

Energy and infrastructure continue to set conditions for this reorganization. Obtaining energy requires an investment of energy, and the net surplus depends on the technological route, location, and accounting boundary; materials age, and maintenance expenditure depends on asset condition and service requirements. No broad historical curve of decline can determine the future of every energy technology. Computing's promised expansion must still be realized through particular power sources, equipment, and maintenance capacity.

The common form of technological paradox is a global reckoning after local resistance falls. Local resistance reduction is not the endpoint. The new equilibrium is the answer.

This step, however, remains qualitative. The six kinds of paradox have their own terminology, settings, and research traditions, and can be placed in one framework because they share an underlying structure, not because a common set of variables already describes them. Whether the costs of lower local resistance emerge in throughput, equilibrium, measurement, risk, or task distribution must still be answered case by case in the current formulation. If this common form holds, the transfer of resistance, the response of throughput, and the formation of new equilibria should admit a reusable set of quantities, beyond a classification by names. That formulation remains to be written.

\subsection{The Ultimate Question: The Paradox of the Post-Tool Age}

The previous section treated the redistribution of the field of resistance as a purely structural matter, yet resistance never falls evenly on people. The resistance that falls is removed from some jobs, while the new resistance is imposed on others. Who bears the transferred viscosity is a question of distribution rather than efficiency; before discussing distribution, we must establish the limits of these judgments, or technological viscosity can easily be read as just another expression of sentiment.

\subhead{The Full Account of Technological Effects}

Digital payments, navigation, industrial simulation, automated experiments, and code tools have reduced transition costs at different stages. Evaluating those improvements requires examining output, execution, verification, maintenance, and the handling of failure together. Costs reduced, burdens transferred, and risks not yet revealed should be recorded separately within the appropriate system boundaries.

Technological viscosity is no universal explanation, either. Politics, culture, capital cycles, business models, organizational capabilities, structures of interest, and social psychology also shape technological deployment. Technological viscosity offers a foundational perspective rather than reducing every social issue to resources, time, and topology: when intelligence tries to move from representational space into real systems, it must encounter resistance from its medium. That resistance is a structural property of the real system itself, rather than incidental noise. The decisive capability in the AI era is therefore not merely stronger generation, but the ability to turn generated results into real changes that can be executed, verified, maintained, and answered for. Future competition will concern verification systems, engineering systems, organizational systems, infrastructure, and institutions of responsibility, as well as model capabilities. Whoever manages viscosity better can turn intelligence into real productivity more effectively.

\subhead{Three Interlocking Paradoxes}

With those limits clear, the chapter's argument can be drawn together into three interlocking paradoxes. The first is the efficiency paradox. People once established their value by becoming faster, more accurate, and stronger, yet the end of that road is the disappearance of the person defined as a tool: the more people optimize themselves in logic, computation, and execution, the closer they come to the biological limits of carbon-based brains, while silicon-based systems advance exponentially on the same track. On this track, the finish line is the line of elimination. The issue is the choice of track, rather than a gap in ability.

The second is the escape paradox. People try to evade the material world's weight through virtualization, only to find that more freedom in the virtual world demands deeper dependence on the physical one. The more people desire a frictionless experience, the more energy-intensive, entropy-producing infrastructure they need in the world of atoms to support it. Trying to sever dependence on physical reality only makes that dependence harder. The desire to ascend intensifies the fall.

The third is the paradox of meaning, arising from the first two together. Modern people's sense of meaning rests on being needed: instrumental value. When the efficiency paradox declares people unnecessary as intelligent tools and the escape paradox declares escape impossible, meaning has a vacancy. People lose the pride of being producers, yet cannot rest content as pure experiencers, like ancient aristocrats, because someone must still maintain the physical foundation. They are caught between useful machines and free agents, unable to enter either position.

\subhead{From Doing to Being}

All three paradoxes share a premise: the problem is one of capability, and running faster will solve it. If that premise fails, technical reskilling and economic compensation are only pain relief, not a solution. Once the path of becoming a better tool reaches its end, and escape into a weightless virtual world is physically impossible, the question must change. The old question was: how can we do better than machines? We cannot. The new question is: when the capacity for \emph{doing} is outsourced to machines, what does \emph{being} consist of?

A turn is needed here, and it does not occur at the level of technology. The historical period that took efficiency as its sole coordinate defined a person's place through function; once function can be copied cheaply, that place is left suspended. The new place lies outside function: in the ability to bear, to judge, and to receive the consequences of action. These capacities cannot be bought centrally like computing power; they develop only in particular people over particular stretches of time. The era in which human civilization secured its right to survive by imitating machines, refining skills, and pursuing efficiency has ended, and the next question is to redefine the exam, rather than score higher on the old one.

A temporal limit must be made clear here. The physical world's lag is not a consequence of people failing to try hard enough; it is a window of time. During that window, people must both accept being surpassed in efficiency and preserve the ground on which machines do not define them. The window will not remain open indefinitely, because the three accounts discussed earlier keep moving: energy costs may fall, robot capital costs may be spread further, and high-entropy settings may be structured piece by piece. The buffer's value lies in giving time for a turn, not in guaranteeing its outcome.

History reveals the direction of that turn. Whenever technology externalizes an ability, it breaks an old bond between capability and value. Writing lightens memory, shifting value from recitation to understanding; printing lightens copying, shifting value from possessing texts to interpreting them and organizing trust; steam engines lighten muscular work, shifting value from doing work to control, maintenance, and dispatch; computers lighten rule execution, shifting value from execution to problem definition; large models lighten symbolic generation, requiring value to move toward verification, authorization for action, and bearing consequences. Each time, the structure repeats: external systems take over an ability, and people move to positions harder to counterfeit. Yet this trajectory also shows that migration never happens automatically. Writing did not naturally turn every memorizer into an interpreter; printing did not naturally bring every scribe into publishing institutions; steam engines did not naturally make every artisan an engineer. Migration requires new interfaces, new institutions, and sustained struggles over those interfaces.

This trajectory has a further qualification, which Chapter 6 develops. Migration is a contest, rather than a gentle upward curve, and high-viscosity positions do not inherently belong to people: the interfaces treated today as evidence of human value can also be absorbed by platforms, priced by capital, divided by contracts, and redistributed between expert systems and institutional machinery. If a few institutions monopolize these interfaces, people gain no automatic promotion, but become objects to be classified, scored, and tuned instead of producers. Migration cannot be achieved by individual effort alone; it requires new channels through which more people can express real experience, reject mistaken objectives, and participate in the distribution of consequences.

Technological progress will not turn the world into a frictionless information space. It lightens some stages while burdening others, accelerates some processes while shifting bottlenecks to verification, maintenance, and responsibility, and rapidly expands representational space while forcing real systems to redistribute resources, time, and structure. Understanding the AI era requires examining how intelligence passes through reality, as well as how capable it is. Durable, effective technological paths belong to people and institutions able to identify and distribute viscosity, reduce what is unnecessary, retain what is necessary, and achieve reliable state transitions under viscous conditions. The future does not belong to fantasies of a world without resistance.

Why intelligence itself encounters these forms of resistance remains unanswered. To answer that question, we must first ask an earlier one: in a world driven by energy gradients and sustained by dissipation, why does intelligence arise at all? Without an answer, all the preceding accounts amount to no more than a checklist.

\chapter{The Physical Boundaries of Reconfiguring Matter: Fundamental Forces and a Generalized Viscosity Model}

Chapter 1 ended with a question that comes before all the others: why does something like intelligence emerge in a world driven by energy gradients and sustained by dissipation? Without an answer, all the constraints of resources, time, and structure that follow can only be read as external obstacles, as though intelligence could otherwise pass lightly through the material world and merely happened to meet resistance. The reality is the reverse: resistance is not an obstacle external to intelligence; it comes from the way intelligence originated.

Intelligence is neither a miracle arriving from nothing nor a decorative faculty that life acquired by chance; it is more like a mechanism for selecting paths that the thermodynamic world produced over the course of evolution. To understand why intelligence emerged, and why it encounters constraints of resources, time, and structure, we cannot start with brains, language, or computers alone, but must begin deeper: with energy gradients, dissipative structures, autocatalytic networks, physical trial and error, and virtual simulation.

\section{Intelligence and the Reconfiguration of Matter: The Physical Limits of Optimization}

\subsection{The Principle of Least Action and the Path Selector}

\subhead{Dissipative Structures in Energy Gradients}

The universe is not still. Wherever differences in temperature, potential, concentration, and chemical energy exist, matter flows, collides, reorganizes, and dissipates. Isolated systems tend toward increasing entropy, but open systems can form locally ordered structures through sustained flows of energy and matter. Storms, cells, organisms, cities, and machines are not the opposite of increasing entropy; they are local channels formed within an increase in entropy on a larger scale. They maintain order not by escaping thermodynamics but by taking in free energy, reorganizing matter, releasing waste heat, and using their own structures to participate in a larger process of energy release.

What sustains this local order requires a clearer account of the mechanism. In \emph{What Is Life?}, Schrödinger posed a question with lasting influence: how do living organisms avoid rapidly sliding into thermal equilibrium? His answer was that life maintains its own order by taking in “negative entropy” from its environment \cite{schrodinger1944}. In more precise contemporary terms, life does not violate the second law of thermodynamics: an open system maintains local order by continuously taking in low-entropy resources and releasing high-entropy waste and waste heat. Life does not acquire its order for free; it must keep paying for it.

Prigogine's theory of \term{dissipative structures} took the question further. Far from equilibrium, open systems subject to sustained flows and nonlinear interactions can form new ordered structures \cite{prigogine1977nobel,nicolis1977}. Their order is dynamic, dependent on inputs and outputs, rather than the closed order of a static crystal. Once the flows of energy and matter stop, they disintegrate, cool, die, or return to a state closer to equilibrium. Life is one of the extreme forms of this dynamic order: a complex, persistent, replicable, and evolvable dissipative structure within thermodynamics, rather than an exception outside it. The maximum entropy production principle offers a heuristic picture: in some open systems far from equilibrium, structures that can stably organize flows may be more readily sustained and amplified \cite{martyushev2006}. Storms organize flows of heat and momentum, organisms capture and convert chemical or solar energy, and ecosystems and cities reorganize flows of energy, matter, and information on larger scales.

A distinction matters here: the maximum entropy production principle is not an uncontested universal law that can be applied directly to every aspect of the evolution of life and intelligence \cite{bruers2007}. This chapter uses it as a picture, not as proof. It helps us see a possibility: \key{Order does not necessarily resist entropy increase; often, order itself is a more complex, stable, and enduring channel of dissipation.}

\subhead{Autocatalysis and the Coupling of Conditions}

Once local order forms, the next problem is persistence. Several critical transitions separate ordinary chemical reactions from life, and one of the most important is autocatalysis. In primordial oceans, hot springs, mineral surfaces, or small chemical environments, thermal motion, random fluctuations, and local differences in concentration can produce transient pockets of molecular order. Most soon disperse into a disordered distribution again. Some structures, however, are unusual: they do more than exist; they promote their own formation. A and B react to produce C, and C promotes further reactions between A and B: this is autocatalysis. Autocatalysis amplifies small pockets of order that arise by chance, giving transient structures the ability to reinforce themselves.

Autocatalytic networks matter because they turn a structure that occurs by chance into one that can persist. They are positive feedback networks, rather than single chemical reactions. Given sustained inputs of energy and raw materials, such networks can expand, replicate, compete, and differentiate. They absorb free energy and maintain local order while releasing heat and waste. More complex structures can process flows of matter and energy more effectively and are more likely to survive competition. Kauffman's work on self-organization and autocatalytic sets sought to explain precisely this: understanding the origin of life requires an account of how chemical networks spontaneously form structures that can persist and expand, as well as an account of external selection \cite{kauffman1993}. This account also has a limit. Autocatalytic networks are not a complete answer to the origin of life. In their discussion of autocatalytic sets, Hordijk and colleagues emphasize that these sets are important conditions for lifelike behavior but are insufficient on their own to constitute life in full \cite{hordijk2018}. A self-reinforcing reaction network also needs boundaries, information storage, variation, replication, selection, and internal regulation before it can approach life. Autocatalysis provides a route from transient pockets of order to structures that persist, rather than explaining the origin of life in a single stroke.

Each missing condition has its own possible origins, and information carriers have received the most attention. The RNA world hypothesis provides another important lead here. RNA is unusual because it can carry sequence information and, in some circumstances, also act as a catalyst. In 1986, Walter Gilbert used the phrase “RNA world” to describe a hypothetical stage before modern life came to be dominated by DNA and proteins, when RNA may have performed both information storage and catalysis \cite{gilbert1986}. This hypothesis does not mean that the origin of life has been solved, but it brings out a crucial point: the emergence of life requires information, reactions, and replication to become progressively linked. With energy flow but no information, structures struggle to accumulate a history; with information but no reactions or energy, structures cannot sustain themselves; with reactions but no boundaries, local order struggles to concentrate and be inherited.

Dissipative structures, autocatalytic networks, RNA, lipid membranes, and primitive metabolism should therefore be understood as several kinds of conditions that must gradually couple, rather than as a single historical sequence already proved in full: energy flows, boundaries, information storage, replication, variation, selection, and internal regulation. Membranes distinguish a system from its environment, RNA or other information carriers preserve inheritable structures, and autocatalytic networks organize flows of energy and matter. Primitive life was not a soul that suddenly appeared; it arose as certain dissipative structures acquired boundaries and the capacities for replication and internal regulation through prolonged selection.

\subhead{Geodesics in Phase Space}

Dissipative structures and autocatalytic networks explain how local order can emerge and persist, but they do not explain where intelligence fits into this picture. To answer that question, we need a different description: treat a manufacturing activity as the movement of a system's state through a high-dimensional space.

Space in everyday language has just three dimensions—length, width, and height—while the state of a simple pendulum can be specified by two variables, position and momentum. Describing the state of a chemical plant or an assembly line, however, requires thousands of independent variables: reaction temperature, pressure, catalyst concentration, material strength, transport distance, inventory cycles, equipment depreciation rates, and the cost of capital, each constituting a dimension. Raw materials occupy one point in this space, the finished product another, and production is the trajectory traced by the state point between them. In this description, a process improvement is a new choice of trajectory.

In state space, engineering optimization compares paths under constraints: can the same objective be reached with less material, lower energy consumption, a shorter schedule, or less risk? The stationary action principle in physics provides another rigorous formulation in terms of paths. It derives equations of motion from a specified Lagrangian and boundary conditions, and cannot be directly equated with minimizing economic cost. Both formulations concern paths, but they use different quantities and criteria.

\begin{equation}
S[q]=\int_{t_{1}}^{t_{2}}\left(T-V\right)dt,
\qquad
\delta S=0
\end{equation}

$S$ is the action, measured in joule-seconds; $q$ is a generalized coordinate; $T$ and $V$ are kinetic and potential energy, respectively; and $\delta S=0$ means that the actual trajectory makes the action stationary under the specified endpoint conditions. A stationary value can be a minimum or have other properties. Nonconservative effects such as friction require the corresponding generalized forces or a description of dissipation. The principle supplies equations of motion; how intelligence develops choice, memory, and learning requires a separate account of the mechanisms.

Industrial waste has specific sources: inaccurate demand forecasts create inventories, inadequate control of operating conditions increases losses, and poorly planned routes cause redundant transport. AI can reduce these expenditures through search, modeling, and control. The size of the improvement must be measured for the same task, quality, and system boundary; “extra action” cannot replace the separate accounts for energy consumption, money, and time.

Intelligence acts here as a \term{path selector}. It compares actions in light of objectives, available resources, and feedback, seeking routes with a higher probability of success and a more manageable cost. This choice can change materials, processes, and initial states, as well as actual losses; the specific lower bound must be recalculated for the task and its physical boundaries.

Path selection moves some expensive trial and error into a model before execution. Comparison itself has a cost, and the selected path must still be executed in reality. We therefore need to distinguish three accounts: a reaction's net thermodynamic cost, the barrier governing its rate, and the operation and maintenance of equipment and structures. The three interact, but they are not the same expenditure of energy.

\subsection{Two Unavoidable Expenditures: Activation Energy and the Entropy Tax}

Change and maintenance face different constraints. Activation barriers primarily affect reaction rates, free-energy differences constrain net work exchange under given conditions, and maintenance concerns damage, disturbances, and the continuity of function. Stable structures such as crystals can persist passively, while life and continuously operating equipment generally require supporting flows. Keeping these separate makes it possible to see which part intelligence can improve.

\subhead{The Thermodynamic Bottleneck of Physical Trial and Error}

Once life emerges, however, it faces a harsher problem: how to find better paths through complex environments. Early living systems relied primarily on \term{physical trial and error}. Mutation, replication, competition, elimination, and death make up the oldest search mechanism. It works because reality selects; it is extraordinarily expensive because every failure is settled in the real world. A harmful mutation changes a body, rather than a line of code; a mistaken action consumes energy, exposes the organism to risk, costs opportunities to reproduce, and may cause death, rather than merely requiring a corrected answer. Natural selection computes in a real environment, and matter, time, and life pay the bill.

This is the thermodynamic bottleneck of physical trial and error. The more complex the environment and the greater the number of possible paths, the more expensive it becomes to select among them through collisions with reality alone. Evolution can search through vast populations and immense stretches of time, but for any particular organism, real-world trial and error is too slow, too costly, and too dangerous. An individual cannot use its body every time to test whether it can leap a cliff, whether it can approach a fire, whether an unfamiliar animal will attack, or whether spoiled food is safe to eat. Reality supplies an answer, but often too late.

Intelligence emerged within this bottleneck. A nervous system does more than let life sense the world: it builds a low-cost model of the environment inside the body. An animal need not try every possible action in reality; it can first rehearse internally where food might be, where danger might lie, which route takes less effort, which movement is likelier to succeed, which object is worth approaching, and which signal must be avoided. Intelligence moves some external collisions inward, converting some physical trial and error into \term{virtual simulation}.

This is a profound substitution of costs. Real-world trial and error requires movement, injury, energy consumption, material losses, and sometimes death; internal simulation requires neural signals, memory, attention, and computation. Neither is free, but their costs differ by orders of magnitude. Intelligence lets a system choose before doing work, compare before acting, and rule out errors before exposure to risk. It does not cancel physical costs; it reduces the number of times they are paid blindly.

From the perspective of biological evolution and systems that act, \key{The primary function of intelligence is to avoid costly mistakes, rather than to think abstractly.} This judgment sounds less like the traditional philosophical celebration of intelligence, but it is closer to the predicament of life. An organism must act with limited energy, limited time, a limited body, and limited information. It need not know the truth of the universe to qualify as intelligent; first it needs to reduce risk before acting, assess objects before contact, choose paths before expending resources, and exclude obvious errors before failure. Intelligence is a mechanism through which a body selects paths that allow it to persist in a heavy world, rather than a luxury of the abstract mind.

\subhead{Information Hubs and Two Kinds of Entropy}

Once this mechanism operates, a finer question arises: what exactly does it reduce? Through internal models, intelligence reduces an agent's uncertainty about relevant environmental states and the consequences of action, thereby reducing the agent's internal information entropy. Two kinds of entropy must be distinguished here. Thermodynamic entropy describes energy dissipation and irreversible processes; information entropy describes uncertainty about states. In founding information theory, Shannon formalized uncertainty as information entropy \cite{shannon1948}. Intelligence reduces an agent's ignorance of its environment and the consequences of action, allowing clearer judgments about paths, rather than reducing the thermodynamic entropy of the external world itself; this reduction in information entropy must be carried by real physical processes. Brains need glucose and oxygen, neural signals require electrochemical processes, and memory and learning require changes in material structures. Intelligence is a highly organized dissipative process inside an open system, rather than mental activity without a cost.

The human brain provides a concrete factual anchor. In discussing the brain's energy budget, Raichle and Gusnard note that it accounts for about 20\% of the body's oxygen and calorie consumption despite comprising only a small fraction of its mass \cite{raichle2002}. That proportion alone shows that intelligence is not free. The brain is expensive because it compresses vast amounts of environmental information, bodily states, memory, prediction, and action selection into an energy-intensive system. Life's willingness to pay a high price for a brain shows how internal simulation can save even more expensive external trial and error.

Landauer's principle also reminds us that information processing cannot be separated from physical costs. In 1961, Landauer pointed out that erasing information in logically irreversible operations entails heat generation \cite{landauer1961}. The principle cannot simply be used to calculate the energy consumed by all thought or all AI training, but it establishes a basic fact: information is no ghost detached from the material world. Recording, erasing, transmitting, and computing information all require a physical substrate. Intelligence reduces uncertainty without escaping thermodynamics; it saves the cost of mistaken actions while still consuming energy itself.

Living organisms consequently develop a functional division of labor. A complex living system needs an energy system, an information system, and a system for doing work. The energy system takes in, converts, and supplies free energy; the work system moves, hunts, builds, escapes, and changes the environment; the information system senses, remembers, predicts, and selects paths. Cells have energy metabolism, genetic information, and protein machinery; multicellular organisms have digestive, circulatory, nervous, and motor systems; human civilization has energy infrastructure, production systems, bodies of knowledge, and computing systems. Intelligence is the information hub of a dissipative structure. It does not directly replace energy or work, but determines where they are directed. The brain is expensive because it compresses a large amount of environmental information; civilization developed language, writing, mathematics, and science because these systems compress scattered experience into a capacity for path selection that can be transmitted, used in simulation, and reused. The more complex the information and the more advanced its compression, the more the system can reduce blind trial and error.

Friston's free energy principle has something in common with this line of thought. It seeks to place perception, action, and learning within a unified framework: organisms maintain their states by reducing prediction error or surprise \cite{friston2010}. This chapter neither simply equates intelligence with free energy minimization nor applies one grand theory directly to every intelligent phenomenon. It borrows a deeper intuition: life continuously predicts, acts, and revises to keep itself within a viable range, rather than passively receiving the world. Intelligence continuously selects paths in a closed loop between body and environment, rather than observing from outside the world.

\subhead{The Activation Barrier: The Cost of Breaking Chemical Bonds}

Reconfiguring matter requires an actual reaction path. The free-energy difference between reactants and products determines the thermodynamic direction of net change under given conditions, while the activation free energy affects the rate of crossing the transition state. Breaking old bonds requires energy, and forming new bonds releases it, so the net account cannot include bond-breaking costs alone. Manufacturing does not always push matter into a higher-energy state; the purpose of a process is to produce the target state at a viable rate, purity, and yield.

At constant temperature and pressure, under the corresponding reaction conditions, the change in Gibbs free energy can be written as $\Delta G=\Delta H-T\Delta S$. A negative reaction free-energy change indicates the spontaneous direction at the given state, but supplies no rate. Changes in reaction quotient, pressure, temperature, and composition also change the direction and the equilibrium position. A catalyst changes the path and the rate, but not the free-energy difference between the same initial and final states.

Ironmaking transfers oxygen from iron-bearing feedstocks to other substances. Carbon and carbon monoxide participate in reduction inside a blast furnace, while coke also supplies heat and supports the burden; energy consumption depends on the feedstock, reduction route, temperature, heat transfer, and equipment \cite{babich2021blast}. Algorithms can improve burden preparation, flow, and control, while alternative reducing agents and process routes can also change the entire cost structure. The energy of a single iron–oxygen bond cannot directly serve as the minimum energy bill per tonne of iron.

Producing cement clinker involves carbonate decomposition and the subsequent formation of minerals. Calcium carbonate decomposition is endothermic and its equilibrium also depends on the partial pressure of carbon dioxide; clinker burning requires specified temperature and residence-time conditions. The theoretical heat consumption of about $1.7\,\mathrm{GJ/t}$ reported in the literature is a process estimate for a particular clinker composition and system boundary, while actual heat consumption also includes heat-transfer, exhaust-gas, and equipment losses \cite{madivate1999theoretical,madlool2011cement}. Changing the clinker proportion, feedstock, or binder route also changes the basis of comparison.

High temperatures affect equilibrium, reaction rates, and transport processes at the same time. Raising the temperature can accelerate some steps while also increasing losses or damaging the product; catalysis and route redesign can achieve the same objective at a lower temperature. The thermodynamic constraints of given initial and final states, the kinetic barriers along the selected path, and the losses in actual equipment must be distinguished. Intelligence can help change the latter two, and can also help find new combinations of initial states and objectives.

\subhead{The Entropy Tax: Maintaining Order and Countering Randomness}

“Entropy tax” here means the continuing expenditure needed to maintain function. Life depends on metabolism, repair, and regulation, while operating equipment needs energy, cooling, and maintenance. Buildings, crystals, and passive storage structures have different mechanisms of stability; not every form of order requires continuous external work. Maintenance costs should be estimated from the specific mechanisms of damage and disturbance.

Agriculture organizes light, water, nutrients, land, and biological processes into harvestable output. Breeding can change the harvest index and improve disease resistance, photosynthesis, root systems, and resource use. Yield and inputs do not simply redistribute a fixed total: they change together with variety, environment, and management. Solar energy flows, external inputs, land occupation, and harvest outcomes should be accounted for separately.

Structural safety requires dealing with uncertainty in loads, materials, construction, and models. Safety factors and partial factors are specified by codes, failure modes, and structural components; they cannot all be interpreted as “one tonne in an ideal case, two tonnes in reality.” Redundant material can also carry loads and dissipate energy. Intelligent design aims to reduce unnecessary expenditure while meeting reliability requirements and retaining structures that withstand disturbances.

The Landauer limit supplies a precise microscopic account: under the corresponding thermal and information conditions, resetting one unbiased bit requires a minimum heat release of $k_{\mathrm B}T\ln2$. At room temperature, this is approximately $2.9\times10^{-21}$ joules. Raising a one-kilogram object by one meter requires about 9.8 joules, but these are entirely different units of operation, and their ratio cannot estimate the costs of complete reasoning and manufacturing tasks. Comparing complete tasks also requires accounting for the number of operations, actual devices, communications, equipment, and auxiliary systems.

\subsection{The Conservation Equation for Reconfiguring Matter}

\subhead{Amplification Through Virtual Simulation}

Human civilization continued and amplified this route. Language compresses individual experience into collective memory, maps turn spatial trial and error into representations of paths in advance, mathematics compresses relationships into forms that support deduction, scientific theories organize scattered experience into testable models, and engineering simulation moves expensive experiments into representational space before execution. Many of civilization's inventions essentially move physical trial and error into symbols, models, and computation in advance. People need not travel every road, because maps can exclude bad routes beforehand; engineers need not let every bridge collapse once, because mechanical models can exclude dangerous structures; doctors need not try every treatment directly on patients, because experiments, animal models, clinical trials, and statistical analysis jointly narrow the space of error.

Artificial intelligence further increases the density of virtual simulation. It can search enormous spaces of possibilities for candidate solutions, discover hidden structures, generate models, predict outcomes, and screen at scale before real action occurs. AI is a new stage of this evolutionary route, rather than a superphysical intelligence outside thermodynamics. Brains simulate the world with neural signals, science with equations and experimental systems, engineering with computer simulations, and AI with high-dimensional statistical models and generative systems. Their common function is to narrow the scope for error, screen paths, and reduce blindness before physical costs are actually paid.

Virtual simulation separates selection from execution, and a classic thought experiment illustrates the distinction. Maxwell imagined a demon stationed at a vessel's valve, able to see the speed of every molecule, admit fast molecules, and block slow ones, thereby creating a temperature difference without consuming energy. From Szilard through Landauer to Bennett, the problem led researchers to include measurement, storage, and resetting in the account of a complete cycle; the preceding section discussed the thermodynamic cost of erasing information \cite{landauer1961,bennett1982thermodynamics}. Applying this thought experiment to industrial systems reveals another account: algorithms have no hands. They can decide when a valve should open or close, but cannot supply the actuator with the mechanical energy needed to move it. AI in industrial systems occupies the information control layer: it can reduce uncertainty about relevant states, resolve airflow vortices in blast furnaces, track vehicles through logistics networks, and detect frequency fluctuations in power grids; it does not directly produce the force of execution, and every change to the state of atoms must pass through actuators powered by electric current, hydraulics, or combustion. From a control perspective, industrial civilization depends on power amplification: in a schematic hierarchy running from neural electrical signals at the nanowatt scale through muscles at the watt scale, vehicles at the kilowatt scale, and factories at the megawatt scale, control signals can mobilize a capacity for work far greater than their own power. Intelligence occupies the information control layer, where signal power can be far below the power of the execution it directs. A control signal is not a power flow: a logic gate can determine whether a dam gate opens or closes, but cannot provide the mechanical energy to lift it; when energy is insufficient, the gate will not move, however correct and timely the command. For an actual amplification chain with an independent energy source at every stage, the power relationship can be written as a product,

\begin{equation}
P_{k}=P_{0}\prod_{i=1}^{k}G_{i},
\qquad
G_{i}=\frac{P_{i}}{P_{i-1}}\gg 1
\end{equation}

Here $P_{0}$ is the power of the control signal at the start of the chain, in watts; $P_{k}$ is the final execution power, in watts; $G_{i}$ is the dimensionless power gain at stage $i$; and $k$ is the number of stages. The examples in the text—neural electrical signals at the nanowatt scale, muscles at the watt scale, vehicles at the kilowatt scale, and factories at the megawatt scale—show the range of power scales that control and execution can span. Each stage treats the preceding stage's signal as a control input, rather than an energy source, and draws power from its own energy system; the product accumulates the ratios of output to input power at successive stages, rather than creating energy from nothing. $G_{i}\gg1$ also shows that the power carried by the signal layer can be small relative to execution power, so “the command is correct” and “the action is possible” are two different conditions. A switch can determine whether passage is allowed, while the actuator still needs energy; the product above is the arithmetic expression of this distinction. The product holds when each gain is defined by actual input and output power and every stage has the power source it needs. Each stage must also meet the next stage's drive requirements; if an energy source or actuator is missing, the chain breaks there, and no amount of upstream computational accuracy can compensate.

\subhead{Virtual Simulation and Its Limits}

Virtual simulation, however, is not reality itself. Intelligence can select a path but cannot replace it, schedule energy but cannot cancel it, reduce wasteful dissipation but cannot make the reconfiguration of matter cease to dissipate. It is the arrangement of forces, rather than a force; a mechanism for choosing where energy is used, rather than energy itself. The essence of intelligence is to reduce the number of times the world is moved in the wrong way while it remains heavy, rather than to make the world light.

AI can design a bridge that uses less material but cannot abolish the mass of steel, gravitational potential energy, or the strength of connections; it can optimize a robot's movements but cannot supply a motor's torque, bear a joint's wear, or handle noise on a sensor's behalf; it can screen drug candidates but cannot perform metabolism, toxicology, clinical validation, or long-term feedback in place of a human body. \key{Intelligence can approach a given task's lower bound on physical cost, but computation cannot abolish that bound.} It can reduce mistaken paths but cannot eliminate the paths themselves; reduce wasted experiments but cannot eliminate verification; reduce waste but cannot eliminate work.

Reconfiguring matter requires connecting descriptions, inputs, processes, and outcomes; a preliminary accounting relationship can be written as follows:
\begin{equation}
\begin{aligned}
&\text{Information (recipe)}+\text{Matter (medium)}+\text{Free energy (work)}+\text{Time (process)}\\ &\longrightarrow \text{Ordered structure}+\text{Waste heat}
\end{aligned}
\label{eq:conservation}
\end{equation}
Each of the four inputs represents a condition that cannot be replaced by the others. Information is the recipe, expressed dimensionally in bits: it specifies what the structure should become but does not itself move any atom; matter is the substrate, measured in kilograms, supplying the atoms the final structure needs; free energy is the work term, measured in joules, with the required net work determined by the initial and final states and the process conditions, rather than invariably pushing matter from a lower to a higher energy state; time is the process term, measured in seconds, because state transitions must follow a real trajectory through time, rather than jump only within a space of representations. The two terms on the right are outcomes: the ordered structure is the target organization formed by the process, and waste heat is an output of actual irreversible processes. For a continuously operating dissipative system, the boundaries for free-energy input and entropy output must be specified; a closed system can still exchange heat and work and must not be confused with an isolated system. Without entropy export, continuing irreversible processes consume available free energy, and local order cannot accumulate indefinitely. This is a relationship among conditions for a process, rather than an accounting balance: with information but no matter, the result cannot appear; with matter but no available driving mechanism, the desired change does not happen automatically; with energy but no time, the process cannot unfold; an ordered system that continuously dissipates cannot sustain its function without the corresponding supporting flows. Intelligence can change selection, not the conditions of existence; it can optimize paths, not reality's physical accounts.
