\subhead{Candidate Proliferation and the Return of Costs}

This is precisely what is most easily misunderstood in the AI era. AI reduces the cost of finding possible paths, rather than automatically reducing every cost of completing a state transition. It can generate a thousand building designs, but the buildings still have to be built; propose ten thousand molecular candidates, but experiments and clinical work cannot expand in step; simulate countless robot movements, but real robots still face friction, collisions, batteries, joints, and maintenance. The search space can expand rapidly, while verification and execution must still return to the physical world.

AI itself also has thermodynamic costs. Training and inference need chips, electricity, data centers, cooling systems, supply chains, and maintenance systems. The cloud is not weightless; it merely hides materials, energy consumption, and waste heat behind an interface. Internally, AI appears as information compression and path search; externally, it appears as a high-density dissipative structure. It converts some physical trial and error into computational trial and error, but computation still needs a physical substrate. Substituting bits for some trial and error with atoms does not eliminate atoms; substituting computation for some experiments does not eliminate energy consumption; screening paths with a model does not mean those paths have been completed.

Greater intelligence does not automatically make reality lighter. What intelligence expands first is the space of candidates. Where only ten solutions could once be tried, ten thousand can now be generated; where only a few conditions could once be simulated, vast parameter spaces can now be explored; where only a few experts' intuitions were available, models can now compress enormous bodies of experience. This is certainly progress. Yet more candidates also push pressure toward verification, execution, and those who bear the consequences. Intelligence lowers search costs but may increase the burden of screening; lowers the barrier to proposing solutions but raises the requirements for confirming them; lowers the cost of trial and error in bit space but brings the verification bottlenecks in the domains of atoms and life into view.

Intelligence forms internal representations, allowing some expensive trial and error to take place in models first. Technological viscosity examines how paths enter reality after screening. The two meet at the question of cost: computation and learning can reduce some execution costs while also adding expenditure on data, verification, and maintenance. Whether a change is worthwhile requires comparing the entire path, rather than counting only how quickly candidates appear.

The distinction becomes particularly clear across the three media of bits, atoms, and life. In bit space, path search can be extremely fast: text, code, images, proposals, and simulations can be generated, revised, copied, and withdrawn at high speed. In the domain of atoms, path selection must be realized in materials, energy, positions, friction, heat, forces, and maintenance; errors cannot be undone as easily as text. In the domain of life, path selection is heavier still, because living processes involve development, metabolism, immunity, reproduction, and long-term feedback; an apparently beneficial intervention may reveal its costs over a longer timescale. The deeper intelligence enters these media, the more it must acknowledge that paths can be screened in advance, while state transitions must still pay real-world costs.

Once a path has been selected, materials, energy, and structures for execution must still realize it. Computation can help reduce this expenditure, but cannot replace the actual process. The next step is to examine resource conditions in detail, distinguishing costs that arise from initial and final states from those that arise from processes and losses.


\section{Resource Barriers: Power Flux, Binding Energy, and Material Abundance}

Once intelligence has selected a path in representational space, the cost must be settled in the medium, and the medium's first account is resources. Of the three kinds of constraint, resource barriers are the easiest to misjudge. Discussions of intelligence's capabilities usually place the constraints on the information side: is the model strong enough, is there enough data, is the algorithm good enough; these conditions are indeed improving rapidly, and the improvements can be measured. For a proposal to become a fact rather than a description, however, it must pass another set of checks with entirely different criteria: can the materials be obtained, can energy be supplied at the required power, can the process finish within an acceptable time, and can the resulting structure be maintained over the long term? The material world does not change automatically because a proposal has been made. A drawing can be generated instantly, a route rapidly optimized, and countless possibilities simulated on a screen, but any proposal entering reality must answer older questions: where do the materials come from, how is energy supplied, how does the process unfold, how does the structure remain stable, how are losses handled, and how is order maintained? This is the resource barrier.

A resource barrier is neither a simple “lack of resources” nor a temporary shortage of supply, but the conditions for state transitions that every material reconfiguration must pass through. A real system's transition from state A to state B reconfigures material positions, energy distributions, structural relationships, and processes in time, rather than merely rearranging symbols. Information can provide the recipe, intelligence can select the path, and organizations can coordinate action, but matter does not rearrange itself automatically because an algorithm is better. Resources are not isolated “things” in nature either: they are neither names in the periodic table nor total reserves in the crust, but matter in a state that permits extraction, separation, processing, transport, control, and maintenance. A resource is a combination of matter, available energy, location, structure, purity, interfaces, and usability, rather than atoms alone. Without a usable state, existence does not amount to a resource; without a route into a technical system, reserves do not amount to capability. The first question about a resource barrier is therefore whether matter can be brought into a usable state, beyond whether it exists.

Iron, silicon, nitrogen, lithium, copper, and aluminum all occur in nature, but natural occurrence does not automatically confer technological usability. To enter a technical system, matter must undergo extraction, separation, purification, transport, processing, stabilization, and maintenance. Every step requires available energy, incurs losses, and depends on equipment, organization, and time. Usability is therefore the result of a technical system's work rather than an intrinsic property of matter, which in turn explains why the same land supports vastly different populations and industries at different technological levels, and why resource statistics always lag changes in technical capability. What we call a resource is usability that a technical system creates in natural matter.

\subsection{Power-Flux Limits and the Kardashev Scale}

\subhead{Levels of Available Energy}

The “available-energy constraint” here does not mean applying one particular thermodynamic potential to every technical system; it refers more broadly to the energy conditions that can drive state transitions, sustain local order, and actually be called upon by technical systems. For an engineering system, the key is the energy's entry into the process in the appropriate form, at the required power and location, within the right time window and with sufficient control precision, as well as its total amount. Heat, fuel, electricity, mechanical work, chemical potential, and potential energy can all contribute to real-world change, but become capabilities only when technical systems can dispatch, convert, and constrain them. Available energy can also be stored in structures: cities and infrastructure lift, fix, and connect vast quantities of material, retaining some energy as gravitational potential energy and in other forms while dissipating the rest during construction; changing a structure requires rearranging these energy accounts, and concentration, location, and purity are prerequisites for state transitions alongside energy.

How much reconfiguring capability a form of available energy can support thus depends on its energy scale. In 1964, Kardashev proposed classifying civilizations by the power they could command \cite{kardashev1964transmission}; the scale is commonly written as
\begin{equation}
K=\frac{\log_{10}P-6}{10},
\label{eq:kardashev}
\end{equation}
Here $K$ is the dimensionless civilization index and $P$ the total power the civilization can command, in watts; the denominator 10 means that a 0.1 change in the index corresponds to one order of magnitude in power, while each increase of 1 in $K$ corresponds to ten orders of magnitude. On this scale, Type I corresponds to $10^{16}$ watts; humanity's present power consumption is on the order of $2\times10^{13}$ watts, or 20 terawatts, giving $K\approx0.73$, about 2.7 orders of magnitude short of 1.0 \cite{smil2017energy}. Another convention often cited in the literature places Type I at the total solar radiation received by Earth, approximately $1.7\times10^{17}$ watts, corresponding to $K\approx1.12$ in this formula; the two conventions differ only in their zero point, which does not affect the conclusion below. In this coordinate system, the gap between 0.73 and 1.0 is not 27\%.

Chemical and nuclear reactions have different energy scales per event, nuclear fission already supplies electricity, and solar, hydroelectric, and wind power do not require humans to burn chemical fuels \cite{jaffe2018physics}. The microscopic energy scale of a source cannot directly determine the macroscopic power available to a factory. Industrial processes are also constrained by energy conversion, transmission, equipment, materials, and control.

This scale, however, is easily misread as a one-dimensional ranking. Total power is only one coordinate of a civilization's capabilities: the same power can produce vastly different results depending on its form, location, and precision of release; conversely, a system with less total power but strong dispatch capabilities can achieve state transitions in particular domains that a more powerful system cannot. The Kardashev index addresses a ceiling rather than the whole problem, and treating $K$ as a civilization score omits three variables: the form of available energy, its release location, and the control window.

From this perspective, technology's primary object is locally ordered structure sustained jointly by matter, energy, and constraints, rather than information. Bridges, chips, batteries, drugs, factories, cities, and data centers are more than “objects.” They are functional structures formed by using energy to move matter away from dispersed, disordered, or unusable states. They must be manufactured, retain their functions amid disturbances, and continually resist wear, corrosion, heat, noise, aging, and failure. Technology involves more than turning ideas into reality: it converts available energy into controllable, stable, maintainable local order, and thermodynamics and energy history repeatedly show civilization to be an open process dependent on energy conversion, material organization, and waste-heat removal, rather than a symbolic system detached from energy \cite{smil2017energy,callen1985thermodynamics}. \subhead{The Step Beyond Chemical Energy}

Nuclear fission supplies power through nuclear fuel, reactors, and thermodynamic cycles, while imposing requirements for fuel supply, materials, waste, and safety governance. Its scope for sustained expansion depends on resource pathways, technologies, costs, and institutions; neither the natural abundance of uranium-235 nor the existence of waste can decide the question alone. The respective constraints of chemical, nuclear, and other energy sources must be assessed across the complete system.

Each deuterium-tritium fusion event releases approximately 17.6 megaelectronvolts. Obtaining useful net energy also requires meeting conditions for plasma confinement, materials, the tritium cycle, heat removal, and equipment operation \cite{atzeni2004physics}. If fusion develops into a mature energy system, it may broaden supply options; until then, industrial capability can continue to improve through existing energy sources, conversion, and processes, without being uniformly confined to a single valence-electron energy scale.

The rocket equation shows that, for a given effective exhaust velocity, larger velocity increments require a rapidly increasing mass ratio. Chemical propulsion has a practical performance range: about 4.5 kilometers per second is representative of high-performance chemical engines, rather than a strict ceiling shared by every design. Missions can also use staging, gravity assists, or other forms of propulsion. The force of these constraints lies in their item-by-item calculability, rather than in declaring a radius of activity directly from the energy of a single reaction.

\begin{equation}
\Delta v=v_{e}\,\ln\frac{m_{0}}{m_{f}},
\qquad
\frac{m_{0}}{m_{f}}=\exp\!\left(\frac{\Delta v}{v_{e}}\right)
\end{equation}

Here $\Delta v$ is the velocity increment gained by the rocket, in meters per second; $v_{e}$ is effective exhaust velocity, in meters per second, determined jointly by the propellant, reaction energy, expansion process, engine efficiency, and other factors, with the text's 4.5 kilometers per second representing the order of magnitude for high-performance chemical engines; $m_{0}$ is mass before ignition and $m_{f}$ mass after propellant exhaustion, in kilograms; their ratio is the dimensionless mass ratio. The logarithm is the key: each additional $v_{e}$ of velocity increment multiplies the mass ratio by $e$; for a given mode of propulsion, the larger the desired velocity increment, the greater the mass fraction that must be reserved for propellant, while the attainable range of $v_{e}$ is constrained jointly by reaction energy and engineering design. This transport cost of chemical propulsion takes the form of a mass ratio rising exponentially with $\Delta v/v_{e}$; staging, gravity assists, and other modes of propulsion require their own mission-specific accounting. The limits of applicability are these: the equation gives an ideal velocity increment, neglecting drag and gravity losses, so a real mission requires more propellant with other conditions held equal; this book substitutes no target $\Delta v$ for a particular mission, since that depends on the mission itself, and uses the equation here only to show how the order of magnitude of $v_{e}$ constrains the cost of macroscopic transport.

\subhead{The Mismatch Between Computing Speed and Power Delivery}

Computation, energy storage, and actuators improve along different paths. A battery's specific energy, specific power, service life, safety, and cost must be balanced together; cell-level values, pack-level systems, and theoretical material values must also be distinguished. Comparisons of fuels and batteries must also account for engine and motor efficiencies and mission mass. Historical annual improvement rates are not eternal constants, and percentage-based compound growth is not linear growth \cite{ziegler2021reexamining,viswanathan2022challenges}. Theoretical limits such as those of Bremermann and Bekenstein concern information processing and information capacity, respectively, under particular assumptions \cite{bremermann1982minimum,bekenstein1981universal}. They cannot predict how many more years commercial chips can improve at their present pace. Practical improvements in devices also face limits in materials, interconnects, memory, cooling, and manufacturing economics; robot motion requires a separate power account for actuators and energy storage.

\subhead{Four Sets of Conditions}

Once technology is understood as the generation of locally ordered structures, the conditions that material reconfiguration must pass through can be listed one by one. The first set concerns materials: real-world change needs a physical medium, bridges need steel and concrete, batteries need metals, separators, and electrolytes, chips need high-purity materials, and drugs need molecules that can be synthesized, remain stable, and enter the body. Without a medium, information remains a description; with the wrong medium, a proposal cannot enter the world. Many technologies fail for reasons of material form, purity, technological chains, service life, and long-term stability, rather than a lack of imagination. The second set concerns available energy: moving a material from one state to another generally requires crossing barriers, with ores to reduce, molecular bonds to break, crystal lattices to rearrange, objects to transport, structures to lift, and equipment to drive. Energy is a condition of state transitions rather than an optional addition; without enough available energy that can be called upon, controlled, and released in concentrated form, matter will not spontaneously acquire a new order merely because humans become more intelligent, and production, transformation, and disposal in economic processes are likewise bound to entropy increase, dissipation, and irreversibility \cite{georgescu1971entropy}. The third set concerns processes, whose distinctive feature is the sensitivity of their rates to temperature. Real-world change takes time: steel must be smelted, cement calcined, drugs synthesized and verified, chips put through many processing steps, and buildings constructed, cured, inspected, and delivered; processes require equipment, sequencing, environments, people, and stable conditions, and many physical processes cannot be copied, rolled back, or restarted like software, while greater precision imposes stricter requirements for temperature, pressure, purity, timing, and surroundings. This sensitivity has a definite physical form: the Arrhenius relation describes the relationship between reaction rate and temperature, with its expression and conditions of applicability given below in the discussion of strong covalent-bond cleavage. For now, retain its conclusion: the higher the activation energy, the more sharply temperature affects the rate; in high-temperature processing, temperature acts as a switch for crossing barriers rather than a linear amplifier.

The fourth set concerns maintenance, which turns the first three accounts from one-time investments into long-term expenditure. An ordered structure does not persist forever once built: machines wear, buildings age, pipes corrode, materials fatigue, data centers need cooling, infrastructure needs maintenance, and pharmaceutical systems need oversight; locally ordered structure is a state of continually resisting dissipation rather than a one-time achievement, and maintaining order is itself part of the resource barrier. These four sets of conditions form material reconfiguration's underlying relationship: information provides the recipe, materials the medium, available energy performs the work, processes unfold the structure, and maintenance mechanisms resist dissipation. Information cannot fully replace any element of this relationship: a recipe without a medium produces no result; a medium without available energy undergoes no state change; energy without a process stabilizes no structure; and local order without continuous maintenance cannot sustain a system over the long term.

The four sets of conditions are easily read as an approval checklist, as though passing each item separately were enough to enter reality. The actual situation differs: all four must be present at once, and if any one is almost absent, investment in the other three cannot deliver; material shortages leave available energy idle, insufficient available energy halts a process midway, and loss of process control can make maintenance cost more than the structure itself is worth. Here lies the core meaning of the resource barrier: \key{Reality consists of executable states, rather than possibilities.} Possibilities can be generated without limit; executable states must satisfy material conditions. A viable proposal does not mean materials are already in place; available materials do not mean available energy has already been supplied; sufficient energy does not mean the process is stable; a completed process does not mean the structure can be maintained over the long term; real-world change must pass through the full chain from materials to available energy, processes to maintenance, and local states to lasting order.

These four sets of conditions do not apply with equal force at every stage of history. For a long time, technical systems bypassed the most expensive one: instead of manufacturing the low-entropy structures they needed, they took products that natural processes had already made. Wood had strength, fibers toughness, rivers a drop in elevation, and coal chemical energy; from that starting point, the accounts for materials, processes, and maintenance were much lighter. The cost of using nature's ready-made structures is dependence on their distribution, stocks, and rates of replenishment; once ready supply cannot meet demand, the costs of forming and processing materials, previously borne by nature, return to the accounts. How long this use can continue determines the form in which resource barriers later reappear.

\subsection{Using Low-Activation-Energy Materials and Reconfiguring Physical Form}

The history of technology begins with selecting matter rather than manufacturing it. Almost none of the materials and power sources humans first used were of their own synthesis; they were structures made in advance by photosynthesis, geological processes, and evolution. Understanding this use of ready-made structures explains both why early technology seemed light and why that lightness could not last.

The earliest technology used parts of the world that the world had already made, rather than manufacturing the world. Wood, cotton, hides, bones, flowing water, wind, animal muscle, coal, and oil were not resources that humans created from scratch. They were structures already organized, or forms of energy already accumulated, by natural processes. Trees turn sunlight, carbon dioxide, and water into fibers, plants and animals organize environmental matter into bodies, rivers and wind fields give energy flows direction, and fossil fuels seal the solar energy captured by ancient life inside chemical bonds. Early technology seemed light because it drew on work nature had already completed, rather than escaping physics; this is the real meaning of low-hanging fruit.

\subhead{Using Structures Prefabricated by Nature}

Low-hanging means that nature has prepaid part of the bill, rather than that the technology is primitive. Humans need not synthesize wood, design cotton fibers, or produce the chemical energy in coal on demand: nature has prepaid energy, structure, and time for the technical system, which merely cuts, carries, weaves, burns, domesticates, and rearranges these ready-made structures. In other words, low-hanging fruit identifies places where nature has already generated low-entropy structures, rather than fruit that is easy to obtain. Wood already has strength, stone hardness, fiber toughness, muscle mechanical work, rivers a drop in elevation, and coal chemical energy; early technology follows the paths of low resistance nature provides, chiefly changing form rather than rewriting matter itself and drawing on existing order rather than creating order from disorder. This also explains why many early technologies seem especially “natural”: a windmill intercepts wind rather than making it; a waterwheel uses a drop rather than creating it; a wooden house comes from cutting trees rather than manufacturing cellulose structures; domesticating animals organizes their existing metabolism and movement rather than manufacturing muscle. Technology has costs, but geological, biological, and climatic processes have already amortized a large share of them in advance.

Cotton brings naturally formed cellulose structures into textile processing. The plant has already synthesized the material; textile machinery chiefly organizes drafting, twisting, and winding \cite{klemm2005cellulose}. This fit of material form to process was an important condition for mechanization, while the Industrial Revolution also involved energy, trade, capital, labor, and institutions; “the energy density for breaking strong chemical bonds was unavailable at the time” cannot explain it alone.

Early rough mechanical processing depended on a fit of microscopic form as well as the material's chemical properties. Cotton fibers have natural convolutions along their axes, related to cell-wall structure and collapse during drying: after the boll ripens and opens and water evaporates, the roughly cylindrical cells become twisted ribbons. Friction between fibers and cohesion produced by twisting allow loose staple fibers to form a continuous yarn. Scales on wool create directional friction and make fibers prone to felting and entanglement, requiring control of carding intensity and fiber alignment; fine flax yarn is often wet-spun to improve fiber slippage, while coarser yarn can also be dry-spun. Cotton requires neither resynthesizing cellulose nor chemical bonding to form yarn, providing favorable conditions for early mechanical processing. Raw-material preparation is the other half of the explanation. Wool's diameter, length, and crimp vary with the animal, body region, and environment, and input variation adds to the control burden of fixed mechanical motions. Cotton, as a seed fiber, also varies in fineness, length, and maturity; grading, cleaning, and blending bring these differences within a range machines can handle. The water frame need not identify each fiber: it repeats drafting, twisting, and winding; biological form and raw-material preparation have already reduced input variation enough for fixed mechanical motions to run continuously \cite{cottonworks_quality,flax_spinning_glossary}. Low-hanging fruit does not extend indefinitely. As demand expands, technical systems cease to be satisfied with the forms nature supplies: wood is not hard enough, requiring steel; natural fertility is not stable enough, requiring fertilizer; natural fibers are not diverse enough, requiring synthetic materials; natural crystals are not precise enough, requiring semiconductors; ordinary combustion is not controllable enough, requiring electricity systems; natural medicines are not precise enough, requiring synthetic molecules and targeted interventions. Technology shifts from drawing on existing structures to actively manufacturing them.

\subhead{The Activation-Energy Staircase}

Moving from existing forms to active manufacture usually makes process conditions more complex. This book calls that change the “activation-energy staircase,” pointing to thresholds in purification, reactions, lattices, defects, and interface control. Individual processes have activation energies with precise physical meanings; a whole factory's capital and maintenance burdens have no single activation-energy value. The two must be measured separately.

Technological usability depends on whether a material has the required purity, form, concentration, and location. Sand is not a wafer, ore is not steel, and lithium in the ground is not a battery. Producing a usable state requires extraction, transport, processing, reactions, and quality control, with costs arising from thermodynamics and kinetics as well as equipment and organization.

Precision manufacturing often needs stricter cleanliness, defect control, measurement, and process windows. As chips shrink, some control tasks become harder, while process innovation may also lower cost per function. The account must cover the energy use, yield, capital, and maintenance of particular steps, rather than assigning every control difficulty to one progressively higher activation energy.

Startup and maintenance belong in the same life cycle. Finer structures may increase control and maintenance requirements, or perform the same function with less material and energy. Deeper penetration into matter does not guarantee that total cost rises in one direction; it requires accounting for the complete path from discovery through manufacture to long-term operation.
