\subhead{Four Layers of Resistance}

The first layer of resistance is power. Changing reality requires work: moving objects, driving equipment, compressing processes, raising output, and speeding transport all require more state transitions per unit time. Energy divided by time is power:
\begin{equation}
P=\frac{\Delta W}{\Delta t},\qquad \Delta W\ \text{held fixed}\ P\propto\frac{1}{t},
\label{eq:power}
\end{equation}
Here $P$ is power, measured in watts, or joules per second; $\Delta W$ is the work required for this state transition, measured in joules; and $\Delta t$ is the time taken, measured in seconds. The inverse relationship assumes that total work remains fixed: the route, process, and materials stay the same, and the task is simply performed faster; if acceleration changes the process or makes $\Delta W$ depend on speed, the relationship must be recalculated. The conclusion follows directly: halving the time doubles the power; reducing time by an order of magnitude raises power by an order of magnitude. Compressing the same energy consumption into less time requires greater power input; without the corresponding supply, transmission, and control capacity, acceleration becomes overload. Industrial production makes this particularly clear: a faster line requires feeding, processing, inspection, packaging, logistics, and maintenance to sustain the faster pace together; a shortfall in power capacity at any stage becomes a bottleneck, and forcing one stage to accelerate creates a backlog at another. Speed is settled across the entire chain.

Power systems build different response speeds into their choice of equipment. Adjusting power faster requires more than pushing the same generating unit harder; it also requires equipment with different ramping capabilities: conventional coal units often adjust output by a few percent of rated capacity per minute, flexible gas units are generally faster, and battery storage can respond within milliseconds to seconds where its inverter and control system permit. Their costs must be compared separately in terms of power, storage duration, fuel, life, and operating conditions; a single “cost per unit of capacity” cannot place them in a fixed order. The wind and solar fluctuations a grid can accommodate depend on ramping capability, network capacity, reserves, storage, demand response, forecasting, and control \cite{irena2017planning,pnnl2019storage}. The same principle appears in manufacturing and transport: cutting delivery from six weeks to one usually means airfreighting some components, running some processes in parallel, and positioning some inventory in advance, as well as running equipment harder; the time saved is bought back at a higher unit cost. Time, power, and capacity can be exchanged in this way; near the limits of a given system, the margin required for further compression can become increasingly disproportionate.

Beyond power, the second layer of resistance is heat. Engineering must account for losses: computation generates heat, mechanical motion encounters friction, power transmission incurs losses, chemical reactions may produce by-products, and production may leave waste; if losses per operation stay fixed, higher speed means more waste heat to remove per unit time. Heat removal is a central boundary to acceleration: many systems could compute, transmit, or manufacture faster if they could remove heat, losses, and by-products at the same rate. Data centers, chips, engines, batteries, factories, and urban transport all face this constraint: energy can enter faster, but waste heat must leave faster too; if incoming flux rises beyond outgoing capacity, the system heats up, throttles, ages, or fails. Heat makes acceleration a question of whether unusable energy can leave as well as whether energy can enter.

Beyond power and heat, the third layer of resistance is stress. Physical objects are not ideal symbols: materials bear forces, structures bear vibration, equipment bears wear, connectors bear shocks, and supply chains bear fluctuations; driving a system faster exposes its weak points faster. Faster machinery increases friction and fatigue, faster construction puts more pressure on quality control, faster logistics reduces buffers, and faster organizational activity leaves less time for communication and repair. Stress is dangerous because it often accumulates as microscopic damage before causing failure; fatigue, wear, loosening, cracks, and quality fluctuations can result from prolonged high-frequency loading rather than a single large shock. Acceleration brings a system closer to its limits while accumulating damage faster.

The fourth layer of resistance, and the easiest to overlook, is inspection and repair. Faster systems need to find errors sooner: in a slow system, an error may have time to surface, be located, isolated, and repaired; in a fast one, a small error may be copied, spread, and amplified before it is found. A faster production line has a shorter inspection window; faster financial trading spreads erroneous orders faster; faster content generation concentrates review pressure; more scientific candidates deepen the verification bottleneck. Inspection and repair form a distinct cross-section because their costs do not fall linearly with speed: doubling inspection frequency often requires corresponding increases in equipment, staffing, standards, and organizational processes, while repair capacity remains constrained by the time needed to locate faults and complete rework.

Taken together, the four layers lead to a counterintuitive conclusion: speed need not mean efficiency. Efficiency means completing an effective state transition at lower total cost; speed measures how much transition is completed per unit time. A system can be fast yet consume much energy, generate large heat loads and losses, spread errors quickly, and be difficult to maintain; it can also be slower, stable, economical, and repairable. The real question is whether going faster reduces the system’s total bill.

\subhead{Speed and Efficiency}

Accelerated testing is engineering’s formal method for trading away time; its boundaries show how far that trade can go. Materials and device life assessments commonly raise temperature to accelerate reactions, then use an Arrhenius relationship to extrapolate service life at ordinary temperatures; a test that would take years can thus finish in months. There is a strict condition: the extrapolation must stay within the same failure mechanism. At sufficiently high temperatures, new reaction pathways, stress states, or failure modes appear, and the life being extrapolated belongs to a different process. Testing time is compressed, while service still unfolds under its own conditions and over its own duration; conversion between them is valid only where the acceleration model applies and the failure mechanism remains the same \cite{nist_arrhenius}. This condition recurs wherever acceleration is applied: directly reducing the time parameter first requires evidence that the shortened process still follows the same path.

Concrete curing illustrates a productive use of this exchange. Twenty-eight days is a common testing age, not the end of strength development; with a suitable mix and temperature–pressure schedule, high-pressure steam curing can produce a 24-hour strength close to the 28-day strength under ambient curing, with the autoclaving stage itself taking on the order of a dozen or more hours. Precast pipe piles and other high-strength components use processes of this kind \cite{psu_accelerating_strength,chen2017autoclave}. The twenty-odd days saved become autoclaves, boilers, pressure vessels, and the energy needed for a continuous steam supply; component dimensions are also constrained by the sealed vessel. High temperature and pressure alter hydration products and long-term properties too, so the exchange involves mix design, microstructure, and performance targets as well as time and energy. The curing route chosen depends on which resources are scarcer on site and what properties the product requires.

AI is especially liable to create an illusion here. It greatly reduces the time spent on search, expression, generation, and preliminary screening; this speed is real and valuable, reducing pointless waits and blind trial and error, narrowing the candidate field, and improving early judgment. Once AI output enters reality, it encounters materials, equipment, bodies, processes, experiments, organizations, and responsibility, rather than an information space that can be compressed in the same way; the faster the generation stage, the more likely execution, verification, and maintenance are to become throughput bottlenecks. Reducing ten thousand candidates to one hundred can be quick; turning those hundred into reliable conclusions requires experiments, tests, replication, environmental exposure, and long-term feedback. Proposals can be generated at high frequency, but real verification cannot run at an unlimited frequency; faster generation demands sufficient verification capacity, or speed merely transfers pressure from generation to verification.

Automation downstream can expand parallelism, reduce waits, and remove steps by improving the route. The remaining constraints must be specified: which steps genuinely have to occur in sequence, how long each requires under current conditions, and which consequences become observable only after exposure. Only with these conditions fixed does the chain have a corresponding lower bound on elapsed time.

Open the acceleration ledger, and benefits and costs appear in different accounts. Cutting a workshop’s cycle time from 60 seconds to 45 raises output by one-third on paper, but feeding, changeovers, inspection, packaging, and logistics must be rescheduled to the new cycle; if one stage cannot keep up, extra work in progress accumulates between operations, tying up space, capital, and subsequent rework time. The equipment account is more direct: higher rotational speed means faster wear and shorter maintenance intervals, so some of the apparent increase in utilization must be offset against maintenance downtime. Speed gained at one stage is forfeited at another; acceleration moves costs from the time account to equipment and maintenance accounts.

Acceleration is therefore no one-way road to efficiency. Effective acceleration removes pointless waits, rework, and needless friction, completing the same state transition at lower total cost; ineffective acceleration merely raises flux density and pushes power, heat, stress, errors, and maintenance into the background. A mature system should seek a sustainable range of speeds rather than the shortest possible time; energy supply, heat removal, load bearing, inspection, repair, and responsibility jointly define that range: below it the system wastes time, above it the system consumes its own structure. Real efficiency means completing a state transition within the throughput the system can bear. Resistance to acceleration is the throughput ledger of compressed time. Time cannot simply be deleted: it is either wasted or used for buffering, cooling, inspection, repair, and revealing hidden effects. AI can help eliminate wasted time, but cannot remove for free the time needed to bear a process; information can arrive first, while reality must still pass through the available cross-section. The physical world accepts speed on the condition that the system can bear it.

The discussion so far concerns one kind of acceleration: compressing a process into a shorter window. Another kind increases how often updates are imposed on the same system, rather than shortening the duration of a particular process. The two face different constraints: the first depends on sufficient throughput capacity, the second on how long a system takes to complete an update. If inputs arrive more frequently than the system can absorb them, the system is being interrupted rather than accelerated.

\subsection{The Bandwidth of Time: Update Frequency and Response Timescales}

Temporal rigidity means more than an inability to compress a process at will. It has a subtler form: real systems cannot be updated at arbitrary frequencies. AI readily creates the illusion that faster generation, prediction, and scheduling should make real systems change faster too: models issue new judgments every second, platforms refresh data in real time, sensors collect signals continuously, organizations revise metrics whenever they like, and algorithms repeatedly recompute plans. Speed comes to be mistaken for intelligence itself, and real-time operation for efficiency itself. But a real system is not a screen that completes a state change whenever an input arrives; after accepting a change it still has to transmit, execute, obtain feedback, correct, and settle again. Only then has it completed an update. This is the bandwidth of time.

\subhead{Bandwidth and Timescales}

A system’s response bandwidth describes how much of the variation in its input appears in its output. Materials, actuators, procurement, and organizations each have their own dynamics; high-frequency signals may be attenuated, or may elicit different responses through the control structure. A new input arriving before the previous round finishes does not automatically cause instability; the interactions among inputs, states, and the feedback loop must be examined.
\begin{equation}
\frac{\mathrm{d}x}{\mathrm{d}t}=\frac{u-x}{\tau},
\label{eq:relaxation}
\end{equation}
$x$ and $u$ have the same state units, and $\tau>0$ is the time constant. With a fixed input, the error decays exponentially, leaving about 37\% after one time constant. With a continuously varying input, the system acts as a stable first-order low-pass filter, attenuating amplitude and introducing phase lag. Closed-loop oscillation requires a separate analysis that includes a controller, delays, or other such structure.
\begin{equation}
f_c=\frac{1}{2\pi\tau},
\label{eq:cutoff}
\end{equation}
$f_c$ is the cutoff frequency of a first-order system, measured in hertz. For a sinusoidal input at frequency $f$, the steady-state amplitude ratio is $[1+(2\pi f\tau)^2]^{-1/2}$; at $f=f_c$ it falls to $1/\sqrt2$ of its low-frequency value. High-frequency response is attenuated, but the equation itself still describes a stable first-order tracking system. Greater tracking bandwidth requires changing the plant or the control structure.

Sampling frequency and a plant’s ability to follow an input are distinct design questions. Faster sampling can provide more state information; the controller must also account for delay, noise, gain, and actuator limits in choosing how to update. A first-order low-pass system responds to high-frequency inputs with reduced amplitude; whether a closed loop oscillates depends on the loop formed jointly by controller and plant. Fast sampling alone neither guarantees stability nor necessarily causes instability.

Some processes can respond faster with faster actuators, shorter coordination chains, and greater sensor bandwidth; others require different materials or structures to change their timescales. Protective action also requires distinguishing measurement, judgment, and execution: fast measurement combined with filtering and thresholds can preserve both responsiveness and resistance to disturbances. Immune regulation, circuit protection, and quality inspection work through different mechanisms; their pace must be designed around the signals being identified and the consequences of errors.

Reality is therefore a system of many timescales, rather than a slow system. Near contact, protection, balance, fault isolation, and immediate safety, fast response is essential; near goals, meaning, institutions, trust, and long-term structure, stability is essential. Planning, scheduling, inventory, maintenance, coordination, and resource allocation lie between: they cannot be too slow, but cannot be driven directly by high-frequency signals either. Mature systems assign update times across levels, rather than letting a central intelligence control everything at one frequency.

The layers of a power system are a mature expression of this principle. In the first tens of milliseconds after a fault, protective relays begin identifying it and issuing trip commands, while actual clearance time also depends on circuit breakers and protection coordination; over the following seconds to minutes, frequency control, stability controls, dispatch, and related functions adjust output, shed load, or isolate areas; above these sit day-ahead and longer-term markets, maintenance, and planning, operating over days, months, and years. Each layer has different authority, action speeds, and grounds for judgment: protection and local control that cannot wait for human reaction rely on automatic action, while goals, rules, and long-term commitments require identifiable people and institutions to take responsibility; dispatch and planning can also use automated optimization \cite{nerc2024frequency}. Repeated accidents and engineering practice have shaped this layering, because no single timescale can handle both faults and planning.

Embodied intelligence makes the point especially clear. A robot cannot simply connect a large model directly to every motor: a body is not a screen, and movement is not text. Language understanding can be slower, vision must update faster, motion planning must turn goals into trajectories, and low-level control must handle balance, force, friction, slipping, and error at high speed. A system can take its time deciding “this is a cup,” but when its fingers touch the cup it must correct pressure and posture quickly; semantic correctness cannot replace force feedback. High-level intelligence handles meaning and goals, low-level loops handle stability and safety, and the levels between must translate across timescales; otherwise greater intelligence can leave the body less controlled. Nor can a power grid be rewritten in real time at any frequency one chooses. Fault protection must be extremely fast, frequency regulation fast, load forecasting somewhat slower, market dispatch slower still, and the generation mix and grid plan slower again. AI can forecast load at high frequency, but cannot rewrite the whole grid at that frequency; protection that is too slow causes accidents, while planning that changes too fast creates disorder. Grid stability depends on each level having an appropriate update time.

\subhead{Forms of Frequency Mismatch}

The same holds for supply chains. Demand signals can fluctuate in real time, while capacity, procurement, inventory, transport, and quality checks have their own cycles; passing high-frequency demand straight into production without filtering can turn short-term fluctuations into excess inventory, shortages, rework, and scheduling friction. A small fluctuation at the point of sale can be amplified through procurement, production, and logistics into oscillation across the whole chain; the problem is a slow system forced to respond to fast fluctuations it should not be following, rather than an excess of demand signals. Organizations provide an even clearer case: data can refresh in real time, metrics can change daily, and AI can offer continuous advice, but trust, capability, habits of cooperation, and relationships of responsibility cannot be rewritten every day. A team needs time to understand its goals, establish a rhythm, and stabilize who is responsible for what; if every day brings a new priority, every week a new objective, and every model update new advice, an apparently more agile organization may lose continuity. Attention fragments, boundaries of responsibility blur, executors keep changing direction, and the system spends its energy responding to change rather than completing work.

The real danger of high-frequency intelligence is updating before completion. The next change arrives before the system has absorbed the last; the next metric replaces the previous one before behavior has fed back; the next plan is issued before the consequences of the previous plan have appeared. The system then switches among unsettled changes instead of accumulating capability; it keeps updating without completing an update, and keeps responding without establishing stable control. Frequency mismatch usually takes several forms: first, noise, as inputs arrive too densely for the system to distinguish real change from short-term disturbance, producing more filtering, explanation, and coordination rather than more action; second, interruption, as high-frequency advice repeatedly cuts into slower processes, forcing people to reinterpret, realign, and reorder their work until time is fragmented into pieces too small to finish anything; third, oscillation, as delayed feedback meets overly frequent adjustment and the system keeps chasing past errors; fourth, drifting responsibility, as automatic advice outpaces confirmation, tracing, and accountability, leaving it hard after a failure to identify which output, interface, person, or organization actually changed the system’s state.

Putting these four forms together can suggest that frequency mismatch only runs one way: fast disturbances striking a slow system. The reverse mismatch exists too, with more immediate consequences: slowing a layer that requires fast response produces accidents rather than mere inefficiency. Late protection burns out equipment, late obstacle avoidance strikes pedestrians, and late emergency treatment misses its window; response time here is part of the function itself, rather than an exchangeable cost. The question is whether each layer’s time constant matches what it must handle; mismatch causes losses in both directions, though the forms of loss differ.

\subhead{Interfaces for Update Times}

High-frequency intelligence therefore needs interfaces governing update times as well as faster output to enter reality. Such an interface requires at least four structures: rate limiting, buffering, holding, and layering. Rate limiting prevents high-frequency inputs from repeatedly rewriting slower structures; buffering keeps short-term fluctuations from striking slow systems directly; holding gives a decision enough time for execution, feedback, and correction; layering keeps fast feedback local and slow judgment at the structural level, so that different timescales do not damage one another. Responsibility also belongs in the time interface: a real system is more than a signal-processing system, and whether a high-frequency recommendation can execute automatically depends on who will bear a failure as well as whether the system can respond. Without an interface for responsibility, stronger high-frequency intelligence can push decisions into automatic processes whose consequences no one bears in full; the more a system operates in real time, the clearer it must be which changes can execute automatically, which need confirmation, which may only advise, and which must not become actions. Likewise, “end to end” cannot simply mean one model controlling everything: it can reduce hand-written rules and learn complex mappings, while real execution still requires layers, rate limits, and boundaries of responsibility. The danger extends beyond the black box to making the time interface opaque: if we cannot see which layers are fast or slow, which feedback is filtered, which commands are held, and who bears which failures, a system may lose its stabilizing structure beneath an appearance of integration.

One further point about interfaces is easily reversed: they are often imagined as brakes, as though lowering all update frequencies would make the system safe. What is required is matching across layers: fast layers must be fast enough, and slow layers must be allowed their time. AI’s value does not depend on making reality match the model’s speed. It can observe frequently without intervening frequently, predict continuously without changing things continuously, generate plans quickly while issuing them on a stable basis, and strengthen decisions while respecting the real system’s own update times. Mature intelligence embeds model capability in the world’s temporal structure. Real-time operation means being timely at the right level: fault protection needs it, strategic planning does not; contact feedback needs it, organizational culture does not; obstacle avoidance needs it, urban renewal does not. Making processes real time where they should not be exposes slow systems to high-frequency disturbances.

The bandwidth of time reminds us that reality’s pace reflects a need shared by every enduring system: allocating time between change and stability. A change is complete only after transmission, absorption, correction, and stabilization; faster intelligence makes it still more essential to distinguish output frequency from the frequency of real updates. High-frequency intelligence must know which layers can be fast, which must be slow, and which changes require rate limiting, buffering, holding, and layering. Intelligence can drive the world, but cannot drive all of it on the same timescale.

An interface can assign update frequencies to ranges each layer can sustain; it cannot change the fact that some results exist only after a process has run its course. A higher refresh rate does nothing for such problems, because what is awaited is the formation of an answer rather than the arrival of one already written. Beyond the boundary of frequency lies another boundary belonging to the process itself.

\subsection{Sequence Dependence in Living Systems}

Rate limiting and buffering address update frequency, preventing overly rapid change from interrupting a system; they do not explain why another kind of time can resist compression. Some changes cannot be skipped because their results do not exist before the process has run, rather than because the system cannot absorb them fast enough. Fatigue accumulates through cycles, side effects appear through metabolism, institutional effects emerge through implementation, and ecological consequences propagate through networks; these facts are products of the process, rather than answers stored at its starting point waiting to be read faster.

\subhead{Materials, Engineering, and Life}

Materials make this particularly clear. Good initial laboratory performance does not establish stability in long-term use: fatigue requires cycles, stress accumulation, corrosion exposure, and aging time. Many failures develop gradually through microscopic damage rather than appearing on day one; short tests screen out obvious errors but cannot fully replace service over time. That time is the process through which loads, temperature, moisture, oxidation, vibration, and maintenance conditions reveal hidden defects. Asbestos gives an extreme timescale: symptoms of mesothelioma may appear twenty to forty years or more after fibers are inhaled; an assessment comparing exposure and outcomes only within the same year will miss such long-latency consequences \cite{medlineplus2025mesothelioma}. Engineering systems work the same way. A design may pass simulation, a device pass initial tests, and a system operate in ideal conditions, while reliability has to develop amid noise, faults, maintenance, scaling, edge cases, and user behavior. Many problems arise only through prolonged operation, use by different people, and different loads, even when designers have anticipated them; reliability is a property of the process as well as the drawing. A system’s reliability depends on how it ages, is maintained, is misused, and degrades under faults, as well as how it was designed. The duration allocated to testing itself makes the point: some semiconductor reliability tests run continuously under high-temperature bias for over a thousand hours, full-scale structures are assessed through load spectra and cycle counts, and cumulative vehicle durability test distances can exceed a hundred thousand kilometers. The object and the standard determine the duration, load spectrum, and equivalence calculation; these numbers matter because they provide enough of a process for hidden defects to emerge.

Life unfolds as material processes in a sequence: gene expression has an order; protein synthesis, folding, modification, transport, and degradation have rates; cell division has cycles; immune responses have initiation, amplification, regulation, and resolution; tissue repair has stages; development and aging are themselves long processes. Biological reality lies in the progressive interpretation of sequences by cells, tissues, environments, and time, as well as in the sequences themselves. That is why AI-accelerated molecule discovery cannot eliminate clinical time from drug development. AI can find candidate molecules, predict structures, and screen targets faster, but a candidate entering a body still faces absorption, distribution, metabolism, excretion, toxicity, immune responses, dose, individual differences, and long-term feedback. Short-term efficacy does not establish long-term safety, a correct local target does not establish that the whole-body network can bear the intervention, and efficacy in an animal model does not establish lasting efficacy in human populations; living systems respond, compensate, rebound, and evolve. Time here is part of biological reality, rather than merely regulatory delay: the body needs time to reveal side effects, disease to reveal its course, the immune system to reveal its response, and population differences to reveal their distribution. A drug truly enters reality by surviving the tests of living processes, rather than by looking plausible in a model.

Drug safety requires effects to become visible in appropriate populations, observation periods, and measurements. Rentosertib reached first-patient dosing in Phase III in September 2026, a new milestone in its discovery and development \cite{insilico2026phase3}. It also shows that generating a candidate, entering clinical trials, and establishing evidence of long-term benefit are distinct milestones. Trial design and regulatory capacity can improve; follow-up results that have yet to occur still cannot be filled in ahead of time.

Not all biological time resists compression. Screening can occur earlier, biomarkers can reveal damage sooner, adaptive trial designs can reduce uninformative enrollment, and well-designed dose escalation can increase the information provided by early participants; these improvements do shorten the time needed to identify individual differences. They compress observation and selection, however, rather than exposure itself: metabolism in the body, accumulation in tissue under long-term load, and the distribution of effects across populations in real use must still unfold through their own steps. Distinguishing compressible observation from exposure that must be preserved lets us judge whether an acceleration shortens the process or moves observation ahead of its endpoint. Verification is how living systems turn candidates into facts.

\subhead{Organizations and Society}

Organizations and societies also require evidence through time. An institution may look reasonable on paper, a policy model effective in simulation, and a management plan logically clear, but implementation encounters incentives, trust, habits, interpretations, resistance, and arbitrage; people cannot simply be assigned values like variables. Institutional effects emerge through implementation, trust through repeated interaction, responsibility through events, and organizational capability through sustained cooperation; social facts form through people’s responses over time, rather than following statically from a proposal. Many reforms look successful at first and reveal costs later; platform mechanisms initially improve efficiency and later generate abuse, competitive overinvestment, and systemic fragility; educational, medical, and urban governance plans improve short-term metrics while producing more complex long-term consequences. Logical completeness does not establish an institution’s success: what matters is how people understand, exploit, bypass, and counter it. Social systems learn and change shape, adapt and push back; time is the space in which social consequences form.

Ecosystems extend this structure across longer timescales. A chemical, an introduced species, a form of land use, or a water project can deliver clear short-term benefits while producing different long-term consequences through food chains, water cycles, soils, species relationships, and climate feedback. Ecology is a network of multiple feedbacks: local changes travel along relationships, short-term gains can become long-term system costs, and consequences are difficult to establish fully in advance because they form as interventions run through an open network. Such processes often span decades: a centimeter of topsoil can take hundreds of years to form, a logged forest commonly needs decades or more to recover its former structure and species composition, and lake sediments can continue releasing phosphorus after nutrient inputs stop, delaying water-quality recovery for years after emissions decline. Earlier conclusions in these systems require observation series, rather than faster reasoning alone.

Several more basic processes lie behind these examples. First, accumulation: microscopic damage, toxicity, erosion of trust, and ecological pressure can build through repeated cycles rather than appearing all at once. Second, thresholds: a system can look stable for a long time, then fail suddenly when a boundary is crossed. Third, adaptation: organisms, organizations, markets, and institutions compensate for, bypass, and counter interventions. Fourth, diffusion: local consequences spread through material cracks, metabolic networks, social relationships, and ecological chains. Evidence through time consists of these processes turning invisible states into observable facts, rather than waiting alone.

A crucial difference between social and material processes makes the former harder to converge. When observation does not significantly disturb a material, it does not adjust its strategy because it knows it is being observed; people and organizations do. Announcing a policy reshapes expectations; putting a metric into an evaluation reorganizes behavior around it; stronger supervision shifts the supervised activity toward areas left unsupervised. The effect of the same intervention can therefore vary across measurement dates, following a trajectory that changes with observation and rules. This is why “run it again and we will know” often fails in social settings: the first run has already changed the initial conditions of the second. Social facts take time to form and, once formed, still cannot be treated as final conclusions established once for all.

\subsection{Evidence Through Time: The Process as a Source of Information}

In the age of intelligence, the time needed for some facts to form is easier to underestimate than the power to generate. A model can quickly generate answers, designs, molecules, strategies, and predictions, compressing search in a space of representations and presenting possibilities that once required prolonged trial. Yet real problems involve more than finding a plausible solution among possibilities: many outcomes gradually form, emerge, and become established as materials, organisms, organizations, and ecosystems operate. A single inference cannot fully replace them, and a static metric cannot directly establish them. This is evidence through time.

\subhead{The Process as a Source of Information}

Evidence through time is neither waiting alone nor a compensation for insufficient intelligence. It means putting candidates into processes, so that cycles, exposure, metabolism, use, diffusion, and responses turn hidden consequences into facts. A candidate may already be complete in representational space, but its validity in reality depends on how it bears cycles in a material, is metabolized in a body, is understood and countered in an organization, and spreads through an ecological network; time is a condition for some facts to form and appear. Computational irreducibility can offer an analogy, but not a blanket claim that complex systems are unpredictable. Many systems can be simulated, predicted at coarse resolution, or assessed early through proxy indicators; the crucial distinction is between what computation, inference, and simulation can compress in advance and what the running process must supply.

The latter are outcomes carried by the process itself: a material’s fatigue history, a body’s metabolic response, an organization’s path of adaptation, and an ecosystem’s long-term feedback are facts formed through interaction with the environment over time, rather than simple labels attached to a static candidate. Processes of this kind have a lower bound on duration:
\begin{equation}
T\;\ge\;N\,\delta t,
\label{eq:steps}
\end{equation}
Here $T$ is the total time required to complete the process along a given path, measured in seconds; $N$ is the dimensionless number of evolutionary steps that must be completed in sequence along that path; and $\delta t$ is a common lower bound on step duration, measured in seconds, such as the minimum duration specified for a fatigue cycle, a metabolic round, a reproductive generation, or an exposure period. Both sides have the dimensions of time; the bound requires dependent steps, each beginning from the result of its predecessor and each taking at least $\delta t$. Where a process contains independent branches, its critical dependency path constrains total duration; the steps of all branches cannot simply be added. This relationship describes the execution time of a specified physical path; computational irreducibility additionally requires showing that a shorter computation cannot produce the output sought. Better algorithms, different paths, and faster individual physical steps are three distinct kinds of progress, whose boundaries cannot simply be transferred from one to another.

The bound is simple in form, but both quantities are difficult to establish; that is what makes it hard to judge whether an acceleration actually shortens a process. $N$ is not an intrinsic property of the process: it depends on what counts as a step. Material fatigue can be counted by stress cycles or by stages of crack growth; different resolutions can change $N$ by orders of magnitude, while coarse-graining cannot change $T$ itself, only the steps we count. Nor can $\delta t$ always be read directly from a parameter: the same metabolic round differs in speed across individuals, and the same exposure period differs in duration across climates and loads. Looking at the two quantities separately gives a practical criterion: technical progress that reduces $\delta t$ changes the process rate; a claim to reduce $N$ requires an account of what changed in the dependency structure, implementation path, or target. A different counting scale alone does not shorten the process.

This distinction also has a symmetrical misuse. The claim that some facts must come from processes can expand into a dismissal of all advance judgments and predictions, as though outcomes could only be awaited. That does not follow: a process that cannot be skipped can still be interrupted, recognized early, or redirected midway. Early signs of failure, intermediate metabolites, changing organizational attitudes, and ecological indicator species all provide information before completion; they do not establish the final outcome, but can turn blind waiting into directed observation. The distinction is between final facts and process signals: the former require the full course, while the latter can be collected along the way; confusing them leads either to premature conclusions when observation should continue or repeated demands for conclusions while the process still needs time.

Specific indicators show the value of process signals. Glycated hemoglobin reflects average blood glucose over roughly the previous two to three months, with greater weight on recent levels; a single glucose measurement captures one moment, while this measure captures accumulated exposure across a period, making it more useful for assessing long-term control but unable on its own to say what happened this morning \cite{niddk_a1c}. Cracks inside metal structures emit acoustic signals before reaching a critical size; monitoring those signals can indicate the direction of damage before failure, but cannot establish service life in the first loading cycle. Such signals have a common role: revealing part of an invisible process early and directing observation, while leaving the process itself to run.

\subhead{What Can Be Compressed, and What Cannot}

AI’s role remains substantial. It can narrow the candidate space, find more promising paths, identify risks early, design better experiments, simulate more scenarios, detect early signals, and reduce unproductive trial and error, making verification more intelligent, directed, and economical. AI still cannot eliminate real verification: it can reduce what we must wait for without abolishing the need to wait, improve prediction without allowing every step to be skipped, and find many errors early without relieving the world of having to run. Mature judgment distinguishes two kinds of time while recognizing AI’s speed: search, candidate generation, and formal deduction can be compressed, while the time in which facts form cannot be canceled at will. Slowing what can be computed is inefficient; skipping what only the process can supply is dangerous. Real technical progress identifies which time is wasted waiting and which is necessary for reality to provide facts.

This is also why cheaper generation makes evidence through time more important. A model can generate a thousand drug candidates, engineering proposals, business strategies, or policy documents, while reality cannot expand clinical trials, long-term tests, service experience, organizational feedback, and ecological observation at the same rate; as information space expands, scarcity shifts toward the capacity to verify a few crucial candidates through real processes. AI reduces the cost of proposing possibilities; evidence through time bears the cost of turning possibilities into credible facts. Some processes resist complete compression into a simple shortcut because they generate new constraints, states, and feedback: a trajectory can be predicted but still has to be traveled, a risk simulated but still tested against reality, and search compressed without eliminating the information supplied by the process. Reality is a process that must unfold, rather than a table that can be filled out in advance.

Whether a result can be obtained quickly depends on problem structure, algorithms, required precision, and the sources of information. Complete initial conditions do not guarantee a shortcut; gradual unfolding does not establish that every approximation or redesign must fail. Only after the necessary sequential steps, conditions per step, and observation requirements are specified can $T\geq N\delta t$ be applied to a given process. Computational irreducibility does not supply a proof for every engineering wait.

This is not technological pessimism. Mature technology makes evidence through time more efficient: better sensors detect fatigue earlier, better biomarkers shorten clinical judgments, better digital twins reduce physical trial and error, better statistical design improves experimental efficiency, and better AI helps select the paths most worth verifying. Technology’s task is to reduce wasted waiting and amplify useful feedback. The key lies in boundaries: which results computation can provide in advance and which only a process can provide; which risks a model can rule out and which must appear through exposure, use, and long-term feedback; which candidates are ready for the next step and which must remain in representational space. Distinguishing time that can be compressed in advance from time that must be preserved is a central form of judgment in the age of intelligence. Evidence through time reminds us that reality does not always preexist in the form of an answer: some reliable facts form through fatigue, metabolism, immune responses, organizational adaptation, ecological feedback, and prolonged use. They have to be produced by the world running, rather than merely thought of by someone clever. AI can compress the search for an answer, but cannot eliminate the time in which the answer becomes fact; some facts can only come from the process.

Once a process has supplied facts, a further gate remains. Verification establishes a candidate at its own scale, without establishing that it can be integrated into an existing system. Real systems consist of interdependent equipment, people, institutions, habits, and interests; the actual cost of changing a node depends on its structural position and how many other parts connect to it. The resistance met by the same verified technology can differ by an order of magnitude depending on where it is installed.


\section{Topological Rigidity: Coupling Density, Phase Transitions, and Structural Memory}

\subsection{Network Coupling Density and Virtual Mass}

The time dimension has made one point clear: some facts can only come from processes; a candidate must enter materials, bodies, and organizations before hidden consequences gradually emerge. But a process has a prerequisite: the candidate must be able to enter it, and the system must be able to accommodate the target. Resource barriers concern the price of changing reality, and temporal rigidity concerns the limits to compressing real processes; topological coupling raises a deeper question: even with a target state identified and resources and time available, does the system have a path to that state? That is the question topological coupling addresses.

\subhead{From Targets to Paths}

Seeing the problem clearly requires a different description of the system. A real system is a network of relationships among variables, rather than a collection of isolated variables. Roads connect to roads, equipment to equipment, departments to departments, rules to rules, people’s behavior to institutional expectations, and technical interfaces to legacy systems. An element derives its significance from its position as well as its own properties; changing it also changes its relationships with the surrounding structure. In a complex system, local improvement therefore has no guaranteed passage to system improvement. A node can be optimized, a process accelerated, and a model made more accurate; whether those improvements change the system’s state depends on their position in the network, the connections, and the boundary conditions. Local optimization improves a point; system change moves along a path. Topology lies between the two.

The effect of connection density can first be seen through the accounts. A node’s own size determines the work required to change the node itself; the relationships that must change with it add another component. As coupling density rises, this additional component grows; the node behaves less like an object that can be moved alone and more like one carrying an extra load: the same push produces less displacement. Accounting for that additional cost separately gives what we can call the node’s virtual mass in the network. This is not physical mass and has no fixed unit; it serves comparisons among positions within the same system, answering a concrete question: why does the same change take a day here and become a six-month project there?

Network science offers corresponding structures. Erdős–Rényi random graphs and regular lattices generally have relatively narrow degree distributions; many real technical and organizational networks have broader distributions, with a few nodes carrying many connections, while transport requires distinguishing structures such as road and airline networks. Stanley Milgram introduced the small-world letter-passing experiment in 1967; in the study published by Travers and Milgram in 1969, 64 of 296 initiated chains reached the target, and successful chains passed through an average of 5.2 intermediaries, near the familiar six-step scale. This does not prove that any two people are connected within six steps \cite{milgram1967smallworld,travers1969experimental}. In 1998, Duncan Watts and Steven Strogatz supplied a network model in which short paths coexist with high clustering; short paths alone do not require extremely high-degree hubs \cite{watts1998collective}. These studies suggest examining path length, clustering, and degree distribution separately: short paths make it possible for disturbances to reach distant locations quickly, while hubs can concentrate the cost of change. A position with large virtual mass may be only a field, an interface, or a table, yet connect an entire system; the number and type of connections, and the commitments crossing boundaries, all affect its weight.

Software engineering has repeatedly observed a correspondence between technical and organizational interfaces: the structure of the organization designing a system tends to be reproduced in the system’s interfaces, as communication boundaries between teams become module boundaries \cite{conway1968how}. In real systems this creates a double coupling, with technical dependencies and organizational coordination reinforcing each other: changing an interface is difficult both because of its downstream systems and because the change crosses departmental responsibilities. Assessing a node’s virtual mass therefore requires asking whether its connections cross organizational boundaries, involve external commitments, or are embedded in contracts and performance evaluations, as well as counting them.

\subhead{Target States and State Transitions}

Whether a path exists first depends on the space in which the proposed state is valid. AI is good at generating target states: a more efficient urban transport plan, a better hospital triage process, a supply chain with less inventory, a more precise teaching evaluation model, or more automated factory scheduling. A target generated in a model establishes only that the state can be described in representational space; it does not establish that a real system can reach it cheaply, safely, and stably. A describable target does not guarantee an executable transition.

Many errors of technological optimism begin here. Knowing a better state is mistaken for being able to enter it. Real systems cannot be changed arbitrarily. Cities already have roads, subways, buildings, utility networks, property rights, residents’ habits, and fiscal constraints; hospitals have departments, medical records, insurance payments, physicians’ responsibilities, and patient trust; companies have legacy software and processes, departmental interests, performance systems, and data formats; education has examinations, admissions, teacher evaluation, family expectations, and social selection. A proposal entering these systems must find a channel through an existing topology, rather than draw lines on an empty plane. The first implication of topological coupling is therefore that a real system’s state space is not uniformly open. Some imaginable states have no affordable path; some locally effective proposals cannot pass through system interfaces; some improvements valid in a model are absorbed, delayed, distorted, or amplified in the opposite direction by the real structure. Deployment requires both a good solution and a system that allows that solution to become reachable.

This explains many familiar outcomes. An AI diagnostic model can be highly accurate on a test set, yet in a hospital it encounters physicians’ workflows, patient histories, equipment differences, insurance rules, liability for misdiagnosis, and clinical trust; its local performance cannot directly rewrite the healthcare system. A traffic algorithm can reduce congestion in simulation, yet in a real city drivers change routes, commercial districts change flows, construction interrupts plans, enforcement changes behavior, and public and private transport feed back on one another; the seemingly better traffic state may lack a stable path through the system.

\subhead{Improvements Absorbed by the System}

One common sign of an unstable path is that the system absorbs the improvement. An AI assistant may help every employee produce documents faster without making the company more efficient overall. Organizational efficiency also depends on judgment, communication chains, approval structures, the allocation of responsibility, and alignment of goals. If everyone produces material faster while review, coordination, and decision-making remain unchanged, the system may simply move from a generation bottleneck to a screening bottleneck. Greater local speed need not improve the overall state.

\key{System change is not the simple sum of local capabilities.} A complex system’s overall state often depends on the structure of its relationships more than on the performance of an individual component \cite{boccaletti2006complex}. In a net, strengthening one node does not mean the whole net can move into a new shape; force must pass along its strands to other nodes, and the connections may disperse, cancel, or lock that local force. Such resistance is often misread as conservatism or opposition to change. Topological coupling offers another explanation: many forms of resistance arise because relationships cannot be rearranged immediately. A technology entering a system often changes who is responsible, who benefits, who bears risk, who must learn, whose workflow is interrupted, and whose power is redistributed. What looks like a tool touches structure; the more complex the structure, the less likely the technology is to be a neutral plug-in.

This absorption has an observable form: improvements farther downstream are more easily flattened by a fixed upstream rhythm. A workshop may cut processing time per piece by one-third, yet if assembly takt, material delivery cycles, and inspection batch rules stay fixed, the time saved becomes waiting between operations rather than a proportional rise in output. Conversely, even a small improvement at the stage setting the pace can propagate along the whole chain. To judge whether an improvement can change the system, first locate the source of its rhythm, then ask whether the improvement touches it.

\subhead{Structural Position and the Distribution of Viscosity}

The same technology can have entirely different fates in different positions. Many AI applications follow a familiar trajectory: easy demonstrations, difficult deployment; successful pilots, slow scaling. Demonstrations usually occur in low-coupling environments, with clear tasks, clean inputs, preset interfaces, responsibility suspended, and failures that can be disregarded; pilots also tend to select cooperative, standardized settings with the best prospects of success. Deployment at scale faces the heterogeneity of real systems: institutions differ in data structures, staff capabilities, processes, interests, compliance requirements, and boundaries of responsibility. Topological costs emerge when a showcase enters the system.

Assessing an AI technology’s real potential therefore requires asking where it will be embedded, as well as whether it can do the task. Low-coupling positions are easier to automate; high-coupling positions face more constraints. Advertising copy generators, meeting-note tools, and first-pass customer service systems are generally easier to deploy than medical diagnosis, autonomous driving, educational assessment, judicial decisions, and energy dispatch, because their structural positions are lighter, their consequences more limited, and their failures easier to roll back—not necessarily because their models are stronger. The same capability encounters different viscosity in different structural positions. Text generation for a marketing draft connects primarily to communication effectiveness; for a medical report, to clinical responsibility; for a judicial decision, to rights, obligations, and coercive power. Similar task forms occupy different topological positions and face entirely different resistance.

Interface counts show the scale of this positional difference. An author bears the risk of changing a function called by a few internal scripts; changing an interface used in fixed formats by more than a hundred downstream systems distributes the risk among all callers, and any change to a field’s meaning must pass through notification, compatibility work, parallel operation, and retirement of the old version. The first change takes hours, the second quarters. A few lines of code can differ by orders of magnitude in virtual mass because of how much they connect to.

\subhead{Technologies That Change Connections}

If resistance comes from position, the entry point for change lies beyond capability alone. Technologies that change systems often do so by changing connections, rather than by offering the strongest capability at a single point. Smartphones changed the world by reorganizing mobile networks, app stores, payments, developer ecosystems, and user behavior as well as improving hardware; electric vehicles spread as battery supply chains, charging networks, policies, maintenance systems, and public understanding developed, as well as through efficient motors. A technology becomes a force within a system by finding or creating its niche. Deployment means giving a tool new interfaces within reality. Clear interfaces, explicit responsibility, closed feedback, and controllable failure ease entry; confused interfaces, unclear responsibility, delayed feedback, and irreversible failures leave technology in demonstrations and pilots. Topological coupling says that system change needs structural channels: the target state does not automatically supply a path; connections, history, institutional interfaces, and patterns of behavior jointly open or close it. A technology needs both a clear answer and a position in which the system can accommodate that answer.

We can now answer the opening question: a path exists because structural channels exist, rather than because the target is clear. Resource barriers say that changing reality requires paying a physical bill; temporal rigidity says it requires going through a process; topological coupling says it requires passing through structure. Without resources, the system cannot be moved; without time, the process cannot unfold; without a path, the target cannot be reached. Deployment gives an answer a structural channel into reality.

Opening a channel is only the first step. Changing one node along it often moves interfaces, data, permissions, training, responsibility, and expectations too; some must move together, and failure may leave no way back. These costs explain both the different speeds of the same improvement in different systems and whether a technology is absorbed as local efficiency or pulls the whole dependency network into adjustment.

\subsection{Topological Phase Transition: Percolation Thresholds and Gelation}

Beyond a certain range of coordinated movement costs, a system changes how it responds. The difficulty of complex systems often changes character abruptly rather than increasing gradually. A few added connections may improve coordination; a few more may merely increase coordination costs. But when connection density, feedback loops, and dependencies reach a critical range, the system takes on a new state: a network spanning the whole, rather than loose parts that can be adjusted locally. Local changes travel along connections to distant places; local errors become harder to isolate and may enter feedback loops across the system. This is the basic meaning of a “gelled system.”

Gelation here is a structural analogy rather than a strict physical equivalence. In polymers, colloids, and material networks, gelation occurs when dispersed units form a spanning structure under particular conditions, giving a flowing system a supporting network. The image points to a shared mechanism across social, organizational, transport, and intelligent systems: \key{Beyond a range of connectivity, the system changes the phase of disturbance propagation rather than merely becoming “a little more complex.”} The system moves from locally absorbable changes to system-wide transmission, from local adjustment to whole-system entanglement, and from a flexible space for trial and error to a taut net.

The physical process itself offers useful comparisons; the analogy has a material source. As cross-linking increases in a polymer solution, viscosity initially rises slowly and then sharply near a particular cross-link density; a gel network spans the sample, while a residual sol fraction can remain. Materials science calls this the gel point: the first spanning connectivity across the sample, rather than a local region becoming hard. Functionality and reaction extent can be used to estimate the gel point; it belongs to the same class of mathematical structure as the percolation thresholds discussed next. Its defining property is worth remembering: before it, a local region can be stirred; after it, local forces can travel through the spanning network, with their range and timing still dependent on the material and loading.

\subhead{Percolation Thresholds and Interdependence}

Models can calculate the width of this region and the location of its threshold. Percolation theory gives a simple, powerful picture: with few connections, nodes form small disconnected clusters and disturbances cannot readily cross the system; near the critical threshold, clusters merge; beyond it, a giant component appears, making system-wide transmission possible \cite{broadbent1957,erdos1959}. The picture matters because additional connections can produce a phase transition, rather than a linear change. The system shifts from one mechanism of disturbance propagation to another.

For a random graph with independent edges, the threshold can be expressed through mean degree. Let $\langle k\rangle$ be the network’s mean degree, the average number of connections per node; the condition for a giant component to appear is
\begin{equation}
\langle k\rangle_c = 1.
\end{equation}
For an Erdős–Rényi random graph, a giant component emerges asymptotically as mean degree crosses 1. This concerns the growth of random branches, rather than a guarantee of spanning connectivity whenever every node has one connection. The mean degree of $G(n,p)$ is $(n-1)p$, giving a threshold edge density of roughly $1/n$. Real dependency networks require examining direction, correlations, weights, and clustering.

In the corresponding infinite-system limit of ordinary percolation, the order parameter can grow continuously from zero above the threshold. Finite networks exhibit changes in spanning probability and cluster size. Let $p$ be the occupation probability, $p_c$ the threshold, and $P_\infty$ the fraction in the giant component; near the threshold the following scaling form can arise:
\begin{equation}
P_\infty(p)\ \propto\ (p-p_c)^{\beta},\qquad p\to p_c^{+},
\end{equation}
Here $\beta$ is the critical exponent, and $P_\infty$ lies between 0 and 1; the expression applies only in the infinite-system limit. The value of $p_c$ depends on network type and dimension: site percolation on a two-dimensional square lattice has a threshold of about $p_c\approx 0.5927$, so a spanning component appears when random occupation exceeds roughly 59\%; bond percolation on the same lattice has a threshold of 0.5; a one-dimensional chain has $p_c=1$, requiring full occupation. A finite system has a transition region that steepens near the threshold, rather than an exact switching point; smaller systems have broader transition regions.

The sensitivity of the threshold to network type matters more for real systems than the number $0.5927$ itself. A two-dimensional square lattice has coordination number 4, while site percolation on a three-dimensional simple cubic lattice has a threshold near 0.31; higher coordination and dimension lower the occupation fraction needed to span. In some large-network models with a divergent second moment of the degree distribution, the retained-node fraction needed to sustain a giant component after random removal can approach zero; the corresponding removal fraction approaches one, indicating tolerance of substantial random losses of ordinary nodes \cite{albert2000error}. Tolerance of random disturbance and vulnerability to targeted attack can coexist in the same network; removing key hubs can disrupt connectivity more readily than removing the same number of nodes at random. Percolation thus gives a differentiated judgment: thresholds depend on structural form as well as total connection count.
