Table \ref{tab:ch2-rtg} lists ways to reduce constraints and the expenditures they may add. More equipment may shorten a schedule, more review may reduce failure risk, and redesigned interfaces may reduce both coordination and maintenance costs. The outcome requires accounting for all relevant stages. Contracts, institutions, and participants’ decision rights also determine who pays and who bears the risks.

\subhead{Parameter Trade-offs}

The three coordinates often move together in engineering. More equipment and parallel operations can ease time constraints while adding capital and maintenance costs; standardization can reduce both resource use and coordination difficulty. Comparing natural and artificial synthesis likewise requires placing sunlight, land, reactors, feedstocks, energy carriers, and control conditions within the same boundary. Changing the path changes the combination of resources, time, and structure; the particular process determines the net benefit.

The trade-off follows directly from \eqref{eq:eta-exp}: hold $\eta$ fixed, take logarithms of both sides, then differentiate to obtain
\begin{equation}
\alpha\,\mathrm{d}R+\beta\,\mathrm{d}T+\gamma\,\mathrm{d}G=0,
\qquad
\left.\frac{\mathrm{d}R}{\mathrm{d}T}\right|_{\eta,\,G}=-\frac{\beta}{\alpha}
\label{eq:exchange-rate}
\end{equation}
The subscripts $\eta,G$ denote fixed generalized viscosity and topology. Within the exponential model, with fixed coefficients and a nonzero resource weight, the slope along the constant-viscosity surface is $-\beta/\alpha$: reducing $T$ by one unit increases $R$ along that surface by $\beta/\alpha$ units. The ratio describes coordinate combinations at the same modeled cost. Whether engineering can move in that direction depends on paths allowed by the equipment, process, and budget.

Coefficient values depend on the task, scales, and reference state. A different normalization changes the exchange ratio. Comparisons across systems require common reference conventions. Where marginal ratios vary with state, coefficients can be calibrated by region or interactions added to log cost, followed by testing the new form.

Taking more time to reduce risk is standard practice where consequences are serious. Drug development includes toxicology, Phase I, II, and III trials, and post-market observation; nuclear facilities undergo repeated reviews and redundant design; aircraft undergo full-life fatigue testing. These processes combine observation with verification in high-consequence systems, involving temporal rigidity as well as $G$: errors can propagate through connections and be difficult to isolate or reverse. Compressing $T$ without replacement evidence or controls may merely move risk exposure into the future. A further trade-off is easy to overlook: adding structure to reduce local friction. Sensors, middleware, adapters, dispatch platforms, data interfaces, and audit modules can smooth the operating layer of a legacy system. If additions neither integrate nor replace old dependencies, $G$ may rise as local friction falls and system entanglement grows.

Power transmission shows another configuration. Raising the voltage of a direct-current link can, under the relevant design conditions, increase capacity and reduce long-distance losses, at the cost of converter stations, insulation, and control systems. Once built, the corridor must operate in coordination with the grids at both ends. Capital expenditure, line losses, and network dependencies are recombined; the net effect requires accounting across the whole transmission chain.

The three trade-offs share a property: they are strategic compromises rather than exact exchanges. What is given up and what is gained depend on the particular structure; there is no universal exchange rate. Benefits must therefore be calculated case by case rather than inferred from a general principle.

\subhead{Where Costs Come From}

Cost transfers and physical lower bounds require separate accounts. Consider a closed reacting system exchanging heat and pressure–volume work with an environment at temperature $T_0$ and pressure $p_0$, with the initial reactants and final products at that temperature and pressure; the Gibbs free-energy difference gives the reversible minimum net input of non-expansion work. Entropy generation in the actual process adds to that requirement:
\begin{equation}
W_{\min}=\Delta G=G_{\mathrm{f}}-G_{\mathrm{i}},
\qquad
W_{\mathrm{act}}=\Delta G+T_{0}\,S_{\mathrm{gen}},
\qquad
S_{\mathrm{gen}}\ge 0
\label{eq:thermo-floor}
\end{equation}
$G_{\mathrm{i}}$ and $G_{\mathrm{f}}$ are the initial and final Gibbs free energies, while $W_{\min}$ and $W_{\mathrm{act}}$ are the reversible and actual net non-expansion work inputs, all measured in joules; $S_{\mathrm{gen}}$ is entropy generation, and $T_0S_{\mathrm{gen}}$ the associated irreversible loss. For the same endpoints and environment, process improvements can reduce losses and bring actual expenditure closer to the lower bound. Total energy use must also include material handling, heat sources, and auxiliary equipment within the boundary.

Aluminum offers a direct comparison. Producing primary aluminum by electrolysis of alumina typically uses more than 13,000 kilowatt-hours per tonne; recycled aluminum bypasses reduction, and under the industry’s common production-energy convention, recycling and remelting can save about 95\% of primary-production energy. The scrap already contains metallic aluminum, leaving remelting and refining to be paid for, rather than reduction from the oxide \cite{quinkertz2001scenario,iai_recycling_energy}. The routes begin in different states: one with oxide, the other with metal. The reference state is therefore set by the actual availability of materials, energy, and waste.

For given endpoints and environmental conditions, theoretical minimum work sets a process floor. Algorithms can screen processes, reduce trial and error, and help reduce irreversible losses. Changing feedstocks, products, or the environment requires recalculating the bound. \key{Intelligence can optimize a path without abolishing the physical conditions of a given state transition.}

Structural costs require separate measurement. Let $C_{\mathrm{loc}}$ be complexity at the operating stage and $C_{\mathrm{rest}}$ complexity elsewhere within the same boundary; with a consistent metric, the change in total complexity is
\begin{equation}
\Delta C_{\mathrm{tot}}=\Delta C_{\mathrm{loc}}+\Delta C_{\mathrm{rest}}
\label{eq:complexity-transfer}
\end{equation}
All three quantities must use the same complexity metric, such as maintained interfaces, dependencies, or an explicitly defined weighted workload. Local simplification accompanied by increased background cost indicates transfer; a negative sum indicates lower total complexity. Modularity, standardization, and removal of redundant elements can produce the latter. Only after fixing the boundary and metric can transfer and net reduction be tested separately.

\subhead{Uses and Limits of the Framework}

Together, the parameters address a difficult question: why can a better technology still fail to move a system? The answer is often a mismatch of dimensions. A proposal improves its own performance—less energy, more speed, or greater accuracy—while entering a system already saturated in another dimension. A more fuel-efficient powertrain requiring a rebuilt fueling network meets $G$; a more precise therapy requiring ten years of follow-up meets $T$; a more efficient industry requiring a new grid meets $R$. The proposal is evaluated on a different scale from the system’s ability to absorb it. In \eqref{eq:eta-exp}, adopting a technology changes all three coordinates:
\begin{equation}
\frac{\eta_{\mathrm{new}}}{\eta_{\mathrm{old}}}
=\exp\bigl(\alpha\,\Delta R+\beta\,\Delta T+\gamma\,\Delta G\bigr),
\qquad
\Delta X=X_{\mathrm{new}}-X_{\mathrm{old}},\quad X\in\{R,T,G\}
\label{eq:mismatch}
\end{equation}
$\eta_{\mathrm{old}}$ and $\eta_{\mathrm{new}}$ use the same task, cost convention, reference, and coefficients. A negative weighted sum of the three increments gives lower modeled cost; a positive sum gives higher cost. Savings in one component’s energy use may be offset by added infrastructure, switching, and verification. Accuracy and response gains must be assigned to the appropriate coordinates; savings and new expenditure within the same resource dimension must first be combined into a net change before entering the formula.

Two contrasting cases illustrate dimensional mismatch. Magnetic-confinement fusion binds $R$ and $T$ closely: confinement requires large magnets, powerful electrical supplies, and cryogenic systems; the Lawson condition connects density, temperature, and energy confinement time, with the idealized ignition threshold for deuterium–tritium fuel in a suitable temperature range taking the following order of magnitude:
\begin{equation}
n\,T\,\tau_{E}\ \gtrsim\ 3\times10^{21}\ \mathrm{keV\cdot s\cdot m^{-3}}
\label{eq:lawson}
\end{equation}
Here $n$ is plasma ion density in inverse cubic meters, $T$ ion temperature in kiloelectronvolts, and $\tau_{E}$ energy confinement time in seconds. At fixed temperature and other conditions, doubling density can compensate for halving confinement time; changing temperature requires recalculating reaction rates, radiation, and energy balance, rather than extending a constant threshold to every temperature range. The triple product is a performance measure for specified fuel and energy-gain conditions; device design and control change the attainable parameter combinations \cite{lawson1957some,wurzel2022lawson}. Messenger RNA vaccine platforms show a different pattern: the $T$ of sequence design and candidate screening can shrink dramatically. In 2020, mRNA-1273’s candidate sequence was selected within days of the pathogen sequence becoming public, while manufacturing, quality testing, and clinical evidence had separate processes; 63 days still elapsed from sequence selection to the first participant’s dose \cite{moderna2020timeline}. Immunogenicity, stability, batch consistency, and long-term safety each require verification; reductions in $T$ must be recorded stage by stage. Both cases lead to the same conclusion: how much a technology reduces $T$ depends on which stage it compresses and what remains connected downstream.

The framework also helps explain apparently cumbersome arrangements that endure. Redundancy, approvals, conservative parameters, human review, and staged releases reduce local efficiency while reducing $G$ and tail risk. Where failure consequences cannot be rolled back, these losses are necessary expenditures. The framework’s explanatory limits also need to be clear. It does not explain political processes, cultural differences, capital cycles, business models, or organizational capabilities. Deployment also depends on who benefits, who bears costs, who decides, budget duration, and capacity to execute. These factors lie outside the book’s three coordinates. Generalized viscosity adds a view of resistance in the medium alongside these factors, rather than reducing all social phenomena to physical quantities.

The book’s domain classifications use explicit criteria and relative grades; the exponential model proposes quantitative relationships requiring separate calibration. The two uses remain distinct. Application begins by fixing the task and outcome standard, then identifying obstacles that can be removed, costs reduced or transferred, and functions taken over by other mechanisms. Time constraints, dependencies, and resource inputs must each be assessed by their particular role.

Distinguishing the three requires separate judgments about resources, time, and structure, each using different methods. So far the chapter provides a static ledger: it locates a state transition in three coordinates and identifies the binding dimension, without yet describing how the medium responds to change. The same potential difference produces different results when applied slowly or quickly; bits, atoms, and life respond differently to loading rates. Local bit operations can be extremely fast, atomic systems also respond at rates set by diffusion and heat transfer, and living systems can change their own structure with loading speed. The viscosity coefficient varies with the rate of change. To examine that variation, attention must move from a state’s position to the behavior of its interfaces.

\chapter{Interface Dynamics: Intelligence’s Phase Transitions and the Rheology of Media}

Chapter 2 separated viscosity into resource barriers, temporal rigidity, and topological coupling, describing a system’s resistance to external action. In that framework, intelligence stood beside the medium: measuring resistance, finding low-resistance paths, or stopping before it. Once intelligence outputs control, executes actions, and intervenes in state transitions, its position changes. It becomes a source of disturbances injected into the medium, which immediately begins processing them. The standard for assessing intelligence must change with its position. The same model faces different constraints and error costs as a solver and a driver; the medium translates its output into diffusion, work, or feedback, or dissipates it at the interface.

\section{Intelligence’s Phase Transition: From Solver to Driver}

In the preceding framework, intelligence selects paths: it reduces uncertainty before action, screens possibilities for better routes, and substitutes internal exploration for some external trial and error. This helps explain why intelligence evolved, but leaves open what happens when it enters execution. Selecting a path takes place in representational space; driving a state transition must occur in a medium. The turning point has two parts: how intelligence’s role changes, and the new constraints that follow.

\subsection{An Ontological Shift: From Solver to Driver}

A path valid in representational space need not be valid in reality. Intelligence first appears as an ability to select paths. That ability appears across bits, atoms, and life. Nervous systems, scientific models, engineering simulations, and AI all seek better paths before paying the costs of matter, energy, time, and failure. Finding a path does not complete it. A model can choose a direction; reality requires its execution.

\subhead{Solver and Driver}

Execution breaks a path into concrete stages. A symbolically valid proposal must become control signals, actions, energy inputs, material rearrangements, bodily responses, organizational coordination, and responsibility to enter the physical world. Moving from abstract representations into embodied reality changes intelligence’s functional role. This is its phase transition from solver to driver. “Phase transition” is a functional analogy here: the role, constraints, error costs, and evaluation standards change together as intelligence enters a real system. Intelligence joins a closed loop capable of changing states, participates in transitions, and drives real processes with mass, inertia, feedback, losses, and responsibility.

A change of role changes the inventory of capabilities. In information space, intelligence is primarily a \term{solver}. It deals with symbols, logic, probability, patterns, and representations. A question produces an answer; a goal initiates a path search; data are compressed into structure. Its products at this level are representations that have yet to enter physical execution: text, images, code, models, predictions, and proposed decisions. An answer valid at the symbolic level completes much of the task.

In reality, intelligence has to do more than solve. It must become a driver. The driver makes information act on a medium with mass, inertia, friction, noise, delay, losses, and risk. Solvers output solutions; drivers output control capable of acting on a medium. Solvers ask whether an answer is valid; drivers ask whether it can pass through actuators, feedback, energy, and responsibility. Solvers handle possibilities; drivers bear consequences.

An early result in cybernetics gives this distinction a quantitative form. Ashby’s 1956 law of requisite variety says that a regulator cannot suppress more varieties of disturbance than it can distinguish and respond to: only variety can destroy variety \cite{ashby1956cybernetics}. Applied to solvers and drivers, the implication is direct. A solver’s variety lies in the proposals it can express; a driver’s in the actions it can apply; the medium’s disturbances include friction, deformation, occlusion, delay, failure, and unexpected interactions. If the driver’s degrees of freedom, bandwidth, and precision cannot distinguish and counter the relevant disturbances, some of even a powerful solver’s capability falls beyond the system’s reach, leaving residual disturbance in its outputs.

Many misjudgments about AI confuse solver capability with driver capability. Generating an architectural proposal does not build it; planning a traffic route does not change road capacity; simulating a robot movement does not ensure a stable grasp of a cup; proposing treatment does not establish that a drug has passed bodily, clinical, and long-term safety tests. A symbolic solution supplies a prerequisite for control rather than the state change itself. Taking the four changes together reveals the weight of this role: larger models, longer contexts, and stronger reasoning continue to improve the solver without changing its role; the transition occurs when value depends on whether a state change happens, remains stable, and permits recovery.

\subhead{Closed Loops and the Meaning of the Transition}

Moving from solver to driver shifts the center of intelligence from answers to closed loops. A solver can give a one-off answer; a driver must continuously sense feedback, correct errors, and control risks. The world is a continually changing dynamical field. Intelligence must join the cycle: sense reality, generate control, observe feedback, correct action, and execute again. Without a closed loop it remains advice; within one it becomes a force in reality.

Closed loops also introduce risk. Feedback is delayed, execution has inertia, and systems have noise. AI entering forecasting, dispatch, trading, supply chains, traffic control, and management often shortens decision cycles and raises feedback frequency, compressing buffers previously supplied by human intervals, review, and waits. The question is whether adjustment frequency matches the response cycle of the system being regulated. A fast intelligent loop regulating a slow physical, organizational, or market system can overcorrect through delay, phase difference, and local misjudgment, even turning negative feedback positive. The bullwhip effect, mistaken feedback in organizational decisions, algorithmic amplification in markets, and delay-induced control oscillations all point to the need to understand response times, buffers, and stability boundaries. Faster judgment is a capability when matched to the system’s frequency; without that match, it can manufacture oscillation faster \cite{lee1997,sterman1989}. The problem of closed loops predates cybernetics itself. During World War II, Norbert Wiener and Julian Bigelow developed a predictor for antiaircraft fire control that had to extrapolate an aircraft's future position from a stretch of observed trajectory; the work produced the 1942 report Extrapolation, Interpolation, and Smoothing of Stationary Time Series, one of the precursors of cybernetics \cite{wiener1948}. The engineering difficulties mattered more than the prediction formula itself: the predictor's output changed the gun's aim, which in turn changed the next round of observations and errors, drawing target maneuvers, observation noise, servo delays, and operator reactions into the same loop. Corrections that were too abrupt, or delays that were too long, could themselves excite oscillations and, in severe cases, disable the aiming mechanism. Cybernetics later discussed these machine failures alongside tremors in living organisms because both arose from phase misalignment within a closed loop. The counterintuitive point is that a system with greater predictive accuracy need not perform better once connected to a loop: its effect is determined by its phase and gain within the loop as well as its own accuracy.

This is what “phase transition” means. Entering reality changes intelligence’s role, constraints, error costs, and assessment standards together. In symbolic space its main value lies in generation, search, and reasoning; in a dynamical field it lies in stable control, reduced dissipation, lower risk, and greater executability. The first centers on answers, the second on state transitions. The crucial AI-era judgment is whether smarter answers can become control that can be executed, verified, maintained, and held responsible. \key{An optimum that cannot pass through its medium remains an elegant figure in symbolic space; a suboptimal solution that enters reality stably may be intelligence of real value.}

Intelligence originates in choosing paths before action; its phase transition occurs when a path must be executed. From solver to driver, it moves from rewritable representations into reality’s friction, inertia, risk, and responsibility. It must drive changes of state as well as calculate possibilities. Understanding physical AI, robots, autonomous driving, and intelligent infrastructure begins with this transition. Mature intelligence recognizes that an abstract optimum will deform, bend, dissipate, and carry consequences on entering reality. Its highest form finds paths that can be executed stably in a viscous world, beyond disembodied calculation. The change of role says what intelligence becomes; it does not yet specify its limits.

\subsection{Four Constraints on Executability and the Deflection of Paths}

Confusing solver and driver capabilities also hides the changing form of constraints. In logical space the limits mainly concern complexity: can the problem be formalized, is the search space too large, are the model and data sufficient, and is the reasoning accurate enough? The central question is whether the result can be computed. Entering a dynamical field shifts those limits. The questions become whether the system can be moved, in time, stably, at sustainable cost, and with consequences someone can bear. Computational solvability gives way to executability in thermodynamics, control, and engineering.

\subhead{Executability and Its Costs}

Executability includes at least four real constraints: power density, medium bandwidth, feedback error, and safety boundaries. Power density asks whether enough energy can act in enough locations within enough time. Robot movements require motor torque, braking requires friction and distance, factory dispatch requires equipment response, and grid control requires capacity and stability. Medium bandwidth asks whether the system can absorb inputs at the required frequency and amplitude. A physical system has natural frequencies, propagation speeds, and relaxation times that constrain how frequently it can be rewritten. Feedback error asks whether correction can continue through noise, occlusion, wear, delay, chance events, and nonlinear responses. Safety boundaries ask whether errors can be bounded, stopped, isolated, and traced to responsibility. Cybernetics and modern feedback theory have long treated stability, bandwidth, delay, robustness, and feedback-error management as central problems of closed loops, beyond finding solutions alone \cite{wiener1948,astrom2008}. The four constraints interact and trade off. Raising control frequency increases power and heat requirements; reducing response delay leaves less room for checks; compressing safety margins reduces tolerance of error. Engineering trade-offs occur among these four: faster actuators often cost inertia, energy, or precision; denser control loops often cost sensors, communication bandwidth, and maintenance. A paper proposal that optimizes all four at once has usually left weight out of the account.

Error costs change character as intelligence enters reality. Errors in symbolic space are usually inexpensive. Text can be corrected, code rolled back, images regenerated, and model outputs prompted again. The error is primarily informational. It may waste time and attention without usually causing direct material damage.

In dynamical space, errors are costly. Failed grasps break objects, driving errors cause crashes, mistaken drug predictions can injure bodies, industrial control errors damage equipment, and medical misjudgments involve lives and responsibility. An incorrect answer becomes irreversible dissipation, physical damage, injury, and institutional consequences. Physical AI, embodied systems, autonomous driving, medical AI, and industrial control therefore cannot simply inherit a chatbot’s iteration logic. Chatbots can improve through many low-cost interactions; real robot falls, collisions, and injuries cannot be treated as cost-free, unlimited trials. A language model can generate alternatives for human selection; a medical system cannot try unverified proposals directly on many people. Real error costs rule out inputs premised on high frequency, little responsibility, and arbitrary rollback.

\subhead{The Deflection of Paths}

Reality is a viscous environment full of dissipation. The mathematically shortest path is often not the feasible one. An algorithm’s shortest, most efficient, resource-saving proposal still encounters friction, hysteresis, maintenance, risk, responsibility, coordination, and long-term stability. The real path undergoes \term{deflection}. Deflection means a planned path shifts as it passes through its medium, toward lower resistance, lower risk, affordable energy demand, and more stable feedback rather than the abstract optimum. Real systems often seek minimum total damping rather than minimum distance, sustainability along the entire route rather than a point optimum, and controllable failure rather than maximum local efficiency.

This explains why seemingly less advanced arrangements can prove more stable. Engineering retains apparently wasteful redundancy to resist failure; healthcare trades time for verification and responsibility; aviation, nuclear power, and financial risk control avoid adopting untested optimal algorithms lightly because local gains do not offset systemic failure risk. Apparent clumsiness can be the price of stability. Research on complex high-risk systems and system safety identifies redundancy, delay, approvals, and conservative strategies as structures that can limit accident propagation, preserve recovery, and assign responsibility \cite{perrow1984,leveson2011}. Entering reality is a dynamical coupling, beyond simple “application.” An intelligent output joins a system with inertia, feedback, history, and responsibility. The system absorbs, filters, amplifies, distorts, or cancels it. A logistics algorithm meets vehicles, warehouses, drivers, weather, and fluctuating orders; a diagnostic model meets physicians’ responsibility, patient trust, insurance, and legal risk; a robot controller meets sensor errors, force feedback, uncertain contact, and wear. Performance depends on the coupling between intelligence and its medium as well as intelligence itself. An otherwise strong model loses much of its practical effectiveness without reliable feedback, actuator control, process compatibility, exception handling, and responsibility. A weaker model may have more real value if it integrates stably, lowers error costs, matches the medium’s frequency, and preserves safety boundaries.

\subhead{Embodied Intelligence and Closed Loops}

This matters particularly for physical AI. Putting a large model in a body does not complete embodied intelligence. Bodies are not screens, and actions are not text outputs. Robots must continually perceive, localize, map, predict, control, make contact, avoid obstacles, and correct errors. They must perform under specific mechanical conditions as well as know what to do. A cup in language is an object; in reality it has weight, material, surface friction, a center of mass, and fragility. A door in an image has hinges, resistance, an opening angle, and environmental changes caused by pushing it open in reality. Behavior-based robotics and embodied cognition have long understood intelligence as continuous coupling among body, sensing, action, and environment, beyond central reasoning alone \cite{brooks1991,pfeifer2006}. Vision–language–action models further illustrate this transition. In 2023, RT-2 combined vision–language models with robot trajectory data, transferring internet-scale knowledge into robot control and representing actions as tokens \cite{zitkovich2023}. By July 2026, Google DeepMind’s Gemini Robotics 2 placed whole-body control, dexterous manipulation, and multi-robot cooperation within one model family \cite{geminirobotics2026}. In Google’s October 13 Gemini 4 Argon demonstration, a Spot robot practiced stepping on a trash-bin pedal and maintaining balance in a MuJoCo digital twin before operating the real pedal, checking its gripper position, and dropping in a soda can; simulation, cameras, and action interfaces brought model reasoning into a closed loop \cite{rao2026argonrobotics}. These cases illustrate a necessary remapping from language and vision into actuators, action spaces, sensor feedback, and real objects when a model moves from answers to actions, rather than establishing that embodied intelligence is solved. The difficulty is keeping understanding effective through contact, friction, delay, and error. Autonomous driving likewise involves more than recognizing roads. It embeds perception, prediction, and control in a tightly coupled traffic system.

Human drivers, pedestrians, roads, weather, construction, law, insurance, and responsibility jointly form the real environment. An algorithm can calculate an optimal strategy, but the vehicle acts within braking distances, limited visibility, complex strategic interactions, and consequences that cannot be rolled back. Every real control action carries consequences. Research on autonomous-driving testing and verification identifies open-road edge cases, nondeterministic algorithms, complex requirements, fail-operational behavior, and safety arguments as far harder than a single recognition task \cite{koopman2016}. RAND’s reliability research also shows that, under common confidence assumptions, establishing safety at or above human levels using road mileage alone can require enormous distances \cite{kalra2016}. Physical intelligence finds paths that pass stably through real media, beyond the mathematical shortest path. It must know when to be fast and when slow, when to seek efficiency and when preserve redundancy, when to experiment and when verify before acting, and when an optimum remains usable or fails under the medium’s damping.

Once connected, a loop’s effect depends on more than the loop itself. When intelligence reduces resistance in one place, other actors respond, rearranging flows, risks, metrics, and responsibility. The link between local reductions in resistance and global outcomes remains to be explained. Output also passes through a translation by the medium before becoming an outcome.


\section{Interface Physics: The Rheological Spectrum of Media and Rate Mismatch}

The preceding chapter’s reachable space described states that a system can stably attain. A path describes a channel, without describing what intelligent input becomes as it passes through. The same open path produces different responses in different media: rapid diffusion, a requirement for work, or a rebound. The medium determines whether input becomes state change.

A medium translates intelligence into change. This is easily overlooked when AI enters real systems. The familiar claim that “AI will change the world” treats a world that is far from uniform. Text, code, images, machines, roads, drugs, cells, bodies, and ecosystems receive intelligent inputs differently. The same model output can spread rapidly through text, must become force and motion in a robot, and can trigger metabolism, immunity, compensation, adaptation, or rebound in life. AI’s real effectiveness therefore depends on the medium absorbing its output as well as the model’s strength: stable translation turns intelligence into useful work; mismatch turns it into noise, heat, wear, oscillation, verification burdens, or resistance by the system. The \term{medium response spectrum} describes how different media turn intelligent inputs into state changes. Bits translate intelligence into diffusion, atoms into work, and life into feedback. These are three absorption mechanisms: bits involve copying, combination, and propagation; atoms involve energy, inertia, and dissipation; life involves metabolism, regulation, and adaptation. One logic of intelligent acceleration applied to all three creates illusions.

\subsection{Three Response Spectra: Bits Diffuse, Atoms Do Work, Life Feeds Back}

\subhead{Diffusion in the Bit Medium}

The basic response of the bit medium is diffusion. Intelligent input readily becomes new information structures: text, images, code, model outputs, design drafts, and search results. They can be copied, edited, distributed, combined, and regenerated quickly. Bit-domain state changes primarily rearrange symbols rather than material positions. AI therefore expands most readily in bits, generating abundant content at very low marginal cost and compressing tasks of expression, search, rewriting, and combination that previously took people substantial time.

Diffusion, however, is not proof. Low bit viscosity occurs mainly in lateral propagation rather than vertical corroboration. Lateral propagation copies more, generates more, distributes faster, and combines more densely; vertical corroboration demands truth, reliability, provenance, explanation, and responsibility. AI readily amplifies the first without automatically reducing the burden of the second. Generated text still needs fact-checking, generated images provenance, generated code security and maintenance audits, and circulating opinions grounds for public trust.

The central tension in bits is between generation and establishing truth. Possibilities can expand cheaply without a cheap guarantee of truth. Cheaper generation makes credible results scarcer; more content increases screening; smoother expression makes judgment more important. Diffusion creates new pressure for corroboration, borne by those who verify rather than those who generate.

Bits also need reality as an anchor. Model intelligence compresses real language, images, experiments, code, behavior, and feedback, rather than growing from a purely logical closed loop. The lightness of bit space comes from turning reality into replicable information structures, whose replicability still depends on real sources. An information system consuming more of its own generated content without fresh contact with reality and external feedback can become smoother and more closed \cite{shumailov2024ai}. It can gain consistency without truth, or fluency while losing variance and external calibration.

Bits hide viscosity in two places: physical infrastructure and corroboration against reality. The first includes chips, electricity, cooling, data centers, and networks; the second real data, fact-checking, human feedback, provenance, and responsibility. Users see cheap diffusion; the system pays infrastructure and verification costs. Faster bit diffusion makes calibration against reality more necessary. When the output must change material positions rather than symbols, the response mechanism changes.

\subhead{Work in the Atomic Medium}

The atomic medium responds through work. A generated information structure does not automatically change atoms: control signals must become energy flows, planned paths motion, and designs materials, processing, assembly, testing, and maintenance. Symbolic elegance must survive force, heat, friction, inertia, material strength, and spatial constraints. Translating intelligent input into physical action requires energy, incurs dissipation, and takes time. Handling needs force, manufacture processes, cooling heat exchange, motion control, construction materials, robots motors and joints, and grids capacity and stability. AI can optimize paths without canceling mass, reduce trial and error without canceling work, improve dispatch without canceling capacity limits, and strengthen control without canceling friction, wear, heat, and failure.

Intelligence drives the atomic medium rather than persuading it. Bit diffusion can approach instantaneous response, while atoms require energy transfer and structural change. A smarter robot policy still needs actuator torque; better logistics still needs vehicles, roads, warehouses, and handling; more precise chips still need cleanrooms, lithography, materials, defect control, and cooling. Intelligence becomes control over physical processes. The atomic medium retains dissipation: some input becomes heat, wear, noise, error, and maintenance rather than useful work. Greater control precision often requires additional sensing and actuation; with energy use and losses per operation fixed, higher speed increases power and cooling pressure; added complexity not absorbed by modularity increases calibration and maintenance. Intelligence must keep the accounts of energy, power, heat, materials, and failure.

The atomic medium also has response bandwidth. Machines have inertia, materials fatigue, heat diffusion takes time, actuators have response limits, grids stability constraints, and traffic braking distances and reaction delays; physical states cannot change at unlimited frequency. High-frequency AI recommendations need not be absorbable at the same frequency. Excessively fast inputs can create oscillation, overcorrection, heat, wear, and safety risks instead of additional useful work.

Intelligence in the atomic medium needs an appropriate way to drive matter. Physical intelligence must know the power, frequency, error, and feedback delay the medium can sustain. It matches output to physical response, enters a stable feedback loop, and seeks executability, low dissipation, maintainability, and recovery rather than output speed and symbolic optimality alone. Work also exposes intelligence to physical losses: a system unable to manage heat, wear, error, and maintenance remains a demonstration regardless of model strength. The atomic medium brings answers down to actions, proposals down to processes, and optima down to sustained operation. Nonliving systems have feedback too. The translation enters the biological layer when the medium processes input through metabolism, self-maintenance, and adaptation.

\subhead{Feedback in the Living Medium}

The living medium responds through feedback. Life is matter with boundaries, metabolism, defenses, repair, regulation, memory, and adaptation; it interprets external action as well as bearing it. Drugs enter metabolic networks, immune systems, tissue environments, and behavioral contexts; gene editing perturbs development, expression regulation, cellular environments, and ecological relationships; treatment acts together with the body’s own feedback systems.

The living medium treats intelligent input as a disturbance rather than passively executing it. It absorbs some, cancels some, amplifies some, delays some, and rebounds against some. Stronger, faster, or more forceful intervention can provoke greater resistance rather than faster change. Immunity, inflammation, drug resistance, compensation, endocrine counterregulation, and ecological rebound show complex adaptive systems inclined toward self-maintenance. Rheology includes media that flow under gentle, slow disturbance but harden under rapid, strong disturbance \cite{brown2014shear}. Life can show analogous responses: mild, infrequent, adaptable intervention may be absorbed flexibly, while frequent, forceful, cross-scale intervention can abruptly raise resistance. Multiple layers of feedback can lose coordination when the driving timescale becomes shorter than the relevant relaxation time, provoking defenses, compensation, or instability.

This explains why life cannot iterate like software. Software permits many versions and reversible code changes; human intervention has limited trials and difficult rollback, physiological feedback takes time despite rapid model updates, and long-term side effects can lag improvements in short-term metrics. Biological feedback often conceals consequences in time: an intervention effective today may be canceled by compensation months later, or an improved metric reveal system costs years later. Nonlinearity also separates local targets from whole-system goals. Lowering one indicator need not improve bodily health, activating one pathway need not produce global benefit, suppressing one response can release another risk, and editing one gene can involve development, expression, and ecology. Every intervention point is a network node; more precise entry points do not stop biological feedback.

AI’s effects in the life sciences will therefore be uneven. It can quickly expand candidates by finding targets, predicting structures, generating molecules, designing experiments, and recognizing patterns. The living medium does not validate them at the same speed: abundant molecules do not become abundant approved drugs, quickly designed gene edits do not establish safety quickly, and quickly trained diagnostics do not remove clinical responsibility. AI accelerates discovery without canceling biological feedback. Life translates intelligence into feedback and sends it into long-term verification. Atomic failures often appear as wear, fracture, heat, and instability; biological failures can appear as compensation, tolerance, delayed side effects, population differences, behavioral change, and ecological consequences. Beyond physical losses, the biological account must include adaptation, self-maintenance, and their responses to intervention.

Three representative models describe responses: first-order tracking, rate-limited progress after a startup delay, and underdamped feedback. Let $y(t)$ be the response of a selected outcome and $y_\infty$ its steady-state value; the models are
\begin{align}
y_{b}(t)&=y_{\infty}\bigl(1-e^{-t/\tau_{b}}\bigr),\qquad \tau_{b}\to 0^{+}\label{eq:resp-bit}\\[2pt]
y_{a}(t)&=y_{\infty}\min\left\{\frac{(t-t_{d})_{+}}{\tau_{a}},\;1\right\},\qquad t_{d}>0\label{eq:resp-atom}\\[2pt]
y_{l}(t)&=y_{\infty}\left[1-e^{-\zeta\omega t}\left(\cos\omega_{d}t+\frac{\zeta}{\sqrt{1-\zeta^{2}}}\sin\omega_{d}t\right)\right],\qquad 0<\zeta<1\label{eq:resp-life}
\end{align}
Time parameters use a common unit, and responses are normalized to the same reference. In the first expression $\tau_b$ is a first-order time constant; in the second $t_d$ is startup delay and $\tau_a$ the duration of rate-limited progress; in the third $\zeta$ is damping ratio, $\omega$ natural angular frequency, and $\omega_d=\omega\sqrt{1-\zeta^2}$. For $0<\zeta<1$, the third response overshoots before gradually returning to steady state. The forms describe rapid tracking, capacity limits, and feedback-driven decline in relevant tasks; response data determine the form and parameters selected.

Analyzing the medium supplies mechanistic clues for model selection. Digital distribution often responds quickly, manufacturing faces startup and throughput limits, and biological intervention often involves compensation and hysteresis. One medium can also exhibit several responses: information networks congest, mechanical systems overshoot, and living processes approach a state monotonically. The comparison concerns particular channels, rather than curves assigned in advance by a medium’s name.

\subsection{Rate Mismatch and Interface Dissipation}

\subhead{Three Clocks, Different Rates}

A subtler problem lies among the three response spectra: the same logic of speed cannot drive them all. Bits can generate at high frequency, atoms require power matching, and life requires relaxation time. Intelligence crosses interfaces between rates as well as between media. Bits can compute, update, and propagate extremely quickly; atoms have inertia, heat transfer, friction, fatigue, actuator response, and safety boundaries; life adds metabolic cycles, immunity, tissue repair, behavioral adaptation, and long-term feedback. A faster input layer gives less reason to assume its absorbing layer will accelerate in step.

This resembles impedance mismatch. In engineering, mismatched source and load impedances can leave energy reflected, dissipated, or oscillating rather than effectively transferred to the load. Its standard expression is the reflection coefficient
\begin{equation}
\Gamma=\frac{Z_L-Z_S}{Z_L+Z_S},\qquad \frac{P_{\mathrm{refl}}}{P_{\mathrm{in}}}=|\Gamma|^2
\end{equation}
For a lossless transmission line with a terminal load, $Z_S$ denotes a positive real characteristic impedance and $Z_L$ the load impedance, both in ohms. $\Gamma$ is the voltage reflection coefficient, and reflected power divided by incident power is $|\Gamma|^2$; for a nonnegative real load, $\Gamma$ lies between $-1$ and $1$. Impedance matching eliminates reflection. Output frequency, review throughput, and execution capacity in intelligent systems have their own units and require separate measurement; queues, dropped outputs, overcorrection, and structural damage are directly observable consequences of mismatch.

Mismatch can be expressed as the ratio of input rate to absorption capacity. Let $r=v_{\mathrm{in}}/v_{\mathrm{abs}}$; measure effective progress in units of absorption capacity, with a damage term for degradation under overload:
\begin{equation}
r=\frac{v_{\mathrm{in}}}{v_{\mathrm{abs}}},
\qquad
u(r)=
\begin{cases}
r, & 0<r\le 1\\[3pt]
1-\kappa\,(r-1)^{m}, & r>1
\end{cases}
\label{eq:rate-mismatch}
\end{equation}
$v_{\mathrm{in}}$ and $v_{\mathrm{abs}}$ use the same unit, making $r$ dimensionless. $u$ is net progress rate divided by absorption capacity. For $r\le1$, all input is absorbed and $u=r$ indicates unused capacity; for $r>1$, the model uses $\kappa(r-1)^m$ for net loss from overload. $\kappa\ge0$ and $m>0$ must be estimated from observation; $u<0$ means damage exceeds current gains. A system that only queues without degrading requires a saturated-throughput model instead. Information networks, machines, and living systems can all suffer overload damage; particular mechanisms and data must establish the differences.

Engineering has long used layered conversion. Primary grid frequency response comes automatically from local controls within seconds; secondary control uses automatic generation control or manual dispatch over minutes to restore frequency and power balance, while reserve deployment and unit commitment span minutes, hours, and days \cite{nerc2024frequency}. Longer timescales allow larger changes in the resource mix but involve scheduling, commitments, and switching costs; making a fast layer take over slow-layer objectives can create control conflicts, while faults requiring immediate action miss their window if they must await a slow layer. Data systems have a similar arrangement: writes enter a log before merging into primary storage, while reads need not await all background maintenance. These structures convert rates between source and absorbing system, spending resources to avoid congestion, instability, or stoppage from mismatch.

Mature AI systems convert rates across media rather than pushing every medium toward the highest frequency. Intelligence improves the match between source and load as well as increasing output. Failure can arise at the interface: too much output to screen, updates too fast for workflows, controls dense enough to cause physical oscillation, intervention strong enough to provoke biological rebound, or metrics frequent enough to consume organizational effort. \key{Intelligence has not vanished; it has been dissipated at the interface.}

\subhead{Adapting to the Medium}

A mature view of intelligence asks how the medium translates output as well as whether the model can produce a better result. Is it stable, or does it oscillate? Does it conserve resources, or create waste heat and maintenance? Is it controllable, or does it provoke biological and systemic rebound? Can it be verified, or does it only look valid in representational space? The medium’s response helps define intelligence’s boundaries. The response spectrum corrects an image of intelligence without a medium: AI hands outputs to bits that diffuse them, atoms that demand work, and life that feeds back; every translation costs, every response has limits, and every absorption has forms of failure.

Effective intelligent systems must adapt to their medium. Bits demand truth and trust; atoms power, dissipation, and maintenance; life feedback, relaxation, and long-term consequences. Generation must anticipate what will absorb it, optimization what residue it will leave, and acceleration when to reduce frequency, buffer, and verify. The opening proposition now becomes concrete: the medium translates intelligence into change, and AI’s real effectiveness depends on stable, economical, controllable, and verifiable translation.

Network protocols offer another version of the same experience. During the congestion collapse of October 1986, throughput on a link from Lawrence Berkeley Laboratory to the University of California, Berkeley fell from 32 kilobits per second to 40 bits per second. Van Jacobson and Michael Karels’s 1988 congestion control constrained senders through acknowledgment pacing, a congestion window, and retransmission backoff; after a timeout, the congestion window restarted from a very small value, with the slow-start threshold reduced to half the former window, followed by controlled growth \cite{jacobson1988}. The source thus followed the absorption capacity of the whole path. A sender advancing only at its own output capacity fills intermediate queues, causes drops, and adds retransmissions that deepen the load, reducing effective throughput. Protocol discipline writes the medium’s bandwidth and feedback into the source’s control law.

A medium already has a history before intelligence adapts to it. Its construction was shaped by human bodies, existing processes, and institutions of the time, rather than intelligent input formats. The central problem is often whether translation can occur without rebuilding that medium’s skeleton; once the skeleton must change, the cost returns to the terms of the atomic world.


\section{Evolutionary Strategy: Cybernetic Parasitism and the Complexity Ratchet}

The reality intelligence seeks to change was built before intelligence arrived. Roads, buildings, hospitals, and factories have existing structures embedded in law, insurance, habits, and responsibility. Models work through those interfaces, making deployment cost depend on the extent of change required. Replacing a component is repair; replacing a load-bearing structure is reconstruction. Once local capability is sufficient, adapting to the old structure must be compared with rebuilding the environment on total cost.

\subsection{The Overlay Strategy and the Three Costs of Reconstruction}

\subhead{Three Costs of Reconstruction}

In theory, the cleanest route is to rebuild the underlying structure. Redesign roads, vehicles, signals, insurance, and traffic rules for autonomous driving; buildings, tools, warehouses, homes, and factories for robots; hospital workflows, records, accountability, and payment for intelligent healthcare. The physical world would better suit machine perception, action, and decisions, with more regular interfaces, less environmental uncertainty during operation, and more stable feedback. But this route is expensive.

Rebuilding the atomic world must overcome three costs. First, resources: roads, factories, hospitals, ports, grids, homes, and utilities embody vast materials, capital, space, and labor; demolition and reconstruction discard existing material structures and pay the energy bill again. Second, temporal rigidity: infrastructure has life cycles, while construction, approvals, migration, coordination, and behavioral change cannot update instantly like software versions. Third, topology: roads connect insurance, law, logistics, real estate, work, and daily life; hospitals connect physicians’ responsibility, patient trust, insurance payment, and legal boundaries. Changing the base pulls on the entire system.

Annual production of cement, steel, and equipment accumulates into buildings, roads, factories, and networks. USGS and World Steel Association reports for 2026 still place global cement output in the several-billion-tonne range and crude steel near two billion tonnes \cite{usgs2026cement,worldsteel2026figures}. Transforming that stock depends on lifetimes, replacement rates, construction capacity, and neighboring systems; one year’s production cannot be equated with stock available for simultaneous reconstruction.

These are the preceding chapter’s three constraints expressed in the built environment. Resource barriers concern material, energy, and space already paid for; temporal rigidity concerns infrastructure processes that cannot be compressed at will; coupling concerns the connections already formed among roads, law, insurance, and work. A built object’s viscosity enters its structure at construction. Assessing an intelligent upgrade requires counting how much of that old structure must be paid for again, alongside its symbolic savings.

\subhead{The Overlay Strategy}

Civilization therefore tends to overlay before rebuilding. An \term{overlay strategy} adds a bit-based control layer over an old physical skeleton without completely changing it. Keep the roads and add navigation, cameras, radar, high-definition maps, and cloud training; keep the factory and add sensors, predictive maintenance, digital twins, and dispatch platforms; keep the hospital and add image recognition, record summaries, triage, and review; keep the city and add cameras, platforms, algorithms, data interfaces, and “smart governance.” A digital film covers the heavy atomic skeleton.

This is a form of cybernetic parasitism. Here “parasitism” describes a structural relationship and an evolutionary strategy, without moral disparagement: the new intelligent layer neither exists independently nor immediately replaces the old layer, but attaches itself to an existing physical system, using its established space, energy, equipment, institutions, and human networks to gain a foothold for action in reality and to change the old system's behavior. The bit layer resembles a layer of neural tissue covering the old world's skeleton; it leaves the bones in place while trying to make them move faster, more accurately, and more readily under coordinated control.

The strategy is widespread because it follows least-cost logic. A local overlay is lighter than rebuilding the world: sensors cost less than roads, dispatch software less than a rebuilt factory, recognition models less than a rewritten healthcare system, and better robot perception and control less than redesigned living spaces. The overlay is a second-best route around a viscous base, finding room to act above its weight rather than removing it. In the short term it works: smoother interfaces, greater management visibility, more immediate dispatch, better risk monitoring, and real local efficiency gains. Navigation, predictive maintenance, assisted diagnosis, monitoring platforms, and automated warehouse sorting make old systems appear lighter by reorganizing processes once dependent on human experience and local judgment.

Overlays predate the digital age. Between the late nineteenth and early twentieth centuries, factories shifted from centralized steam transmission toward distributed electric motors; diffusion had begun in the 1890s, but major productivity gains waited for layouts, transmission, machine placement, and production organization to be rearranged around distributed power, a lag of two or three decades \cite{david1990dynamo}. Containerization likewise required docks, cranes, truck chassis, railcars, warehouses, union rules, and customs systems to change after the modern era’s landmark Ideal X voyage in 1956; entire handling areas moved, and widespread adoption followed in the 1970s \cite{bernhofen2016estimating}. In both cases the old skeleton’s ability to change was often the bottleneck for the new layer.

Recent cases make the limits of overlay gains clearer. China’s Ministry of Transport reported in 2019 that pilots in Jiangsu, Shandong, Sichuan, and Chongqing cut normal average provincial-border passage times from 15 seconds to 2 for cars and from 29 to 3 for trucks; on January 1, 2020, 487 provincial-border toll stations in 29 connected provinces were abolished \cite{mot2019tolling,mot2020tollbooths}. The Pennsylvania Turnpike introduced open-road electronic tolling east of Reading and on the Northeast Extension in January 2025, allowing vehicles to pass gantries at highway speed; in May 2026, equipment was still being installed in the west for a planned systemwide conversion in 2027 \cite{paturnpike2026ort}. The bit layer changed toll collection, while lane, ramp, mainline, and service-area capacities still required separate accounting. Peak flows still pass through physical channels; removing the toll-point constraint can expose mainline or interchange bottlenecks. The gains are real, and the whole corridor’s constraints determine how far they extend.

The old world is heavy because historical decisions have become physical dimensions. After 1,435-millimeter standard gauge emerged in the nineteenth century, the tunnels, bridges, platforms, and vehicles adopting it took shape around it. International container standards formed in the 1960s into major series including 20- and 40-foot lengths, shaping cranes, yards, truck chassis, and railcars. Stair-riser limits, doorway sizes, outlet shapes, AC frequency, and keyboard layouts reflect the bodies, processes, and industry compromises of their time. They remain because changing them incurs atomic-world costs shared across the entire chain, rather than because they are optimal.

Overlays also spread because they put costs in another ledger. Sensors, cameras, and dispatch platforms appear in current capital and operating budgets; the old skeleton’s failure to accommodate machine perception and action appears in no explicit cost item. One is expenditure; the other an implicit debt. An old system’s digital upgrade delivers visible gains quickly. The costs emerge as overlays become dependent on one another, by which time they are necessary for operation.

\subsection{The Complexity Ratchet, Compatibility Tax, and Deployment Tax}

\subhead{The Complexity Ratchet}

An overlay requires sensing, data, communication, permissions, monitoring, maintenance, and exception handling. Interfaces that require supporting changes in old structures can add coupling; when structure needs further structure to keep running, a \term{complexity ratchet} forms. Modularity, standardization, and retirement of old interfaces can also lower net complexity; architecture and operating records establish the direction.

A recurrence expresses the process:
\begin{equation}
C_{n+1}=(1+\alpha)\,C_n+c
\label{eq:ratchet-recursion}
\end{equation}
Here $C_n$ is complexity counted consistently, $c$ the direct addition from a new layer, and $\alpha$ the proportion added to existing structure by that layer. With fixed $c>0$ and $\alpha>0$, the recurrence grows exponentially; with $\alpha=0$, linearly. It describes one case of accumulating dependencies; layer count alone does not establish that a real system follows a fixed proportion.

Expanding \eqref{eq:ratchet-recursion} reveals the ratchet’s form. For initial complexity $C_{0}$, after $n$ layers,
\begin{equation}
C_{n}=(1+\alpha)^{n}C_{0}+\frac{c}{\alpha}\bigl[(1+\alpha)^{n}-1\bigr],
\qquad
C^{\min}_{n}=\beta\,C_{n},\qquad 0<\beta<1
\label{eq:ratchet-floor}
\end{equation}
The first expression solves the recurrence for $\alpha>0$; for $\alpha=0$, its limit is $C_n=C_0+nc$. The second records retained complexity after removal as $\beta$ times the current level, with $\beta$ estimated from the particular exit plan. Existing dependencies can be transferred, rebuilt, or removed, so $C_n^{\min}$ is a reachable level for a scenario rather than a universal physical floor.

The difference is a lock-in band; its accumulation is the compatibility tax payable to unload the first $n$ layers:
\begin{equation}
K_{n}=\sum_{k=1}^{n}\bigl(C_{k}-C^{\min}_{k}\bigr)=(1-\beta)\sum_{k=1}^{n}C_{k}
\label{eq:compat-tax}
\end{equation}
$K_n$ aggregates successive differences into a compatibility-burden index, with units set by the complexity convention. Shared interfaces can make direct addition double-count; converting the index into exit expenditure requires separate estimates for removal, migration, verification, and replacement support. Concentrated reconstruction can also lower actual cost; the sum alone does not establish an inevitably exponential exit bill.

Autonomous driving is a characteristic overlay dilemma \cite{kalra2016}. Roads were not designed for machine vision, traffic rules for algorithmic responsibility, or insurance for driverless actors, and people do not follow machine protocols completely. Simplifying autonomy through closed roads, separated traffic, common vehicle–road communication, standardized participants, and clear responsibility would rebuild urban transport at great cost. The overlay route instead puts more sensors on cars, asks algorithms to handle long tails of behavior, and adds safety drivers, remote intervention, regulatory sandboxes, insurance arrangements, and data logs. The environment stays complex, so vehicles acquire complexity; insufficiently standardized roads leave algorithms more uncertainty. Replacing a driver also transfers road-reconstruction costs into onboard intelligence, redundant perception, cloud training, and responsibility systems. Mixed traffic adds a transitional difficulty: human driving has established interaction rules, highly standardized machine traffic might form stable protocols, and the mixed stage must accommodate both behaviors alongside old roads, law, nonstandard actions, insurance, and expectations, creating a mixed region of high uncertainty. Stronger intelligence need not simplify the system; much compute pays for the old environment’s disorder.

\subhead{Compatibility and Deployment Taxes}

Embodied intelligence faces the same cybernetic parasitism, across a wider range of spaces. Homes, hospitals, restaurants, warehouses, shopping malls, and streets were not designed for robot bodies: door handles assume human hands, stairs assume two legs, kitchens assume coordination between eyes and hands, tools assume human touch and common sense, and household objects assume the human ability to handle ambiguity. To enter these spaces, robots must pay a compatibility tax: more degrees of freedom, more complex sensors, more demanding real-time control, stronger safety redundancy, and more expensive maintenance systems. Industrial robots succeed because they are usually placed in low-entropy environments with fixed positions, repetitive movements, standardized materials, separated workspaces, and clearly specified tasks; general embodied intelligence is difficult because it must enter high-entropy human environments, where object positions vary, task goals are ambiguous, layouts differ, human behavior is unpredictable, and contact feedback is complex. Installing a large model in a robot does not automatically eliminate friction, collisions, errors, occlusion, material differences, or liability risks.

This cost distribution has an earlier formulation. Hans Moravec observed in 1988 that adult-level performance on intelligence tests or chess was relatively easy for computers, while a one-year-old’s perception and mobility were extremely difficult \cite{moravec1988}. More than thirty years later, the distinction persists in embodied intelligence: explicit reasoning can be formalized, labeled, and searched, while grasping, walking, and obstacle avoidance depend on tacit regulation learned through perception, action, and feedback; simulation supplies some training, while real contact still calibrates and verifies, concentrating costs in adaptation that is difficult to copy. The compatibility tax pays for regulation that human bodies acquired through long evolution, beyond the robot’s apparent intelligence.

The “deployment tax” appears when a model touches reality. Every world model compresses reality and leaves residuals; simulation cannot exhaust real noise, edge cases, material changes, and human contingencies. Action changes what is modeled: lifting a cup changes its position, pushing a door changes its state, and entering a room can change people’s behavior. Physical AI continually corrects within an environment it perturbs. An overlay’s difficulty includes both model capability and an old world not rebuilt for low-cost intelligent action. AI pays compatibility, residual, and maintenance taxes in that world. Local bit-layer efficiency carries atomic weight, disorder, and consequences that cannot be rolled back.

\subhead{Between Overlay and Reconstruction}

Overlays can be mistaken for reconstruction. They extend old systems’ lives, improve local efficiency, and add control to old infrastructure, but cannot accumulate without limit. Does each layer remove more friction than complexity it adds? Do its labor savings cover its maintenance burden? Do its efficiency gains justify its added fragility? A system that only overlays without rebuilding gradually forms an efficient but fragile network. It looks intelligent in normal operation; failed interfaces, bad data, faulty sensors, platform outages, and broken responsibility chains turn complexity into a risk amplifier. Old problems remain under intelligent layers, while responsibility is redistributed across platforms, algorithms, operators, users, regulators, and human backstops.

Mature physical AI therefore requires more than larger models, more sensors, and finer control: it requires deciding when to overlay, when to reconstruct, and when to abandon an approach. Settings with low risk, weak coupling, and extensive standardization suit an overlay: closed campuses, industrial production lines, warehousing and logistics, and fixed-route transport can all benefit substantially from the added layer. High-risk, open, tightly coupled settings demand more than an overlay: autonomous driving, medical care, home robots, and urban governance ultimately require changes in environmental design, institutions, and responsibility boundaries together. Future competition in physical AI will concern more than model capability: it will concern the ability to reduce environmental entropy, standardize interfaces, reconstruct infrastructure, and design institutions of responsibility; reducing the compatibility tax makes intelligent action cheaper, reducing environmental disorder makes embodied systems more reliable, and recognizing the boundary between overlay and reconstruction prevents the complexity ratchet from pulling systems toward fragility. Cybernetic parasitism is physical AI's starting point, rather than its endpoint. AI often first enters the world of atoms as an overlay attached to existing systems; if it remains there forever, civilization will acquire an ever more complex network of patches. Reliable physical intelligence requires finding the path of lowest total viscosity among overlaying, reconstructing, and retaining existing structures, rather than endlessly attaching sensors and algorithms to the old world.

The old world does not vanish when intelligence arrives. It is first overlaid, monitored, dispatched, and patched. Physical AI begins with this reality: intelligence first parasitizes the atomic world it seeks to change; maturity ultimately depends on moving toward real environmental reconstruction. Overlay or reconstruction, intelligence keeps feeding a viscous system. The system may divert along lower-resistance paths, accumulate inputs it cannot absorb, or oscillate under overly urgent feedback. Strategy changes input, structure, and feedback; the resulting system dynamics explain these responses.


\section{Dynamical Responses: Detours, Accumulation, and Instability}

An input gains no priority merely by coming from outside the system. The system’s dynamics process it, absorbing some inputs, delaying some, and amplifying others. An overlay adds structure and interfaces, bringing new coordination and conversion stages into the path from input to effective change.

\subsection{Probabilistic Shortcuts and Detours}

Intelligence entering reality has several possible outcomes. It may find a low-resistance path that opens an unexpected solution, accumulate at interfaces as inputs outpace real change, or generate oscillation through delayed feedback and overcorrection. The three forms are detours, accumulation, and instability. They do not lie entirely on one axis. A detour is a strategy for passing resistance successfully; accumulation and instability are two failures of pushing a viscous system—too much input for absorption, or correction too urgent for feedback. The three responses describe three fates: getting through, becoming stuck midway, or rebounding into fluctuation.

Resources, time, topology, and medium response explain resistance; we now ask how a resistant system moves under sustained intelligent input. A viscous system absorbs, filters, delays, accumulates, rebounds, and amplifies. A common AI-era mistake treats intelligence as a one-way accelerator: stronger models mean faster systems, more proposals faster progress, more predictions better decisions, and denser control a more controllable reality. Yet resource limits, process times, structural paths, feedback delays, and safety boundaries can turn intelligent inputs into inventory, congestion, fluctuation, and oscillation as well as useful change. The crucial assessment therefore asks what dynamical form the inputs take after entering the system, beyond proposal counts and improved local metrics.

\subhead{Detours: Moving Trial and Error into Information Space}

The first form is the detour. Intelligence searches state space for a lower-resistance path rather than breaking straight through a barrier. With high resource barriers and tight coupling, the direct route may cost too much to be feasible even when the destination is describable. Intelligence often finds a route with fewer collisions against walls.

This is the meaning of a \term{probabilistic shortcut}. A probabilistic shortcut uses models, simulation, search, and combination to discard clearly unproductive routes and retain a few promising ones, reducing expensive real trials. It pays some costs in information space before they fall due physically; real trials remain but are compressed, reordered, and pruned. AlphaGo’s inspired moves offer an accessible bit-domain example: within unchanged Go rules and the board’s physical constraints, it found paths through a huge state space that human experience rarely reached \cite{silver2016mastering}. The surprise comes from reorganized search: seemingly natural human paths need not be best globally, while large-scale search discovers feasible channels beyond experience.

Sampling as an alternative to analytic solution long predates deep learning. In 1946, Stanisław Ulam’s thoughts about card-game probabilities led to repeated random trials as an alternative to difficult combinatorial calculation; he and von Neumann subsequently applied the idea to neutron transport and other problems. Nicholas Metropolis named it “Monte Carlo,” and Metropolis and Ulam published their methods paper in 1949 \cite{lanl2021montecarlo}. The cost per sample remained, while the problem became how many samples and what error were sufficient, rather than whether an analytic solution could be found. Weather prediction later expanded from single deterministic forecasts to ensembles, using perturbed initial conditions and model configurations to produce probability distributions. Models and random simulations move some real trials into computation, permitting replay, parallel batches, and failures with little damage while still requiring checks on model bias and sampling error.

The atomic world has similar mechanisms, with heavier costs. Materials discovery, drug screening, structural optimization, and process-parameter searches seek low-resistance paths in high-dimensional state spaces; AI can remove some fruitless experiments, avoid clearly failed combinations, and concentrate resources on promising regions. Candidate materials still need synthesis, drugs verification, processes stability, and products maintenance; intelligence reduces blindness rather than eliminating reality. Computational lithography, process optimization, and defect control show the same logic: near microscopic limits, direct scaling becomes harder, and computation, control, and complex processes find manufacturable paths within narrower windows. Progress continues by detour through more complex, costly arrangements with less tolerance for error when direct paths are blocked.

Even detours encounter barriers they cannot bypass, and specific energy is one. Aviation kerosene has a specific energy of about 12,000 watt-hours per kilogram; taking lithium-ion cells at 250 to 300 watt-hours per kilogram for comparison gives a gap of roughly fortyfold. Allowing for a heat engine's efficiency of about one-third and an electric motor's efficiency of more than 90 percent still leaves a gap of more than tenfold. This barrier sets the feasible limits of several strategies for taking a detour: on the ground, all-electric mobility can avoid some costs through lightweight construction, charging networks, and route constraints; in aviation, the same detour incurs a direct penalty in takeoff weight, because batteries retain their mass throughout the flight while fuel is continually consumed. A detour works only if the costs it shifts are smaller than the costs it adds in the new medium; once the latter are greater, the detour has merely moved the obstacle elsewhere.

Protein structure prediction extends this logic to a larger scale. The space from amino-acid sequences to three-dimensional structures is vast; difficult samples may take months or years to resolve experimentally, while AlphaFold and related models compress patterns from known sequences and structures into parameters, greatly reducing the cost of candidate generation \cite{jumper2021alphafold}. Predictions already assist screening, interpretation, and experimental design; specific structural or functional conclusions still require attention to confidence, applicability, and relevant evidence. More candidates make screening and focused corroboration more important; verification resources should prioritize candidates capable of changing conclusions and actions.

Biological detours are subtler. Drug design, gene editing, and synthetic biology seek intervention paths in living networks; an effective intervention may use a low-disturbance leverage point rather than force. Compensation, redundancy, and feedback can cancel a seemingly easy path over time; a rare mutation may offer a therapeutic opportunity and unforeseen risk. Biological probabilistic shortcuts need even more verification than atomic ones. A detour changes how costs are paid rather than eliminating all cost. It distributes concentrated costs as risk, moves some physical trials into simulation and search, and substitutes path selection for some direct reconstruction. A successful detour looks like a sudden drop in resistance, but usually finds a more bearable payment route rather than making total cost vanish.

\subsection{Accumulation, Inventory, and Fluctuation}

\subhead{Accumulation and Inventory Formation}

The second form is accumulation. Inputs exceed absorption: the system has activity in abundance but cannot turn it into effective change. It looks busier, denser, more automated, and more immediate without a proportional change in real state. Accumulation begins when incoming flow exceeds absorbed flow: execution, verification, coordination, and responsibility determine how many proposals, commands, investments, experiments, metrics, and recommendations can become change, regardless of what the source produces. Beyond that bandwidth, more input queues, silts up, creates rework and friction, or becomes a maintenance burden instead of automatically raising output.

A stock equation expresses the relationship:
\begin{equation}
\frac{\mathrm{d}S}{\mathrm{d}t}=I(t)-A(S),\qquad A(S)\le A_{\max}
\end{equation}
$S$ is the stock at the system interface, counted as tasks, queue length, or unverified candidates; $I(t)$ is input rate in items per unit time; $A(S)$ is absorption rate; and $A_{\max}$ is the maximum execution, verification, and coordination throughput with given resources. For constant input with $I>A_{\max}$ and saturated absorption, time measured from the start of the saturated segment gives $S(t)\approx S(0)+(I-A_{\max})t$, linear stock growth. For homogeneous tasks, first-in-first-out service, and fixed capacity, the work ahead translates into an approximate wait of $S/A_{\max}$. Reducing $I$ limits arrivals; raising $A_{\max}$ expands capacity: the former changes arrival pressure and waits, the latter maximum processing capability.

Inventory formation is the first form of accumulation. Inputs not absorbed promptly become inventory, queues, tasks, backlogs, unverified candidates, and untreated risks. Inventory makes temporal rigidity visible: inputs have arrived without the capacity to turn them into change; growing stocks can represent future processing pressure piled up at an interface rather than acceleration. In information systems this appears as screening work: AI generates texts, images, code, plans, and hypotheses faster than human and organizational judgment expands, increasing review, verification, and decision burdens. Scarcity shifts from generation to corroboration; acceleration without expanded verification builds information stocks. In research and engineering, discovery outpaces verification: high-throughput experiments, automation, and AI expand candidates, while replication, stability tests, mechanism explanations, scale-up, and long-term reliability remain. Drug candidates still pass through toxicology, pharmacokinetics, dose, population differences, clinical trials, and regulatory review. More candidates do not automatically mean more reliable drugs; faster discovery makes verification more binding. High-throughput methods and AI move the bottleneck, reducing early search costs while potentially increasing pressure on verification, resource allocation, and failure screening; discovery expanded alone can leave many apparently innovative possibilities stranded before reliable results. In organizations, accumulation appears as internal friction: compute, capital, metrics, and commands arrive quickly, while learning, judgment, execution, and responsibility form more slowly.
