Without absorption capacity, new recommendations, live metrics, strategic slogans, optimization plans, and management tasks create more meetings, reports, pilots, presentations, and short-term goals rather than greater intelligence.

Internal friction can be understood as input failing to become useful work. More information, resources, and competitive pressure arrive without increased structural response, leaving energy circulating within the system as repeated coordination, metric chasing, local competition, review congestion, dissipated attention, and maintenance rather than changing external states. “Heat” here means unproductive motion left by intensive input, rather than heat in the strict physical sense.

\subhead{Fluctuations and Cycles}

Accumulation does not always sit quietly in place. When input exceeds absorption capacity, a stock first builds up; if it cannot be absorbed locally, it propagates through the structure. In traffic, vehicles keep moving forward while a congestion wave may travel backward; in an organization, tasks keep flowing downstream while unresolved matters surge back to upstream management; in a technical system, candidates keep appearing while a verification bottleneck exerts backpressure on the initial search strategy. What moves here is the state that cannot be absorbed, rather than the entities themselves. This can be called an accumulation wave. Traffic congestion waves also offer an analogy for backpressure in other high-viscosity systems: when a local channel reaches capacity, the flow it cannot absorb becomes a pressure wave through the system; individuals may still move forward while pressure travels backward, tasks may still advance while a bottleneck presses back on earlier stages, and intelligence may still generate proposals while the verification burden constrains the direction of search. The waves in high-viscosity systems often consist of propagating failures of absorption rather than material waves.

When a system adjusts stocks rather than light variables, accumulation can become cyclical. Inventory, capacity, factories, teams, cities, and institutions cannot appear or disappear instantly: expansion responds to shortage, but conditions may change before supply arrives; contraction responds to surplus, but a new shortage may appear before it finishes. The difficulty can lie in heavy stocks and slow responses rather than impatient control. Cycles arise as stocks of different weights correct at different speeds.

Short cycles often involve light stocks. Goods, tasks, review queues, and candidate proposals can grow and be cleared relatively quickly; their short cycles reflect faster feedback and visible correction. Even light stocks can overshoot under delayed signals: the supply-chain bullwhip effect amplifies small changes in final demand through orders, inventory, production, and procurement, using delayed information and stock adjustments \cite{lee1997information}. Medium cycles involve equipment, capacity, teams, factories, supply chains, and capital expenditure; investment takes longer than days or weeks, and conditions may change before expansion or contraction is complete. The stock being adjusted is productive capacity, with longer cycles and more expensive correction. Longer cycles involve spatial and structural stocks—buildings, cities, roads, schools, hospitals, housing, and infrastructure—which fix expectations in space and resist rollback; changing populations, industries, public finances, and lifestyles can leave excess buildings, debt, and underused infrastructure, a hysteretic echo of sunk structures. The longest fluctuations involve technological paradigms, energy systems, and institutions, as capital, infrastructure, education, regulation, organizations, and daily life reorganize through expansion and imagination, surplus and selection, then liquidation, restructuring, and stable absorption; these long waves are neither precise clocks nor inevitable laws, but historical revaluation and recoupling of heavy structures.

Different cycles can thus be understood as delayed corrections of stocks with different weights: light goods inventories adjust briefly, fixed capital over longer periods, buildings and cities longer still, and technological, energy, and institutional structures across extended historical periods of expansion, surplus, liquidation, and reorganization. Heavier stocks bring slower feedback, making correction more liable to create another imbalance. Money, credit, psychology, institutions, shocks, and technological change also shape actual cycles; the general mechanism here is a system adjusting heavy stocks using delayed signals, with a changed world awaiting the correction. Cycles often reflect obsolete signals correcting heavy stocks rather than an intrinsic rhythm.

Inventory can buffer fluctuations or amplify adjustment delays. Whether accumulation becomes a cycle or instability depends on replenishment, feedback, service, and control. Once input exceeds absorption, the options include reducing unproductive arrivals, improving candidate quality, expanding processing, and changing schedules, beyond increasing generation alone.

\subsection{Instability, Damping, and Three Forms of Governance}

\subhead{Instability and Damping}

The third form is instability. Construction and feedback delays can make stock adjustment cyclical, while control itself can amplify fluctuation. Delayed feedback combined with excessive gain, action amplitude, or unsuitable update timing can turn correction into error amplification. Periodicity does not automatically mean instability: bounded oscillations can persist, while instability appears when small disturbances grow enough to undermine the target state or take the system outside safe operation. The preceding discussion emphasized a slow world; here we ask whether the hand is too fast or pushes too hard. Both can occur in the same loop.

In an ideal feedback system, a controller detects deviation and applies a correction that restores stability; real systems have delays in measurement, judgment, execution, physical response, and behavioral change. Continual corrections to outdated states can apply the right action at the wrong time; by the time it takes effect, the system has moved, turning correction into overcorrection. Such oscillation reflects mismatch among control action, the plant, delays, and feedback cycles. Fast measurement can still help; control gain, action amplitude, and update timing need examination.

Algorithmic flash crashes show a similar mechanism. High-frequency strategies adjust rapidly to prices, orders, and liquidity, while market liquidity, risk-bearing capacity, and institutional safeguards may not replenish at the same speed; interacting algorithms can respond, cancel orders, and amplify signals until prices diverge from fundamental value \cite{sec2010findings}. On May 6, 2010, the Dow Jones Industrial Average briefly fell about a thousand points intraday and then rebounded sharply; investigations identified interaction between high-frequency and algorithmic trading as an important cause. Multiple fast feedback loops can couple into collective instability beyond the error of one algorithm. Organizations can oscillate too: frequent adjustments to strategy, metrics, resources, and staff direction can interrupt feedback from previous adjustments. Metrics change before teams finish learning, resources move before projects stabilize, and new advice arrives before a process has been absorbed. Apparent agility can conceal a lost rhythm under overly dense control.

Actual loops must be examined for causes of oscillation: gain, delay, model error, actuator limits, and coupling can all contribute. Fast measurement and computation can also stabilize a slow plant. Damping, inertia, and active compensation have different physical effects and require separate accounts; their shared goal is correction along recoverable trajectories.

Damping devices can themselves fail. China introduced index circuit breakers in January 2016, with CSI 300 declines of 5\% and 7\% triggering two levels; January 4 and 7 both saw halts followed by early closes, with liquidity contracting near the thresholds, and the mechanism was suspended from January 8 \cite{csrc2016circuit}. The intended cooling-off period split a continuous decline into stages and could also induce selling before a threshold arrived. A damping device must act compatibly with the behavior of the system it seeks to damp. Industrial control has a counterpart: common electromechanical low-frequency grid oscillations occur around 0.1 to 2 hertz and are suppressed through phase compensation in excitation loops, with stabilizer parameters tuned to inertia and operating configuration; higher sampling rates do not replace tuning.

Power systems make the differences among inertia, fast response, and control coordination concrete. In Britain’s August 9, 2019 blackout, multiple sources of generation were lost after a lightning strike, frequency fell, and low-frequency demand disconnection operated \cite{nationalgrid2019technical}. Inertia affects the initial rate of frequency change, damping and frequency response affect subsequent behavior, and protection settings determine when load is disconnected. These functions require joint design; calling inertia damping obscures the mechanism of stability.

\subhead{Three Forms of Governance}

Detours, accumulation, and instability are three basic dynamics under intelligent input to viscous systems. Detours use information search to change how barriers are paid for; input beyond absorption bandwidth creates inventories, queues, waves, and cycles; overly urgent control or dense feedback can turn negative feedback into an amplifier in a system otherwise capable of slower adjustment. The forms correspond to three kinds of governance. Detours require verification: a shortcut may be a discovery, chance correlation, overfit, unmanufacturable design, or unmaintainable process; counterintuitive paths need tests of repeatability, executability, and boundary conditions. Reality must still establish the path intelligence finds. Accumulation requires rate control: expand absorption as well as generation, screen candidates by level, match experimental verification to discovery and organizational input to execution, and match policy and capital to real capacity; input beyond absorption becomes inventories, waves, and cycles. Instability requires damping: slow variables constrain fast feedback, long-term goals correct short-term metrics, safety boundaries constrain rapid control, and algorithmic loops need delay management and amplitude limits. Stable intelligence knows when to stop accelerating. \key{Viscous systems need mature dynamical control, beyond stronger intelligence alone.} Search finds detours, absorption prevents accumulation, and damping avoids feedback instability; together they allow intelligence to become stable real change.

The design of damping devices is itself contested. Theoretical work on price limits and circuit breakers shows how thresholds can move trades ahead of a halt and accelerate prices toward the limit, the magnet effect \cite{subrahmanyam1994}. Some Taiwan and Shanghai samples show price acceleration and changed trading near thresholds; other samples and identification methods produce different results \cite{cho2003magnet,wong2009pricelimits,kim2013pricelimits}. The four U.S. market-wide halts in March 2020 offer another observation: S\&P 500 declines of 7\%, 13\%, and 20\% from the prior close define three thresholds; the first two halt trading for fifteen minutes during specified hours, while the third ends trading for the day. March 9, 12, 16, and 18 each triggered Level 1, marking the return of such market-wide halts after 1997 \cite{nyse2021mwcb}. Behavioral effects and recovery can differ across market structures; parameters need testing against rules, liquidity, participant responses, and transaction data.

Mature intelligence must know whether a path is real, input excessive, or feedback too fast, as well as how to find answers. Viscous systems require detours, rate control, and damping to change. All three first require a more basic question: what exactly is the output of intelligence? A proposal’s complete form does not establish confirmation by objects, rules, execution, and reality; a seemingly compliant generation is not yet something that can be relied on.


\section{The Limits of Form: When Can an Output Be Confirmed?}

The three judgments left by the previous section point to an object we have yet to examine: what, exactly, does intelligence produce? The questions people first encounter when using large models are usually concrete. Why does a model sometimes answer like an expert and sometimes invent facts? Why can it write a plausible proof yet skip the crucial step? Why does code look perfectly conventional yet call an interface that does not exist? Why does a smooth causal explanation fail when applied to an experiment, an engineering problem, or organizational action? Will hallucinations disappear if the model gains access to search, databases, code execution, proof checkers, and external tools?

These apparently separate questions lead to a deeper one: does a large model generate forms, or forms that have already been confirmed? Paper titles, proof steps, code structures, causal explanations, experimental hypotheses, and action plans can all appear in language. A model’s ability to generate them shows that it has recovered certain stable structures from human traces; recovering a structure does not establish that it refers to a real object, obeys strict rules, passes execution checks, or can enter reality and bear consequences. Large models change more than where answers come from: they allow forms to be generated in vast quantities without simultaneous confirmation. The separation of form generation from form confirmation is the starting point for understanding large models’ capabilities, hallucinations, and limits in reality.

\subsection{The Dual Identity of Form and the Limits of Its Guarantees}

\subhead{The Dual Identity of Form}

This is also why large-model errors can be so perplexing. Their errors are often neither crude nor unstructured gibberish. They arrive in remarkably complete forms: nonexistent papers have plausible titles, authors, journals, and abstracts; false proofs have theorems, lemmas, a deductive tone, and orderly symbols; unrunnable code has good style, clear function names, and thorough comments; unverified medical advice has pathological explanations, dosage recommendations, and risk information. The model resembles someone fluent in these forms who keeps generating where confirmation is absent, rather than someone speaking in ignorance. The issue is whether objects, rules, execution, and real feedback have confirmed the forms it possesses.

Form means more than symbols, axioms, or formulas: at a deeper level, it is a transferable constraint that reduces uncertainty. How a sentence continues, a proof advances, a program calls a function, an action unfolds, or a failure is explained is not arbitrary. Whenever a structure repeatedly constrains subsequent possibilities across content, contexts, and tasks, it becomes a form that intelligence must retain. Form frees experience from individual cases, lets judgment transfer, makes reasoning checkable, and allows action to be organized in advance. Here lies the significance of formal logic: it separates the validity of reasoning from its specific content, rather than inventing reasoning. Syllogisms, propositional logic, predicate logic, and symbolic calculi make the same point: validity depends on preserving structure rather than keeping the objects unchanged. If the structure is preserved, the content can be replaced. Form is thus one of intelligence’s most powerful means of compression, retaining extensive transferability with very little redundancy. Its transferable skeleton lets humans carry judgments between objects, turn one class of problems into another, and distill experience into rules.

Historically, this approach went a long way. Euclid’s Elements organized scattered experience of measurement into axioms and deductions, making conclusions depend on the chain of reasoning rather than on the accuracy of any particular measurement. Boole expressed logical operations algebraically in 1854; Frege’s Begriffsschrift of 1879 brought structures such as “all,” “there exists,” and “if” into a symbolic calculus. By Russell and Whitehead’s three-volume Principia Mathematica, axiomatization had reached arithmetic itself. A clear conviction sustained this approach: with sufficiently explicit axioms and strict rules, proofs could be checked mechanically, making the validity of reasoning independent of who performed it. Compression reaches an extreme here: one rule can cover infinitely many instances, one structure can stand in for all the particular content, and the content compressed away need not be remembered.

In the early twentieth century, this approach became a program. The second of Hilbert’s twenty-three problems, presented at the International Congress of Mathematicians in Paris in 1900, asked whether the consistency of arithmetic could be proved. Returning to the question in Bologna in 1928, he also identified completeness and decidability as goals; the latter became known as the Entscheidungsproblem. The program sought to organize mathematics into explicit axioms and rules, establish consistent formal foundations, and find a general mechanical method for deciding whether a first-order logical formula is universally valid. This ambition pushed the transferability of form to its limit and brought the question of its guarantees into the open. If a form can guarantee only what it covers, can it guarantee itself?

\subhead{The Limits of Formal Guarantees}

Formalization makes deduction independently checkable and also establishes precise general limits. A sufficiently strong, consistent, effectively axiomatizable arithmetic theory contains undecidable sentences and, under the relevant conditions of the second incompleteness theorem, cannot prove its own formalized consistency \cite{godel1931}. The halting problem rules out a general algorithm that decides the behavior of every arbitrary program; algorithmic information theory studies description length and incompressibility \cite{turing1936,chaitin1987}. These results constrain different objects without invalidating reliable checks of particular programs and proofs.

These results reveal distinct limits on provability, decidability, and describability; they cannot be collapsed into a blanket claim that form can never justify itself. They make the conditions of a guarantee part of the problem: which axioms, which procedures, and which objects? Form remains one of intelligence’s most powerful means of compression, but information relevant to a task must be recovered elsewhere if that compression discards it. Gödel, Turing, and Chaitin addressed different boundaries within formal systems. Real systems add another: a form’s validity at one scale does not establish its validity at another.

Complex systems bring this warning back to reality. The real world is neither a completed table of propositions nor a simple machine that produces the expected output whenever an input is supplied. The same system presents different effective variables at different scales: particles, interactions, and fluctuations microscopically; temperature, pressure, flow, and phase transitions macroscopically; function, homeostasis, adaptation, and repair biologically; institutions, strategies, trust, and feedback socially. Scale is a way of compressing the world rather than an incidental label attached to it. A form valid at one scale need not transfer to another without loss. Intelligence often fails when forms overreach: a causal narrative in language is treated as an intervenable causal relationship in reality, a local regularity as system control, short-term feedback as a long-term objective, accuracy at one point as deployment reliability, or deduction within rules as action beyond them. Detached from task, medium, scale, feedback, and boundary conditions, form can turn from intelligence’s skeleton into a source of error.

Such overreach is common in engineering. A simulation accurate under training conditions fails under different conditions; risk rules that perform well on historical data misjudge unseen behavior; scheduling algorithms stable with standard cargo require human intervention for nonstandard loads. These failures need not come from errors within the rules; the rules’ domain of applicability may have been mistaken for the extent of the world. To judge where a form is valid, we need to know the data, boundary conditions, and costs of failure under which it was established—information often absent from the form itself.

Engineering has achieved formal confirmation, at a measurable cost. A lookup-table defect in the Intel Pentium’s division instruction led the company to take a charge of roughly \$475 million in 1994 for replacements, inventory write-downs, and related costs; the episode strengthened the standing of formal methods in hardware verification \cite{intel1995fdiv}. An extreme software case is the seL4 microkernel. Its initial 2009 results verified that about 7,500 lines of C conformed to an abstract specification, while boot and assembly code lay outside that proof. The proof, frameworks, tools, and libraries totaled about 200,000 lines of Isabelle script and approximately twenty person-years of proof work: nine on general infrastructure and eleven on the seL4-specific proof \cite{klein2009sel4,sel4proofstatistics2009}. The compiler counterpart is CompCert, which uses a proof assistant to verify preservation of observable program behavior under the formal semantics of its supported languages and target machines; its guarantee has a specified language scope, behavioral conditions, and trusted base \cite{leroy2009compcert}. These figures indicate the scale of formal confirmation costs: shrinking the trusted core, specifying requirements clearly, decomposing proofs, and reusing tools can make confirmation affordable. As the object expands to open environments, hardware timing disturbances, concurrent interactions, and human use, the specification itself can become difficult to establish.

\subsection{Where Compressed Forms Come From, and the Illusion of Low Loss}

\subhead{Where Compressed Forms Come From}

AI’s development can also be understood along this line. Early symbolic AI captured the expressible, composable, and checkable aspects of intelligence. Rules, predicates, expert systems, theorem proving, knowledge graphs, and symbolic planning demonstrated the indispensability of form; the limitation was heavy reliance on hand-written forms, which struggled to cover open-world common sense, context, exceptions, bodies, goals, and consequences. Real action does not unfold naturally from a static library of axioms. Symbolic systems excel at deduction within explicit boundaries but struggle to absorb the vague, ambiguous, tacit, embodied, and historically formed structures of human experience. Large models mark a turn toward learning forms from text, code, papers, laws, conversations, proofs, programs, and experimental records rather than relying chiefly on people to write them down. Language is a deposit of human experience, reasoning, institutions, failures, corrections, and recorded actions, rather than a heap of words. Logic, classification, implication, negation, recursion, causality, counterfactuals, proof templates, program structures, goal achievement, and correction recur in these deposits; reducing prediction error presses models to absorb these relational skeletons with their low redundancy, broad transferability, and strong constraints.

Variable binding, reference, function calls, proof patterns, and goal relationships in a corpus have reusable structures; learning them helps reduce prediction error. Whether training acquires them, and how reliably they can be called upon, must be tested on tasks. Energy, data distributions, objectives, and optimization play distinct roles; dissipation alone does not guarantee logical or causal ability. The physical accounting of information processing contains a definite lower bound:
\begin{equation}
E_{\min}=k_B T\ln 2
\end{equation}
Here $k_B$ is Boltzmann’s constant, $1.38\times10^{-23}\,\mathrm{J/K}$; $T$ is ambient temperature in kelvins. Under the usual assumptions of an isothermal process, symmetric memory, and a complete reset cycle, $E_{\min}$ is the lower bound, in joules, on heat released to the environment when erasing an unknown logical bit with equally probable states. At room temperature, $T\approx300\,\mathrm{K}$, the bound is $E_{\min}\approx2.9\times10^{-21}\,\mathrm{J}$. This is entropy accounting: resetting two equally probable logical states to one state reduces the memory’s logical entropy by $k_B\ln 2$, and the environment must receive the corresponding entropy. The expression bounds this reset process. Many operations in current general-purpose computers dissipate far more; devices, memory hierarchies, power delivery, and cooling determine the actual account. It reminds us that information processing has a physical substrate; known states, correlated side information, and logically reversible operations involve different conditions, so every write cannot simply be charged as this one-bit erasure.

Dissipation is a necessary condition here, but an insufficient one: dissipative systems do not all produce transferable logical structures. Several conditions work together: electricity, chips, and cooling provide real energy flux; human records provide highly structured data distributions; the loss function makes prediction deviations comparable; and optimization continually presses these differences into parameter space. Dissipation makes computation possible, the data distribution supplies compressible structure, the loss function supplies selection pressure, and optimization shapes the result. Form is selected jointly by structured data and error pressure through energy-driven optimization, rather than emerging automatically from energy.

This image is no strict physical law, but helps explain why large models develop linguistic, logical, and code structures: an untrained network resembles unformed terrain, training data prolonged rainfall, and optimization continuing erosion. The material matters, yet with enough data, training, and error pressure, the channels repeatedly selected by the water shape the landscape. Language, logic, code, and causal narratives are paths through human records that reduce resistance and error and recur stably. Models appear to understand language and logic because these structures efficiently reduce prediction error, rather than because explicit rationality has been poured into them. A modern large model is therefore neither a collection of if-else rules nor a conventional symbolic rule base. It more closely resembles a highly constraining, low-redundancy structure sustained by physical dissipation, shaped by information gradients, and carried in parameter space—figuratively, an information crystal grown jointly by electricity, data, and error gradients. This “crystal” is dynamic rather than static: training, use, and updating require continuing energy input. Its order is purchased through substantial external dissipation; its stability is maintained, rather than absolute, across the training distribution, parameter structure, inference context, and confirmation mechanisms.

\subhead{Low Loss Does Not Establish Truth}

The boundary emerges here as well. Optimization selects low-loss paths rather than truth itself; predictive training elicits formal structures rather than forms already confirmed. A recurring structure that reduces prediction error may be absorbed from a corpus, but whether it refers to a real object, follows strict rules, can execute, or can enter real action requires further confirmation. \key{Low loss does not establish truth, fluency does not establish validity, and compatibility does not establish executability.} The GPT-4 technical report offers a useful historical anchor: it demonstrated strong performance on many standardized examinations and tasks while acknowledging hallucinations, reasoning errors, and the need for care in high-stakes uses \cite{openai2023gpt4}. This juxtaposition matters: capability and limitation can coexist. A system can be remarkable at examinations, writing, reasoning, coding, and multimodal understanding without automatically turning its outputs into confirmed facts, verified proofs, runnable programs, or deployable plans. Its recovery of many forms makes it powerful; the credibility of unconfirmed forms makes it dangerous.

Hallucination thus becomes a prominent problem between form generation and confirmation. It can accompany powerful associative ability, but cannot be attributed solely to that ability. High-dimensional association connects related domains, formats, arguments, and goals into low-resistance generation paths; without constraints from objects, rules, and evidence, a path can continue into structurally compatible but unconfirmed content. A nonexistent paper can combine a real field, real terminology, authentic authorial styles, journal formats, and argumentative conventions; a false causal chain can join similar scenarios, familiar explanations, local correlations, and narrative sequence; a false proof can retain the tone, steps, and symbolic appearance of proof while losing the constraints of its rules at the decisive turn. The problem here is form generation outrunning reference checks, rule checking, and real feedback. There are internal routes to reducing hallucinations: improving training data and objectives, calibrating confidence, allowing abstention, and changing inference. Research in 2026 further showed how accuracy-centered evaluations reward guessing under uncertainty, while interventions in some models’ internal mechanisms for answering or abstaining can improve decisions \cite{kalai2026incentives,nguyen2026commitabstain}. These results support neither the claim that fewer hallucinations necessarily mean less creativity nor the disappearance of errors on arbitrary tasks. The key is to coordinate generation, evidence, rules, and conditions for abstention. Reviews generally describe hallucinations as fluent, coherent outputs that are factually false or unsupported by evidence, tracing their causes through data, training objectives, model architecture, inference, and evaluation \cite{huang2023hallucination}. “The model is not large enough” cannot explain the whole problem, and “connect it to search” cannot handle it alone: large models generate candidates quickly, while their reliability requires confirmation appropriate to the task.

\subsection{Where Confirmation Happens, and What It Costs}

\subhead{Three Sites of Confirmation}

Proof provides a second important case. A mathematical proof is more than the tone of proof, connectives such as “clearly,” “hence,” or “it is easy to show,” or the appearance of theorems, lemmas, and corollaries: every transformation must be permitted by the rules, and the entire chain must be checkable. AlphaGeometry illustrates this distinction. It solved twenty-five of thirty recent International Mathematical Olympiad geometry problems, approaching human gold-medalist performance \cite{trinh2024alphageometry}. More significantly, it combined neural generation with symbolic deduction rather than relying on a language model to produce proof-like text: the neural component proposed useful constructions, and the symbolic engine performed deductions and checks. Form generation matters enormously, but a reliable proof needs rule-based confirmation: a model can suggest a direction, while the rules must make the proof hold. Code provides a third case. Large models’ coding ability is already changing software production, yet code also makes the need for confirmation especially clear: looking like code, running, passing tests, solving a real issue, and operating reliably with its dependencies are distinct levels. SWE-bench Verified comprises 500 human-filtered real GitHub issues used to assess whether models or agents can solve problems in actual repositories \cite{swebench2024}. Its value goes beyond another leaderboard: it brings code from text generation back to confirmation through execution. The repository, dependencies, tests, issue description, patch, environment, and regression checks form a chain of confirmation; without that chain, code remains a formally complete candidate.

These three cases point to the same structure. Citations need confirmation of their referents, proofs of their rule-governed validity, and code of its execution. Large models may be extraordinarily fluent in all three appearances, but appearances provide no confirmation: a citation requires retrieval and source tracing, a proof step-by-step checking, and usable code execution, testing, and adaptation to its environment. Form generation can take place within a model; confirmation requires independent constraints from evidence about objects, rule systems, and execution results. Form is confirmed in at least three places. First, representational confirmation: does the form refer to a stable object? Papers, authors, concepts, interfaces, facts, and relationships must be retrievable, traceable, and open to cross-checking, beyond looking true. Second, inferential confirmation: can the form be transformed reliably under the rules? Proofs must be checkable, code executable, calculations reproducible, and causal chains able to withstand counterfactual constraints. Third, confirmation through action: can the form change a real state and bear the resulting feedback? A plan needs more than linguistic completeness: it must pass through interfaces, permissions, resources, time, failure recovery, and boundaries of responsibility. The same structure can pass through all three places: causality can be recognized as a textual schema, computed as an inferential structure, and tested through real intervention. Validity in language does not establish validity in inference; validity in inference does not establish feasibility in reality; feasibility still faces resources, time, structure, and responsibility. Form gains reliability through different tests at different places, rather than acquiring it all at once. Pearl’s formalization of causality makes precisely this point: causality requires intervention and counterfactual structures that let a dependence face the question “What would happen if the conditions changed?”, beyond making a correlation sound more persuasive \cite{pearl2009causality}. These three places occupy the middle of Chapter 1’s verification pyramid, which rises through formal, semantic, causal, engineering, long-term biological, and social-responsibility verification. Representational confirmation concerns meaning and evidence about objects; inferential confirmation concerns formal rules and causal assumptions; confirmation through action enters engineering execution and connects to long-term verification and social responsibility. The classifications overlap rather than corresponding one to one. Large models drive candidate-generation costs extremely low, releasing text, code, explanations, hypotheses, and plans rapidly. Dependable results require an ascent through confirmation of objects, rules, and action, then of integration into systems and the ability to withstand disturbances, exceptions, audits, and responsibility over sustained operation.

\subhead{The Costs and Limits of Confirmation}

Training dissipates energy to compress forms; verification dissipates energy to make them trustworthy. Generation can be amortized in advance in parameter space, while confirmation must be paid for at each level of objects, rules, action, systems, and responsibility. Generation takes place at the pyramid’s base; reliability is acquired step by step during the ascent. Confirmation costs can therefore grow nonlinearly: they may be low for low-risk, weakly coupled, reversible tasks, but rise rapidly in medicine, finance, law, engineering, public policy, and biotechnology. Higher up, confirmation approaches reality—and resources, time, organization, responsibility, and the bearing of consequences. This difference can be expressed in terms of pass rates:
\begin{equation}
N_{\text{cand}}=\frac{M_{\text{use}}}{\prod_{i=1}^{k}p_i}
\end{equation}
$k$ is the number of confirmation stages, and $p_i$ is the conditional probability of passing stage $i$ after passing all earlier stages; multiplying these probabilities requires no independence assumption. Under stable, comparable repeated attempts, $M_{\mathrm{use}}/\prod_i p_i$ gives an expectation or planning approximation, without guaranteeing success in any particular batch. An additional independence assumption is needed if unconditional pass rates are used instead; correlation has no uniform direction of effect on the estimate. Model improvements may also raise pass rates, improve trials, and reduce rework.

Retrieval, databases, execution engines, proof checkers, test environments, APIs, sensors, and feedback loops belong here: they are different interfaces for confirming forms rather than a catalog of technologies for this section. Retrieval confirms objects, execution rules, tests boundaries, tools interfaces, and feedback the consequences of action. They can reduce hallucinations without automatically guaranteeing zero error, because confirmation paths can themselves fail: sources may be unreliable, tests incomplete, interfaces misused, feedback delayed, and responsibility impossible to assign. As some generation errors are eliminated, reliability questions also extend to the confirmation loop composed of model, tools, and environment. RAG, tool calling, code interpreters, and agent frameworks are consequently no “eliminate hallucinations” button. They extend the confirmation chain and introduce further objects requiring confirmation: are retrieved results real, databases current, tool calls correct, execution environments representative, proof checkers given a correctly formalized problem, and sensor feedback correctly interpreted? When a model begins calling the outside world, errors can involve retrieval, interfaces, execution, coverage, permissions, and responsibility as well as generation; confirmation migrates rather than disappearing. This yields a testable boundary claim: assertions of general reasoning or real-world action capability must face three tests. Without external confirmation interfaces, can the system consistently avoid representational hallucinations? Can it keep its deductions within the rules? Can it complete real actions with feedback, rollback, and accountability? These tests distinguish the ability to generate candidates, the ability to check them internally, and the degree to which task results have actually been confirmed. Increasing model size does not automatically remove this boundary; tools, environments, and feedback redistribute it across a larger confirmation loop.

This also explains the distance between large models and world models. Large models learn forms from traces; world models must also calibrate those forms against real responses. A causal account can be sustained narratively in language but needs intervention-based testing in reality; a goal can be expressed in a sentence but must pass through resources, time, structure, and responsibility in reality. A form effective for prediction is not a sufficient representation of a world we can intervene in; it must be confirmed through the consequences of action. At the level of action, form confirmation meets technological viscosity. Confirmation has a cost: facts require retrieval, databases, and source tracing; inference requires execution, testing, and coverage; action requires sensors, interfaces, permissions, trials, monitoring, and rollback; systems require redesigned workflows, safety redundancy, audit logs, assigned responsibility, and social absorption; long-term confirmation requires time, exceptions, distorted incentives, and consequences across generations. Higher levels of the verification pyramid encounter viscosity in resources, time, structure, verification, and responsibility. Large models make candidate generation extremely cheap without canceling the real accounts due when candidates become dependable results. The same large-model application proceeds at vastly different speeds across media. In bit space, text, code, retrieval, summaries, and preliminary analysis can iterate rapidly; errors can sometimes be retracted cheaply and candidates rewritten at low cost. In atomic space, action requires materials, energy, sensors, interfaces, operating conditions, tests, and maintenance, while errors may cause damage, downtime, or safety incidents. In biological space, confirmation is more expensive still: drugs, gene editing, development, immune responses, ecological effects, and consequences across generations cannot be undone repeatedly like text. As form reaches deeper into reality, confirmation grows heavier and viscosity becomes more visible.

The large-model revolution changes how forms are produced. It moves forms from hand-written rules into high-dimensional representations, from explicit inscription into statistical learning, and from a few axioms into vast collections of traces, without abolishing their limits. Predictive training can elicit structure, gradient erosion can shape low-loss channels, and external tools can add confirmation paths; none automatically confers reliability in reference, rules, action, and responsibility. Once forms enter tools, environments, and feedback, their boundaries are redistributed within the system’s loop. Intelligence therefore includes knowing what confirms a form, at which scale it holds, and when it needs replacement, beyond generating it. Large models compress the forms in which logic, programs, causality, and action appear in human traces, rather than logic itself. Their boundary is that high-dimensional associations formed through prediction have not automatically acquired reliability under representational, inferential, action, system, and long-term tests. Form makes intelligence possible; testing brings form into reality. Testing first needs a place where it can occur: a channel must already exist between model and object through which consequences can pass.


\section{World Models and Intervention-Ready Compression}

Where forms can be tested and where actions obtain correction signals are two questions that lead to a much-discussed but rarely precisely defined object: the world model. To understand the term, we first need to sidestep a more familiar dispute. One of the easiest arguments to fall into about AI is whether it has “real intelligence.” If real intelligence means autonomous consciousness, self-generated purposes, subjective experience, and humanlike understanding, the question quickly enters philosophy and science fiction. We have no definite answer today about whether, when, or in what form such AGI will emerge. Engineering does not wait for ultimate definitions. Aircraft flew without humans first understanding avian consciousness, and computers calculated without first possessing a mathematician’s mind. Technological paths usually start with useful capabilities and expand through tasks, tools, and feedback, rather than working backward from an endpoint. From this perspective, a large model begins as a powerful imitation-and-compression system, rather than a completed general mind: it learns patterns from vast amounts of text, images, code, and interaction data, statistically compressing language, knowledge, style, program structures, and task relationships. Its capabilities emerge through similarity matching, structural completion, and probabilistic generation across a vast space of experience rather than strict deduction in the traditional sense. Calling it an increasingly articulate parrot is not entirely wrong, but can obscure the crucial point: deep enough imitation, broad enough coverage, and connections to tools, memory, feedback, and task environments can turn imitation beyond mechanical repetition into useful approximate intelligence. Imitation can be the beginning of intelligence in a feedback loop, even if it is not its endpoint.

\subsection{From Imitation to Useful Approximation: Where World Models Come From}

\subhead{From Imitation to Useful Approximation}

AI’s history is a series of experiments in how intelligence gains a world. Early symbolic AI tried to construct intelligence through formal logic and rule systems: write the world as propositions, rules, and inference chains, and intelligence could unfold like a mathematical proof. This inherited an older drive toward formalization: the world could be encoded, reasoning made rule-governed, and intelligence reduced to symbol manipulation. The underlying assumption was that sufficient description would let intelligence acquire the world through rules. Open reality is not a closed system with all its axioms already written. More rules create more combinations; more open-ended goals make contexts harder to exhaust; closer contact with reality makes exceptions, noise, bodies, history, and consequences harder to enumerate completely. Reality is an ongoing process changed by action, rather than a static table of propositions. Intelligence entering it must submit its judgments to environmental tests rather than relying only on internally closed rules. Modern neural networks take another route: they learn structure from data distributions rather than starting with explicit rules, obtaining usable patterns through fitting, compression, and generalization rather than first stating the world’s logical axioms. CNNs, Transformers, and other deep networks are not deductive machines in the traditional sense. They excel at learning resemblance, likely continuations, and recurring structures from many examples. This imperfect, hallucination-prone route lacks strict provability, but bypasses the difficulty of explicitly enumerating the world in a purely symbolic system: capabilities can appear before the world has been fully written into rules.

Vast resources were once committed to that symbolic route. Japan launched its Fifth Generation Computer Project in 1982, organized through the Institute for New Generation Computer Technology around predicate logic and parallel inference. The Information Processing Society of Japan records approximately ¥54 billion in spending over the eleven fiscal years from 1982 through 1992. The project built five parallel inference machines, including the 512-processor PIM/p and 256-processor PIM/m, but did not achieve the anticipated broad commercial adoption. Meanwhile, improvements in general-purpose computers reduced the value available to dedicated inference machines \cite{aiso1988fifth,feigenbaum1993japanese,ipsjfgcs}. The lesson concerns competition among explicit knowledge acquisition, software ecosystems, specialized architecture costs, and advances in general-purpose hardware, rather than the incapacity of rule systems. Writing the world into rules alone cannot ensure a computing approach’s success.

The central value of the large-model approach is that it offers a practically scalable approximation to intelligence, regardless of whether ultimate understanding has been solved. It can imitate before combining, complete before planning, and generate before being corrected by external feedback. Value can precede a complete world model; many intelligent capabilities stabilize through repeated coupling with external environments rather than forming all at once within a closed interior.

\subhead{Where World Models Come From}

Here we encounter the question of world models. A common claim is that AI must first possess a world model to acquire real intelligence. The claim has force: without some internal structure of the world, a system cannot predict consequences, plan actions, distinguish appearances from regularities, or transfer experience across situations. With no world structure at all, it can only react locally between inputs and outputs and struggles to sustain stable action. But the claim immediately raises a question: where does the world model come from? If it comes from experience, that experience may come from the system’s own perception, actions, and feedback or from others’ records of observation and intervention. If feedback must correct it, the system must submit its judgments to environmental tests; if it supports action, action cannot wait for complete model maturity. The system must act with an incomplete model and use action to improve it; it cannot first stand outside the world, model it completely, then return to perform tasks. This is the world model’s circular dependence: models guide action, while action and its records provide sources and corrections for models. Models supporting action need calibration against the world’s responses, and action needs models for guidance. They shape one another within the same loop rather than following a simple sequence. The loop also has an irreducible direction in time: models compress past experience, data, and failures, while actions bet on future consequences that have yet to appear. Weakly coupled tasks stabilize more easily because the future can largely be extrapolated from the past; strong feedback-loop tasks are harder because action changes subsequent conditions; highly coupled reflexive tasks are harder still because objects reorganize in response to models, predictions, and interventions, making the future more than an extension of the past.

A deeper misunderstanding is hidden here. “World model” easily suggests that intelligence should hold an internal map: a world outside, a model inside, the world as object, and the model as representation—as though intelligence must first acquire a fairly complete map before acting with it. An actor embedded in the world has no such outside perspective. It cannot first take a complete photograph from outside and return to execute its plan; it is inside from the beginning. Bodily position, task goals, tool interfaces, experience, and action capabilities already shape its perception. It sees a world related to its possible actions rather than a pure world. A world model is therefore a compression of action consequences rather than a photograph of the world. Intelligence may need less a complete internal picture than a structure of expectations about what will happen if it acts: which paths are more likely to succeed, which actions bring danger, which errors can be corrected, and which failures cannot be rolled back. A model reduces expensive mistakes before action, absorbs feedback afterward, and helps avoid one more collision next time, rather than moving the world inside. Large models’ success offers a clue: without physical bodies or direct contact with reality, they perform many useful tasks by compressing human symbolic experience. Intelligence can often begin with local patterns, task structures, symbolic compression, and feedback correction; a complete world model may be a deposit left by sustained intelligent action rather than its prerequisite. The better question is therefore how strongly a system’s model must couple to action for a particular task, rather than whether AI already possesses a world model.

\subhead{Digital Agents and Embodied Intelligence}

AI agents express this logic in digital environments. A large model on its own has an evident boundary: it can generate text and plans, but without calling tools, observing results, and revising plans, its ability remains at the level of one-off output. Agent systems connect models to files, browsers, code environments, databases, software interfaces, and task-management workflows so they can decompose goals, execute steps, observe feedback, and adjust strategies. The model enters a task loop—plan, act, observe, revise, act again—beyond answering questions. This changes the structure of capability without immediately establishing autonomous intelligence. Many problems once demanding a correct single inference become problems of repeated trials and feedback control; a model can approach correctness through environmental feedback. Its effective intelligence is distributed across tools, interfaces, memory, logs, tests, and external feedback as well as its parameters. Tools belong to the intelligent loop itself. This gives the other half of the answer about where world models come from: part of the model grows in toolchains, logs, and failure records rather than parameters. While those external structures remain, the model need not fit the entire world inside itself.

Embodied intelligence faces the same kind of problem in a heavier medium. Large models currently learn mainly from text, images, code, and human knowledge: a world expressed by humans through secondhand, compressed, and symbolic experience. This is already powerful because so much civilizational knowledge resides in symbols, but it still lacks much firsthand feedback: touch, force, spatial continuity, physical contact, long-term causality, and consequences of action. Embodied intelligence reconnects AI to the real physical world, giving the system consequences of acting in the world alongside descriptions of it. Descriptions can unfold fluently in symbolic space; consequences appear in the world. A model can write about a cup or recognize its image, but lifting it confronts weight, friction, center of mass, contact angle, slipping, collision, and feedback delay. A model can recommend treatment, but drugs entering a body encounter absorption, metabolism, immunity, toxicity, individual differences, and long-term side effects. A model can design a traffic plan, but implementation encounters roads, property rights, regulation, habits, accident liability, and behavioral responses. A model unable to pass through this feedback remains language about the world rather than a capability to enter it. All three cases require feedback, but of different kinds: the cup involves residual physical state changes after contact, drugs involve metabolism, compensation, and individual differences, and traffic involves institutions, responsibility, and behavioral responses. Together they resist entry into the world without reducing to one kind of coupling. Internal symbolic consistency is consequently powerful and dangerous: a large model can construct complete arguments and strong consistency across styles, analogies, and concepts, yet without external correction it may mistake linguistic smoothness for real effectiveness. It can expand possibilities without knowing which can pass through real resistance, and generate answers without knowing what their entry into the world will change.

\subsection{Three Degrees of Coupling, Residuals, and Reflexivity}

\subhead{Three Degrees of Coupling}

Coupling can be divided into three working situations. With low coupling, candidates can be checked before outputs change external states; in a strong physical feedback loop, each action changes the object encountered next; in a reflexive loop, other actors also interpret the model and adjust strategies. These situations can coexist within one system. Social systems may form stable equilibria or keep drifting; reflexivity alone does not establish the absence of a fixed point.

Differences in timescale across the three kinds of coupling can be measured. Franka’s real-time interface exchanges states and control commands at 1 kHz, updating every millisecond. Update rate is not physical closed-loop bandwidth: the latter is also constrained by transmission flexibility, sensor and actuator placement, workpiece stiffness, and delays; excessive gain can excite unmodeled vibration \cite{frankafci2026,eppinger1987}. Large-model response latency varies with the model, hardware, output length, reasoning, and tool calls: fast interactions may begin producing output within hundreds of milliseconds, while a complete decision may take seconds or longer. Contact tasks therefore cannot simply connect large-model outputs directly to servo loops. Semantic judgments can be slow; force and position loops must be fast. Hierarchical control and timescale conversion must bridge them, or residual errors will continue accumulating between high-level decisions.

\subhead{Residuals and Reflexivity}

The circular dependence of world models is a basic condition of intelligence embedded in the world, rather than a defect of immaturity. Models and actions do not simply follow one another: models form through action, actions find direction through models, and intelligence gradually acquires a world relevant to itself by acting within it. Whether this loop can bootstrap depends on whether its update operator drives deviations back down:
\begin{equation}
\begin{split}a_t&=\pi(m_t),\quad m_{t+1}=U(m_t,a_t)=F(m_t),\\ DF(m)&=\frac{\partial U}{\partial m}+\frac{\partial U}{\partial a}D\pi(m).\end{split}
\end{equation}
$m_t$ is the model state and $a_t$ the action. Stability requires examining the composite map $F$; the second term retains the path by which the model changes the action and the action changes the update. If $F$ maps a complete invariant domain into itself and is uniformly contractive there, iteration converges to a unique fixed point in that domain. A derivative at one point or a local linearization offers only a local assessment; environmental change, noise, and delay can alter the result. SLAM demonstrates a feasible route to building a model while moving, though convergence depends on observability, sensing, and motion conditions.

Embodied intelligence’s real difficulty runs deeper than mapping. SLAM generally assumes a largely stable map: the world does not actively change itself because it is measured. This shows how a world model can bootstrap around stable objects, but does not capture action’s full weight. Cups, floors, and bodies do not actively change because they are modeled either. Their difficulty is that contact leaves consequences: touching a cup changes its position, orientation, frictional state, and subsequent graspability; an unstable step changes posture and ground contact; an excessively tight grip may deform or break an object. The problem is action rewriting the next step’s initial conditions, rather than an object understanding the model. This is the difficulty of medium coupling: the world is not actively reflexive, but action leaves residuals. An object has not evaded the model, yet no longer occupies its earlier state. The typical challenge for embodied intelligence is consequently strong physical coupling in a feedback loop, before highly reflexive coupling. Cups do not anticipate robots, floors do not understand algorithms, and door handles do not adapt strategies around models; contact changes their states and carries those changes into the next action. Reflexive high coupling arises when tasks include people, organizations, road users, or other actors that interpret and respond to models. Ordinary physical objects are rewritten by action even without responding to the model itself, and this already creates embodied intelligence’s central difficulty. The system must keep acting in a world continually rewritten by its own actions.

The physical world does not automatically return to its starting point after each step. Text can be rewritten, code rolled back, and images regenerated, but physical actions leave consequences: a small recognition error changes the grasping posture, a contact error changes an object’s position, and a control delay amplifies the next planning error. Residuals travel along the task chain rather than clearing automatically between actions. Embodied intelligence must manage consequences so that action remains possible afterward, beyond describing a static world completely. A useful world model therefore cannot be an isolated module whose construction brings intelligence automatically. It manages consequences as well as describing objects, drawing on observation and action, prediction and correction after failed prediction, compressing past experience while tracking changes it has caused. It is an actionable compression built by an actor’s continuing interventions, rather than a complete atlas drawn by an external observer.

\subhead{Steps in Coupling and the Management of Consequences}

Technological viscosity reveals changes in the type of model–action coupling, beyond a simple increase in model weight. The bit domain permits cheap generation and rollback, so models can remain relatively light. Atomic actions leave residuals that do not clear automatically, requiring feedback. Living systems change intervention outcomes through metabolism, compensation, adaptation, and individual differences. Social systems interpret, respond to, exploit, and even resist interventions, making the model part of the dynamics. A step separates medium from high coupling, beyond a continuous dial of increasing strength: one concerns objects rewritten by action, the other objects that respond to the model. Their central difficulties are rolling residuals and reflexive drift, respectively. The heavier the world, the less a model can remain merely descriptive; the more objects respond to the model, the less it can pretend to stand outside the world. The crucial question is how and in which medium a model couples to action. Low coupling lets models flow like language; strong physical feedback loops require online correction during action and tracking of its residuals; highly coupled reflexive tasks make models part of the world’s dynamics. A world model is a family of structures anticipating action, varying with task, medium, consequence intensity, and object reflexivity, rather than one uniform thing.

This also gives circular dependence a new meaning. Circular dependence is normal for intelligence embedded in the world, rather than a defect to eliminate completely. A model is more than a pure image preceding action, and action more than mechanical execution following a model: action validates and invalidates models, while models guide actions that change the world they must face. Intelligence learns to remain correctable, recoverable, and able to continue acting within the loop. Embodied intelligence therefore needs continuing correction of consequences more than an ultimate map: it can act without possessing a complete world, but must know how its action changes the world encountered next; it need not contain all reality internally, but must maintain stable relations between action and feedback for relevant tasks. Failure occurs when the world after action moves beyond what the system can continue handling, rather than simply because the model lacks omniscience. This judgment has limits: if task outputs scarcely change subsequent objects, errors are cheap to roll back, and feedback can be filtered externally, a world model may remain weaker, looser, and more symbolic. As action increasingly rewrites subsequent states, residuals roll along task chains, and recovery becomes harder, stronger model–action coupling is needed. The world model then becomes an online compression of action consequences rather than a static internal representation.

From this perspective, AGI may be better understood as something other than a complete subject arriving suddenly. A more plausible route gradually assembles capabilities within feedback loops: language models provide symbolic compression, agents task execution, tool environments external memory and computation, embodied systems physical feedback, long-term interaction causal data, and verification mechanisms corrective constraints. Larger actionable structures form across multiple loops rather than erupting from one point. This less romantic route is more realistic: it requires neither complete consciousness at the outset nor prior mastery of the world’s ontology, but the ability to act with limited models, obtain feedback, correct models, and expand the range of action afterward. Whether large models resemble parrots matters less than whether the “parrot” connects to tools, memory, feedback, a body, and real tasks. Repeating language in a cage is mainly imitation; gaining feedback through action, revising plans, and turning failure into subsequent adjustment begins intelligence’s bootstrapping. Managing the changes it causes and tracking objects rewritten by its own actions reaches the core of embodied intelligence. The fundamental difficulty exceeds the world’s size or the model’s weakness: “world model” can make us forget that intelligence can possess a world only from within it, obtaining consequences through action, correcting itself through those consequences, and acting again afterward. Intelligence acquires its world through action, and the world it acquires has already been changed by its own actions.

\subsection{Intervention-Ready Compression: Causality and Scale}

Saying that models must learn from the world’s responses is simple; implementing it requires answering an earlier question: what kind of compression captures those responses? Compression here is a basic way finite intelligence handles the world, beyond a data-processing technique; it determines how broadly a model remains useful. A more specific question follows: how far can compression go while capturing the world’s responses rather than merely remembering its traces? Large models sharpen an old question: if intelligence is compression and the real world itself is full of probabilities, can probabilistic models represent it? There is no simple yes or no. Probability is not the obstacle: quantum measurement, thermal noise, chaotic systems, and limited observation show that descriptions at many scales must be probabilistic. The issue is whether reality constrains those probabilities, and whether the model can predict the world’s response after action, beyond generating plausible continuations. \key{Large models mainly learn the traces the world leaves; the threshold for world models is learning how the world responds to intervention.} Traces can be copied, replayed, sliced, annotated, and trained on repeatedly; newly measured responses require contact with the world, bringing cost, delay, noise, risk, and irreversibility, while existing response records can be reused. Text, images, video, and code are traces from experience, observation, institutions, narratives, experiments, and operations. They are not the world itself: recovering many structures from them does not automatically confer the ability to change real systems.

\subhead{Intervention-Ready Compression}

Compression is a basic way finite intelligence handles the world, beyond a technique used by large models. Reality’s state space cannot be copied completely, and finite intelligence keeps no high-resolution duplicate. It dynamically selects variables to retain, ignore, or observe again according to task, error, and risk requirements. Particles, materials, boundaries, historical paths, noise, others’ actions, and structural coupling coexist, yet any action occupies a tiny slice. Intelligence selects a few action-relevant state variables in an uncopiable world; without this selection, perception, concepts, causality, planning, and action would be impossible. \term{intervention-ready compression} means coarse-graining the world’s responses when its entire state space cannot be copied: discarding details that do not dominate transitions at the present scale and retaining variables effective across interventions, boundary changes, and counterfactual comparisons. Coarse-graining selects effective variables for action rather than simplifying arbitrarily. It discards details that do not affect the current task’s results and retains structures that change transitions; a world model is thus an action model valid at a specific scale, for a specific task and boundary conditions, rather than a copy of the world.

Causal inference already offers an explicit framework distinguishing observation, intervention, and counterfactuals \cite{pearl2009causality}. Records can contain experimental and mechanistic knowledge, and models may learn causal structures from them; accurate prediction of records does not automatically establish an intervention’s reliability in reality. Intervention-ready compression requires making that reliability concrete for specified tasks, scales, and feedback.

\subhead{Causality and Scale}

Causality enters here. A world model needs structures that change state transitions under intervention, rather than every co-variation: correlation indicates what often appears together, while causality indicates which changes alter outcomes. A drug need not work in every patient to change the distribution of benefits and side effects; a control signal need not reproduce a robot’s trajectory exactly to change the direction of transitions. Causality need not be a deterministic chain; it is a minimal structure that acting systems must retain when compressing the world’s responses. Causality also requires counterfactuals and scale selection. Actors must compare acting, refraining, choosing B over A, acting later, or acting differently; planning, correction, and judgments of responsibility require these comparisons. Causal variables differ across molecular, mechanical, task, and organizational scales. The difficulty is identifying variables that change state transitions at the current scale rather than treating every correlated clue as a cause.

A local first-order sensitivity condition can provide an initial screen for which variables to retain or discard:
\begin{equation}
\left|\frac{\partial f}{\partial x_i}\right|\sigma_i>\theta
\end{equation}
$f$ is a selected output component of the state transition, $x_i$ a candidate state variable, and $\sigma_i$ its typical fluctuation amplitude within the current task and time window. The local sensitivity $\partial f/\partial x_i$ multiplied by that amplitude approximates the output change caused by one variable’s fluctuation, with the same units as the tolerance $\theta$; division by $\theta$ makes the comparison dimensionless. Variables exceeding the tolerance deserve priority for retention; those below it cannot simply be discarded, because nonlinear interactions, correlated fluctuations, accumulation of small terms, and rare tail risks can change the conclusion. The condition is a screening clue: it neither identifies causality nor proves a granularity minimally sufficient. Usable granularity still depends on task, timescale, risk level, and coupling scope. Too coarse a scale misses variables that change outcomes; too fine a scale drowns action in irrelevant detail. Developing these conditions into testable quantitative criteria remains an open problem, informed by modeling, exploration, failure, and revision.

Causal structures need not always appear in clear, stable, low-dimensional forms. With strong noise, strong chaos, or irreducible randomness, small disturbances may amplify rapidly and individual outcomes resist precise prediction. Variables governing transitions may not compress into simple relationships; models then retain probabilistic constraints, robust boundaries, and risk distributions rather than deterministic chains. Intervention-ready compression assumes no universally masterable causal structure. At a given task and scale, it seeks to retain structures that can still change outcome distributions, constrain transitions, or bound failure risk. Probability is compatible with causality; in many real systems, causal structure can be retained only probabilistically. A good world model therefore knows which things cannot be ignored at the current scale, rather than simply knowing the most. For grasping a cup, molecular detail can usually be discarded, while friction and center of mass cannot; for material fatigue, microcracks matter; for congestion, individual neural activity can be omitted, while aggregate flow and response delays must remain. Patterns and constraints should not be opposed simplistically. Constraints are stable structures that continue limiting transitions under changing contexts, scales, and interventions. Frequent patterns indicate what usually happens; constraints indicate the bounds of validity, what cannot hold, and how failure follows a boundary crossing. A model that learns frequent surface patterns without structures constraining transitions can generate plausible scenes without reliably guiding real action.

\subhead{Frontier Approaches and a Shared Threshold}

Video models, interactive models, vision–language–action systems, simulation training, and online feedback all connect records with responses to action. Google DeepMind’s Gemini Robotics 2 work in July 2026 further combined whole-body action with high-level capabilities \cite{geminirobotics2026}. The common interfaces requiring examination are task, hardware, feedback, recovery, and evidence of generalization.

The same underlying problem appears: records can be copied; responses must be paid for. Text, images, video, and demonstration trajectories can be replayed at scale, while real responses to action bring cost, delay, noise, risk, and irreversibility. Simulation reduces trial costs without eliminating the gap between simulation and reality \cite{tobin2017domain}. Rewards can drive policy optimization without guaranteeing coverage of long-term risks; online interaction can reveal errors, but in atomic, biological, and social systems many errors are themselves costs. The threshold for world models is their ability to turn limited, expensive, risky responses into generalizable, verifiable judgments of action whose consequences can be borne, beyond coherent appearances, interactive environments, or complete action interfaces.

Reversibility also constrains compression. Risk is lower when discarded variables can be observed again, higher when restoring them requires expensive trials; variables cannot be discarded lightly when action leaves a state that cannot be restored. Errors in bit space can often be undone, while those in atomic, biological, and social systems may leave irreversible consequences. Intervention-ready compression chooses how much to discard according to error recoverability, verification cost, and irreversible consequences, rather than discarding as much as possible. Together these conditions set different thresholds for the same criterion across media: omitting contact details in simulated grasping incurs almost no direct physical damage, while doing so on a real production line may damage workpieces or injure people.

\subhead{Viscosity and the World’s Responses}

This is where technological viscosity appears. The world’s responses are feedback filtered through resources, time, and structure, rather than free information. Resource constraints determine the energy, materials, space, compute, equipment, maintenance, and redundancy costs of obtaining one real response; time constraints determine when it appears and whether waiting, aging, training, feedback, or recovery cycles resist compression; structural constraints determine how a local action passes through a coupled network to be amplified, canceled, routed back, or locked in. Technological viscosity is the cost structure of the world’s responses themselves, rather than resistance outside the world model. A useful world model judges transitions under resource, time, and structural constraints, beyond generating the world’s appearance.

High coupling and multi-agent systems deepen the problem. Other actors adjust expectations, strategies, and constraints in response to the model’s actions. The model must calibrate a response distribution changed by its own intervention rather than transitions in a fixed environment. Entering the system makes the model part of it: its predictions change the world’s responses to it. This is reflexive drift, discussed above, appearing in world modeling. Intervention-ready compression is especially vulnerable when its object responds, learns, and changes the model’s inputs in return rather than remaining a static environment.

Verification checks whether compression retains the structure action needs, rather than serving as an external patch: the coarse-graining discussed here discards information, and the question is whether that information becomes important again during action. Failure can reveal this boundary: failed grasping may point to omitted contact, friction, posture, or sensor variables; driving errors to rare scenes, occlusion, judgments of intent, or feedback delays; drug failure or toxicity to omitted metabolic paths, dose relationships, or long-term effects. Failures can also realize known risks or result from actuator faults or stochastic outcomes; omitted variables cannot be inferred from every failure. Compression selects what to discard; verification checks when those choices make action pay a price.

This is also why world models need feedback loops. A fixed corpus can record how the world responded to interventions; an action loop lets the system keep testing those relationships under current objects, policies, and conditions. Every action exposes the model’s internal compression to external reality; new feedback can test and revise its selection of state variables. Learning a world means gradually finding structures sufficient for action through intervention, failure, correction, and recompression, rather than acquiring a complete picture at once. A world model is a transition model continually calibrated by the world’s responses rather than a static knowledge base. Intervention-ready compression can therefore be defined as coarse-graining the world’s responses to interventions into variables, relationships, and structures that still support stable judgments of transitions, constraint boundaries, counterfactual consequences, and failure modes, when intelligence can neither copy the entire state space nor try actions without limit. This definition describes the conditions world models must meet when entering real systems rather than replacing the concept: they must retain sufficiently reliable action structures from limited, expensive, risky responses. Probability uncalibrated by the world’s responses undermines fidelity to reality; compression unable to withstand intervention tests undermines action. Probability and compression themselves are not the obstacles.

\subhead{Judging Actions from Limited Responses}

Large models have demonstrated something important: the traces left by the world can be learned to an astonishing extent. World models face a harder demonstration: can they learn a defensible criterion for action from limited, expensive, risky responses? The former occurs in continuations of symbols, images, and video; the latter in intervention, cost, failure, and correction. The leap is from learning the world’s traces to learning its responses to action, rather than from probabilistic to nonprobabilistic models. Records can teach how the world is described and how it has been changed; new responses to action continue testing when that knowledge still holds. Intelligence entering reality must learn how the world can be changed as well as how it is described.
