The cost of obtaining a response can be estimated from the accounts of pharmaceutical research and development. In 2016, using a sample of 106 new drugs from ten pharmaceutical companies, DiMasi, Grabowski, and Hansen estimated that out-of-pocket R\&D expenditure averaged about US\$1.395 billion per approved new drug in 2013 dollars; capitalized to the date of approval at a real discount rate of 10.5 percent, the total was about US\$2.558 billion, also in 2013 dollars \cite{dimasi2016}. Typically, around 10 percent of compounds entering clinical trials ultimately receive approval, with a still lower proportion for drugs targeting the central nervous system. These figures describe the same reality: a record can be copied indefinitely, but each real response must be paid for, project by project, year by year, with failures factored in, and payment does not necessarily buy a usable conclusion.

Once the problem reaches this point, models alone are no longer the subject. Responses require bodies to contact the world, and residuals require bodies to absorb them. Compression criteria determine which variables a model retains; bodies determine what corrects them during contact, with what delay, and whether recovery remains possible after failure. A criterion calculable within a model must be borne through materials, structures, and reflexes in physical contact: this is the problem addressed by the tradition of morphological computation. Bodies are only one layer of these supporting structures. On much longer timescales, another layer performs a similar role: generations replace sensors and reflexes in recording which variables cannot be discarded, while reproductive failure tests which compressions were wrong. Its verification cycles are measured in generations, its errors cannot be rolled back, and variables once encoded impose continuing costs on subsequent actions. Judging how far intelligence can go in physical media first requires understanding how this older mechanism of compression works.

\chapter{Life, Bodies, and Movement: The Divergence of Intelligence}

Chapter 3 ended by pointing to an older mechanism of compression: generations replace sensors and reflexes in recording which variables cannot be discarded, while reproductive failure tests which compressions were wrong. Its medium responds in fundamentally different ways from mobility systems. Act on a road and the responses are friction, inertia, and queues; act on a living system and they are metabolism, repair, immunity, compensation, and memory. The difference exceeds response speed. Some parameters of mobility systems can be calibrated during design; living systems keep evolving in response to intervention, carrying consequences invisible at design time far into the future. Once a medium is understood to interpret an input, a single imagined axis can no longer answer what form intelligence should converge toward.

\section{Life Is Not Software: The Physical Meaning of Genetic Code}

\subsection{Where the Code Metaphor Fails: Hyper-Embodied Information}

Living systems display medium response most fully: an input is reinterpreted by the system itself. Changing a system requires knowing what it is. Mobility systems can be decomposed through mass, energy, and topology because their parts are connected externally: engines, roads, airspace, and regulations can each be described and replaced separately. Living systems are organized differently. Their components are materially embedded in one another; their structures have been selected and compressed by environments over long periods. The most convenient way to describe such objects is often the easiest way to get them wrong.

\subhead{The Code Metaphor and Physical Execution}

Comparing genes to code is a useful but dangerous metaphor. It is useful because DNA does carry information. Base sequences can be copied, mutated, read, used to influence protein synthesis, and passed between generations. Without this informational structure, life could maintain no continuity and evolution could accumulate nothing. The danger is the next inference: if genes resemble code, life resembles software; if software can be edited, debugged, and refactored, life can be rewritten in the same way.

That inference overlooks a fundamental fact: genes are not programs running independently of hardware. Their meaning depends on physical and chemical execution within cells, beyond the symbolic arrangement of A, T, C, and G. In eukaryotic cells, DNA sequence function depends on a system of nuclear and chromatin structure, transcriptional regulation, RNA processing, protein translation, folding, modification, transport, degradation, metabolic state, cell type, developmental stage, and external environment. Prokaryotes lack nuclei but have their own regulatory and physicochemical environments of execution. \key{Genes are not software written into the body; they are part of the body itself.} Its meaning is not simply read out; it is physically enacted in the cellular environment.

Software code’s meaning is usually determined by formal rules. A function has relatively well-defined input–output relationships within a given language, compiler, and runtime. Despite software engineering’s dependencies, compatibility problems, interfaces, and legacies, code’s meaning can largely be analyzed through symbolic structure and execution rules. Genes differ. They have no pure meaning independent of the cellular environment. A sequence may be silenced, activated, spliced, modified, or amplified in different cells; the same protein may have different consequences under different metabolic states, tissue environments, and developmental stages. It is a physical trigger embedded in a network rather than an instruction running on its own.

Genotype to phenotype is therefore a multilayer reaction network rather than a linear translation. DNA sequence is one starting point among others. It passes through successive filters of chromatin accessibility, transcription-factor binding, RNA splicing, translation efficiency, protein folding and interactions, cellular signaling, metabolic flux, mechanical environment, and tissue structure. “One gene causes one trait” has strong explanatory power for some Mendelian traits, but complex traits and diseases usually involve multiple genes and the environment \cite{manolio2009finding}. Most biological phenomena arise from network states rather than single-gene instructions. Genes supply possibilities, cellular environments determine how they are realized, and the body as a whole and external environment further change the consequences.

This is why genes’ physical implementation cannot be bypassed. A base mutation can change molecular shape, binding energy, folding pathways, reaction rates, stability, spatial conformation, and regulation, beyond replacing an abstract character. Changes in binding energy can be written as a concrete quantity:
\begin{equation}
\Delta\Delta G=RT\ln\frac{K_{\text{d}}^{\text{mut}}}{K_{\text{d}}^{\text{wt}}}
\label{eq:ch27-ddG}
\end{equation}
$\Delta\Delta G$ uses the convention “mutant minus wild type” for binding free energy, and $K_{\mathrm d}$ is the corresponding dissociation constant. The ratio is dimensionless. A tenfold increase in the mutant’s $K_{\mathrm d}$ indicates weaker binding and a positive free-energy difference, approximately $5.9\,\mathrm{kJ/mol}$ at 310 kelvins. A local sequence change can thus substantially alter affinity, while functional consequences still pass through concentration, kinetics, localization, and network state.

Biological “semantics” is thermodynamic and kinetic rather than dictionary meaning. A sequence’s function ultimately appears in its changes to material, energy, and signal flows and structural stability. Genes change local boundary conditions within a complex physicochemical system rather than commanding a machine to act. This distinguishes living systems from ordinary symbolic systems. Language tolerates substantial ambiguity because interpreters supply context; software can operate in strict environments because its rules are designed to be discrete, explicit, and traceable; life operates amid continuity, noise, thermal disturbance, and strong coupling. Temperature, pH, ion concentrations, protein conformations, molecular crowding, membrane structure, mechanical pressure, and stochastic fluctuations \cite{ellis2001macromolecular} can all affect the actual consequences of the same genetic structure. Life maintains order in warm, wet, crowded, noisy matter rather than executing code in a clean logical space.

\subhead{Hyper-Embodied Information}

If execution environments determine genes’ meaning, those environments cannot be mere background: the selection constraints imposed by long adaptation leave traces in genetic structures. More strongly, life has a property of \term{hyper-embodiment}. Ordinary embodied intelligence gives a model a body through which sensors and actuators connect it to an environment; life does not begin with an abstract model installed in a body. Life’s informational structures are themselves deposits of prolonged interaction between bodies and environments. Genes record more than how to build a body. They compress traces of billions of years of environmental selection: which molecular structures remain stable, metabolic pathways sustain energy supplies, modes of perception and action improve survival, and developmental programs remain viable under particular temperatures, nutrition, gravity, microbes, predators, and reproductive pressures. Genes are history engraved within life by its environment rather than blueprints detached from that environment.

Genetic information is thus interactional information retained through natural selection, genetic drift, mutation, and historical dependence, beyond symbolic information in the ordinary sense. It contains viable structures left by repeated trials in a particular physical world rather than a complete world model. Eyes are shaped jointly by light, media, nerves, movement, predation, and escape, beyond an isolated “eye-building code”; lungs reflect constraints from atmospheric composition, metabolic demands, body architecture, and circulation, beyond sequence-specified parts; immune systems are dynamic legacies of prolonged encounters with pathogens, symbionts, tissue damage, and environmental exposure, rather than isolated programs. Life’s “code” is material memory shaped jointly by environmental pressures, bodily structures, and historical selection from the outset; it also retains neutral changes and historical contingencies \cite{nhgrigeneticdrift}. This makes gene editing different from software modification. Software usually runs in environments designed and kept relatively stable by people; gene editing changes a system that has internalized environmental history within its structure. A sequence may persist because of hidden synergies formed over evolution, or through neutral retention, drift, and linkage; continued existence alone does not establish usefulness. It may participate in developmental timing, metabolic buffering, immune regulation, tissue stability, or stress responses. We see a sequence but touch a compressed layer of long coupling between life and environment. The older and deeper this layer, the less readily it reduces to a clear engineering table of functions.

\subsection{Evolutionary Layering, Pathway Regulation, and Four Entanglements}

\subhead{Evolutionary Layering and Topological Rigidity}

Life’s hyper-embodiment also means that living systems were not designed from scratch. They accumulated through evolution. Ideally, engineering can begin with an objective, choose a clean architecture, remove redundancy, and rebuild foundations. Life did not arise this way. Living systems are historical deposits of prolonged evolution. A structure sufficiently usable in one environment may be retained; a mechanism serving one function may be repurposed; a local patch may later become an indispensable interface; a contingent path may become irreplaceable as countless subsequent structures come to depend on it. Life accumulates viable designs rather than achieving an optimal design.

This evolutionary layering fills living systems with functional legacies. They may be neither simple nor elegant, nor satisfy an engineer’s desire to refactor, yet remain deeply embedded. An apparently redundant pathway may provide a backup under stress; an apparently inefficient mechanism may regulate, buffer, or serve a hidden developmental function; an apparently irrelevant segment may affect chromatin, expression timing, or distant regulation. Biological “scrap” is often part of a historical structure rather than entirely useless waste. It may contribute to overall stability without having one clear function. This is one source of life’s topological rigidity.

Long-standing dependencies entangle living systems, beyond assembling independent modules. A local change may trigger distant consequences; a beneficial short-term edit may alter long-term development; an enhancement at one point may disrupt metabolism; inhibiting one target may trigger compensation through bypass pathways; a local repair may redistribute pressure throughout the system. The difficulty exceeds incomplete knowledge: the mechanisms themselves have multilayer coupling, historical dependence, and state-dependent effects. Such rigidity comes from the density of dependencies among known structures, rather than a particular unsolved problem. Rigidity does not mean closure: medicine and biotechnology can change life precisely because pathways remain available.

\subhead{Pathway Regulation and Four Entanglements}

Hormones can change whole-body states, neurotransmitters behavioral tendencies, receptors signal amplification or suppression, enzymes metabolic flux, immune checkpoints immune responses, transcription factors cell fate, and delivery systems access to particular tissues. Life is a complex network with entry points, levers, vulnerabilities, and control surfaces, rather than an inaccessible black box. The crucial distinction is between pathway-based regulation and software-style rewriting. Drugs change system states through receptors, enzymes, ion channels, signaling pathways, immune nodes, and metabolic nodes rather than rewriting an overall bodily program; gene editing changes local structures in specific cells, at specific times, under specific delivery conditions, rather than freely reconstructing life. Effective interventions often find a sufficiently important, accessible control point with tolerable side effects to move the system between states, rather than rewriting everything.

Pathways have different physical forms. Many small-molecule drugs depend on shape and interaction matching with receptors, enzymes, or other targets; antibodies on accurate epitope recognition; gene editing on carriers’ distribution across tissues; cell therapies on homing and survival after entering the body. These material forms constrain intervention precision and whether the same molecules can reach the same location in different people. A “target” therefore implies an entire path to be traversed inside the body, beyond a molecular site.

Pathway capacity and selectivity can be quantified. Adeno-associated viral vectors are important gene-delivery tools, with a conventional single-vector genome capacity of about 4.7 kilobases, including regulatory sequences. Oversized payloads reduce intact packaging and expression efficiency; splitting payloads adds requirements for reconstitution and co-delivery. Tissue distribution depends on capsid, dose, and route, with liver uptake particularly prominent after intravenous delivery \cite{naso2017adeno}. Lipid nanoparticles offer more flexible mRNA payload designs. Transient expression can make a lasting gene edit or, through repeated dosing, sustain protein replacement, so it does not rule out long-term treatment. Clinical trials of the propionic-acidemia candidate mRNA-3927 used repeated dosing; in January 2026 its developers announced a collaboration for further development and commercialization upon approval. It remained investigational at that point \cite{koehberl2024mrna,moderna2026recordati}. Repeated dosing has immune and tolerability constraints of its own: a 2026 mouse study observed reduced expression efficacy after repeat administration of the PEG-containing formulations tested, within those formulations and experimental conditions \cite{lnp2026repeat}. Delivery influences which cells can be reached, how long effects last, and how often dosing can recur. Constraints extend beyond editing-tool precision: pathways’ physical forms help set the limits of intervention effects.

Biotechnology’s central difficulty is finding intervention paths whose consequences can be borne, beyond whether life can be manipulated. A good target must meet several conditions: importance within the disease network, accessibility to a drug or editing tool, stable benefit after modification, tolerable side effects, no destructive long-term feedback, and individual differences that do not make risk unmanageable. This is a demanding set of conditions. Life can be regulated, but intervention requires understanding pathways, networks, environments, time, and consequences together.

Technological viscosity identifies four entanglements behind the high viscosity of living media. The first is physicochemical. Gene function must be realized through molecular folding, reaction rates, binding energies, and spatial conformations. Symbolic changes must pass through material execution. The second is network entanglement. Genes are nodes in regulatory, metabolic, signaling, and developmental networks rather than isolated instructions. The system can amplify, cancel, or transfer local changes.

The third is historical entanglement. Living systems are evolutionary inheritances rather than machines designed anew. Many structures exist because past constraints retained them and later structures came to depend on them, rather than because they are optimal. The fourth is pathway constraint. Regulation must enter through accessible pathways: delivery routes, target specificity, dose windows, timing windows, tissue distribution, and feedback boundaries determine whether an intervention works. Together these four entanglements explain why genes are not software, life is not a clean code repository, and the body is not a freely replaceable hardware platform. Genes, bodies, environments, and history are embedded in one another at the atomic scale. Life’s code has its full meaning only within living matter.

This does not deny genetic technology’s power. Its ability to reach foundational biological structures gives it great capacity for change. Greater capability makes reducing life to editable text less defensible. Mature biotechnology recognizes the physical, networked, historical, and pathway-dependent nature of genetic meaning, rather than treating bodies as inferior hardware. It asks which pathways an edit will use, in which state, which networks it will disturb, and who will bear long-term consequences, beyond whether editing is possible.

Genes are not software. They are physical structures executed by living systems, and material memories compressing environmental history. Life can be manipulated, but not rewritten at will. The key is finding tolerable regulatory paths within hyper-embodied evolutionary systems, rather than imagining changes to code.

The four entanglements show that intervention must act through pathways. The existence of a pathway answers only half the question. Once used, it brings intervention into the system’s own operations: metabolism, compensation, repair, immune recognition, and consequences unfolding over time that remain invisible initially. Whether a regulatory path tolerable at design time remains tolerable after the system responds requires another analysis.


\section{Shear Thickening in Life: Why Faster Intervention Can Meet Greater Resistance}

\subsection{Responsive Systems, Pathways, and Control Surfaces}

A tolerable regulatory path at design time need not remain tolerable once used. Living systems respond to the change itself, rather than passively receiving it. This changes the intervention problem: stronger external input need not produce greater effects.

\subhead{Responsive Systems}

Living systems are no ordinary load. Force a piece of metal and it deforms, fractures, or recovers; modify code and it compiles, reports an error, or runs; intervene in a living system and it interprets the intervention. It metabolizes, mounts immune responses, repairs, compensates, adapts, remembers, and rebounds. Life is a dynamic system tending to maintain itself, rather than passive material receiving external input. An input changes states and also triggers responses to the change itself. This is the primary difficulty of biological intervention: the object is a responsive system rather than a static object.

This does not make life inaccessible to intervention. Medicine, drugs, vaccines, surgery, hormone treatment, immunotherapy, gene therapy, and regenerative medicine have all demonstrated profound biological change. Living systems have pathways, targets, windows, and levers. The crucial questions are how manipulation enters, whether the system absorbs it, and whether the consequences can be borne.

Many technological visions assume that sufficiently precise targets would let us adjust life like a machine. Suppress an overactive pathway, replace a missing protein, repair an abnormal gene, or restore an unfavorable metabolic indicator. This works in some cases but underestimates biological networks. Living systems do not always accept a change at one point. They may bypass an inhibited pathway, amplify backups, change receptor sensitivity, adjust upstream inputs, shift metabolic pressure, or develop tolerance and rebound over time.

Biological intervention consequently often encounters nonlinear resistance. Low-intensity, infrequent intervention aligned with system rhythms may be absorbed; high-intensity, frequent intervention that overruns feedback cycles may sharply increase resistance. Rheology offers an analogue. \term{shear thickening} is non-Newtonian behavior in which apparent viscosity rises with shear rate, sometimes sharply over a narrow range in concentrated particle suspensions. Lubrication, interparticle repulsion, stress-activated frictional contacts, dilation, and boundary confinement jointly determine flow, sometimes approaching jamming; particles simply “failing to move past one another quickly enough” is an inadequate explanation \cite{brown2014shear}. Over a limited range, a power law can describe this behavior:
\begin{equation}
\eta(\dot\gamma)=\eta_b+k\dot\gamma^{\,n}
\label{eq:ch28-thickening}
\end{equation}
Here $\eta$ and $\eta_b$ have units of pascal-seconds, $\dot\gamma$ of inverse seconds, and $n$ is dimensionless, giving $k$ units of $\mathrm{Pa\,s^{n+1}}$. The expression describes a thickening branch over a specified interval; low-rate thinning, abrupt jamming, and complete flow curves require further mechanisms and forms.

With $k>0$ and $n>0$, viscosity increases with rate. The point at which the plateau and power-law terms are equal defines a crossover scale within the model:
\begin{equation}
\dot\gamma_c=\left(\frac{\eta_b}{k}\right)^{1/n}
\label{eq:ch28-gamma-c}
\end{equation}
The right-hand side has units of inverse seconds. This crossover is defined by equality of the two terms and need not coincide with the measured onset of thickening. Biological use also requires separate definitions of intensity, frequency, duration, and measured “resistance,” and identification of the compensation, saturation, or damage mechanism producing a similar curve.

For a particular intervention, we can test whether increasing intensity or pace reduces marginal benefits or raises compensation and side effects. Dose, frequency, and speed are different variables; some interventions must be sufficiently strong or timely to work. Shear thickening proposes a response hypothesis here; mechanisms and measurements determine the actual relationship.

\subhead{Pathways and Control Surfaces}

Because resistance comes from internal feedback structures, the point of intervention becomes decisive. Drug treatment offers the most direct example. An entering drug encounters a system of absorption, distribution, metabolism, excretion, immunity, tissue barriers, receptor regulation, and individual differences, beyond one target. Improved short-term indicators do not establish improved long-term system states, effective inhibition at one point does not establish lower overall risk, and higher doses may produce toxicity, side effects, tolerance, counterregulation, and systemic pressure rather than linear benefits. Living systems are deformable webs rather than straight lines.

Drugs work precisely because this web is heterogeneous. Some nodes offer greater control. Receptors, enzymes, ion channels, transcription factors, immune checkpoints, hormonal axes, and metabolic bottlenecks can all provide regulatory pathways. Much medical progress finds critical nodes within complex networks that can be reached, amplified, and adjusted safely, rather than suppressing life by force. A good target must be accessible, adjustable, verifiable, and tolerable as well as important.

Biological intervention thus changes system states through local channels rather than directly controlling the whole. An effective drug need not understand every bodily detail, just as a rudder need not push every steel plate in a ship. The task is to find a control surface that can change direction. But biological control surfaces are not stable. They change with age, disease stage, genetic background, tissue environment, immune state, and prolonged drug use. A pathway effective today may be compensated tomorrow; a target effective in one person may produce greater side effects in another.

Gene editing follows the same logic. Editing tools can grow more precise while life’s responses remain complex. A local sequence change has consequences passing through expression, folding, regulation, cellular environment, developmental state, and long-term feedback. Editing is a beginning. The living system reinterprets the result within its own operating network. A change apparently correct in the short term may reveal new consequences across tissues, ages, genetic backgrounds, or environmental stresses.

Gene editing therefore requires delivery, appropriate changes, stable expression, controllable feedback, and long-term safety, beyond cutting accurately. Delivery systems, tissue specificity, editing efficiency, off-target effects, immune responses, cellular selection pressures, and developmental timing all belong to the intervention pathway. Deeper biotechnology requires pathway design rather than treating the problem solely as editing precision.

The immune system illustrates the dysregulated responses examined through this analogy with shear thickening. Immunity is a highly sensitive recognition and regulatory system, beyond a simple defense mechanism. Insufficient responses fail to protect, excessive ones can injure the body; inadequate or delayed responses can be overwhelmed by infection, while excessive, dysregulated activation can contribute to cytokine storms \cite{fajgenbaum2020cytokinestorm}. Intervention mismatched to immune timing and intensity can turn treatment into disturbance. The difficulty is the abundance, complexity, and timing dependence of life’s responses, rather than an absence of response.

Biotechnology consequently cannot simply copy software’s iteration cycle. Software can be released frequently, rolled back, tested on limited deployments, and patched quickly; biological interventions cannot freely repeat high-frequency experiments on people. Some software errors can be isolated and recovered within information systems, while biological errors enter bodies, tissues, metabolism, and long-term risk directly; software controlling medical devices, transport, and infrastructure also has physical consequences. One wrong intervention may alter irreversible development, leave lasting injury, or emerge later through immune memory, cell states, or ecological relationships. Living systems offer no unlimited supply of cheap rollbacks.

\subsection{Sources of Viscosity, the Cost of Robustness, and the Limits of Online Maintenance}

\subhead{Sources of Viscosity and the Cost of Robustness}

Technological viscosity traces the proposed biological thickening to three sources. The first is temporal rigidity. Biological feedback takes time. Drug effects must unfold, side effects be observed, immune responses develop, and tissues repair; development and aging emerge over longer cycles still. Interventions judging only short-term responses can mistake long-term feedback that has not yet returned for feedback that does not exist. Life often hides costs in time.

The second is structural coupling. Biological pathways form networks of connection, compensation, and mutual constraint rather than isolated pipes. Changes at one point can propagate to distant sites, and local benefits may carry global costs. Greater complexity makes improvement in one indicator less adequate as evidence of an improved biological state.

The third is maintenance pressure. Life is a dissipative structure far from equilibrium, requiring continuous energy input, damage repair, waste removal, boundary maintenance, and regulation of internal states. Many critical biological functions cannot wait for the whole system to shut down for maintenance. The heart, immunity, nervous system, metabolism, endocrine regulation, and cellular repair must operate during maintenance. Much repair takes place while the system continues performing its functions. This constrains intervention intensity and precision: too weak has no effect, too strong disrupts operation, too fast outruns feedback, and too slow misses the window.

This also illuminates the problem of drug-development efficiency. Modern biotechnology, automated experiments, and AI can greatly expand the candidate space. Targets can be discovered, molecules generated, structures predicted, and experiments screened faster. Accelerating discovery does not automatically remove bottlenecks; they shift toward biological verification, compensation, and long-term safety. More candidates create screening and verification pressure, and greater target precision still requires understanding system feedback. Without corresponding improvements in verification and selection, candidates advanced faster may also push failure costs into later clinical stages. Eroom’s phenomenon \cite{scannell2012diagnosing} has no single simple explanation, but reminds us that better discovery tools do not automatically penetrate life’s highly viscous verification layers.

Drug-development time and costs vary with disease, trial design, allocation of failures, and capital accounting. A company-sample study in 2016 offered a relatively high capitalized estimate, rather than a fixed price for every new drug \cite{dimasi2016}. A more recent observation is rentosertib: its developer announced the first patient dosed in its Phase III program in September 2026 \cite{insilico2026phase3}. Reaching that stage is progress; Phase III results still require subsequent observation.

The gap between discovery and verification can be measured in work in progress:

\begin{equation}
L=\lambda W
\end{equation}

$L$ is average work in progress within a stable process, $\lambda$ average throughput across the same boundary, and $W$ average time in the process. This is Little’s relationship; exits, withdrawals, and early failures must be counted consistently. Changing arrivals, capacity, selection, and time in process jointly affects inventory and output. When arrivals persistently exceed service capacity and the queue keeps growing, a steady-state average cannot directly describe the entire process.

Alongside these three sources, life has a property working in the opposite direction. Robustness cuts both ways. It lets bodies resist disturbances, repair damage, and maintain stability while making external intervention less likely to have linear effects. A fragile system is easy to change and easy to collapse; a robust system survives and resists change. Life can be hard to treat precisely because it is still trying to maintain itself. Many chronic diseases are states of bodily networks formed under particular historical, genetic, environmental, and behavioral conditions, rather than errors that can be independently deleted. Treatment moves the system between stable states rather than simply deleting a mistake.

This transition need not be blind. Systems medicine, network pharmacology, precision medicine, and synthetic biology seek to identify its pathways. They recognize structures, nodes, and control surfaces embedded in feedback networks and temporal processes, rather than treating life as an unknowable whole. Effective intervention often best matches the system’s state rather than applying maximum force: the right target, dose, timing, population, and verification framework help move a system beyond a pathological stable state.

The technological intuition that faster is better consequently often fails in biology. Intervention can outrun relaxation times; abrupt indicator adjustments trigger counterregulation; stronger local control move pressure elsewhere; and greater candidate generation accumulate before verification bottlenecks. Biological systems require technology to enter their rhythms. Good biotechnology understands feedback, redundancy, compensation, timing, and irreversibility rather than treating life as slow software. So far, shear thickening is a cross-sectional judgment; its limiting form over time remains to be examined.

\subhead{The Limits of Online Maintenance and the Rhythm of Intervention}

Aging can be viewed as a limit of online maintenance. From birth, organisms continually repair themselves through DNA repair, protein quality control, cell renewal, immune clearance, metabolic regulation, and tissue regeneration. Repair remains imperfect. Damage accumulates, errors remain, redundancy is depleted, regulatory networks grow less responsive, and resilience gradually declines. Aging involves maintenance pressure, informational noise, structural damage, and dysregulated feedback across a long-running system rather than one broken component \cite{lopezotin2013hallmarks}. A 2026 study of mammalian transcriptomes further showed that lifespan-modulating interventions can produce opposing health-associated changes across cell types and functional modules \cite{tyshkovskiy2026aging}. Improving one clock or indicator cannot replace assessing whole-body function, risk, and long-term outcomes.

Death reveals the boundary of an individual’s online maintenance. For an individual, death is an end; at population and evolutionary scales, generational turnover provides renewal. Reproduction, variation, selection, and recombination continue the search at a higher level, without endlessly repairing the same individual. This grants death no romantic meaning or benefit to the individual. Many individuals face limits to online maintenance, reproduction and development can rebuild some states in offspring, and variation and selection continue changing populations; this does not establish death as a renewal program necessarily favored by selection.

This also explains the distinctive viscosity of living media. They have bit-like properties because genes can be copied, inherited, and edited; atomic properties because genes require physicochemical execution; and biological properties because execution enters feedback, compensation, repair, and evolution. Life occupies the overlap of bits, atoms, and biology, rather than a light medium. AI can accelerate informational search within it without canceling physical execution, temporal unfolding, or system responses.

Mature biotechnology must pursue more than stronger editing, faster screening, and larger models. It must find pathways, match timing, control doses, verify in layers, buffer risk, and respect feedback. Some situations permit strong intervention, others only gentle adjustment; some targets permit quick verification, other consequences require long observation; models can absorb some residuals, while others must be borne within clinical, institutional, and ethical boundaries.

Life is neither software nor an ordinary machine. It is a dissipative structure that maintains itself, interprets interventions, resists disturbances, and delays feedback. Biological intervention is not difficult because life cannot change. It certainly can. Effective change must find pathways, pass through feedback, respect rhythms, and withstand long-term verification. \key{Pushing faster can make a system harder to move.} This is shear thickening in life.

Shear thickening pushes costs back toward the bearer. However precise the intervention design, disturbance, compensation, irreversible consequences, and long-term verification must fall on a system that is still running. Bearing has limits in capacity and time: disturbances absorbed, feedback postponed, and irreversible changes endured are all finite. What can be borne, by whom, and for how long are questions more fundamental than the intervention technology itself.


\section{After Morphological Computation: Bodily Encapsulation and Evolutionary Amortization}

\subsection{Residuals in Physical Intelligence and Three Layers of Bodily Encapsulation}

Something concrete must always bear the consequences. Life has embedded much residual correction in the co-adaptation of evolution, development, and environment. Machines lack that inherited structure and must absorb deviations through explicit engineering each time they act physically. Chapter 3’s compression criterion selects the variables retained by a model; what corrects them during contact, with what delay, and whether recovery remains possible after failure are questions outside the model alone.

One of the easiest mistakes about physical intelligence is treating the body as a peripheral. On this view, intelligence resides in a brain, model, or controller; the body is a mechanical port executing commands. Understanding comes first, then planning, then bodily implementation. Strong enough models, enough sensors, and sufficiently precise control should let machines enter reality as humans do. The real difficulty is sustained action in open reality, beyond generating an action. Sustained action requires acknowledging that reality continually produces deviations the model has not specified in advance.

\subhead{Residuals in Physical Intelligence}

Reality is an open system continually producing residuals, rather than a static object awaiting execution. The model supplies actions; reality supplies deviations. Floors may be more slippery, objects heavier, cup surfaces wetter, or door handles looser than expected; people may suddenly lose balance, light change, sensors become occluded, or actuators respond late. Each deviation may be small, but a physical task is a chain rather than a single question and answer: recognition errors change grasping postures, contact errors change object positions, localization drift enters the next plan, and feedback delay amplifies control error. Residuals propagate along task chains rather than clearing automatically between actions.

A \term{residual} here means deviations not fully absorbed by the current model, body, controller, or operational arrangements during open physical action, rather than one error term. It includes at least four classes: model residuals, state variables omitted by world or policy model compression; perceptual residuals, estimation errors from noise, occlusion, drift, and asynchronous modalities; contact residuals, incompletely predictable friction, slipping, deformation, impacts, and force transmission; and operational residuals, systemic burdens of exception handling, maintenance, verification, takeover, and tracing responsibility. The issue is whether residuals are absorbed promptly along continuing tasks or propagate across interfaces beyond recovery limits; open action always contains them. Embodied intelligence must therefore keep residuals recoverable across sustained tasks, beyond being able to perform individual actions.

Grasping a cup is the smallest example. Robots face room cleaning, elder care, table clearing, goods handling, construction-site collaboration, crop harvesting, and hospital medication delivery. Each links many actions, each action changes the next one’s initial conditions, and the system must demonstrate recoverability over long, disturbed, consequential task chains rather than one successful attempt. The difficulty has a threshold: beyond some residual level, capability may abruptly become a stop, misgrasp, collision, loss of balance, or request for human takeover rather than declining smoothly. This focuses attention on structures bearing residuals. Human bodies’ distinction lies in embedding much correction in bodily, experiential, and environmental co-adaptation rather than possessing a complete world model.

\subhead{Three Layers of Bodily Encapsulation}

Lifting a cup requires no prior explicit calculation of its exact geometry, friction coefficient, center of mass, surface wetness, contact angle, and force distribution: a person looks, reaches, and touches. Fingers immediately sense slipping, muscles feel weight, joints adjust posture, and tiny slips trigger automatic changes in grip through finger pads and muscles. Many errors are absorbed before reaching consciousness: this is \term{bodily encapsulation}. \key{The body is a residual-management system, not a peripheral of intelligence.} It contains many deviations from open reality within low-latency, continuously sensing, self-correcting loops.

Bodily encapsulation means that the body itself is a residual-absorbing structure, beyond simply being important. Skin, muscles, tendons, joints, bones, the vestibular system, proprioception, pain, and reflexes form a continuous system of sensing, actuation, buffering, constraint, and correction rather than appendages to the brain: soft fingers fit surfaces, elastic muscles absorb impacts, joint limits restrict dangerous movements, pain marks overload, and experience indicates ignorable details and signs of danger. The body processes part of reality directly through contact rather than sending everything to the brain and waiting for computation.

The body contains residuals by turning some physical laws into action structures, rather than circumventing them. Exchanges between gravitational potential and kinetic energy during leg swing, elastic storage in muscles and tendons, local finger-pad deformation, and joint limits excluding dangerous poses are constraints built into morphology before central compensation. They confine some errors within manageable dynamical channels. In many situations a mature body lets gravity, inertia, friction, and contact constrain, select, and correct actions rather than continually opposing them through active control. Morphological computation thus converts some residuals otherwise requiring sensing, estimation, and control into cheap constraints in materials, geometry, and passive dynamics, beyond having a body participate in computation \cite{paul2006}. Passive-dynamic walking robots directly demonstrate this: suitable morphology and dynamics can organize some movement without intensive central control \cite{mcgeer1990,full1999,collins2005}. Encapsulation occurs at at least three levels. First, material encapsulation: skin, muscles, tendons, and joints absorb errors physically. Soft finger pads enlarge contact areas, muscle elasticity buffers impacts, and bodily elasticity helps stabilize gait. This “computation” is material and morphological participation in control rather than symbol manipulation. Morphological computation matters because it includes shape, compliance, passive dynamics, and environmental coupling in control, allowing bodily structures to share complexity otherwise handled centrally \cite{paul2006}. Second, feedback encapsulation: vision, touch, proprioception, vestibular sensation, and muscle tension sample reality continuously during action. Pressure underfoot tests slipperiness, a touch tests looseness, and contact with another person’s body triggers adjustment to imbalance. The world can be queried locally through action without being fully preinstalled. Impedance control became fundamental to robotic manipulation because contact tasks cannot be reduced to position tracking: operator, actuator, object, and environment form one coupled dynamical system, requiring control of interactions rather than isolated trajectories \cite{hogan1985}. Third, experiential encapsulation: countless encounters with cups, handles, stairs, wet floors, knives, hot pans, tired bodies, and crowded spaces supply actionable lossy compressions rather than a complete model. People know which details usually can be ignored and which need immediate attention. Bodies permit incomplete models; experience lets action begin somewhere other than zero \cite{gibson1979}. This approach connects to Moravec’s paradox, embodied cognition, and morphological computation \cite{moravec1988,pfeifer2007,varela1991,gibsonpick2000,pfeifer2006,hauser2011}. Moravec’s paradox suggests that abstract reasoning may be easier to engineer than a toddler’s sensorimotor abilities; embodied cognition locates intelligence across body, environment, and action as well as the head; morphological computation further emphasizes materials’ and forms’ roles in control. The more specific claim advanced here is that bodies encapsulate low-latency residual absorption rather than an abstract quantity of computation. This can too easily imply natural bodily superiority. A distinction is needed: humans externalize some residuals into handles, stairs, furniture, roads, and tools built around bodily scales, while machines internalize some through soft grippers, elastic joints, mechanical stops, and compliant materials. Humans do not only internalize complexity, nor machines only externalize it. The deeper differences concern the timescale for amortization and substrate affordances, developed in this section’s final subsection. First comes another question: with so many routes to residual correction, why do machines still seem heavy?

\subsection{Making Machine Complexity Explicit: Interface Debt}

\subhead{Making Machine Complexity Explicit: Interface Debt}

Machines have many ways to correct residuals. Sensors expose deviations: cameras, depth cameras, lidar, touch, torque sensing, IMUs, and proprioception reveal drift, slips, collisions, and posture errors. Control algorithms correct them through feedback, impedance control, model-predictive control, and real-time replanning. Bodies absorb some through soft grippers, underactuated hands, elastic joints, compliant materials, mechanical stops, and passive stability \cite{mason1985,birglen2008}. Stronger models anticipate residuals: vision–language–action models, world models, imitation learning, and policy models infer more states from fewer inputs and avoid dangerous actions in advance \cite{shao2025,li2025}. Environmental redesign reduces them through standard shelving, QR codes, dedicated fixtures, fixed routes, closed sites, tracks, V2X, and structured warehouses. Task restriction and operational support also contain residuals: cleaning, warehouse transport, inspection, surgical assistance, welding, harvesting, and delivery each narrow the task boundary, while remote takeover, safety operators, exception tickets, audit logs, maintenance staff, and insurance place residuals within larger operating structures. The question is why machines often must expose residual correction as engineering systems where humans have embedded much of it in bodies, experience, and environments, rather than whether enough methods exist.

This is \term{explicit machine complexity}. Making complexity explicit means more than adding sensors or judging machine hardware inferior: reality’s complexity, handled continuously, locally, and with low latency in human bodies, is separated in many machines into structures that can be measured, synchronized, controlled, verified, maintained, and held accountable. A finger senses slipping where a machine may need tactile sensors, slip-detection algorithms, feedback control, and safety policies; muscles buffer impacts where a machine may need compliant materials, force-control policies, and mechanical protection; experience interprets “gently,” “don’t break it,” and “hold steady,” where machines must convert these vague constraints into action rules, risk boundaries, and responsibility records. What is connected within a body is divided into modules, bringing interfaces and further paths for residual propagation.

This can be called \term{interface debt}: splitting residual correction implicit in bodily loops into multiple engineered modules creates continuing structural burdens of synchronization, calibration, delay compensation, fault propagation, maintenance, and verification. Human perception, actuation, buffering, correction, and safety boundaries are not five independent systems. At contact with a cup, touch, muscle tension, joint angle, skin deformation, and experiential judgment already correct locally within one bodily loop. Variables need not all be named, errors fully expanded, or control separated into independent modules. A machine must detect slip, calibrate touch, synchronize vision and force, compensate delay, absorb actuator errors, judge safety boundaries, log behavior, verify reliability, and trace responsibility. Separating another variable adds an interface; another interface adds a synchronization problem, failure mode, and maintenance point. If module coupling is approximated by allowing every pair to interact, interface growth can be written as:
\begin{equation}
N_{\text{if}}=\frac{n(n-1)}{2}
\end{equation}
$n$ is the number of explicitly separated modules and $N_{\text{if}}$ the potential pairwise interfaces in the fully connected approximation. Both are dimensionless counts; $1/2$ avoids double-counting unordered channels. Counting at most one undirected relationship per pair gives this potential upper bound for a fully connected network; counting interface types or directions separately requires a different convention. Increasing $n$ from five to ten raises the bound from ten to forty-five, faster than module growth. Actual dependencies are usually not fully connected, leaving many potential channels inactive and the count below that bound. Hierarchy and decoupling can limit growth; a potential quadratic upper bound is not an inevitable growth law for real systems. Making complexity explicit converts implicit complexity into explicit coupling structures, beyond merely seeing it clearly.

Interface debt is more than ordinary integration cost. Integration cost emphasizes the trouble of many modules; interface debt emphasizes propagation: perceptual errors enter control, control errors enter actuation, actuation changes the environment, and the changed environment contaminates the next perception. More modules offer more propagation paths; longer tasks let local errors become system drift. Machines become heavy through accumulating coupling debt among explicit structures, rather than one component. A subtler temporal debt lies within this: machine vision, touch, torque sensing, proprioception, planning, and actuation usually differ in sampling rates, delays, and phases. Each handles the world at some time slice, and those slices do not naturally coincide. The controller’s “current state” is often an engineered object assembled from asynchronous signals through timestamps, filtering, extrapolation, and fusion. During fast contact or continuous manipulation, residuals cross misaligned temporal phases as well as modules. A system may correct an error that has just passed rather than the present one, and the next action writes the delayed correction into a new physical state. More interfaces make a stable, shared, actionable “now” harder to maintain as well as integration harder. Bodily seams need not each be named; machine seams must each be maintained.

Conversely, making these requirements explicit is not the same as throwing more hardware at them. Mature engineering does not necessarily make everything more general and complex: a compliant gripper may handle soft objects better than a precision hand with an elaborate tactile array, a fixed fixture may be more reliable than a general recognition model, a mechanical stop may be more stable than a complex software safety policy, and a closed campus may be easier to drive autonomously than open roads; the real question is not whether there are enough sensors, but who corrects residuals, where, and at what physical and engineering cost. Soft robotics and underactuated structures follow this direction: instead of merely imitating biological shapes, they bring material compliance, contact geometry, and passive deformation into control, so that robots need not turn every contact into precise measurement and central computation; Rus and Tolley's review shows how compliant materials open routes beyond the design, fabrication, and control of rigid robots, while soft structures introduce new difficulties in modeling, sensing, actuation, and control \cite{rus2015}. A body can therefore absorb residuals while introducing new explicit complexity of its own: it is another way of allocating complexity, not a free solution. If complexity must be allocated somewhere, assigning some of it to a stronger model becomes the next seemingly direct way out.

\subsection{Prediction Cannot Remove Consequences: Task Chains and Cliff-Edge Failure}

\subhead{Prediction Cannot Remove the Need to Bear Consequences}

Models reduce errors, avoid dangerous contacts, and let existing hardware perform more tasks. Physical feedback loops also need adequate force, speed, sensing, and recovery: contact and control structures must catch slips after they occur, and damaged components need repair or replacement paths. Prediction, execution, and recovery capabilities should be examined separately.

This does not deny the value of a better brain. Better vision, world, action, and policy models let existing sensors and actuators do more. Many tasks require neither human-level bodies nor full tactile skins and dexterous hands: clear task boundaries, relatively stable environments, and controllable consequences can let a good model and existing hardware form a usable loop. A stronger brain extends capability boundaries without abolishing them: it cannot create actuator force or material compliance from nothing, prevent all sensor drift, or remove the need to verify open-world tail risks. Stronger brains can move some complexity from sensors and hardware into models, but atomic action still requires managing remaining deviations somewhere—absorbing, transferring, isolating, recovering, and genuinely reducing or eliminating particular errors. Assessments should track whether errors decrease, where costs fall, and whether remaining deviations are handled promptly.

End-to-end models, simulation, teleoperation, and new sensing can reduce or eliminate particular faults, and can also transfer some burden into data, support, and maintenance. Residuals obey no fixed conservation law. Evaluation should record real error reductions, changes in error location, and recovery costs in long tasks. The testable mechanism is when residuals propagate and amplify, rather than a prior assertion that they can only move elsewhere.

\subhead{Task Chains and Cliff-Edge Failure}

The first implication of this empirical mechanism is that short task-chain successes in laboratories do not establish long-term reliability in open environments. Grasping on a standard tabletop does not establish competence in an unfamiliar home; moving among standard warehouse shelves does not establish competence with hospital crowds, privacy, emergency priorities, and temporary closures; driving on ordinary roads does not establish reliable handling of construction, glare, rain, snow, unusual gestures, and liability disputes. Real tasks lengthen chains, add disturbances and responsibility, and circulate small errors across interfaces. The residual mechanism challenges a costless, indefinitely smooth extrapolation of embodied capability, rather than the possibility of reliable embodied intelligence.

Clearing a household table looks simple but forms a task chain rich in residuals. First a robot identifies cups, tissues, medicine boxes, keys, charging cables, glasses, a half-full glass of water, and fragile ornaments. Vision may handle transparent surfaces, reflections, and occlusion well while leaving uncertainty about water in a cup, a damp base, glasses beneath paper, or whether a medicine box is empty. Grasping converts state residuals into contact residuals: a slightly wrong gripper angle rotates a cup, lifts paper, or tangles a cable around another object. Contact then changes the environment: the cup moves, the paper stack collapses, visible keys become occluded, and the tabletop no longer matches the previous plan’s input. The result is a new task state with errors written into the environment, rather than one isolated mistake. Without low-latency touch, compliant grasping, local recovery, and task-level rollback, a small slip can escalate from insecure grasp to dropped object, spilled liquid, interrupted task, and human takeover. Here is the embodied capability boundary: whether the system keeps residuals recoverable at a given task length, disturbance intensity, and consequence level, beyond generating a plausible action.

Abrupt exposure at boundaries also reflects the multiscale structure of physical contact. Finger pads, skin, muscles, joints, and proprioception operate across scales: fine texture, local slip, contact area, overall posture, and muscle tension change together in continuous media. Materials and low-level sensorimotor loops absorb many deviations before they become explicit errors. Machines often separate these scales: materials bear microscopic contact, tactile or force sensors detect local slipping, vision or estimation corrects posture, and planners handle task drift. Residuals unabsorbed at one scale can jump upward: a tiny slip changes grasping posture, posture changes object state, and object state contaminates the next perception and plan. Cliff-edge failure often occurs when a residual crosses a gap between scales and turns a local disturbance into a system event, rather than through linear error growth. Such failure is an outward symptom of inadequate bodily and cross-scale encapsulation and excessive interface debt.

This mechanism admits concrete tests that could count against it. If large numbers of open-world robots in homes, hospitals, construction sites, farms, and public roads sustain graceful degradation—recovering errors, avoiding residual accumulation along tasks, showing gradual rather than abrupt rises in takeover rates with disturbance, and avoiding substantial maintenance and verification cost increases with task length—the claim about propagation and boundary amplification should be weakened. Better models, bodies, environments, and operational systems would have returned residuals to a continuously absorbable range. Important technical signals already exist: Bongard, Zykov, and Lipson demonstrated recovery of motion after damage through continuous self-modeling, \cite{bongard2006} while Cully and colleagues demonstrated rapid discovery of compensatory behavior through intelligent trial and error \cite{cully2015}. These works show the role of residual-recovery structures in reliable embodied intelligence rather than overturning the mechanism. Mature embodied intelligence can degrade gracefully near boundaries, bringing errors back within manageable limits rather than requiring an absence of error. Why this looks effortless in humans is a question of time, beyond the present moment.

\subhead{Evolutionary Amortization and Residual Management}

The ease of human action is not free; its costs have been amortized over immense timescales. Hundreds of millions of years of biological evolution shaped skin, muscles, bones, joints, reflexes, and motor control through innumerable failures, injuries, deaths, and reproductions. Development recalibrates bodies through infancy, childhood, and daily falls, collisions, grasps, trials, and corrections. Social environments build handles, stairs, furniture, tools, kitchens, roads, hospitals, and factories around human scales. A person enters a niche co-evolved, co-designed, and co-domesticated with human bodies rather than a neutral space: this is \term{evolutionary amortization}.

Evolutionary amortization distributes bodily costs across immense timescales, countless individual trials, development, and environmental redesign. An adult’s easy grasp rests on encapsulation deposited by evolutionary, developmental, personal, and environmental histories rather than a simple calculation at that instant. Developmental systems theory and ecological psychology both emphasize action capabilities formed through coupling among bodies, environments, and historical processes rather than unfolding solely from an internal program \cite{thelen1994,clark1997}. The two axes introduced earlier can now be developed. The time available for amortization determines how complexity can be spread: evolution, development, and civilizational design have spread human bodily and environmental costs over long periods, while machines seek to rebuild those encapsulations within short engineering cycles. Substrate affordances determine which residuals are readily absorbed: skin, muscles, tendons, nerves, pain, and self-repairing tissues suit compliant contact, continuous feedback, damage sensing, and local repair. Metal, motors, gears, silicon, cables, and rigid structures excel at precision, repetition, and high power, but do not naturally provide living materials’ low-power compliance, self-healing, and continuous sensing. Humans hide complexity in time and living substrates; machines often make it explicit in engineering systems.

This allocation can be written as an accounting relationship:

\begin{equation}
\bar{c}=\frac{C}{N}
\end{equation}

$C$ is the accumulated cost of forming a capability, including evolutionary trials, developmental calibration, and social environmental redesign, first expressed on a consistent basis such as energy, time, or number of individuals. $N$ counts all uses across the capability’s history, summed over individuals and generations in the population considered; it is dimensionless. The allocated cost per use, $\bar{c}$, has units determined by the accounting basis for $C$. On this basis, the ease of human action may partly reflect a large denominator of uses: even when $C$ is large, a sufficiently large $N$ can make $\bar{c}$ small enough to leave historical costs outside present decisions. Machines rebuilding such encapsulation within short engineering cycles have a much smaller $N$ than evolution and development provide; the same $C$ would mean a higher cost per use. Actual machine and biological costs $C$ differ, so this alone cannot compare total costs. The applicable conditions are sunk investment and continuing use: amortization requires that $C$ is already sunk and the capability keeps being used. If environmental change makes it obsolete, future $N$ stops increasing and further allocation ceases; the original $C$ was already a sunk cost. This is an accounting convention, providing neither measured $C$ and $N$ nor a claim that living bodies are cheaper at every capability.

Living bodies are not superior in every dimension. Machines often far exceed them in precise repetition, heavy loads, high-speed processing, heat, radiation, and standardized manufacturing. Living materials are not inherently “higher”; open-world compliant contact, continuous feedback, damage sensing, local recovery, and sustained action form a capability combination to which life has long adapted. Machines can exceed individual bodily capabilities while still needing redesigned encapsulation for the combination. Human ease also relies on long-calibrated priors about bodily state. Normally, people need not re-establish hand location, joint existence, muscle response, or basic bodily coherence before every action. Proprioception, vestibular sensation, motor experience, and homeostasis provide a continually updated range of confidence that does not reset to zero each time. Machines must engineer this trust through calibration, redundant measurement, estimation, anomaly detection, and safety assertions; their self-state must continually be measured, synchronized, checked, and logged. Default bodily trust appears in machines as an entire verification structure.

Together these axes reconnect physical intelligence to technological viscosity. The bit layer rapidly generates models, policies, and simulations; the atomic layer bears contact, friction, inertia, materials, and safety consequences; the biological layer has spent immense time forming bodies adapted to reality. AI moving directly from bits to atoms while reproducing long-amortized bodily capabilities meets a fundamental rate mismatch: model updates are fast, bodily redesign slower, and environmental co-adaptation slower still. Fast engineering attempts to take on slow evolution’s accumulated history, beyond simply making machines smarter; practical engineering routes therefore divide rather than converging on one solution. First, redesign environments to reduce residual sources: closed sites, warehouses, factories, ports, dedicated roads, and standardized interfaces make reality more observable, predictable, and free from ambiguous contact. They structure local environments rather than requiring machines to understand the entire open world. Second, redesign bodies to absorb residuals: compliant materials, tactile skins, dexterous hands, elastic joints, underactuated structures, and low-latency proprioceptive feedback improve physical support. Humanoids are attractive partly because so many environments, tools, and interfaces already fit human scales, but this also imposes the complexity of bipedal balance, whole-body coordination, dexterity, safe contact, and long-acquired bodily experience. Third, strengthen models to extend capability boundaries: better brains infer more states from fewer inputs, anticipate errors, and let existing hardware do more. This may genuinely improve efficiency or move burdens into models, data, training, simulation, and verification; whole-system costs must be checked. Fourth, narrow tasks and provide operational support. Many usable robots rely on precise task boundaries rather than general bodies: machines handle stabilized ordinary conditions, while people or operational systems handle exceptions and residuals beyond the boundary. Autonomy has been redistributed through the system at a cost.

Physical AI matures by building a sufficiently reliable \term{residual-management system}, beyond improving models or piling up sensors. Bodies, models, sensors, controllers, environmental design, task boundaries, and operational support can jointly form it; different solutions absorb residuals and expose complexity at different locations rather than ranking along one simple scale. Mature physical intelligence often actively limits the dimensions of contact with open reality and sets physical boundaries it can handle. Structured environments, standardized tools, restricted tasks, compliant bodies, safety control, remote takeover, and operational audits define a fault-tolerant region for action. Residuals, delays, and errors can exist there without readily penetrating the successive absorption structures of body, model, control, and operations. Reliable physical intelligence forms a recoverable, verifiable, maintainable action niche jointly with the world, rather than requiring boundaryless understanding of it.

After morphological computation comes the question of how bodies encapsulate residuals across timescales and how machines bear them without the same historical amortization and living substrate. Bodies let humans act with incomplete world models. Machines can learn human actions without endlessly adding sensors, but must find residual-correction mechanisms to replace missing bodily encapsulation. The primary scarcity in physical intelligence is a residual-absorbing structure amortized over long periods and carried by a suitable substrate, beyond abstract reasoning alone. Entry into the open world depends on residual-absorption structures matched to the system’s medium. Yet “residual absorption” groups different kinds of work: exploring possibilities can be retried cheaply in symbolic space, containing risks compresses degrees of freedom within safety boundaries, and exposing errors requires evidence chains and long observation. They demand different resource structures, timescales, and levels of certainty. If where residuals are absorbed determines a system’s weight, might residuals at different locations require intelligence to differentiate into different modes?


\section{Modes of Intelligence: The Constraint Triangle of Resources, Time, and Certainty}

\subsection{Three Sides of the Constraint Triangle and Their Tensions}

Where residuals fall determines the resource structures, timescales, and certainty levels needed to absorb them; these demands do not always align. Intelligence will not evolve along one straight line. A common vision imagines greater intelligence becoming more general, faster, more reliable, and cheaper until it converges on one omnipotent system: real-time understanding, instant plans, stable physical control, accurate prediction of consequences, and minimal resources for every task. This treats intelligence as a single-axis capability whose growth improves every dimension together. Real intelligence operates under constraints. It needs resources for computation, sensing, storage, cooling, and execution; time for receiving information, reasoning, verification, feedback, and correction; and certainty for reliable results, stable behavior, controlled risk, and traceable responsibility. Technology can improve all three, but pushing them together toward extremes without cost is difficult.\key{The central mistake of single-axis thinking is assuming that constraints disappear as capability grows.}

\subhead{Three Sides of the Constraint Triangle}

The constraint triangle brings resource allocation and engineering tradeoffs into one analytical framework; tasks, performance metrics, and architectures determine the specific tensions. Better algorithms, more efficient chips, stronger energy supplies, better sensors, and more mature control architectures can move the boundary. Moving a boundary does not abolish it. Technology can enlarge the triangle without making speed, certainty, and low cost improve without limit and without new costs.

Each side has a physical meaning. Resources are intelligence’s physical account: computation needs energy, models storage, sensing equipment, inference processor time, execution power, control communication and feedback, and high reliability redundancy, backups, audits, and maintenance. Even apparently pure information structures operate on chips, electricity, networks, cooling, and manufacturing systems. Larger systems, higher-frequency feedback, and more consequential tasks make intelligence harder to keep light.

Data centers expose intelligence’s physical foundations. IEA reports in April and October 2026 examined efficiency, demand, and power-supply conditions: efficiency per task can improve while usage growth still raises total electricity demand \cite{iea2026questions,iea2026powering}. Comparisons must distinguish all data centers, AI-related facilities, and individual tasks, and separate earlier projections from actual 2026 results.

Separating total consumption into demand and energy per unit puts evidence pointing in both directions into one expression:

\begin{equation}
E=De,\qquad \frac{1}{E}\frac{dE}{dt}=\frac{1}{D}\frac{dD}{dt}+\frac{1}{e}\frac{de}{dt}
\end{equation}

$E$ is total electricity use over a given period, in terawatt-hours; $D$ is computing demand served over that period, in normalized units of computation; $e$ is energy per unit, in terawatt-hours per computational unit. The first expression decomposes the total, and logarithmic differentiation with respect to time gives the second. Its three terms are instantaneous relative rates of change, in inverse years if time is measured in years. Efficiency improvement can coexist with a moving resource boundary: total electricity use still rises when demand growth exceeds the decline in energy per unit. Masanet and colleagues’ historical estimates for global data centers illustrate this: computing instances increased 6.5-fold from 2010 to 2018, while electricity use rose about 1.06-fold. Energy per computational unit fell to roughly one-sixth of its earlier value, or about 20 percent annually on average, allowing both changes to coexist \cite{masanet2020recalibrating}. Comparable computational quantities and consistent statistical boundaries are required. With mismatched definitions—for example, separate accounting of training, inference, and cooling—or structural changes in demand, the meaning of $e$ changes. Defining it as total electricity divided by demand preserves the identity, but need not isolate efficiency changes for comparable tasks. This describes an accounting structure rather than forecasting energy trends.

Time is the process through which intelligence exchanges information with the world. Intelligence cannot know all consequences before information arrives or complete real verification before processes unfold. Fast responses often mean acting on incomplete information, long-term verification slowing down, and complex feedback waiting for results from the system. More immediate decisions tend to rely on narrower views; greater global robustness demands more observation, checks, and feedback cycles.

Verification time comprises proofs, simulations, trial preparation, real exposure, follow-up, and review. Better tools can accelerate some components; aging, long-term responses, and sufficient observation have conditions of their own. Projects should distinguish waiting that generates evidence from waiting caused by process congestion.

Certainty here names requirements for controlling errors, risks, and consequences, made concrete through reliability, safety margins, recoverability, and traceability. Low-risk text generation can tolerate ambiguity, noise, and regeneration in ways high-risk control cannot. Autonomous driving, nuclear plants, grids, financial clearing, surgical robots, flight control, and drug approval must examine tails, boundaries, responsibility, explainability, auditability, and recovery as well as averages. Greater model intelligence alone does not buy certainty; restrictions, redundancy, verification, and institutions do.

In its September 2026 introduction, the FDA reported more than 1,600 AI-enabled devices authorized for marketing in the United States \cite{fda2026aidevices}. Its periodically updated list specifies how devices are identified and the limits of coverage \cite{fda2026ailist}. Each authorization concerns a particular product and use: the count shows bounded functions entering practice rather than a general qualification to practice medicine.
