Producing a world once called for myth, a city drawings, a character fiction, a molecular design professional chemistry, and an institution prolonged political imagination. Text, images, voices, code, characters, plans, drug candidates, city designs, and future scenarios now appear rapidly in models. Representation begins generating possible realities at scale alongside preserving and rehearsing reality. The ontological question itself is old. Humans long knew that drawings differ from bridges, maps from land, legal texts from social order, money symbols from grain, and fictional characters from real people. Machine intelligence expands representational existence at unprecedented scale and fidelity, bringing an old question into everyday life and technical systems rather than first asking whether generated things exist.

Laying out these levels changes the inquiry. Asking whether generated things exist is too coarse a question. It lacks precision. The answer is simple: they exist in a particular way.

A generated city exists as an image and plan without yet having land, buildings, roads, residents, property rights, maintenance, or public finances. A designed molecule exists as a candidate structure; its synthesis, purification, metabolism, safety, dosage, and clinical consequences remain to be established. A robot action successful in simulation exists as a model state; real friction, collisions, wear, errors, and responsibility boundaries must still test it. A fully articulated persona in language exists as a narrative object; embodiment, temporal continuity, returning consequences, and accountability require separate examination. These exist at lighter levels.

The sharper question is at which level an entity exists, through which edge it enters reality, and who bears its consequences. Something can exist as text, image, code, simulation, candidate, physical structure, living process, social institution, or object of responsibility. Different levels face different constraints, maintenance conditions, and reversal difficulties. Representations can be spoken, drawn, generated, copied, and changed; material entities occupy space, bear loads, consume energy, and maintain structures; living entities metabolize, repair, adapt, reproduce, and respond; social entities require recognition, enforcement, trust, and accountability; subjects maintain boundaries over time and bring action consequences back within them. Passage between levels becomes more urgent than the levels alone.

\subhead{Decoupling Weight from Reach}

Here technological viscosity meets ontology. Viscosity means more than slow execution, conservative organizations, or scarce resources. Light-to-heavy transformations pass through materials, free energy, time, structure, verification, and responsibility. Represented cities, molecules, actions, institutions, and personalities arise quickly; real cities, drugs, capabilities, institutions, and subjects must settle accounts with the world. Machine intelligence sharply reduces candidate costs and may improve verification and execution; actual changes must still determine the target level’s material, operational, and responsibility expenditures.

Existence is therefore more than a ladder. A ladder marks different weights: representations lighter, matter heavier, life heavier still, and social entities and subjects facing more conditions of settlement. Intelligence reveals another crucial fact: \term{conversion edges} connect levels without requiring passage up every intervening rung. Some edges are heavy, others light; technology opens previously near-absent edges, while some apparently easy edges move costs elsewhere. Low resistance often reflects deferred, outsourced, or relocated costs within structures whose burdens are not yet visible.

Separating levels from edges lets us locate systems. A system’s conversion signature defines its ontological identity here: where it generates, where accounts settle, which edges connect them, and who bears maintenance, reversal, and responsibility, beyond technical architecture alone. Generative intelligence chiefly opens low-resistance edges from representation to society: outputs enter attention, trust, opinion, workflows, and collective judgment. Embodied intelligence opens execution edges into material action: policies connected to sensors, controllers, and actuators face friction, inertia, collision, energy use, errors, and safety boundaries. A heavier edge enters living processes: sequences, structures, and regulatory plans read, expressed, replicated, and spread through inheritance or ecology enter metabolism, development, reproduction, evolution, and ecological consequences rather than remaining candidates.

The ontological novelty of machine intelligence lies in changing the connections in the graph of transitions between forms of existence, rather than building a new floor. More precisely, \key{It decouples weight from reach.} In the old world, heavy forms of existence were usually hard to reach: bridges, cities, drugs, institutions, identities, and responsibility all required materials, time, organization, execution, and recognition, and the heavier they were, the slower and harder they were to reach. The new channels opened by machine intelligence let some lightweight carriers reach layers of substantial consequence at low cost. A generated artifact may itself be light, yet become heavy at the social level once it changes people's choices, relationships, expectations, and distribution of responsibility; a strategy may itself be light, yet enter material settlement once it drives a vehicle, robotic arm, or drone; a sequence may itself be light, yet enter deeper irreversibility once living processes read and replicate it.

\subhead{Where Weight Falls}

Light entities have not escaped settlement. Accounts settle elsewhere: in attention, platform rules, organizational decisions, trust structures, physical forces, living processes, and later paths of action that are hard to reverse. A light generated object can mobilize heavy responses; deleting its carrier need not reverse its consequences. Creation costs and deletability alone therefore cannot measure its weight. Maintenance, reversal of consequences, and the structures ultimately bearing those costs matter more. The most dangerous combination may be an extremely light carrier and extremely heavy consequences.

Weight always falls somewhere. Physical burdens take physical effect: rock mass is independent of recognition, and disbelief cannot remove bridge loads or fatigue. Social weight differs. Debt weighs through recognition, collection, and enforcement; identity through institutional and personal recognition; money through exchange networks; machine personas through users’ attention, emotion, trust, and time. At the levels of society and subjecthood, weight increasingly becomes relational rather than intrinsic. A persona may weigh heavily for a dependent user and almost nothing for a system that does not recognize it. The same output can weigh heavily in an organization’s decisions and remain mere text to an observer. Its weight depends on who pays for its maintenance, alongside creation and platform-operation costs.

Intelligence also changes representation by creating self-reinforcing loops. Representations once drew chiefly from reality. Maps came from land, drawings pointed to engineering, accounts to transactions, photographs to scenes, and models required empirical calibration. Generated content now enters data that train models, \cite{shumailov2024ai} which generate further content entering attention, distribution platforms, and the next information environment. Representations can form self-replicating loops beyond reflecting reality. This is a branching: a representational layer reproduces with inadequate real calibration while entering society through platforms, relationships, and trust to produce actual consequences, rather than virtuality replacing reality. The danger is a poorly calibrated representational environment continually influencing judgment, relationships, and action, beyond a virtual world replacing the real one.

A related logic carries more weight in living processes. A candidate structure stably read, replicated, inherited, spread, and selected within life may cease depending on its original designer’s continuing maintenance. It propagates through life’s own mechanisms. Generation has then opened an entry into self-replication rather than producing an ordinary representation. This grants no power to create arbitrary life. Metabolism, development, stability, reproduction, ecology, and evolution constrain biological space: combinability does not establish viability, nor design continuity. The weight lies in sequences being read, maintained, and replicated with hard-to-reverse consequences, rather than merely written.

\subhead{Ontology as an Operation}

Ontology is thus a basic operation of intelligence itself, beyond abstract philosophy outside it. Intelligence does not work within an already completed partition of the world. It first divides continuous reality into recognizable, memorable, predictable, actionable units. Life divides benefit from harm; animals prey, threats, paths, and companions; humans names, tools, institutions, and responsibility; science variables, models, scales, and systems; computers data structures, state spaces, and algorithmic objects. Machine intelligence carries this partitioning into mass generation, rapid conversion, and settlement across levels.

A deeper fault line lies here. Human ontology works with objects, boundaries, identities, and responsibility. We partition by one person, one thing, one organization, one action, and one consequence. Machine representations are not wholly organized around familiar discrete objects; much processing instead uses directions, similarities, distributions, and interpolable regions in continuous spaces. Generated objects appear as objects at human interfaces; internal processing need not use objects in the same sense. Human action, responsibility, law, and memory need boundaries, while machines can process similarity in continuous spaces before returning intelligible objects. Images, text, personas, plans, and answers on interfaces temporarily conceal the difference and suggest a shared ontology. Internal partitions need not match the partitions through which humans bear responsibility.

The sharper question concerns how many light carriers machine intelligence sends into consequential levels without corresponding boundaries for bearing consequences. Models influence public judgment; algorithms change prices, rankings, traffic, and opportunities; agents order, screen, recommend, reject, dispatch, and execute; personas become emotional objects and references for decisions. Social consequences need not be borne at the level of a subject: systems can act without committing a body to the outcome, cause consequences without a life history, influence others without necessarily bearing the effects internally, and be relied on without stable boundaries of responsibility.

Entities causing consequences without being constrained by them collide with an old social rule. The actor should also bear responsibility. Natural persons do; companies, organizations, and states build responsibility through law, institutions, property, representatives, and accountability chains despite lacking natural bodies, allowing suit, punishment, constraint, dissolution, compensation, and answerability \cite{dewey1926historic}. Machine intelligence loosens this coupling. Developers, deployers, platforms, users, organizations, and models may all join a consequence chain while responsibility disperses, transfers, and thins into residuals no one bears completely. Rollback capability supports machine intelligence’s power while also explaining why accountability does not arise naturally. Rapid generation, copying, replacement, and reset permit cheap judgment and execution; accountability requires a continuing boundary that consequences change and cannot readily escape.

Here ontology leads to the question of subjecthood. Machine intelligence creates entities with social, material, and even biological consequences but uncertain boundaries as subjects, beyond questions of human resemblance. They are neither nothing nor complete subjects, neither ordinary tools nor traditional legal persons; without being alive they enter relationships, and without bearing responsibility they change consequences. The ontological mistake is forgetting their level of existence, sustaining edge, and ultimate bearer when support fails, rather than believing virtual entities exist.

From the early universe to machine intelligence, existence can be viewed as layering structures while opening new channels. There is nothing wrong with that trajectory. Representation allows reality to be rehearsed, planned, and changed rather than merely happening. Intelligence gains power by making the world tractable before action.

The trajectory also has limits. Lighter representations make real weight easier to forget, faster generation makes conversion costs easier to underestimate, and greater possibility-making demands attention to levels, routes into reality, and consequence-bearers. The world can be represented faster while reality still requires material support, temporal unfolding, biological response, social recognition, and responsibility. Generation is a beginning. Existence needs support, consequences reversal, and responsibility a bearer.

The questions now concern where costs fall, who maintains, who acts, and who bears consequences, beyond what exists. Before cost allocation comes an earlier question. What makes these partitioned, preserved, transmitted, and generated representations reliable?

\subsection{Evidence for Knowledge: What Can Be Relied On After Candidates?}

As representations are expressed, preserved, and relied on more widely, their grounds for reliance become a harder question. An entity can be light yet reach heavy consequences, but we must first ask what supports the judgments directing action before those consequences occur.

\subhead{Calibration Before Propositions}

Knowledge is neither the world itself nor representation itself \cite{ogden1923meaning}. The world runs independently of understanding, and speaking a representation does not make it knowledge. For life, the earliest “knowing” is calibration before propositions: what can be approached, what destroys, what maintains boundaries, and what damages them. Error is a survival problem before it is a logical problem. Mistaking poison for nourishment damages structure rather than merely inviting refutation. Knowledge begins as the formation of dependable distinctions under worldly constraints, beyond pure observation.

\term{evidence} here concerns knowledge that will be relied on, guide action, and enter chains of consequences. Pure mathematics and formal logic provide limiting cases: their evidence comes chiefly from proof, structural consistency, and axiomatic boundaries \cite{godel1931} rather than empirical contact; applications in engineering, computation, finance, governance, and scientific modeling return them to real consequence chains. Evidence takes different forms, but judgments offered for reliance must specify their supporting structures, conditions of transfer, and stopping boundaries. Humans took calibration beyond bodies into language, writing, images, numbers, and institutional records. Experience became transmissible, cumulative, and reusable—and open to forgery, drift, and entrenched prejudice. The crucial achievement was making claims answerable to constraints, beyond speaking. Measurement gives sensation a scale, experiments expose judgments to outcomes, replication loosens dependence on authority, and mathematics and instruments turn differences intuition cannot stably resolve into comparable, inferable, testable structures. Science gives the world a mechanism for rejecting human claims rather than merely multiplying them \cite{popper1934logik}. \subhead{Two Layers of Evidence}

Knowledge needs evidentially supported representations; appearance alone is insufficient. Evidence is not its only condition: Gettier’s counterexamples show that justified true belief can still fail to constitute knowledge \cite{gettier1963justified}. Fluency, completeness, coherent narrative, and authoritative tone cannot confer evidence. Two layers matter: formation through contact, calibration, and review; realization through boundaries and consequences. Contact exposes candidates to constraints, calibration returns errors to judgment, and review moves beyond isolated output; boundaries specify validity and failure, while consequences specify what reliance changes and who bears costs. Both layers matter: formation without stated boundaries and consequences leaves failure conditions unclear; demands about consequences without contact and review leave judgments resting on authority.

How does evidence form? Media change its forms without changing the basic structure. Contact exposes candidates to objects, materials, bodies, environments, behavior, or structural constraints; calibration returns errors to the scale of judgment and changes subsequent judgments; review moves isolated outputs into public testing across people, tools, and settings. Mature knowledge recognizes where it holds and fails rather than projecting boundless confidence; reliance takes judgments into actions that change paths, resources, bodies, organizations, and futures. Unconsequential candidates can remain imagination, drafts, inspiration, or play; bodies, engineering, transport, finance, governance, and biological processes demand more than formal completeness.

Formation and realization of evidence set conditions for machines’ roles without excluding them. Machines can participate in verification. They run tests, compare data, detect anomalies, assist reviews, seek counterexamples, simulate, check consistency, and automate substantial confirmation processes in some closed environments. The question is how real contact sets ultimate verification costs and consequence structures determine sufficiency, rather than whether machines can participate. Synthesis meets materials, treatment bodies, transport roads, engineering loads, biological interventions metabolism and ecology, and institutions human behavior. Accelerating stages alone does not settle how much evidence is enough; boundaries, consequences, risk, and those bearing it determine that standard.

The knowledge question is therefore more than whether machines “really understand.” That question remains within inherited vocabularies of human minds. A firmer question asks whether outputs face sufficient contact, calibration, review, boundaries, and consequence constraints: whether scope, sources, and conditions are explicit, failure traceable, and correction by reality possible. Knowledge is a traceable path of formation rather than an isolated answer. That path begins with contact, tools, settings, and institutions beyond representation alone.

\subhead{Candidate Expansion and Evidence Bandwidth}

Machine intelligence redistributes pressure along this history. Epistemically, it is the largest expansion of representational technology since writing. Writing freed memory from bodies and shifted emphasis from recitation toward understanding, discrimination, and interpretation; printing freed copying from handwriting and shifted emphasis from possessing texts toward screening, checking, and interpretation; computation freed formal deduction and search from mental calculation and shifted emphasis toward model boundaries, data sources, and result verification. Machine intelligence extends this line by sharply lowering candidate costs and improving some verification, while evidential sufficiency remains task- and consequence-dependent. Cheap, abundant candidates reposition humans from answer producers toward designers of evidential structures, judges of boundaries, and builders of dependability.

Machine intelligence first expands candidate space rather than abolishing ignorance. Candidates include explanations, code, policies, experiments, molecules, protein conformations, routes, diagnoses, financial operations, institutional drafts, and biological sequences and regulatory plans, beyond text and screen images. Intelligence produces possible paths awaiting tests rather than automatically established knowledge. Different media require different constraints and verification, but the epistemic question remains: what makes these candidates dependable?

\key{Intelligence expands candidates; verification establishes evidence.}

Both sides of that judgment can now be accounted for. This is the epistemic counterpart to the decoupling of weight and reach. The previous section asked how light carriers cheaply reach heavy consequences; here candidates appear cheaply without necessarily carrying evidence. Ontology asks how light entities produce heavy consequences; epistemology how fast candidates acquire slow evidence. Generation automatically establishes neither existence at a target level nor knowledge: it separates the speed of possibility-making from the speed of bearing real costs. Scarcity once often lay in obtaining information; amplified expression, combination, and search now shift scarcity toward sufficiently constrained claims and dependable paths rather than the mere availability of claims and paths. \term{candidate flux} decouples from \term{evidence bandwidth}: generation accelerates while contact, calibration, review, boundaries, and consequences remain constrained by materials, bodies, time, institutions, and responsibility. Two failures follow: light carriers reach consequential levels without clear bearers, while candidates claim knowledge’s appearance before passing through reality.

Put these rates into one flow relation:

\begin{equation}
\frac{dQ}{dt}=\lambda_{\text{candidate}}-\lambda_{\text{evidence}}
\end{equation}

$Q$ counts candidates not yet through contact, calibration, review, boundary statements, and consequence tests; $t$ is time in years. The candidate arrival rate is $\lambda_{\text{candidate}}$; $\lambda_{\text{evidence}}$ counts candidates completing the required confirmation, including acceptance and rejection. Both rates are candidates per year, matching the right-hand side’s units. Their decoupling requires no additional mechanism: the rates differ. When arrivals exceed confirmation, the stock grows monotonically by their difference without generating its own evidence—the structure behind abundant claims and scarce dependable claims. The rates must use matched granularity and counting units. This simplified queue assumes candidates leave only through confirmation; withdrawal, discarding, deduplication, or direct elimination require additional outflows. It gives a direction rather than a long-term prediction, since rising stocks change screening standards, attention, and institutions, making $\lambda_{\text{evidence}}$ stock-dependent. The relation describes structure without providing measured values.

\subhead{The Shell of Knowledge and Epistemic Viscosity}

Dependability becomes a central scarcity. A fast answer need not be reliable, a complete explanation establish a mechanism, a successful simulated action establish real safety, or a written sequence establish biological controllability. Candidates acquire knowledge’s appearance without automatically gaining grounds for reliance. Errors can be polished, ignorance articulate, and falsehood free of obvious defects. They can be fluent, courteous, systematic, and professional, completing every surface act of expression. Beyond hallucination lies the separation of candidate production from confirmation: formal completion outpaces real calibration, and possibilities expand faster than evidence forms.

This changes intuitions about knowledge. Fluent expression, organized concepts, steady tone, conventional format, and logical coherence long served as credibility signals because producing them usually required training, experience, and institutional backgrounds. Machine intelligence retains the signals’ shell while lowering the threshold for producing it. Epistemology must therefore distinguish evidenced candidates as well as the presence or absence of information. Technological viscosity can in this sense be understood as epistemic viscosity. The world requires judgments to pay contact costs and candidates to face constraints before reliance, rather than lagging behind generation or rejecting intelligence. Generation rapidly explores representations and produces parallel candidates; verification for real action must retain evidential connections to objects, reusing existing records and results where possible, while facing materials, time, experiments, bodies, settings, institutions, and responsibility. Generation is often light; verification grows heavier as candidates pass through real resistance.

Representation’s self-reproduction with inadequate real calibration can enter society through platforms, relationships, and trust, creating the light-carrier, heavy-consequence branching already discussed. Its epistemic consequence now matters. A system drawing chiefly from its own echoes reduces contact, becoming better at internal consistency and potentially worse at withstanding external refutation. Simulations, metrics, models, platform feedback, and organizational reports can form similar self-feeding loops \cite{cinelli2021echo}. Replacing external contact with internal products can yield coherent candidate worlds that no longer know where reality interrupts them. Knowledge retains an interface for refutation and converts it into calibration, beyond being an attractive representation supported by reality.

\subhead{Allocating Verification}

After candidate abundance, allocating verification becomes as difficult as verification itself. Materials, experiments, time, settings, organizations, attention, and responsibility cannot be allocated equally to every candidate. Humans need paths through the flood rather than individual checks of every output: prioritizing irreversible consequences, postponing reliance beyond boundaries, escalating reviews for delayed errors, distinguishing inspiration from permission to act. Verification allocates scarce contact budgets as well as performing technical operations. Knowledge institutions serve this function. Libraries, laboratories, universities, standards, journals, audits, trials, certification, accident investigations, court evidence, and peer criticism form evidence and allocate verification rather than standing outside knowledge \cite{merton1942normative}. Slow, costly, cumbersome, sometimes conservative and rigid, they serve a basic function: preventing fluent representations, elegant models, and successful simulations from bypassing contact and impersonating dependable judgments.

Machine intelligence makes these structures more important rather than eliminating them. Scarce candidates once justified concentrating attention on generation; abundance calls for more screening, verification, tracing, boundary judgment, and prioritization. The scarce capabilities build evidence for answers, identify real constraints for plans, and judge which conclusions merit expensive contact, beyond supplying answers, plans, or conclusions alone. Finite verification budgets shift epistemic work from production toward ranking.

Epistemology in the age of intelligence must ask more than true or false. Truth matters, but earlier comes the question: which constraints has this candidate faced? Where does its evidence come from? Who can review it? How will failure become visible? How are its boundaries stated? What consequence chain will its use enter?

Without answers, it remains a candidate rather than knowledge. Candidates are valuable—human exploration depends on them—but they are a beginning. Epistemology must prevent unsupported candidates from impersonating knowledge and formal completeness from impersonating passage through reality.

Humans’ epistemic role changes rather than disappearing. People increasingly design verification paths, judge boundaries, allocate contact budgets, and build dependability alongside producing answers. Machines can expand candidates and perform many verification steps; selecting worthwhile contact, dependable judgments, sufficient evidence, and priority consequences returns to subjects, values, and consequence-bearers. Placing machine intelligence properly gives it power: mistaking candidates for knowledge creates false certainty, while treating candidates as candidates greatly expands exploration.

After candidates, what can be relied on? Neither maximal fluency, expertise-like appearance, fulfilled expectations, reassurance, nor speed supplies the answer. Expressive appearances alone confer no evidence. Dependability lies in judgments, structures, and paths tested through contact, calibration, review, stated boundaries, and consequences. Knowledge is the form candidates retain after surviving real constraints, rather than language’s victory. Machine intelligence delivers unprecedented candidate abundance rather than an automatic harvest of knowledge. The scarcity is turning those candidates into evidenced, dependable judgments through reality. The question becomes what can be verified, relied on, and permitted into action, beyond what is generated.

\subsection{Permission to Act: When Can Representations Cross Conversion Edges?}

Candidates need evidence; evidence still does not automatically permit action. Knowledge and action meet at a conversion edge rather than a continuous slope. Knowledge makes judgments dependable; action takes them into real processes. One remains representational, while the other begins changing the world’s state. Statistical advantage, local tests, simulation stability, or theoretical institutional coherence leave a heavier question unanswered: may the system consume resources, occupy time, touch bodies, mobilize organizations, alter institutions, and place residual consequences on specific cost-bearing structures?

\subhead{Conversion Edges}

The preceding sections examined existence’s weight and knowledge’s evidence: light carriers reach consequential levels as weight separates from reach, and candidates accelerate beyond evidence bandwidth. A third break now appears: representations gain the power to trigger real change without automatically carrying structures that bear consequences. The question is under which conditions a representation may trigger a real transition, beyond whether it can produce outputs or be believed.

\key{Decoupling the power to trigger action from the structures that bear its costs is the new problem machine intelligence poses for theories of action.}

Actors themselves often supplied cost-bearing structures in earlier settings, though externalities, delegation, and divided responsibility already existed. Action was usually tied to a bounded subject. Acting commits a body, identity, reputation, responsibility, time, and future to a path, beyond issuing instructions or expressing wishes. The actor is a boundary to which consequences return as well as a trigger. Where this coupling holds, failure changes the actor, losses fall on them, responsibility traces back, and future obligations continue constraining them. Committing the actor to consequences gives path selection weight, beyond a light representation \cite{arendt1958human}. Machine intelligence changes the coupling rather than the significance of this structure. Models generate instructions, call tools, alter files, send messages, execute code, access databases, trigger approvals, change rankings, and dispatch equipment. Permissions, interfaces, and workflows trigger real changes that need not return to the model. Models can trigger change without bodily injury, select paths without a lived world, and amplify consequences without asset boundaries, continuous reputation, or sensitivity to punishment. The trigger operates, but costs settle outside its boundary.

\subhead{The Limits of Action Theory}

Traditional theories of action matter without governing this entire chapter. They have long asked what makes an event an action. Is action organized by intention, reasons, desires, beliefs, or plans? \cite{davidson1963actions} Why can a behavior be attributed to an actor? Underlying these questions is the coupling of action attribution and returning consequences. Intentions, reasons, and plans connect why a path is chosen, who chooses it, and who sustains that choice, beyond being inner facts. Planned action lets subjects constrain the present through the future and incorporate consequences into their continuity in advance \cite{anscombe1957intention}. AI agents bring this framework to a boundary. Whether AI has genuine intentions need not be the first question. Systems can trigger real transitions without full intention in the traditional sense. They move money, drive equipment, initiate processes, spread information, alter rankings, and rearrange opportunities. Action theory shifts toward the interfaces by which representations reach reality, their radius of effect, and structures bearing residual consequences, beyond attribution to a subject alone.

This is why agents change the shape of risk. Ordinary generative models first create content risks: error, hallucination, bias, misleading claims, and fabrication. Agents reach action boundaries: permissions, identity, logs, rollback, stopping, monitoring, continued operation, and responsibility scope \cite{openai2025chatgptagentsystemcard}. Reading, understanding, transcription, approval, execution, and review once separated many outputs from action. Reading, writing, querying, dispatching, changing, initiating, calling, and execution can now join one workflow. Models gain triggering power at interfaces beyond expressing possibilities. OpenAI’s March 2026 account of prompt-injection defenses analyzes attacker-influenced sources and consequential tool capabilities along the same path; defenses therefore also constrain actions possible after manipulation \cite{openai2026agentinjection}. Agents lower friction across conversion edges, beyond making models smarter. Organizational friction once delayed errors reaching reality; automation compresses some of it into permissioned calls. Suggestions that once required human translation can now pass continuously through calls into execution. Risk shifts from representation’s correctness toward how it acquires triggering power. Permission to act becomes a primary boundary of entry into real systems rather than an ethical appendix.

\subhead{The Boundary Between Knowledge and Action}

Knowledge and action must be distinguished. Knowledge reduces uncertainty; action spends irreversibility. Verification chiefly accounts for contact budgets, action for irreversibility budgets; physical verification experiments are themselves actions and also need authorization and cost-bearing structures. Reliability increases grounds for reliance without automatically permitting execution. Judgments remain in representational space; actions enter real histories. Many candidates coexist in representation, while real systems follow particular paths. Executing one plan delays, excludes, or removes conditions for others; policies rearrange social incentives; treatment initiates metabolism and immune processes. Knowledge asks what can be believed; action asks whether to spend an irreversible commitment.

Action applies knowledge and exposes its incompleteness to reality. No action waits until its entire future has unfolded. Even substantial evidence reduces uncertainty without completing the future in advance. Action transfers some residual uncertainty from models, text, plans, or simulations into real systems. This is a structural state change rather than rhetorical risk: bodies, equipment, markets, organizations, institutions, and ecologies begin bearing unknown consequences.

Action’s weight lies in its disposition of reachable space as well as the motion itself. Representation holds unrealized possibilities; action realizes one path, using resources, time, and structures while closing some future possibilities. Medication commits bodies to metabolic paths; automated trading puts risk into markets; hiring rules narrow opportunities; grid, traffic, and factory schedules make physical systems respond to their rhythm. Even local rollback cannot fully restore time, opportunities, trust, damage, and historical dependence to their earlier state.

\subhead{Action and Reachable Space}

The discussion returns to structure and reachable space. Chapter 2 showed that withdrawal is not restoration: history, robustness, and structure leave finite plasticity rather than unlimited possibilities. Action reshapes reachable space, closing some options and potentially opening paths. Every irreversible action changes future reachability to some degree. Cheaper path selection, triggering, and execution make irreversible commitments easier. Without authorization, systems may rapidly consume plasticity before recognizing the cost.

Permission to act thus reconnects to RTG. Action turns R from estimated resources into resources occupied, locked, or spent; T from waiting or verification into irreversible history; and G from a structural diagram into activated feedback, coupling, and responsibility chains. RTG coordinates become real accounts at the moment of action. Possible paths become actual paths, and model residuals system residuals.

Different conversion edges carry different weights. Representations entering social judgment first change attention, trust, and expectations. False images, fabricated citations, professional-sounding explanations, and automatically distributed conclusions enter beliefs, organizations, and public discussion. Consequences may contaminate judgment rather than directly injuring bodies.

Physical execution makes consequences more direct. Policies connected to vehicles, robot arms, grids, drones, factories, or medical devices become forces, heat, speeds, movements, collisions, wear, and faults, beyond probability distributions. Entry into biological processes crosses a heavier edge. Life reads, metabolizes, amplifies, repairs, resists, compensates, and evolves rather than serving as a passive carrier. Institutional decisions bring consequences especially easy to underestimate. Scoring in hiring, risk models in credit, prediction in policing, and allocation algorithms in education or medicine rearrange people’s reachable spaces rather than merely offering advice \cite{oneil2016weapons}. \subhead{Rebuilding Cost-Bearing Structures and Sustaining Authorization}

Permission to act does more than add another safety requirement. It reconnects triggering power to the structures bearing costs where they have separated. In many traditional actions, subjects supplied part of the gate by committing themselves to consequences; organizations and institutions still had to handle externalities and divided responsibility. Machine triggering can detach from that commitment, so authorization must reattach cost-bearing structures at the point of action. Without this reconstruction, triggering operates without a structure to settle its costs.

Several mechanisms reattach that structure. Verifiability, stoppability, rollback, traceability, and accountability rebuild cost-bearing relationships rather than forming a flat governance checklist. Verification helps identify residuals, stopping interrupts propagation, rollback contains local consequences, tracing locates sources, and accountability supplies a boundary for returning consequences. Together they ask whether uncertainty entering reality has structures to carry, contain, and return its effects, beyond checking compliance.

Permission to act is not a stamp on knowledge; it rebuilds the structures that bear costs before action is triggered.

A human in the loop is insufficient by itself. The person needs a real position within the cost-bearing structure rather than a formal presence. Someone reduced to clicking confirmation is a liability buffer in automation rather than a gatekeeper. Without seeing model boundaries or consequence chains, changing execution paths, or having time to judge, a person carries nominal responsibility rather than supervising. Effective oversight requires seeing boundaries, understanding residuals, changing paths, stopping processes, and occupying a real place in the return of consequences \cite{santoni2018meaningful}. In May 2026, Anthropic reported that users approved roughly 93\% of permission prompts in its Claude Code telemetry, discussed approval fatigue from repeated confirmations, and emphasized environmental isolation and access boundaries to limit action \cite{anthropic2026contain}. Conversion edges are often crossed gradually. Assistance becomes recommendation, recommendation default, default automation, and automation infrastructure that no one fully understands or questions. Interfaces, workflows, performance pressures, and organizational inertia move representations toward reality incrementally. The result is an entrenched path rather than one sudden overstep.

Continuously operating agents need authorization beyond deployment. Tool calls, feedback, and adaptive policies form a sustained causal pipeline rather than one action. Authorization must specify radius of effect, permissions, update frequency, monitoring, stopping conditions, and responsibility loops. One passed test supports starting under particular conditions rather than unlimited authority through every future feedback state. Continuing action requires continuing authorization. The assessment concerns cost-bearing structures once representations gain triggering power, beyond brilliance, coherence, or inspiration. Representations with no clear bearer for residual uncertainty can remain candidates, explanations, simulations, or assistance without receiving execution authority. The threshold for action is making residuals bearable, rather than completing knowledge.

The threads converge: light carriers reach heavy consequences, fast candidates acquire slow evidence, and triggering power requires reconstructed cost-bearing structures. Otherwise machines generate more candidates while spending irreversibility faster, narrowing reachable space, and externalizing residuals onto unprepared bodies, organizations, and institutions. Action places residual uncertainty in reality, but locating consequences does not identify their bearer. Bodies, markets, organizations, platforms, deployers, users, and affected parties may carry consequences without clear boundaries of return. The next question is what kind of boundary qualifies as a bearer of consequences.


\section{Boundaries of Consequence-Bearing: Where Do Consequences Return?}

Once action occurs, consequences fall on particular people, organizations, and environments. The sites producing and bearing consequences can differ, while control and responsibility disperse. Subjects of responsibility considered here need stable identities, reachable resources, records, and mechanisms returning consequences. Human personhood and fundamental rights have their own ethical and institutional grounds; responsibility structures determine who explains, corrects, and compensates for an action. “Reaction” here means the damage, losses, and future restrictions arising from action, with attention to whether they return to the same boundary of responsibility.

\subsection{Subject Boundaries: Returning Consequences and Visible Responsibility}

Residual uncertainty entering reality needs a boundary to bear its costs, and boundaries have a long intellectual history. For much of that history, inquiry began with the world rather than the subject. Ontology asked what exists, what is real, whether change conceals stable structures, and how things become what they are. Humans were in the world without necessarily occupying inquiry’s center, facing a larger order of nature, gods, substance, form, laws, and cosmic structure. The focus was how the world holds together.

\subhead{From Ontology to Subjecthood}

Modern philosophy brought the knower into greater prominence. The world is experienced, known, judged, and expressed as well as existing. The subject came to the foreground. Experience and judgment prompted the question: who knows? What makes knowledge reliable? Where does judgment obtain certainty? Humans became a center of appearance and meaning-making as well as occupants of the world. The subject became a condition of how the world is grasped, beyond one existent among others \cite{kant1781kritik}. The inquiry can also move from knowledge to action. People change the world as well as observing and interpreting it. Technology, industry, experiments, organizations, engineering, and institutions turn judgments into real forces. Who acts therefore joins who knows. Action changes states and produces irreversible consequences, making the world an intervened-in, reconstructed, damaged, or repaired process rather than an object alone. Modern intelligence pushes the question further. Systems judge, trigger processes, operate machines, participate in experiments, and affect transport, medicine, finance, education, and living processes, beyond expression and assistance to knowledge. The question becomes where consequences return after change, beyond who knows or changes the world.

This line of inquiry connects ontology, subjecthood, action, and consequence-bearing. Ontology asks how the world exists, epistemology how it can be grasped, and theories of action how it can be changed; in the age of intelligence, the question of the subject must also ask who bears the consequences of that change. Intentions, bodies, actions, and consequences were often bound within one living or institutional boundary; generation, execution, gains, and harms can now disperse across different sites. Action occurs and the world changes, yet the consequences need not return to the site producing the difference. The question of the subject becomes urgent as intelligent systems enter reality and effects separate from their returning consequences, beyond machines merely learning to speak like people. Can a boundary count as a full subject if it only changes the world without being changed by those changes in return? At least from the standpoint of consequence-bearing, it remains a site from which unowned action arises.\key{Another route into subjecthood runs beyond narratives of consciousness: where do consequences return, and whom do they keep changing?}

The previous section asked when candidates, judgments, plans, or instructions may cross representations into real systems. Here we ask where the reaction returns once action enters reality. Without authorization, action may come too soon; without subject boundaries, consequences lack a bearer. The shortage is not action: it becomes easier to generate, trigger, and amplify. What is scarce is reconnecting action to boundaries that bear its consequences.

\subhead{The Boundary to Which Consequences Return}

Saying “I” does not establish subjecthood. Self-reference, explanation, preferences, plans, and admissions of error can produce its appearance. Action capability alone does not establish it either. Changing the world does not show that the resulting reactions return to the system itself.

A subject first appears where action and reaction close: action originates there, consequences return there, costs accumulate there, and future actions become constrained. The defining feature is the destination of consequences rather than the starting point of action alone. Model judgments, embodied actions, and proposals for biological intervention are insufficient by themselves. Errors, damage, failure, shame, broken trust, reputational change, bodily costs, lost time, and future restrictions must return within one continuing boundary. Without returning consequences there is only output; without accumulated costs no subject forms.

Feedback and bearing consequences differ, though one system can contain both. Feedback can be light. Thermostats and control systems have feedback; models update from errors and robots adjust paths after collisions \cite{wiener1948}. Feedback describes correction and improved effectiveness. Consequence-bearing differs. Costs return to actors, leave traces that cannot freely be erased, and change future action possibilities. Parameter updates are not remorse, replanning is not responsibility, and reducing a loss function is not paying a price. Feedback returns information; consequence-bearing returns costs. Subjecthood begins with bearing consequences rather than feedback alone.

Human bodies directly show where consequence-bearing begins. They form subject boundaries because life processes are difficult to escape, rather than through a mysterious human privilege \cite{merleauponty1945}. Mistakes can bring pain, shame, lost time, damaged relationships, changed reputations, and memories repeatedly returning to consequences. People cannot easily reset versions like models, replace themselves painlessly like components, or outsource aging, injury, and death to another instance. Humans naturally approach subjecthood because escaping themselves has a cost, rather than because they are nobler.

\subhead{Two Ways to Encapsulate Consequences}

\term{encapsulation of consequences} means consequences cannot disperse at will. Bodies remember wounds, nerves fear, habits repetition, relationships betrayal, reputations choices, and time irreversibility. An “I” is a continuing boundary formed by consequences returning, folding, and compacting through body, memory, relationships, and time, beyond self-narration. The subject is continuity rewritten by past action rather than a static core. Living subjects cannot completely reset after each action; they carry accumulated consequences onward.

Bodies, perception, and action can make embodied machines appear to have acquired subjecthood. That inference fails. Shells, joints, sensors, and actuators form physical boundaries without automatically forming subject boundaries. Machines break, parts and models are replaced, bodies scrapped, data recovered, and costs transferred. Many consequences fall on manufacturers, users, deployers, environments, and affected people rather than returning to the machine. Bodies become meaningful to subjecthood when consequences accumulate within them, rather than when they merely execute \cite{dreyfus1972what}. Living organisms differ. Their bodies are long-evolved structures for bearing consequences rather than temporary interfaces. Morphology, reflexes, pain, recovery, habits, and finite lifespans encapsulate much complexity. Machines do not naturally inherit that evolutionary amortization. They can act without necessarily bearing consequences, enter space without necessarily bringing its reactions back within themselves, and change bodies without necessarily bearing the aftermath. This separates embodiment from subjecthood.

A natural body is not required for every form of subjecthood. Organizations lack pain, flesh, and biological death, yet assets, accounts, history, reputation, identity, and long-term constraints can establish institutional boundaries \cite{dewey1926historic}. Past actions change future capabilities, trust, and restrictions. Consequences accumulate institutionally, letting the past rewrite the institution. Biological bodies hold no monopoly on subjecthood. Living and institutional structures can both encapsulate consequences. What matters is sustained closure within a boundary rather than material alone.

\subhead{Unowned Action and Visible Responsibility}

Whether closure exists is readily apparent in most intelligent systems. The problem with most current systems is that their boundary of closure has yet to form, rather than that they fail to resemble humans. Large models generate judgments, but their consequences do not naturally return to the model; embodied systems execute actions, but the consequences need not accumulate within the machine itself; intelligence applied to living systems proposes interventions, but the people classified, screened, treated, and optimized bear the long-term results. The more intelligence can generate, act, and intervene in life, the wider this gap becomes: the system produces differences, while the consequences fall elsewhere. Beneath the question of who is responsible lies another: does the action belong to anyone? Without a subject boundary, action becomes mere output; without consequence-bearing closure, reality becomes feedback data; without costs returning, errors are distributed to places no one sees. A system can become more effective while bearing less, and more capable of action while having less of an owner. This reduction of the world to pure output is what must be prevented.

Making responsibility visible brings consequences swallowed by the system back into view, beyond adding an external clause. When an action affects only the actor, consequences often register directly: falling hurts, failure leaves a memory, relationships can break, and time cannot run backward. When models, machines, organizations, and biological technologies amplify action, consequences can be delayed, concealed, reduced to statistics, or passed on, becoming losses no single site truly feels \cite{matthias2004responsibility}. Responsibility thus exceeds a moral label attached afterward. It gives a subject boundary social expression. Action must leave an answerable destination as well as an effect.

Subjecthood is therefore a matter of how strongly consequences close back on a boundary, rather than a binary label. Tools have almost no such closure: when a hammer injures someone, the consequences return to its user. Ordinary agents have goals and feedback but need not bear consequences. An institutional subject has no natural body, yet consequences can accumulate in organizational memory and long-term constraints. Living subjects possess the strongest encapsulation of consequences: body, memory, relationships, aging, and death lock consequences into one life process. Engineered subjects may emerge, but their status would depend on persistent identity, memory that cannot be arbitrarily reset, accumulated real costs, an externally answerable boundary, and enduring constraints on their future, rather than the ability to say “I” \cite{parfit1984reasons}. An account of subjecthood need neither defend some human mystery nor rule out a form of subject status for machines. It offers a criterion: what is continually rewritten by the consequences of its actions begins to approach subjecthood; what only produces differences while always shifting their costs remains a conduit. The danger in the age of intelligence is the multiplication of actions whose consequences disperse until no one owns them, rather than machines coming to resemble humans.

A subject is more than something that can say “I.” A subject is where consequences can no longer be passed on at will. It binds action, reaction, memory, cost, and future constraints together. Without that boundary, intelligent systems become more capable of changing the world and less susceptible to being changed by it: actions multiply while owners dwindle. Machine bodies sharpen the question. Engineering can strengthen perception, execution, wear resistance, and self-maintenance; material boundaries and consequence-bearing boundaries remain distinct, and a stronger body does not automatically close the loop of consequences.

\subsection{Consequence-Bearing Closure: From Machine Bodies to Engineered Subjects}

Engineering raises another question that is easier to misjudge: does a machine with a body, able to perceive, act, wear out, and repair itself, come closer to being a subject? The question matters because intelligence has several distinct entry points into reality. Large models bring outputs into social judgment, embodied intelligence brings bodies into the material world, and intelligence applied to living systems brings proposed interventions into metabolism, development, immunity, heredity, and ecology. Each carries more weight than words on a screen, and each invites the same mistake: assuming that greater contact with reality means greater subjecthood.

\subhead{Entry into Reality and the Subject Boundary}

An entry point into reality does not establish a subject boundary. A system can produce judgments without bearing their consequences, possess a body without bearing the costs of its actions, or propose biological interventions without bearing their metabolic, developmental, and intergenerational effects. Entry into reality establishes that an effect has occurred, not that its consequences have returned to the same enduring boundary. Subjecthood does not grow automatically from output, a body, or the ability to intervene in life. It appears where consequences return, accumulate, and constrain the future of the same boundary.

The first step is to distinguish body, embodiment, and subjecthood. The body is a material boundary: it specifies the physical structure through which a system enters the world. Embodiment couples that material boundary to its environment through action: it specifies how the system perceives, consumes energy, undergoes disturbance, corrects itself, and continues acting. Subjecthood concerns returning consequences and consequence-bearing closure: after action, do costs return to a continuous boundary that cannot simply be escaped? The three are connected, but none can substitute for another.

Bodies can be engineered. Sensors can be added, actuators upgraded, joints maintained, materials made compliant, energy allocated, local control accelerated, and self-diagnostics run continuously. Future machine bodies may develop stronger abilities to maintain and repair themselves: detecting wear, repairing surface cracks, reallocating energy, and continuing at reduced capability after local damage \cite{terryn2017self}. These remain, first of all, achievements of bodily engineering rather than the creation of a subject.

This distinction can be expressed as a ratio measuring only the coverage of returning consequences. Let $B$ be an enduring boundary, $a$ an action it initiates, $C(a)$ the set of all consequences of that action, and $\rho_a$ a map assigning each consequence to the boundary that ultimately carries it. Define the proportion of consequences returning to $B$ for action $a$ as

\begin{equation}
\kappa(B,a)=\frac{\bigl|\{\,c\in C(a):\ \rho_a(c)=B\,\}\bigr|}{\lvert C(a)\rvert},
\qquad \kappa\in[0,1].
\label{eq:ch33-closure}
\end{equation}

Here $C(a)$ is assumed to be finite, nonempty, and consistently itemized, with $\rho_a$ assigning each item to one boundary. $\kappa$ records only the coverage of returning consequences on this list. Actual consequences may be shared or impossible to count; both itemization and weighting change the result. The ratio helps us ask where consequences belong; it does not measure consciousness, moral status, or subjecthood as a whole. Insurance and public assistance can legitimately distribute consequences, so complete return cannot be a universal goal.

\subhead{Absorbing Residuals and Bearing Consequences}

Residual absorption and consequence-bearing must be distinguished. Once an embodied system enters the physical world, slippage, friction, inertia, contact errors, sensor drift, and deviations across a task sequence all require handling. The body can absorb them, the controller correct them, environmental constraints contain them, and external support structures share them. Residual absorption determines whether action can continue. Consequence-bearing asks to whom the action belongs. Embodiment invites confusion because it brings these questions so close together: the machine really does handle real-world residuals, making it appear to bear real-world consequences as well.

Being changed by reality does not by itself make something a subject that bears reality’s consequences. Stone weathers, bridges fatigue, tires wear, batteries degrade, databases receive writes, models undergo fine-tuning, and machines retain logs. All leave traces through time, but those traces need not constitute an actor’s history. Being changed is a physical fact; bearing consequences incorporates them into a continuity that can be held to account. The distinction is between carrying consequences and bearing them. Tires carry friction, robotic arms reaction forces, batteries discharge cycles, and casings impacts and wear. Once a machine enters the physical world, consequences necessarily reach some components. Carrying means that consequences reach a \term{physical carrier}; bearing requires them to enter the same enduring boundary, change its future space of possibilities, and prevent it from escaping its past at no cost.

If a service robot damages the corner of a wall, its casing may be scratched, its wheels misaligned, its logs updated with an anomaly, and its control policy revised. Physical consequences have reached the machine, and information has returned to the system. Yet the substantive consequences may fall on the user, manufacturer, deployer, physical environment, and affected people. The machine body carries one part of the chain without necessarily being its final destination. It has been affected, but need not have become a bearer of consequences. Consequence-bearing therefore requires at least several conditions: consequences return to the same boundary rather than merely reaching replaceable parts; they change that boundary’s future possibilities rather than merely triggering repair or parameter adjustment; gains, restrictions, and repercussions constrain the same continuing entity rather than dispersing across different sites; and that boundary remains externally answerable rather than disappearing among versions, instances, supply chains, and maintenance chains. Without these conditions, even a machine body that wears out is only a material interface through which consequences pass, rather than a subject boundary to which they belong.

\subhead{Self-Protection and Living Encapsulation}

Many discussions treat self-protection as evidence of subjecthood; this inference also needs unpacking. Avoiding obstacles does not establish fear of injury; returning on a low battery does not establish concern for the future; detecting faults does not establish an understanding of vulnerability; repairing itself does not establish that a robot has borne trauma. Obstacle avoidance can be a control objective, returning an energy strategy, and self-repair a material mechanism. These mechanisms can be complex and effective, but their immediate role is to maintain function rather than establish an “I” that cannot escape itself \cite{metzinger2003being}. Why do living organisms differ? Life encapsulates consequences more deeply; no mysterious subject hidden inside an organism is needed to explain the distinction.

Body, metabolism, pain, recovery, development, memory, relationships, and death press consequences into the same process, which cannot be replaced at will. Bodily injury changes the capacity to act and the time ahead, beyond a fault in one component; pain brings damage within the same living boundary, beyond an indicator light; death ends continuity, beyond scrapping a casing. Life has greater difficulty passing costs elsewhere, rather than greater nobility. An organism cannot freely replace its entire body, painlessly migrate its memories into another instance, restart from a clean version after failure, or have an equivalent copy bear aging and death in its place. Subjecthood arises from continuity that cannot escape itself at no cost, rather than simply from moving flesh.

A machine body does not automatically inherit this continuity. It may have a serial number, location, casing, sensors, and maintenance records while remaining a replaceable instance. Worn joints can be replaced; faulty models rolled back; retired bodies succeeded by identical machines; failed policies erased in a new version. Machines can certainly have histories, but these often belong to a platform, fleet, manufacturer, external operating structure, or database rather than to the individual executing the action. Recording a history does not establish that it is borne.

\subhead{Conditions for Consequence-Bearing Closure}

Machines may develop subjecthood, but a body alone does not establish it. Any future engineered subject would need more than a humanlike shape or finer tactile skin: it would need engineered consequence-bearing closure, including persistent identity, a history that cannot be arbitrarily reset, accumulated real costs, future actions constrained by past consequences, an externally answerable boundary, and a structure that cannot pass every cost to users, deployers, the environment, and affected people. Such a structure need not be biological. Organizations have no natural bodies, yet assets, reputation, legal identity, historical records, and long-term constraints can establish institutional boundaries. They feel no pain, yet consequences accumulate; they have no flesh, yet their identity can end. Flesh has no monopoly on subjecthood, but subjecthood requires consequences that cannot simply disperse.

This explains three mismatches in intelligence’s entry into reality. For large models, representations influence real judgments without bearing their consequences; for embodied intelligence, bodies absorb real-world residuals without necessarily owning the costs of action; for intelligence applied to living systems, proposals enter biological processes without necessarily bearing their long metabolic, developmental, hereditary, and ecological consequences \cite{floridi2013distributed} \cite{nissenbaum1996accountability}. The later the entry point, the greater the burden carried by the receiving medium, yet the system itself need not become more of a subject. The risk is intelligence entering domains of ever greater consequence while continuing to leave costs elsewhere, rather than increasingly resembling people.

To judge whether an intelligent system approaches subjecthood, examine its consequence-bearing closure rather than human resemblance or bodily presence alone. A system can combine high output with little subjecthood, extensive embodiment with little subjecthood, or deep biological intervention with no consequence-bearing closure; conversely, an organization can establish a subject boundary institutionally without a natural body. Representation opens a route to real-world influence, the body to material coupling, and biotechnology to living processes; subjecthood concerns the strength of closure through which consequences return and remain continuously borne.

\subhead{Coupling, Self-Correction, and Replaceability}

At a deeper level, intelligent systems enter reality through several distinct couplings. Representational coupling concerns which candidates a system can generate and which judgments it can influence. Material coupling concerns whether it can act reliably in the physical world. Biological coupling concerns which living structures read, amplify, resist, retain, or propagate a proposed intervention once it enters a living process. Consequence-bearing coupling concerns whether consequences return to an enduring boundary. The first three explain entry into reality; the last reaches the question of subjecthood.

This also explains why self-correction alone does not establish subjecthood. Large models can reconsider outputs, embodied systems can monitor wear and schedule maintenance, and systems working on biological problems can update candidates, optimize doses, and adjust interventions in response to experiments. All appear to correct themselves, but correction does not establish consequence-bearing. Correction begins to approach consequence-bearing only when an error does more than produce a new version, policy, treatment course, or candidate: its consequences must alter the future of the same enduring boundary in a way that cannot simply be transferred elsewhere.

The deeper dividing line concerns replaceability. As an engineering object, a body tends toward modularity, maintainability, replaceability, and replicability. Engineering seeks to reduce dependence on irreplaceable points: damaged parts can be replaced, errors rolled back, instances migrated, capabilities reused, and effects isolated. This improves reliability while weakening the automatic emergence of subjecthood. A subject requires continuity that cannot be wholly replaced, whereas engineering often improves resilience through replaceability. The better a machine is as an engineering object, the less that fact alone establishes its subjecthood.

The goals diverge without contradicting each other. An engineered body seeks maintainability; a subject boundary requires answerability. Engineering seeks fault isolation; subjecthood requires accumulated costs. Engineering seeks instance migration; subjecthood requires continuity of identity. Engineering seeks to minimize external effects; the criterion for subjecthood asks where consequences ultimately return. A body can become stronger, more flexible, and more internally coherent, yet remain a conduit into reality rather than the destination of consequences if those consequences are still borne elsewhere.

\subhead{An Inescapable Boundary}

Bodies can be engineered while subjecthood is not automatically inherited: this is the dividing line. Bodily engineering handles disturbances, reducing downtime, damage, and loss of control; a subject boundary prevents consequences from disappearing. One absorbs residuals; the other asks who retains the costs. Mature engineering can hide faults within maintenance, replacement, redundancy, and external support; clearer subjecthood requires those hidden consequences to return to an answerable boundary. The two can support each other without establishing each other.

The hardest criterion is this: \key{Judge subjecthood by whether a system can escape its consequences, rather than whether it can protect its components.} If a system distributes harm to users, assigns risk to external structures, files errors under versions, leaves damage to maintenance, migrates identity to a new instance, and then reappears as clean capability, it has yet to become a subject. Conversely, a boundary begins to approach subjecthood, even without being biological, if it cannot escape in this way: past actions continue to constrain it, define it, hold it to account, and alter the paths available to it.

Subjecthood is no automatic upgrade from having a body. Bodies bring machines into the world, embodiment closes action loops within it, and biotechnology brings intelligence into the heavier processes of life; subjecthood requires the world to return the consequences of action to the same enduring boundary. It emerges where costs can no longer be passed on, rather than from sensors, actuators, biological intervention, or self-description alone. No single entry point into reality therefore establishes subjecthood automatically. Output, bodies, feedback, self-maintenance, and biological intervention show only that a system has connected to reality in some way; they do not yet show where consequences return. A boundary begins to acquire the significance of a subject only when consequences continually return to it and change how it can exist, act, and be held to account. Embodiment brings a machine into reality; consequence-bearing makes a boundary a subject.

Closure within one boundary supplies only half the criterion. An action rarely crosses just one boundary: platforms, developers, deployers, organizations, users, and affected people each bear some consequences, through multiple return paths and at multiple destinations. When consequences disperse across these paths, where does closure occur, who decides which boundary bears which part, and how are costs allocated among bearers? These questions remain open.

\subsection{Distributed Consequence-Bearing: What Companies Establish and Models Lack}

The preceding section left a question unanswered: when consequences disperse across several return paths, where does closure occur, and who decides which boundary bears which part? To answer it, start with an example that already has an operational arrangement. One kind of subject neither eats nor breathes, has no nervous system, and has neither a life history independent of its members nor bodily pain. It can own property, enter contracts, be sued, be fined, and be compulsorily dissolved. It answers for its actions. That subject is the company.

\subhead{A Problem Given Institutional Form}

Corporate liability is now so familiar that its constructed nature passes unnoticed. A company is no natural object. It is a boundary for bearing consequences assembled through legal devices. Assembling those devices took centuries; a crucial step was limited liability, which separates shareholders’ liability from the company’s. Under Chinese company law, for example, shareholders of a limited liability company are liable to the company up to their subscribed contributions, shareholders of a joint-stock company up to their subscribed shares, and the company answers for its debts with all its property. In a UK company limited by shares, members’ liability is generally limited to the amount unpaid on their shares \cite{prc2023companylaw,uk2006companiesact}. Limited liability is often treated as an economic policy encouraging investment. Its structural role is more basic: separating corporate from shareholder property gives responsibility an identifiable property and legal boundary. Within that boundary are assets to seize, accounts to inspect, representatives to summon, and an entity to dissolve. The boundary makes accountability an operational procedure rather than an endless search backward. This arrangement establishes an entity to hold accountable without guaranteeing compensation for every loss: finite assets, bankruptcy, and the scope of remedies can still leave consequences with creditors, victims, or society.

This provides a yardstick. It identifies conditions a system needs to become a bearer of consequences. Applying it to machine intelligence reveals what is missing, but first the yardstick itself needs explanation.

\subhead{Four Conditions for a Consequence-Bearing Boundary}

Disassembling the corporate structure reveals four things working together. The first is \term{identifiable, bounded resources}. A company has its own assets and liabilities. Compensation removes actual value from its balance sheet rather than merely expressing regret. A resource boundary gives sanctions a measurable magnitude. The second is \term{stable identity}. A company persists across years, changes of management, and employee turnover. Today’s company answers for conduct ten years earlier because the two are recognized as the same legal person. Identity carries accountability through time.

The third is \term{internal state changes following sanctions}. A fine can reduce investable funds, affect credit ratings, raise financing costs, compress pay, or even trigger bankruptcy. Sanctions thus change what that boundary can do in the future. This is the substance of bearing consequences: being changed rather than merely being named. The fourth is \term{a traceable chain of accountability}. A company has directors, senior managers, legal representatives, employees, and shareholders whose powers and responsibilities follow the relevant law and organizational arrangements.

An act can be traced to specific decision points rather than disappearing into the collective. Together, these conditions make consequence-bearing operational. \key{A company can answer for its actions because institutions anchor consequences to a traceable boundary, not because it is conscious.} This section uses the four conditions to examine consequence-bearing structures: a missing condition leaves a corresponding break in the return of responsibility.

\subhead{What Models Lack}

The same yardstick makes the gaps in machine intelligence systems clear. First, the resource boundary is missing. A model as ordinarily deployed does not independently hold assets in law. Can it be fined, and who would pay? If its deploying company pays, the company bears the consequences; the model itself has not become the legal entity paying compensation. This looks like accounting but concerns structure: without identifiable resources, a sanction cannot land on the system and instead falls on people outside it.

Second, establish who maintains continuity of identity. A new model version need not sever responsibility: deployers can retain versions, configurations, records, and continuing obligations. The question is whether past actions remain traceable after an update and whether the boundary bearing the obligations persists.

Third, establish whom sanctions actually change. Fines reduce an institution’s resources, service restrictions alter operating capabilities, and model updates change behavior. These responses can be connected, but people or institutions usually bear the costs and obligations. Calling all of them “punishment of the model” hides where the consequences actually land.

Fourth, a traceable chain of accountability is missing. The problem extends beyond technology. Model creation, fine-tuning, deployment, integration, invocation, and use often span different actors. An output may pass through a model provider, application developer, platform operator, end user, and affected third parties on its way into reality. Each link can introduce an accountability gap, weakening the trail through which responsibility is attributed.

This weakening can be represented by a schematic chain of transmission,

\begin{equation}
R_n=R_0\prod_{i=1}^{n}\alpha_i,\qquad 0\le \alpha_i\le 1
\end{equation}

Here $n$ is the dimensionless number of layers crossed by the action; six or seven layers can serve as an illustration. $R_0$ is the initial share of attribution evidence traceable to decision points and can be normalized to one for comparison; $\alpha_i$ is the dimensionless proportion of attribution evidence retained after transmission from layer $i$ to the next, ranging from 0 to 1; $R_n$ is the share still reaching an answerable boundary after all layers. If each layer loses some traceable evidence, the remainder decreases as a product; adding a link with a retention proportion below one reduces it further. This expresses how responsibility can disperse, shift, and dilute until a residual remains that no one fully bears. Concentrated attribution, recordkeeping duties, and arrangements governing the burden of proof can improve traceability, appearing schematically as increases in some $\alpha_i$, or changing the whole path. The expression assumes separable contributions at each layer without repeated attribution across layers; when one entity provides the model, application, and platform, the chain contracts and $n$ decreases, but traceability still depends on records and institutions. The expression identifies structural positions for investigation rather than a conservation or multiplication law of legal responsibility; estimating $\alpha_i$ requires operational definitions, records, and validation.
