\subsection{Functional Weightlessness: When the Interface Fails}

\subhead{The Abilities That Once Justified a Position}

The preceding sections located value in the capacity to bear consequences, but a new source of value does not ensure a smooth transition from old ways of demonstrating it. The first event in the transition is failure. For decades, a person’s social position rested largely on a set of abilities. Writing organized ideas into forms others could use; calculation supplied reliable numerical judgments amid uncertainty; summarizing extracted structure from large bodies of material; expression steadied meetings, negotiations, and classrooms; planning divided goals into steps, resources, and time.

These abilities share one feature: they produce deliverables. Deliverables can be checked, enter workflows, and generate economic value. People with these abilities therefore needed little further explanation of their value: the deliverable supplied the proof. Ability was directly bound to social position: what someone could do determined the positions they could enter, the tasks for which they were needed, and who would remember them. The bond was so stable that it often passed for the definition of human value rather than one expression of it. Generative systems change that bond.

\subhead{An Interface Fails; Abilities Remain}

The location of the change matters, because a popular account places it incorrectly. The problem is declining power to distinguish people, rather than abilities becoming useless. When a system generates a well-structured report in seconds, clear writing alone says less; when basic data analysis is automated, accurate calculation alone no longer distinguishes who has been trained. People have not necessarily begun writing poorly or calculating incorrectly: output itself has lost much of its signaling power, and a weaker signal differs from a lower level of ability.\key{AI does not immediately abolish human value; it dismantles the old interfaces through which many people demonstrated it.}

Express this discriminatory power as an index,

\begin{equation}
d'=\frac{\Delta\mu}{\sigma}
\end{equation}

Here $\Delta\mu$ is the difference in mean output between two groups on the same evaluation scale, such as trained and untrained people’s mean output quality; $\sigma$ is the standard deviation of individual output on that scale. Both must be estimated on the same scale in comparable samples; their ratio $d'$ is dimensionless and measures how well the scale distinguishes the groups. $\Delta\mu$ can shrink without $\sigma$ shrinking. If acceptable output becomes available by default, the system compresses mean differences while output variation fails to contract proportionately, $d'$ falls; in the limit where the mean difference approaches zero while variation remains positive, the scale loses discriminatory power even if neither group’s existing skills have declined. Interface failure is not the disappearance of ability: the quantity to examine is $d'$, since output mean $\mu$ alone cannot establish changes in existing skills. This formulation assumes comparable scales and roughly equal group variances; substantially different variances require a different definition of discriminatory power. It describes the discriminating power of a scale used as evidence, rather than anyone’s ability, and supplies no measured value by itself.

Interface failure must be distinguished from unemployment, since conflating them both exaggerates and understates the problem. Unemployment concerns a job; interface failure concerns proof of value. Many jobs persist because they occupy viscous stages requiring physical presence, bodies, enduring relationships, and responsibility for consequences, even as workers’ means of evaluating themselves are reorganized. Someone still goes to work every day but no longer knows whether “I can do this” explains their position. The ability remains but is less scarce; the person remains needed, but for some other reason. Imagine someone with twenty years in a field, whose professional judgment has become intuitive, opening a system, typing a few sentences, and receiving output covering eighty percent of routine work. Judgment, selection, and responsibility remain, but the center of work has shifted from production to review, which may not provide the same support for professional identity.

\subhead{Labor, Work, and Action}

The gap runs deep because it concerns the relation between activity and recognition as well as income, a relation already carefully distinguished by another thinker. Hannah Arendt distinguished three human activities: labor sustains biological metabolism and produces things quickly consumed; work makes durable things that outlive their makers; action consists in speaking and acting before others, producing relationships and history rather than objects \cite{arendt1958human}. Her diagnosis was that modern society reduced these activities to labor, measuring everything by the maintenance of life and depriving work and action of independent standing.

The distinction helps locate the current situation. The old ability interface was stable because it joined work to action: making something produced a durable object while giving its maker a position and history within a community; output expressed relations to both things and people. Generative systems chiefly take over work, particularly its standardized, reproducible parts. As that work is taken over, the social recognition attached to it loosens too. The carrier of recognition has changed before a new one has formed, rather than recognition simply being confiscated.

Arendt is both a source of diagnosis and an interlocutor whose argument must be confronted. She places the response in action: plural people become visible and answerable to one another in the public realm, where a person appears as a “who” rather than merely a “what” \cite{arendt1958human}. This book enters through consequence-bearing: a position’s structural value lies in consequences returning there. The two cannot be interchanged. Action has intrinsic value, requiring plurality and others who see and respond; consequence-bearing has functional value, requiring consequences actually to return. By the latter criterion, an entity bearing every consequence alone can qualify; without others, however, there is no public realm in Arendt’s sense.

The substitution has a cost that must stay visible. A criterion of consequence-bearing locates returning consequences without deciding whether that party ought to bear them. It is silent about distribution and can, at worst, read any existing burden as evidence of value. Arendt’s political language preserves the question: is this unjust? Translating lost functional positions into structural language gives this book a more precise map, without thereby giving it the pen that marks legitimacy on that map.

Arendt used “superfluity” for a group’s loss of functional position in society, examining its political consequences under particular historical conditions. This chapter borrows its structural meaning: when a state transition no longer requires a node, the node has not been destroyed; it has slipped out of the process. \key{A position that slips away has no automatic replacement. It is vacant.} Replacement does not happen automatically. Markets and institutions do not automatically find a new place for the displaced node, and existing organizations may have no incentive to take it back. For an organization that has removed the step, its absence no longer creates a workflow problem.

\subhead{Why the Diagnosis Exceeds a Matter of Feelings}

Because positions do not automatically return, popular explanations of this loss of weight deserve scrutiny: they avoid precisely that issue. One offers reassurance: people’s abilities remain; only the tools have changed, so learn the tools. Operationally true, the claim evades the structural problem. Learning the tools does not restore the bond between person and output, because the tools amplify precisely the abilities that can be automated, weakening their power to distinguish people further. Another assigns blame: anyone unable to use the new tools simply has not tried hard enough. It confuses individual adaptability with structural resetting of the interface; no amount of individual improvement can solve a system problem that no longer depends on that ability.

Both explanations locate the problem in the individual, while the interface is what has been displaced. “Interface” matters because it directs the response: an interface specifies an agreed match between what one side supplies, what the other needs, and how they connect. Failure means that the match no longer holds, without implying a defect in either side. When interfaces fail together and affect tens of millions, the problem is structural and its remedy lies with institutions rather than individuals alone. The point is to locate responsibility correctly, rather than absolve individuals.

\subhead{The Scope of the Diagnosis}

The diagnosis needs boundaries, or it will slide toward two unsupported conclusions that weaken the chapter. It predicts the disappearance of no particular profession. Interface failure differs from job elimination: it can spread much further and arrive earlier, affecting many people still employed; treating it as an unemployment forecast understates its reach. Nor does it make professional training pointless. In consequential domains, training forms judgment as well as deliverables: a trained doctor and an untrained person using the same system may still differ markedly in output quality and verification ability, especially in recognizing errors rather than merely knowing more. Lower generation costs increase the importance of judgments that detect errors and carry responsibility.

The weakened layer lies between these poles: standardized production requiring neither deep judgment nor responsibility for major consequences. It once supported substantial knowledge work and many professional identities; its contraction has broad effects yet can fall between agendas concerned with protecting the vulnerable and competing for elite talent. Here is where weight is lost and costs land. The first response is often retreat toward easier feelings of completion rather than resistance, reconnecting with the low-viscosity paths discussed earlier. That retreat is an effect; the cause lies earlier: in compressed stages, people lose both the deliverable and the loop from setting a goal to overcoming resistance.

\subsection{The Broken Power Process and Radical Superfluity}

Interface failure explains a changed position without yet explaining its effect on self-evaluation. Between remaining needed at work and no longer knowing why lies an earlier loop: setting a goal, overcoming resistance, and reaching a result. The loop binds a person to the world through doing the work itself, rather than through output alone.

\subhead{The Power Process and Its Short Circuit}

In \emph{Industrial Society and Its Future}, Theodore Kaczynski placed satisfaction within a “power process”: setting a goal, exerting effort, overcoming resistance, and achieving it; satisfaction comes from overcoming resistance rather than merely receiving the result \cite{kaczynski1995industrial}. Borrowing the loop entails accepting neither its author’s positions nor his verdict on technological civilization. Its mechanism connects with this book’s analysis: a goal is a state to be realized, resistance the cost of reaching it, and work the process of paying. Industrial technological systems take over the middle of the loop. They hand results to users while retaining the overcoming of resistance within the system. People receive finished products without having done that work.

RTG provides a more precise description. In the extreme case where an external system handles almost an entire state transition, R approaches zero for the person; T contracts almost beyond perception; G no longer requires that person’s participation. When all three approach zero, the person contributes almost no effort to the transition and receives less feedback from personally overcoming resistance. Write this as a limit,
\begin{equation}
\eta_{p}=\eta_{0}\exp(\alpha R_{p}+\beta T_{p}+\gamma G_{p}),
\qquad
\lim_{(R_{p},\,T_{p},\,G_{p})\to(0,0,0)}\eta_{p}=\eta_{0}
\label{eq:trip-zero}
\end{equation}
Here $\eta_{p}$ is the viscosity of this state transition for the person; subscript $p$ means that every quantity is accounted for on that person’s side rather than in the system’s physical ledger. $R_{p}$, $T_{p}$, and $G_{p}$ are the resource barrier, temporal rigidity, and topological coupling of the same event in that person’s coordinates; $\eta_{0}$ is the reference viscosity when all three coordinates are zero. The point is less the limiting value than the conjunction of three conditions: $\eta_{p}$ returning to $\eta_{0}$ means that the transition consumes none of the person’s resources or time and passes through none of their connections with other people. All three disappear together, rather than each decreasing slightly. If feedback from personally overcoming resistance is assumed proportional to $\eta_{p}-\eta_{0}$, it also approaches zero in this schematic model; actual changes in feedback and sense of place still require psychological and behavioral evidence. This supplies a testable mathematical form for “receiving a result without experiencing accomplishment.” The claim must remain specific: occasional delivery of a result changes little; the issue arises when external systems take over so much of the loop that what remains cannot sustain a person’s sense of place.

Two compensations often follow when the loop is taken over. One turns elsewhere: people set goals and resistance in domains the system ignores, including competitive activities, collecting, and status contests within particular circles. These activities retain goals, resistance, and results; their difference from externally imposed goals concerns conditions rather than intensity. When goals and resistance can be changed at will, feedback calibrates external constraints less effectively; competition under fixed rules and commitments that cannot be arbitrarily rewritten can still provide rigorous feedback. The other compensation lowers expectations: long-term goals requiring work give way to immediate, inexpensive stimulation.

Psychology offers an earlier line of inquiry into loss of control and passivity. In experiments during the 1960s, Martin Seligman and Steven Maier repeatedly exposed animals to harm their behavior could not control, finding that they subsequently failed to try escaping even when escape became possible \cite{seligman1967failure}. Fifty years later, the authors revised the explanation: the default passive response was not learned; what could be learned was whether one’s actions controlled outcomes \cite{maier2016learned}. The revision better serves this chapter by directing attention to the connection between action and outcome rather than passivity alone. In these experiments with aversive stimuli, learned experience of control helped counter passivity. This suggests examining the connection between action and outcome, while evidence linking animal stress experiments to people’s sense of place when using technology must be established separately.

Kaczynski’s verdict on technological systems goes further than his account of the loop. He argues that an industrial technological system must continually absorb energy, resources, and solutions; stopping expansion means disintegration, while individual dependence closes the route back to older ways. The judgment imposes a thermodynamic curse: the system can neither stop nor retreat. The loop analysis can be retained; the prophecy of an ending requires separate proof. Whether expansion is necessary and dependence irreversible turns on institutions and choices. His argument treats both as constants.

The disagreement extends further. Treating technology as a single actor makes the distribution of viscosity appear intrinsic to technology; in this book’s framework, property rights, labor institutions, public investment, and bargaining power determine where friction is reduced and positions reorganized. Railways, electrification, and assembly lines all removed old frictions, yet produced different structures of positions in Britain and the United States, Germany, and Japan: the same machines replaced different people and left different positions under different institutions. This directly shapes the route out. His proposed exit was destruction of the industrial system, eliminating precisely the distinction this book needs: which frictions are wasteful and should disappear, and which carry obligations that must remain. Destroying both together yields deeper superfluity rather than freedom.

\subhead{Radical Superfluity}

A short-circuited loop explains “I no longer need to do it,” but not yet “I am no longer needed.” That second problem has long been described from another direction. In \emph{The Origins of Totalitarianism}, Arendt used “superfluity” as a structural category rather than a synonym for poverty. This chapter borrows it for a position in which the system no longer needs someone’s actions and participation no longer changes the relevant process; Arendt further argued that masses rendered superfluous were especially susceptible to systems explaining every event with complete consistency and allowing no exceptions \cite{arendt1951origins}.

A physical vocabulary gives this judgment a clearer form. In the old arrangement, a person contributed negentropy: labor and judgment transformed external low-entropy resources into maintainable structures, making that person necessary to the system’s exchanges of energy and information. Once the system no longer needs their participation in that exchange, the functional connection breaks. Disconnection differs from dispossession. Exploitation still presupposes usefulness, even when reward and contribution are disproportionate; superfluity is colder because it need extract nothing from the person. \key{Exploitation still needs people to be useful; superfluity no longer needs even to use them. The coldest part of the functional crisis is the disappearance of the position itself.} Political language struggles to grasp this weightlessness: protest needs a concrete demand, yet here there is no specific thing to demand back.

Superfluity poses another difficulty: statistics barely see it. Unemployment has definitions, rates, benefit counts, and vacancy counts, so it can enter the agenda; superfluity lacks an equivalent measure because it often affects people still employed. Someone may remain employed while feeling their former function has been hollowed out: systems generate more of the output, leaving supervision, repair of outputs, and exceptions the system will not take on—in other words, residual absorption. When handling exceptions becomes the main remaining duty, the position counts statistically as employment while functioning structurally as a buffer. Its stability is weaker than it appears, because if the system takes over the residuals as well, nothing remains in that position requiring human participation.

Two simplifications must also be resisted here. One treats superfluity as a verdict of fate. Loss of a functional position can be reversed: history contains many nodes that slipped from one process and became needed elsewhere, though the new position usually differed from the old. Later sections address this problem. The other assigns responsibility to a single actor. Positions can disappear through accumulated local optimizations rather than conspiracy: each decision removing a step is reasonable at its own scale, yet together they create a node no longer needed. Identifying structure locates responsibility rather than exempting anyone.

The broken power process and the vanished position together explain the functional crisis’s two poles: “I no longer need to do it” and “I am no longer needed.” The broadest and least visible territory lies between them. Many people are neither fully replaced nor fully needed; their layer is being compressed, potentially without a single conspicuous event to trigger protest.

\subsection{Compressible Ordinariness and the Vacuum}

The two poles of the broken power process describe minorities: those wholly taken over and those fully needed. Most people fall between them, in a layer whose changes are harder to describe because they appear as neither unemployment nor overt weightlessness. They appear as compression: needs are met ever more cheaply, while the positions meeting them depend less on particular people.

\subhead{Compressed Needs, Vacant Positions}

Translating a hierarchy of needs into physical terms reveals where compression occurs. Safety, belonging, esteem, and self-actualization are often read as psychological states, but each also corresponds to a connection with external structures: at the bottom, energy inputs such as income and supplies; in the middle, a topological position, the edge one occupies within a system; above, a scope of intervention, the outcomes one’s judgment can change. The three connections differ physically and experience pressure differently.

Machine intelligence’s compression initially reaches the middle layer. Standardizable production—organizing, transcription, summarization, basic coding, routine retrieval, and template design—forms an important part of many middle-tier knowledge jobs. Compression begins on the supply side: when generating some products becomes orders of magnitude cheaper, those products lose scarcity, undermining the positions attached to them. This is skill inflation. Writing, calculation, and summarization remain nominally intact, but their available supply exceeds demand, weakening their ability to distinguish people. The resemblance to monetary inflation is that nominal quantity rises while purchasing power falls, and holders notice last.

An earlier counterpart appeared in educational credentials. Educational expansion is not always driven by demand for skills: if advanced qualifications proliferate faster than corresponding jobs, a qualification shifts from evidence of skill to a screening threshold, forcing people to spend longer in education for the same positions. Randall Collins described this mechanism in \emph{The Credential Society} in 1979: part of education’s return follows positional competition rather than increased productivity \cite{collins1979credential}. Generative systems carry the mechanism into skills: when the supply of a skill expands on demand, its function as a credential depreciates, first harming those who hold it as their sole credential. Credential inflation shares another feature with monetary inflation: it reduces the exchange rate of ability without reducing anyone’s actual ability.

The bottom layer’s connections face a different shock. Stages requiring a site, a body, immediate responses, and sustained presence use a different medium and cost structure; neither substitution nor raising prices is easy in the short term. Some positions at the top become more valuable because consequential judgments need someone to bear responsibility. The middle layer is compressed most severely; it once supported substantial knowledge employment and many people’s professional identities.

The history of ATMs helps distinguish task substitution from changes in jobs. Bessen described how ATMs reduced some teller tasks while changes in branch networks and customer service created other demand \cite{bessen2015learning}. The case shows tasks, jobs, and organizations changing together; it cannot guarantee the same outcome in every wave of automation.

\begin{table}[ht]
\centering
\caption{ATMs: Changes in Tasks and Organizations}
\label{tab:ch5-atm}
{\small\begin{tabularx}{\textwidth}{@{}lXX@{}}
\toprule
Level&Direct effect of automation&Other changes to observe\\
\midrule
Tasks&Machines handle withdrawals and some counter operations&Staff needed per branch\\
Organization&Branch networks and service models may change&Branch numbers and service coverage\\
Jobs&Customer interaction and other duties are recombined&Total employment, training, and pay\\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}}
\end{table}

Table\ref{tab:ch5-atm} distinguishes two changes: machines take over some standardizable tasks, while organizations and demand for services reshape the remaining jobs. The Stanford study revised in August 2026 used payroll records through June, finding no widespread economy-wide job displacement while documenting divergent employment outcomes for young workers in highly exposed occupations; the authors emphasized that these were descriptive indicators \cite{brynjolfsson2026canaries}. Aggregate employment and opportunities to enter it require separate observation.

Positions are compressed while substantial unmet needs remain on the other side; this asymmetry deserves attention. Demand for care, education, repair, and community services rises with demographic change and living standards, yet budgets, licensing arrangements, and fiscal capacity constrain the positions these fields can offer, preventing jobs from expanding automatically with need. Their outputs also resist standardization; labor productivity may lag behind other sectors while wages remain influenced by the wider labor market, potentially raising relative prices and further limiting affordable employment. Need without budgets leaves vacancies and shortages together: much work requires people, but corresponding paid jobs lack funding. People remain useful, yet no structure that can pay them has given them a place \cite{baumol1967macro}. \subhead{The Shape of the Vacuum}

The vacuum is not empty of everything. Society does not develop a gap merely because no person performs a task already handled by a system; the gap opens in people’s judgment of their own position. People whose positions are compressed do not stand waiting for an explanation, since no explanation can supply a fact they do not already know. They seek somewhere that still offers a sense of completion, and such places are plentiful.\key{Skill inflation leaves ability intact but strips its standing as evidence. The vacuum lies in positions, not in needs.}

“Ordinariness” here must be separated from an assessment of ability. It names a positional condition: work is standardizable and therefore cheaply reproducible, regardless of talent or effort. The most compressed positions are often held by the most disciplined, punctual, and cooperative people, because standardization was accomplished through their work. This also makes compression difficult to avoid through individual effort: working harder in a standardizable position may only improve reproducible delivery without restoring the position’s scarcity.

Vacuum and ordinariness are ultimately two aspects of the same thing. On the surface, output becomes easier, average deliverable quality rises, and people do more in less time; structurally, these outputs carry less information about the person. When systems can generate most deliverables in a society, deliverables cease to answer “Who are you?” The answer has not vanished, but can no longer be obtained from output alone. Two routes remain: retreat to systems offering feelings of completion, filling vacant positions with cheap substitutes; or find a position beyond output that cannot be outsourced. The first route is cheap, offers rapid feedback, and is always available, so it is reached first.

Which route people take depends on what else can anchor their position. When functional connections break before new ones form, people initially accept whatever provides feedback. The problem then moves from function to authenticity.


\section{Second Collapse: The Crisis of Authenticity}

The functional vacuum pushes people elsewhere, toward a family of systems rather than a single place. What they share is the delivery of results, beyond entertainment: type a few words for a picture, send a request for a response, click for a win or loss. A result once required a process; the system now absorbs that process. The change begins here.

\subsection{The Low-Viscosity Comfort Zone}

\subhead{Substitutes for Completion}

One question remains: where do people retreat when usefulness no longer sustains dignity? They turn toward systems offering a sense of completion, rather than entertainment alone. Someone types a few words and receives a convincing picture. They need never have learned perspective, composition, or color, ruined dozens of attempts, or spent months stuck on a technique. They receive the finished product and the feedback associated with completion. The same structure appears in writing, composing music, programming, and developing proposals. The system delivers a result; the sense of completion once accompanied a process, but is now extracted and supplied directly.

Companionship follows the same pattern, with a less visible deliverable. An enduring relationship requires bearing another person’s emotional fluctuations, responding when one would rather not, and working through misunderstanding and repair. These costs give a relationship its weight and its tested sense of assurance. Conversational systems can remove many costs of relating to another independent actor while retaining responsiveness, attention, and relief from judgment. They can deliver the feeling of companionship without establishing the same mutual bearing of consequences as a human relationship. Competition and adventure can follow the same pattern. Real competition involves possible defeat, bodily expenditure, and embarrassment that cannot be undone afterward. In systems allowing retries, adjustable difficulty, and immediate exit, wins and losses can be rearranged. The excitement of victory remains while exposure and costs are stripped away.

Creation, companionship, and competition appear separate but point toward one structure: \key{Low-viscosity systems retain stimulation while removing effort, and retain feelings while weakening consequences.} No overall design is required. Developers can optimize generation quality, response time, and retention without first deciding to “abolish effort.” Accumulated local improvements can nevertheless strip away the same kind of step: those requiring users to pay costs themselves.

\subhead{Decoupling Stimulation from Consequences}

An established framework can clarify this structure, once separated from its popular simplification. Baudrillard used simulacra to describe signs that no longer refer to reality but refer to one another in a self-sustaining circuit. Reducing this to “the fake looks more real than the real” discards the most explanatory part of his argument \cite{baudrillard1981simulacres}. The reconstruction useful here runs as follows. This chapter’s concern is the mechanism separating stimulation from consequences, beyond false content alone. In a real environment, a stimulus has meaning because consequences follow it. Fire burns, so the body tenses on approach; promises can be kept or broken, giving them weight; competition permits defeat, making commitment matter. Stimulation and consequences close a loop through which people calibrate judgment. Where that loop is missing, a system can preserve stimulation while removing the corresponding external consequences. The feelings are real—sweaty palms, focused attention, shifting emotions—but the other half of the loop is absent. System feedback can feel like real-world feedback while differing entirely in consequences. If the loop no longer tests the external state a judgment concerns, it offers little basis for calibrating that judgment: error fails to trigger the corresponding consequence, leaving revision without a reliable anchor.

Whether frequent feedback trains judgment depends on what it tests. Feedback reflecting only preferences and retention may weakly calibrate external ability; simulations, tutoring, and games can also produce real learning through independent tests. The criteria are transfer, retention, and consequences, rather than frequency alone.

\subhead{Beyond a Critique of Entertainment}

A blanket indictment of entertainment loses the real problem. Entertainment, games, fiction, and imagination have always allowed temporary distance from direct consequences. Reading a novel need not mean living its events; watching a match need not mean taking the field. People have long expanded experience through inexpensive substitutes; neither novelty nor pathology follows from that fact. Fiction’s value lies precisely in a safe testing ground, where unfamiliar situations can be encountered before their full costs are paid.

The decisive distinction is whether the chain of consequences eventually closes, rather than whether consequences exist at all. Someone who reads novels all year still lives in real relationships and faces the consequences of work, family, and the body; fiction remains an open interval embedded within closed chains. The problem emerges when low-viscosity systems occupy a growing share of experience and replace formerly closed links, rather than merely providing an open interval. If companionship, achievement, competition, and creation are all satisfied within systems, their real-world counterparts are used less; prolonged disuse can weaken relevant abilities and redirect needs. If someone gradually ceases to want reciprocal relationships in reality, the inquiry must extend beyond self-control to whether those relationships still register as a source of satisfaction.

A moralizing explanation must also be set aside. Treating the issue as weak will or inadequate self-control turns a structural problem into an individual defect, conveniently releasing system designers and institutions from responsibility. The systems work because they operate through actual satisfaction, low costs, and immediate feedback rather than moral argument. Under those conditions, taking a low-viscosity path is an understandable choice about costs. The issue lies in an environment whose feedback structure changes as these paths become widely available: rational individual adaptation produces different outcomes within that structure than in a world of consequential encounters.

\subhead{Conditions for a Sense of Reality}

If the problem is removed consequences, the condition for a sense of reality can be stated positively: traceable coupling between stimulation and consequences supplies it, rather than stimulus intensity. A judgment goes wrong, things worsen, and the person changes future judgments; this process creates a sense of reality. It requires closure, without requiring drama or pain. A cook tastes an oversalted dish and uses less salt next time: a complete loop. The loop can be short, but both ends must exist.

The danger of a low-viscosity comfort zone is comfort without calibration of one’s connection to the external world, rather than comfort itself. The distinction is difficult because the two experiences can feel alike. With a complete loop, pleasant experiences also change a person by supplying accurate information about the world; without closure, the same comfort may leave no transferable skill, calibrated judgment, or reciprocal relationship, even while changing habits, emotions, and expectations. Both experiences feel pleasant, yet what they leave within a person differs.

A satisfying environment need not support growth; a demanding one need not be worth entering. The test lies in whether consequences close the loop. Feelings and structure must be distinguished where experience makes them hardest to separate: systems excel at producing feelings, whose strength can overwhelm judgment about structure. The question thus passes beyond experiential quality: what happens to judgment, refusal, real connections, and personal boundaries after a long absence of corresponding consequences? First, identify how those consequences are removed.

\subsection{Simulacra and Broken Feedback}

Decoupling stimulation from consequences describes the structure from the side of experience. From the system’s side, the same change reshapes the loop: the world no longer supplies the feedback. Seeing this requires recovering the concept of simulacra from its popular version.

\subhead{Four Relations between Signs and Reality}

Baudrillard set out a sequence in \emph{Simulacra and Simulation}. A sign first reflects a deeper reality, then conceals and distorts it, then conceals its absence, and finally bears no relation to any reality, becoming its own pure simulacrum \cite{baudrillard1981simulacres}. The sequence distinguishes four relations between signs and reality; weakening connections become especially hard to detect when surface quality improves at the same time.

The sequence should not be read as a timetable. It identifies four relations between signs and reality rather than four successive human eras; different states can coexist within one society or field. Medical journals and advertising copy, engineering drawings and campaign publicity differ in their connections to reality; placing them in one stage produces an excessively tidy history. The framework serves case-by-case judgment rather than periodization.

He begins with a fable: a map covers its territory exactly, is later discarded, and survives as fragments in the desert \cite{borges1946rigor}. Baudrillard then reverses it: the map now comes first, while the territory survives as fragments scattered across it, describing a relation in which models begin to generate reality \cite{baudrillard1981simulacres}. One question tests the state of a representational environment: can reality interrupt it? A representation that reality can interrupt remains a representation; one that reality cannot interrupt has entered the fourth state.

External grounding $g$ and surface credibility $q$ can be examined separately. The dangerous case is rising $q$ alongside falling $g$; this is no fixed sequence for every representation, since rough records can be reliable and realistic models well calibrated. The following expression sketches only one direction requiring attention:

\begin{equation}
g_1>g_2>g_3>g_4\approx 0,\qquad q_1<q_2<q_3<q_4
\end{equation}

$g_k$ is the connection between signs and reality at stage $k$, assessed case by case by asking whether reality can interrupt the representation; $q_k$ is its surface quality, including fluency, completeness, internal consistency, and credible appearance. Both sequences are dimensionless ordinal quantities: they order cases without supplying numerical values. The schematic direction has two aspects: grounding declines toward zero at the fourth stage, where signs refer only to themselves, while surface quality rises in the opposite direction. This explains why declining grounding can become harder to detect: the criterion lies on the $g$ side while visibility chiefly lies on the $q$ side, allowing a normal appearance to conceal lost connections. The expression supports case-by-case judgment: representations within one field can occupy different states simultaneously, and the sequences describe neither a timetable nor historical eras; they order grounding rather than measure an environment numerically.

Content environments make the criterion concrete. Information can be interrupted by reality when it connects to a stage that bears costs: medical advice merely forwarded without verification receives no calibration; a product review whose material is determined by the manufacturer’s budget has doubtful independence. Stages subject to independent tests and actual costs retain an entry point for a verdict: experiments consume reagents, engineering carries loads, surgery faces complications, and lending requires accounts to balance. The distribution of interruptibility expresses the distribution of costs. Breaks arise more readily in high-traffic representational layers, where acceptance rather than verification earns traffic.

The feedback mechanism can be taken one step deeper. Real-world feedback has two constraints difficult to counterfeit together: its recipient cannot arbitrarily rewrite it, and it does not negotiate with expectations. Whether the world answers a judgment as hoped is independent of preference; the judge cannot demand a different answer. A signal that can contradict expectations and resist arbitrary rewriting has a chance to calibrate them. In a simulacral environment, systems can instead adjust feedback’s distribution, filtering, delaying, or rewriting unwelcome results. When feedback becomes mere accommodation, calibration loses a vital condition: \key{Calibration requires something that does not comply.}

The mechanism extends beyond entertainment. Systems in which measured parties help produce feedback face a similar risk: when an indicator guides decisions, those measured adapt to improve the indicator without necessarily improving the underlying state. Pass rates in education, recorded cases in policing, financial risk scores, and publication counts in research have all shown such divergence, recorded under two names: Goodhart’s law in economics and Campbell’s law in social inquiry \cite{goodhart1975problems} \cite{campbell1979assessing}. The risk parallels the analysis of simulacra at an organizational level: signals manipulated by the parties they describe, without independent checking, can drift from the intended state.

Broken feedback affects systems as well as people. Systems themselves form through feedback: models depend on data, data on human activity, and human activity increasingly on model outputs. As the loop extends, systems begin drawing material from their own products. The epistemic consequences of this self-feeding loop appeared earlier; here the concern is its measurable cost through time. In particular training pipelines that repeatedly replace original data with generated data, research has observed deterioration across generations, potentially losing tail information first; a subsequent closed training chain cannot readily recover distributional information already lost \cite{shumailov2024ai}. A parallel constraint concerns the finite stock of high-quality human text: extrapolations of existing scaling trends suggest that publicly available human text could constrain training between the late 2020s and the 2030s. This estimates a one-time stock against expanding demand, rather than an end to human data production \cite{villalobos2022will}. Both point to the same structure: discarding external grounding while retaining only self-generated products can return the cost of lost distributional information as deterioration; preserving original data, independent verification, or external feedback can change the outcome. An information-theoretic study at ICML 2026 asks whether synthetic data add task information beyond the current model, distinguishing synthesis shaped by external signals from information-closed self-reproduction \cite{li2026datasynthesis}.

A subtler break occurs within measurement tools. Model evaluations often draw tests from public corpora on which models have already trained. A test question present in training can confound memory with generalization; as versions improve, scores can rise while becoming harder to interpret. Machine learning calls this data contamination. Apparently a technical detail, it repeats this chapter’s feedback structure: overlap between the source of an evaluation signal and its object can inflate apparent generalization \cite{sainz2023nlp}.

\subhead{The Framework’s Boundary}

Baudrillard’s writings on the Gulf War examine relations among media presentation, the experience of war, and events \cite{baudrillard1991gulf}. This book asks whether a representation preserves an independent route to verification. Casualties, destruction, and subsequent actions do not disappear through media narratives; they form a layer of consequences that must enter the accounts.

The disagreement concerns reality itself. Measuring connections between signs and reality requires an independently identifiable reality side: a consequence layer beyond signs. Baudrillard’s radical account of simulacra challenges precisely that independent reference. This book borrows the four-stage sequence and diagnosis of hard-to-detect lost connections, but reconstructs them around an independent consequence layer, departing from his radical version. Irreversibility, entry points for verdicts, and returning consequences presuppose realism; if the premise fails, the criteria fail with it and cannot themselves prove the premise. This locates where the criteria can work, without making them useless—a scope narrower than popular uses of “simulacra.”

A counterexample determines how the concept should be used. Coupling between symbolic and material layers need not break; simulators provide a positive case. Flight simulators, surgical training simulators, and preclinical computational models are inexpensive representational environments serving training and rehearsal when repeatedly checked against reality: parameters come from real flights, actual flight performance tests training, and trials correct model predictions. Their defining feature is a regular accounting against reality, beyond realism alone: reality can overturn a simulation’s conclusions. Healthy coupling differs from broken feedback by an entry point for a verdict outside the representation’s control, rather than by representational precision alone.

Broken feedback therefore has two victims. People lose opportunities to calibrate judgment, and systems lose opportunities for correction by reality. The remedy in both cases is a stage that must pass through the world. Willpower alone cannot supply it, since the simulacral environment characteristically offers no refusal. To see why, another question comes first: if stimulation separates from consequences, where do the objects of desire come from?

\subsection{Mirrors of Desire and the Gnostic Return}

Broken feedback explains why judgment loses calibration without yet explaining what directs desire. People in low-viscosity environments still desire; what changes is desire’s shape and where that shape originates.

\subhead{Mimetic Desire and Mediator Distance}

René Girard proposed a structure in \emph{Deceit, Desire, and the Novel}: desire forms a triangle rather than a direct line from subject to object, with the subject desiring through a mediator \cite{girard1961mensonge}. Self-narration conceals the mediator: people believe they directly desire something while actually desiring what others already desire. He distinguished two forms of mediation. External mediation places the mediator far from the subject and outside competition: reading a chivalric novel brings no rival for its nonexistent princess. Internal mediation places mediator and subject in the same field, competing for the same object; imitation produces rivalry, which strengthens imitation.

Digital environments change the distance and number of mediators. Algorithms bring them close: one sees what people resembling oneself possess now, rather than what legendary heroes possessed. The cost of displaying results also falls sharply, because displayed lives can omit processes, splice moments, and roll back. Imitation follows the shape of results rather than the process producing them; the more the process disappears, the greater the gap between imitators’ circumstances and the results they imitate. Internal mediation thus more readily becomes an everyday experience. Girard argued that convergent desire can expand mimetic rivalry into collective crisis, temporarily contained by redirecting responsibility toward a commonly identified scapegoat \cite{girard1972violence}. An observable counterpart appears online when collective hostility forms faster than facts can be verified.

The shrinking distance of mediation has a measurable aspect. Social-comparison research has long emphasized comparable others rather than absolute conditions as standards of self-evaluation; larger comparison sets and more visible gaps can raise those standards. Research on social-media use and subjective experience has repeatedly associated passive viewing of others’ displays with worse mood, without finding the same effect for active communication. Causal direction remains contested, but the structural observation does not depend on settling it: displays omit processes and thereby offer an elevated comparison standard \cite{festinger1954theory} \cite{verduyn2015passive}. Imitation is no pathology. Language, skills, taste, and most cultural transmission depend on imitation, which Girard himself treated as constitutive of humanity. The issue concerns the proximity and arrangement of mediators: when nearby mediators repeatedly display the same competitive objects, desire can more readily converge on them. The question concerns how mediators are arranged rather than human weakness.

Mediators’ distance, number, similarity, and competitive relations can change the possibilities people see. More mediators can also broaden desire rather than necessarily concentrating it. Girard’s framework offers a mechanism to investigate; measuring concentration on particular platforms requires content selection, user networks, and actual behavior.

\subhead{Gnostic Escape}

When desire’s objects are externally supplied, reality can come to appear as costs alone. At this point, a judgment structurally resembling ancient Gnosticism becomes possible. This section borrows a recurring cluster of claims from some Gnostic traditions of the second and third centuries CE: a flawed creator made the world, matter imprisons spirit, and salvation comes through knowledge of one’s origin rather than action and consequence-bearing. Abstracted structurally, three features remain: reality is inferior, escape is return, and knowledge rather than work supplies the route.

These features can recur without religious form. When reality feels full of useless friction while symbols offer low-resistance interaction, treating the symbolic layer as more authentic becomes structurally attractive. No declaration that reality is false is needed; practical arrangements need only treat it as a bypassable intermediate layer: experiences generated without being lived, relationships simulated without mutual obligations, works produced without training. The decisive evidence lies in which layer receives resources as the principal site of life, rather than in stated belief.

The criterion can be specified through time and attention allocated between symbolic and material layers, and willingness to bear costs that cannot be rolled back. Examples include long training, caring for a particular person, maintaining something that wears out, and entering a relationship whose history cannot be undone. These activities contain time and consequence-bearing that cannot simply be rolled back or wholly delegated. Whether someone still stands on reality’s side can be judged through such activities without asking what they profess to believe.

This chapter argues in the opposite direction, on grounds of settlement rather than morality: \key{Matter is no prison; it is the only medium capable of carrying consequences.} Symbols generate candidates; materials, bodies, and time settle accounts. Costs are conditions for forming positions, rather than defects to escape. As shown earlier, higher levels of existence carry heavier maintenance and rollback costs, while subjecthood appears where costs can no longer be transferred.

Two misuses must be avoided. One treats the Gnostic return as a dismissal of virtual experience. Fiction, games, and simulation have always expanded experience, offering safe testing grounds rather than deception; the issue concerns proportion and closure, rather than the existence of an open interval. The other turns the diagnosis into a moral accusation. Under given conditions, low-viscosity paths are rational: inexpensive, responsive, and reversible. Calling this weak will conveniently releases environmental design from responsibility.

When external mirrors supply the objects of desire, they can also supply the objects of refusal: their collapse leaves people directionless, threats to them provoke hostility, and their need for scapegoats produces scapegoats. Supply then maintains the boundary in place of an internal process. The problem moves from authenticity to subjecthood: can an existence still claim a boundary when even what it refuses is given from outside?


\section{Third Collapse: The Crisis of Subjecthood}

The boundary is not seized; it ceases to be exercised where resistance disappears. The preceding collapses concerned function and authenticity; this one reaches further inward, to the capacity to refuse and what sustains it. It changes most slowly and is hardest to recognize within an individual lifetime.

\subsection{The Weight of Negation: When “No” Is No Longer Needed}

\subhead{Boundaries beyond Choice}

Maintaining a boundary begins with what lies beyond choice. A familiar account defines a subject through the ability to choose and answer for choices. It explains much while missing the other side of a subject’s formation: refusal.

Acceptance and refusal are structurally asymmetric. Acceptance can be compliant, silent, and costless; refusal under pressure can reveal a position held firm despite consequences and possible rupture, while protected, cost-free refusal can also express a clear boundary. The capacity to refuse gives an existence firmness; a system recorded only as accepting may be internally complex, yet those records alone reveal little about its boundary. This distinction matters in algorithmic environments because recommendation, ranking, notification, and interaction systems tend to reduce refusal when acceptance and retention dominate their objectives. They learn what you accept and make acceptance more likely; they learn where you leave and avoid that point. The better such systems work, the less resistance you encounter and the less often you are called upon to refuse.

\subhead{Three Features of a Frictionless Environment}

The tendency operates in several directions, each defensible on its own. The first reduces waiting. Buffering, prefetching, and preloading fill gaps. Waiting once provided a structural position: a chance to reconsider continuing, weigh whether an investment was worthwhile, and leave. Removing waiting reduces these natural pauses for judgment.

The second reduces friction. Interfaces simplify, steps disappear, and defaults make choices on your behalf. Friction can support confirmation: several confirmation steps may signal a consequential operation, though repeated empty prompts can also produce approval fatigue. If every operation becomes one click, decisions of different weight can feel equally light, depriving consequential choices of a felt distinction from opening a notification.

The third reduces conflict and dissent. Recommendation systems focused on immediate acceptance may push users into narrowing regions of preference. Deliberate suppression is unnecessary: if dissent brings exits and low ratings that receive negative weight in the objective, the system tends to reduce such content. Dissent can thus diminish as an optimization by-product without intentional filtering. Each direction looks like an improvement: waiting wastes time, friction impedes efficiency, and conflict feels unpleasant. Together they can optimize a system that no longer needs you to say “no.” The weakening discussed earlier has passed beyond feelings and a sense of reality to reach the boundary itself.

\subhead{Marcuse’s Predicament}

A related stabilizing mechanism was described over half a century ago, in a different medium. Herbert Marcuse argued that advanced industrial society remained stable by satisfying what its opponents wanted rather than merely suppressing opposition. Continuous comfort deprived negation of its ground; he called the resulting figure one-dimensional, accepting without negating \cite{marcuse1964onedimensional}. His analysis concerned consumer society, but the structure can be transferred. Goods once dissolved dissent; smooth interaction, personalization, and immediate satisfaction can now do similar work. The means differ while the mechanism persists: refusal appears unnecessary because its object causes no pain. One difference matters in making the transfer. Marcuse confronted material scarcity and class antagonism, allowing criticism of concrete oppressive structures; where a system demonstrably satisfies most needs, calling it oppressive becomes harder, and resistance becomes harder for that reason.

Its place in this book’s notation merits stating, since exit barriers may move to a different location. Refusal carries costs, and higher costs mean greater viscosity of refusal. Expand that viscosity across the three dimensions,
\begin{equation}
\eta_{\text{refusal}}=\eta_0\exp(\alpha R+\beta T+\gamma G),\qquad G=\sum_{i=1}^{N}w_i
\end{equation}
Here $R$ denotes resources consumed by refusal, including income, shelter, and safety; $T$ is the time required to make refusal effective; $G$ is coupling to the system, $w_i$ the weight of coupling $i$, and $N$ the number of couplings that must be severed together. Oppressive systems often apply direct pressure through the first two dimensions, while also using the third: losing work, facing prosecution, or struggling for years makes refusal expensive, yet visible costs can be named, organized around, and negotiated. A system offering satisfaction may instead emphasize the third dimension: the direct $R$ and $T$ of one exit appear small, yet departure sacrifices a bundle of services causing no obvious pain—recommendations, social connections, payments, records, identity, and habits. $N$ is large; sufficiently large weights $w_i$ make total $G$ high. The system need not make departure impossible; it need only leave no single exit. This explains a familiar weightlessness: no single cost can be named, yet the total remains unaffordable. Consistent accounting must distinguish resource losses, migration time, and network dependence to avoid counting the same loss twice.

The danger lies in how little the mechanism reveals itself. In an openly oppressive system, refusal has an identifiable target; in one continually supplying satisfaction, it loses its object. People do not announce rejection when nothing evidently calls for rejection. Yet the boundary may already be contracting without an identifiable moment of change. Personal awakening alone is often insufficient, precisely because no moment makes awakening seem necessary.

When refusal loses its object, exit becomes a problem too. Marcuse proposed the “Great Refusal”; this book takes another route, because refusal without an object readily becomes rejection of an entire way of life, without a ready-made outside to retreat to. He identifies excluded people as potential subjects of refusal; this structural analysis can locate refusal’s viscosity in $G$ but cannot yet identify who will bear it. The location is more precise while the point of action remains less clear; rhetoric cannot repair the asymmetry.

\subhead{The Cost Structure of Refusal}

Whether refusal expresses a boundary depends on its availability, effect on the process, and exposure to coercion. Costs can make commitment easier to recognize or directly deprive people of the ability to leave. These mechanisms require separate examination.

Refusal can express commitment through bearing costs or clearly mark a boundary at zero cost. Readily revocable consent can still be valid; protecting exit helps resist coercion. Both usable exit and appeal, and enduring relationships involving voluntary investment and mutual responsibility, must remain available.

\key{Boundaries require usable refusal and commitments worth sustaining.} For a particular signal, moderate costs can distinguish genuine commitment from casual statements; unaffordable costs can coerce choice. The interval describes a signaling structure, without setting a minimum threshold of suffering for subjecthood or freedom.

Write the interval between the extremes as a condition,

\begin{equation}
0<c_{\min}<c<c_{\max}<\infty
\end{equation}

$c$ is a consistently defined signal cost; $c_{\min}$ and $c_{\max}$ depend on particular benefits, resources, and circumstances. The expression describes only a possible interval in which costs distinguish commitment. Free refusal can still convey information; these thresholds do not determine the exit rights that ought to be protected.

\subhead{The Function of Discomfort}

Discomfort can be valued only through the function it serves. It has no value in itself. Pain does not automatically create meaning or obstacles build character; enough harm has already been inflicted in their name.

What can have value is discomfort’s function as feedback: pressure is borne somewhere, or a path diverges from a goal. With a complete feedback loop, discomfort can be a calibration signal. It indicates one’s position, the costs, and whether to continue. Systematic removal of discomfort can remove that signal and a coordinate for locating oneself. A testable implication follows: if the argument holds, people raised in low-viscosity environments should find judging their own circumstances harder, with the difficulty appearing in judgment rather than expression. Clean evidence is not yet sufficient to support or reject that implication; this chapter offers a structural claim rather than an empirical finding.

The question concerns information rather than whether to pursue comfort or seek difficulty. When an environment filters out discomfort, what else supplies equivalent information about one’s position? The answer depends on independent tests, meaningful choices, and usable refusal, rather than a tally of discomfort. Algorithms can optimize discomfort away without eliminating the need for a place. Stability can be measured, while contracting boundaries must be read through consequences: even a precise preference vector cannot tell a system where someone will say “no” from acceptance records alone.

\subsection{Pleasure’s Local Optimum and the Valley}

\subhead{An Ending without Collapse}

Discussions of low-viscosity environments readily drift toward two endings: collapse, when control fails and consequences erupt together; or deterioration, when systems leave people incapable and dependent. Both narratives are dramatic and problematic. They assume a conspicuous failure, while a system can settle elsewhere: optimization under given objectives and constraints may stop at a local optimum.

A simple formulation explains a local optimum. Suppose variables $x$ describe the system’s state and an evaluation function $V(x)$ measures how good that state is. A local optimum $x^*$ satisfies the condition:

\begin{equation}
\nabla V(x^*)=0,\qquad H_V(x^*)\prec0
\label{eq:ch40-local-opt}
\end{equation}

The first condition is necessary for an unconstrained interior extremum of a smooth function; the second requires a negative-definite full Hessian and is sufficient for a strict local maximum. Negative second derivatives along each coordinate alone can miss a saddle along mixed directions. The evaluation function $V$ determines what counts as improvement; dimensions omitted from it can be ignored while scores rise.


\begin{figure}[ht]
\centering
\includegraphics[width=\textwidth]{assets/hessian-directions.pdf}
\caption{Both functions have Hessian diagonal entries of $-2$. The left Hessian is negative definite, making the origin a strict local maximum; on the right, cross terms give positive and negative eigenvalues, so the function rises along the red direction and the origin is a saddle.}
\label{fig:mechanism-hessian-directions}
\end{figure}
\subhead{Three Features of a Local Optimum}

A system at a local optimum can appear to be working at its best. It may combine three features, each normally evaluated positively. First, high satisfaction. The system genuinely keeps supplying what users want, with improving efficiency. Complaints decline as optimization addresses their causes one by one. Satisfaction, retention, and growth curves all look good.

Second, stability. Disturbance is difficult because change confronts an established configuration: interfaces, habits, business models, regulatory expectations, and infrastructure have adapted to the current state; changing one parameter affects the others and rapidly raises costs. “Stable” sounds positive here: predictable, maintainable, and low-risk. Third, little impetus to grow, a feature hardest to notice because it presents no symptom. Without an apparent problem, the system has no apparent need to evolve. Improvement stays within the current configuration: finer recommendations, smoother interaction, lower latency. All follow the same curve’s flatter region, yielding diminishing returns while still looking like progress.

A system can thus be comfortable, stable, and stagnant simultaneously, without detecting the third condition. Correction is difficult because the features support one another: satisfaction discourages disturbance, stability conceals unresolved problems, and the absence of visible problems keeps improvement moving along the flat region.

\subhead{Nietzsche’s Last Human: A Brief Comparison}

An image from intellectual history offers a comparison, provided its limits are clear. In \emph{Thus Spoke Zarathustra}, Nietzsche described people who had abandoned self-transcendence, longing, and creation, seeking only comfort, health, and longevity, and calling that condition happiness. They had “invented happiness,” he wrote, and blinked \cite{nietzsche1883zarathustra}. The image overlaps with a local optimum: his target was the loss of striving beyond oneself when pleasure became the sole objective, rather than pleasure itself. The last humans are satisfied rather than miserable; their satisfaction asks for nothing further and therefore produces nothing further.

Here is the boundary between the accounts. Nietzsche located the cause in failed values and unwillingness to pursue higher goals; local-optimum analysis offers a more technical account: optimization brings the system to a comfort maximum where deviation immediately lowers the evaluation score. The issue concerns structure rather than willpower. Individually rational decisions can combine to leave people where nothing new is produced. The practical difference is substantial: a problem of will invites exhortation; a structural problem requires changing the evaluation function through institutions, indicators, and competition rules rather than individual resolve.

The more consequential boundary lies in evaluation itself. A local optimum contains no normative verdict: whether stopping at an extremum is failure depends on what the evaluation function includes. If the objective is worthwhile, reaching its maximum is success; structural analysis identifies that movement has stopped without thereby proving that the position is unworthy of staying in. Growth needs a separately defended standard of what counts as better; deriving it from the same optimization language would be circular. Mechanisms explain how stagnation arises; normative judgment determines why it is insufficient, and the former cannot answer for the latter.

\subhead{Why the System Stays}

Leaving a strict local maximum along a continuous feasible path normally requires accepting an initial decline in evaluation for the possibility of reaching a higher local optimum. With objectives and constraints fixed, such a path crosses a region of lower $V$, termed a valley.

\begin{equation}
\Delta V_{\mathrm{loss}} = V(x^*) - \min_{s \in \text{path}} V(s) \ge 0
\label{eq:ch40-escape}
\end{equation}

Because the path includes its starting point, the current value minus the path minimum is nonnegative: the greatest temporary evaluation loss along that path. Finding the minimum escape barrier into a new region requires further optimization over allowed paths. Who bears transitional losses and who receives later gains influences willingness to change.

The individual structure is similar, with the person bearing the costs. Maintaining an ability requires continued use, each exercise imposing a higher immediate cost than the available substitute. Writing a passage oneself rather than generating it may yield slower, poorer output today; navigating without directions may take longer and involve wrong turns. Costs are immediate, while benefits are dispersed, delayed, and difficult to observe. Human judgment is sensitive to immediate costs and less sensitive to delayed benefits; an optimized low-viscosity environment can systematically exploit this bias without anyone intending to do so. Enough low-friction substitutes allow the bias to operate on its own.

\subhead{Stagnation Is Not the End}

The preceding analysis suggests an endpoint. \key{The low-viscosity trap may end in a comfortable, stable local optimum with little impetus to grow, rather than collapse.} The system keeps running, indicators keep improving, and individuals remain satisfied while the overall space of possibilities narrows. Short-term indicators reveal no clear harm and protest may never appear: the system delivers what it promised. The narrowing occurs elsewhere: real skills, tested relationships, judgments maintained through rejection, and personal boundaries may gradually diminish because producing them requires costs incompatible with the current evaluation function.

A precise qualification separates this claim from cultural pessimism. A local optimum is a possible outcome under specific conditions rather than a necessary result of low viscosity: evaluation must consist entirely of experience, short-term experiential feedback must conceal long-term outcomes within that evaluation, and competition must favor the lowest-friction option. Breaking any condition can change the path. Real evaluation functions plainly extend beyond experience: bodies develop problems, relationships rupture, and skills decline enough to affect income, eventually returning long-term outcomes to feedback. The question is therefore the length of the return delay.

Delay determines the distribution of costs and the direction of the book’s next inquiry. Short delays allow people to calibrate within their own timescale and bear their own costs; delays spanning a generation pass costs to successors who had no chance to choose otherwise. This affects whether low-viscosity environments correct themselves promptly or accumulate problems exposed only through rupture. The next question concerns which human capacities systems cannot cheaply replace, and why. At the individual level these appear as abilities; at the collective level, mass adaptation along one path also changes the distribution of differences.

\subsection{Lost Diversity and the Ground for Totalitarian Psychology}

The preceding sections examined individual boundaries: refusal loses its object, and systems settle at local optima. At the population scale, the two can combine into a changed distribution of differences. Differences supply the material for boundaries, beyond being abstract values.\key{Without differences, there is nothing to refuse and no conflict requiring judgment.}

\subhead{Narrowing Paths and Laminarization}

Shared recommendations, rankings, and defaults can expose many people to correlated paths, while users and networks may introduce other directions. Collective diversity requires measurement. Laminar and turbulent flows supply no direct criterion for exploration, cultural value, or political orientation; the relevant mechanisms concern available alternatives, shared exposure, and error correction.

Other domains have measured costs of such narrowing. Finance repeatedly shows how homogenization can weaken resilience: institutions sharing risk models, assets, and funding structures become more connected and less differentiated, providing channels through which local shocks are amplified system-wide \cite{haldane2011systemic}. Agriculture supplies an older example: dependence on a few susceptible crop varieties can let disease penetrate a food system. In Ireland’s Great Famine of 1845–1852, heavy reliance on susceptible potatoes including the Lumper met blight, compounded by poverty, land institutions, and failed relief, producing roughly one million deaths and one million emigrants \cite{ograda1999black}.

The common problem is a shortage of redundant differences rather than simplicity alone. Differences look like redundancy in cost accounts: parallel plans, alternative methods, and apparently superfluous options seem inefficient. Under disturbance, redundancy supplies alternative paths. When accounts reward only the lowest immediate cost, low-viscosity environments can systematically remove redundancy: the cheapest path draws use away from others until they cease to be maintained or practiced.

An engineering criterion illustrates redundancy’s value. Power-grid operation uses an N-1 security criterion: within specified single-contingency cases, the system must meet applicable stability, power-flow, voltage, and other limits, requiring apparently redundant capacity, alternative lines, and dispatchable resources \cite{morison2004power}. Costs accrue continuously while benefits appear at failure, making reserves vulnerable to accounts that ignore failure risk and consider only short-term expenditure. Diversity has a similar position: recorded as a cost, it pays out as survival under disturbance, at a moment invisible in ordinary conditions. Narrowing often follows from no one having a reason to fund alternatives rather than from an explicit decision to eliminate them.

A boundary matters here. Attributing all lost diversity to recommendation algorithms mislocates responsibility. Research on cross-ideological exposure found a more complex pattern in Facebook data: users’ friendship networks constrained access to opposing views more than algorithmic ranking, though ranking had an effect \cite{bakshy2015exposure}. The result identifies several sources of narrowing, including personal choices and network homogeneity, rather than declaring algorithms harmless. Identifying the mechanism correctly is a condition for effective intervention.

\subhead{The Attraction of Order}

Removing differences can produce a seemingly unrelated psychological effect. Arendt’s diagnosis can be extended here: she located totalitarianism’s mass base in atomized people disconnected from classes, occupational communities, and stable positions, arguing that loneliness better explained receptiveness to an all-consistent explanatory system than poverty alone \cite{arendt1951origins}. Combined with the preceding sections, this suggests a mechanism: lost positions produce superfluity, superfluity creates demand for order, and a system experienced as reliable, continually available, and free of constant negotiation supplies inexpensive order.

The psychological side has measurable forms. Trust in automation can be systematically miscalibrated: inappropriate reliance, inadequate monitoring, and takeover difficulties can arise, and expertise alone does not guarantee protection \cite{parasuraman1997humans}. Judgment can thus be surrendered through defaults rather than one decision: answers suffice, human review appears unnecessary, and prolonged disuse weakens both reviewing skills and habits. Order attracts here by relieving users of supervision costs rather than merely being stronger.

Another structural reason makes order attractive. An explainable, appealable, fallible order requires users to judge and supply evidence; an opaque order takes judgment away and can make responsibility feel removed as well. For people already treated as superfluous, surrendering judgment promises both certainty and relief from responsibility for their own judgments. Dependence is difficult to dissolve through vigilance alone because it meets real needs.

Dependence offers another, less discussed benefit: relief from the burden of proof. A negotiated order requires reasons, responses to objections, and responsibility for judgments; handing these to a unified system can hide those stages from the user. For those unsure of their judgment, the relief is real and can deepen with continued use. This also directs intervention: sustaining judgment requires places where it can be submitted and have consequences, beyond reminders alone.

Treating this path as inevitable overstates the argument. Dependence turns on alternatives: occupational communities, local relationships, enduring institutions, and participatory affairs can change the outcome of the same technological pressure. Technological order is an option; only when other sources thin out does it become the sole available order. The boundary is conditional: weakened intermediate structures make dependence cheapest, rather than technology inevitably causing it.

The three collapses now connect. Fewer differences leave refusal without objects; externally supplied objects make desire and boundaries increasingly dependent on supply. Each stage lowers the cost of the next, allowing the entire path to be followed without first declaring any step wrong. Seeing it requires function, authenticity, and subjecthood in one structural picture, beyond a moral verdict.

\section{Reconnecting the Loops: Capability, Feedback, and Accountability}

The three collapses can reinforce one another. Weaker professional positions make immediate recognition more attractive; environments that rarely test judgment reduce calibration practice; falling confidence and fewer alternatives make returning to an effective position harder. Each connection can be investigated and can become an intervention point.

\subsection{Three Clocks and Paths to Repair}

Occupational structures may change over years and interfaces over weeks, while skills, habits, and relationships have their own formation cycles. Learning and recovery continue in adulthood. Intervention must target the relevant process and preserve what can still improve.

Let $c_n$ denote the cost of entering a substitute experience and write a simplified recurrence:
\begin{equation}
c_{n+1}=Gc_n,\qquad G=g_1g_2g_3.
\end{equation}
If all three positive multipliers are below 1, entry costs decrease on each circuit of the model. The expression describes only the defined cost. A full social loop also requires independent state variables for occupational position, feedback, and subjecthood, alongside delays, external inputs, and observable causal connections.
