Inquiry can begin with narrower questions: has entering an occupation become harder? Do assistive tools improve skills on independent tests or only immediate output? Can users recognize, challenge, and correct a consequential error? Does an appeal change the decision? Are alternatives affordable and usable?

These questions need different evidence: longitudinal observation, task tests, institutional records, and concrete cases. Indicators also need reverse checks, so that counting appeals does not masquerade as counting resolved problems. Repair mechanisms must have actual power to change the process.

\subsection{Four Functions of Accountability}

Consequences need a route into a response. Accountability structures must supply at least four functions.

\textbf{Detection.}Monitor harm, near misses, and important deviations; allow users and affected people to report problems. Operators’ dashboards must connect to external complaint channels.

\textbf{Tracing.}Reconnect an event to the relevant decisions, versions, configurations, and tool actions. The scope, retention, access permissions, and privacy protections of records must be designed around their uses.

\textbf{Harm containment.}Give someone usable authority to pause, isolate, recall, or restrict. Emergency control can precede complete attribution, preventing harm from growing during investigation.

\textbf{Remedy.}Allow affected people to seek correction, obtain appropriate compensation, and press for prevention of recurrence. Assets, insurance, and organizational capacity behind responsibility determine how much of a promise can be fulfilled.

\begin{figure}[ht]
\centering\includegraphics[width=\textwidth]{assets/accountability.pdf}
\caption{Four functions of accountability. Monitoring and reporting bring consequences into the record; tracing supports explanation and correction; harm containment can begin immediately, while remedy addresses consequences already incurred. The functions connect and can operate in parallel.}
\label{fig:accountability-loop}
\end{figure}

The four functions can run in parallel and supply one another’s inputs. Each needs actors, resources, and operational interfaces. Aviation combines design assurance, production control, maintenance, operating permissions, reporting, and investigation; aircraft and institutions jointly produce reliability. Other fields must arrange these functions around their own consequences and control conditions.

Machine systems need equally clear interfaces: who controls updates, who can suspend access, which records survive a service shutdown, who hears challenges to model decisions, and who can provide remedies?

Responsibility can be allocated through control, contractual roles, legal duties, and other legitimate standards. Insurance and compensation funds can share some losses; independent investigations help separate learning from immediate attribution of blame. Incentives, enforcement, and funding together determine whether these arrangements work.

Accountability can also expand deployment. Risks become easier to assess and accept when they have clear control, recording, and remedy paths. Knowing how to act when uncertainty becomes consequence gives some formerly unpromisable applications conditions for operation.

\subsection{Judgment Requires Standing}

Three questions remain central to decisions: which consequences are acceptable, how much evidence warrants action, and who has the right to impose costs on whom?

Models can estimate outcomes, compare proposals, expose contradictions, and help people express positions. Adopting standards and imposing consequences also require appropriate rights, authorization, and duties. This book argues: \key{People bearing consequences should retain effective channels for voice, representation, and challenge.}

Direct exposure provides one basis for standing; legitimate delegation, professional duties, democratic authorization, and protection of absent and vulnerable people provide others. Patients bear bodily risks and physicians professional responsibilities, connected through informed consent, professional standards, and accountability procedures. Jurors usually do not bear the same consequences as defendants; their authority comes from legally assigned roles, duties, and procedures \cite{kalven1966american}. Captains, physicians, and jurors have different grounds for authority. They share a requirement: decisions have explainable reasons, permissions have defined scope, and someone must answer a challenge. Reviewers also need competence, time, and power to change decisions before a “human in the loop” becomes an actual position rather than a paper assurance.

\subsection{Human Value When Output Becomes Cheap}

A society valuing people only through scarce output loses part of its evaluative basis as output becomes abundant. Participation, care, relationships, judgment, and finite lives need a fuller place in evaluation.

Consequences falling on someone give that person grounds for protection and voice. Allocating burdens also requires attention to legitimate relations of power and control. Bearing burdens need not be romanticized; avoidable harm should be reduced.

Another person can advise, work, or make delegated decisions, without thereby living your finite life or automatically occupying the same relationship. Assistance expands a person’s capabilities while leaving that person’s stake in outcomes intact.

Repair has concrete destinations: rebuild paths to useful contribution, preserve corrective feedback, keep exit, dissent, and enduring commitment viable, and reconnect consequential actions to people and institutions able to respond. Each arrangement requires investment. The next chapter distinguishes costs that merely obstruct from those preserving the conditions that make progress worth having.

\chapter{Reconstructing Value: Living in the Shear Zone}

The previous chapter showed why consequences need a bearer, and how bearers can be separated from decision-makers. Where value goes also depends on demand, property rights, bargaining power, and public arrangements. This chapter distinguishes the social necessity of work, the pay and standing of those doing it, and human dignity and the meaning of life. The three influence one another without automatically converting into one another. Abundant generation may make verification, care, enduring relationships, and responsibility scarcer; whether those positions receive resources remains a question of institutions and distribution. Historical externalizations of capability offer several ways to examine this change.

If intelligent systems can already write copy, summarize, translate, retouch images, code, and develop proposals, how much weight remains in ordinary people’s skills? If they can also read the literature, propose hypotheses, design experiments, run simulations, analyze data, and write papers, how does research training demonstrate its value? If they participate in mathematical proofs, search for lemmas, and check derivations, is even research’s hardest formal intellectual labor beginning to loosen? If robots drive, manufacture, carry, inspect, operate, and provide care, how much room remains for people in work once grounded in bodies, experience, and situated judgment? Beyond the fate of particular occupations, external systems are dismantling the capability interfaces once used to establish training, experience, and standing as a subject.

Questions about disappearing occupations and depreciating skills reach a deeper issue: how did people once demonstrate their value? Writing, calculating, making, judging, researching, proving, and acting could each sustain a social position. External systems now remove, amplify, and reorganize these abilities layer by layer. The unsettling question is where people move after a capability is externalized, beyond finding something machines will never do.

\section{Historical Echoes: The Physics of Value Drift}

These questions have been asked before, and their answers rewritten before. Chapter 1 offered a claim: externalizing a capability breaks its old bond with value, because what moves is also an interface through which society recognizes training, experience, qualification, and responsibility. This chapter follows the break: where does value land, and why there? Three forms of proof fail together: output no longer automatically establishes a subject, form no longer establishes experience, and capability no longer establishes legitimacy. Each depends on a stage that an external system can take over; where those stages sit shapes the direction of migration.

An interface here is a concrete institutional arrangement. Guilds establish craft through apprenticeship years, imperial examinations establish qualification through tested knowledge, universities establish training through degrees, professional licenses establish admission through exams and practice, and academic communities establish credibility through publication records. All anchor proof of ability in a process not quickly acquired: seven years of apprenticeship cannot be compressed into seven months of reading, examination scores cannot replace a resident physician’s case experience, and authors’ assurances cannot replace peer evaluation. The interface gives such processes recognizable form; if an external system takes it over, an entire procedure for recognizing qualifications is disturbed alongside the scarcity of ability \cite{spence1973job}. History’s answer has repeatedly been a new anchor for value rather than the end of human value. Different ways of moving capabilities break old bonds differently, yet each leaves the same question: where does the value released from its former position go next? Following that line needs the hardest step at each turning point rather than a complete history of technology.

\subsection{Socrates’ Fear: Wisdom without the Viscosity of Internalization}

\subhead{Externalized Capabilities and Broken Bonds}

The inquiry follows several turning points in externalization: memory, copying, timekeeping, work, rule execution, symbol generation, formal exploration, action, and biological intervention. Human beings have experienced this weightlessness before. Writing lightened memory, printing copying, clocks time, steam engines muscle, and computers rule execution; large models lighten symbol generation, reasoning models and scientific agents formal exploration, embodied intelligence begins externalizing action, and intelligence applied to life brings biological intervention and the definition of life into technical systems. Each technology resembles a deep relocation, moving capabilities once lodged in bodies, skills, and identities into external systems and loosening old interfaces of value. Human value need not disappear, but must find new places, some deeper, heavier, and harder to outsource. Together, these nine turning points trace repeated rearrangements of where value lands; technology alone does not determine who receives the gains.

These turning points are organized by modes of large-scale externalization, showing how formalization affects migration rather than supplying a technological chronology without overlaps. Their order can be understood through operational forms: speech becomes writing, copying becomes an arrangement of type, muscular work passes to machines and energy systems, and rule execution, symbol generation, and formal exploration enter procedures, statistical patterns, and searchable spaces. The easier a capability becomes an operational external form, the easier it is to move beyond the body under the relevant technical conditions. Externalization first unsettles those whose identity rests on an ability: their position depends on doing what others cannot, while the external system makes that act cheap.

The old bond contains identifiable parts. Training must be verifiable, showing sustained preparation; experience traceable, showing encounters and remembered consequences; qualification exclusive, limiting who can occupy a position; responsibility attributable, determining who answers when things go wrong. Old institutions bundled the four, allowing one capability to attest to all of them. Externalization cuts the cord: models supply some outputs once requiring training, retrieval supplies some experience, subscriptions can supply signals formerly used to recognize qualifications, and responsibility disperses among systems. Where the bond breaks, value needs a new home.

\subhead{External Memory and the Work of Internalization}

Memory is the first turning point, externalized earliest and most thoroughly. Before writing, memory sustained order itself. Law, myth, genealogy, ritual, exchange, taboo, and experience depended chiefly on memory, speech, and ceremony, assisted by material markers. Those able to remember, recount, and transmit carried a community’s time as well as its information. Forgetting could break an order, beyond being a personal lapse. Writing changed this. It let extensive experience settle into symbols beyond a particular body. People die, voices fade, witnesses depart; words, contracts, laws, poems, accounts, and knowledge can remain. In Plato’s \emph{Phaedrus}, Socrates warns that writing can act as a remedy for memory while encouraging people to mistake external preservation for inward understanding \cite{plato_phaedrus}. The warning recognizes an early \term{migration of value} rather than simply rejecting technology: as memory grows lighter, understanding grows heavier; texts fix answers without replacing questions, and possessing words need not mean possessing the judgment behind them.

Socrates’ fear has a precise target: when knowledge moves from living neurons to parchment and other external carriers, its felt understanding does not necessarily travel with the words. Recitation here is internalization rather than primitive storage: content repeatedly passes through the body and meshes with experience, a viscous and expensive process. Writing sharply reduces resistance to external preservation and transmission, shifting scarcity from remembering toward reasoning. Writing changes wisdom’s fulcrum rather than destroying wisdom: value drifts from storage to logical construction, from the vessel of knowledge to its processor. The question was already posed in the fourth century BCE and remains: external preservation can fix an answer without doing the work of understanding for us.

Research on oral societies supplies a measurable comparison. Recording South Slavic epic singers in the 1930s, Milman Parry and Albert Lord found that skilled singers did not merely memorize tens of thousands of lines: they mastered metrical formulas and reassembled songs during performance, with one singer’s versions of the same epic differing by thousands of lines \cite{parry1960singer}. Memory was ongoing construction rather than a warehouse, combining creation, transmission, and checking. Writing separates them: creation goes to authors, transmission to manuscripts, and checking to later readers. As the unified burden of memory dissolves, understanding, editing, and interpretation gain weight—the aspect Socrates perceived.

The migration has another side: externalizing memory can also expand thought. Writing preserves existing ideas and creates new objects of thought. Positional notation and algebraic symbols let calculations unfold on a page, proofs be checked beyond a speaker’s memory, and geometric constructions be retraced by later readers. Moving reasoning out of a head allows others to pause, challenge, and rewrite it, expanding inference as well as reducing the burden of memory. Lower internalization costs are exchanged for publicly inspectable forms; costs and benefits coexist.

Controlled experiments offer a measurable answer to what follows outsourced memory. In studies published in 2011, Sparrow, Liu, and Wegner found that expecting later retrieval reduced recall of information itself while improving recall of where it was stored, a pattern known as the Google effect \cite{sparrow2011google}. The result concerns the distribution of remembered content rather than a net loss of memory ability, and establishes no general harm from external storage. Examinations offer a related illustration: open-book tests allowing retrieval can emphasize organization, judgment, and expression over direct recall, while closed-book tests persist because some domains require sufficient internal knowledge for judgment, beyond reverence for memory itself. Both point to changed locations of scarcity rather than a changed total quantity of humanity.

Memory’s lightening came first; copying changed on a larger scale, disturbing authority rather than individual understanding alone. Mass reproduction shifted scarcity from possession of texts toward the right to interpret them. The earlier migration changed individual capabilities; this one changed communal power.

\subsection{Gutenberg’s Reduction: The Collapse of Interpretive Monopoly}

\subhead{Cheaper Copying and Contested Interpretation}

Printing further lightened copying. In manuscript culture, owning, copying, and preserving scarce books conferred power. Printing sent texts out of a few confined spaces into wider social circulation. Eisenstein saw it as a force transforming early modern Europe’s intellectual order, changing textual comparison, transmission, debate, and the formation of authority alongside copying speed \cite{eisenstein1979printing}. Human value shifted from reproduction toward selection, interpretation, editing, organizing trust, and establishing public judgment. More texts make judgment scarcer; cheaper copies make trust more costly. Printing made interpreters, verifiers, and makers of reliable editions more consequential rather than making people irrelevant.

The reduction concerns copying rather than language itself. A scribe’s physical speed limits daily output; scarce scripture concentrates interpretation among those controlling manuscripts and therefore the entrance to truth. As reproduction became much cheaper than handwriting, information followed lower-resistance paths and scarcity moved toward interpretation: Luther’s \emph{Ninety-Five Theses} entered print in 1517 and spread rapidly across Europe, enabled by cheaper copying rather than ecclesiastical permission. Interpretations multiplied, and old authorities lost their foothold; the panic concerned control of interpretation changing hands, beyond information overload alone. Value drifted from possessing information toward defining belief and then establishing trustworthy versions, a line repeated in later externalizations.

Cheaper reproduction had a quieter consequence: textual criticism and edition comparison became scalable technical work. Versions could be placed side by side, variants systematically organized, errors corrected in reprints, and authors’ works repeatedly revised during their lives. Tasks once grounded in particular scriptoria became routine functions of publishers, libraries, and learned societies. As copying grew cheaper, establishing trustworthy versions became more demanding, creating positions for editors, compilers, and publishers. Scarcity shifted from whether a text existed to whether it could be trusted.

Cheaper copying and generation can expand knowledge while increasing demand for selection and trustworthy versions. Tools can accelerate confirmation too. The question is which function becomes relatively scarce across the chain, and whether the organizations performing it receive resources.

\subhead{Rule Execution and Symbol Generation}

Once copying grew lighter, externalization moved into mental work that could be written as a procedure. Rules have no weight in tons or watts, yet the structure of migration is similar. Computers carried this migration further into mental labor. They reduced the costs of formalizable, rule-governed, programmable processes rather than all thought. Manual calculation, accounting, tables, storage, retrieval, sorting, repeated execution, and deterministic workflows passed to machines at scale. Faster human calculation alone could not win that value back. Human positions moved upstream: defining problems, building models, choosing variables, understanding context, and judging whether outputs met real needs. Computers lightened execution while making problem definition heavier. Simon’s account of artificial systems and bounded rationality already situated intelligence within goals, constraints, information, and organizational structures, designing viable paths rather than solving in isolation \cite{simon1969sciences}. With execution outsourced, scarcity moves toward deciding what merits execution, why, which problems admit formalization, where models end, and whether results should enter reality.

Accounting makes the distinction between tasks and jobs concrete. Spreadsheets and accounting software take over much bookkeeping, trial balancing, and report consolidation, while audit, tax planning, internal control, and financial interpretation still require professional judgment. In BLS projections released in 2026 for 2025–2035, employment of bookkeeping, accounting, and auditing clerks is expected to fall 6\%, while accountants and auditors grow 5\%; these are distinct occupational categories and forecasts rather than observed outcomes \cite{bls2026bookkeepers,bls2026accountants}. The change concerns what demonstrates ability as well as workload: balancing accounts differs from judging the treatment of a transaction and whether it can withstand later scrutiny. The case makes the separation of rule execution and professional discretion tangible without guaranteeing that every externalization moves people into more valuable positions.

Large models strike deeper, entering the territory people most habitually use to establish themselves: language, expression, explanation, code, proof, proposals, style, synthesis, planning, and preliminary judgment. Steam engines displaced muscle, computers rule execution, and large models now begin displacing substantial symbolic output. They mark one of the major events in symbols since writing, beyond a smarter writing tool. Writing detached experience from bodies, printing reproduced it at scale, computers executed symbols under rules, and large models recombine externalized human experience into responses, generation, and agentic action. External memory no longer merely preserves and awaits retrieval; it begins to speak, explain, plan, and invoke tools.

The change already extends beyond answering questions, coding, and passing examinations. The GPT-5.5 system card describes complex real-world work: coding, online research, information analysis, document and spreadsheet creation, and progress through tasks in environments with multiple tools \cite{openai2026gpt55systemcard}. The o3 and o4-mini system card connects reasoning to browsing, Python, image and file analysis, automation, file search, and memory \cite{openai2025o3o4minisystemcard}. Deep Research and ChatGPT Agent further show research, retrieval, web interaction, code execution, data analysis, and file generation converging \cite{openai2025deepresearchsystemcard,openai2025chatgptagentsystemcard}. Together they indicate a move from symbol generators toward task systems acting through tools and agents. Human value cannot therefore remain a contest over who writes better. If models write, search, calculate, execute code, use tools, and generate reports, value must find deeper positions: who confirms information, defines problems, admits results into reality, takes over failures, and bears consequences?

A mirror is still no world. A large model can produce the shape of knowledge without automatically having experience; the shape of proof still requires checking against rules; the shape of care need not bear the corresponding relationship; a proposed action need not touch its consequences. A judgment once usually implied a speaker, experience, and responsibility behind it; forms can now proliferate without experience, verification, or consequence-bearing. The old link between form and experience weakens. Civilization’s external memory learns to speak, while speaking itself loses some of its former weight.

\subhead{Verification after Generation}

When external memory begins to speak, the locations of value need rearranging. Verification can be classified by its objects into formal, semantic, causal, engineering, long-term biological, and social-responsibility layers; ordered instead by depth of consequences, the chain becomes a sequence of growing stakes, with intersecting stages whose speed and costs still require separate accounting. The distance between candidates and evidence is where value must find a new place to settle.

After large models, an initial source of human value is reconnecting symbols to reality rather than producing still more symbols. Cheaper generation makes verification relatively scarcer; more candidates make judgment more consequential. An answer is not yet knowledge, explanation not yet understanding, a proposal not yet action, simulation not yet consequence. The age of intelligence brings an explosion of candidates rather than an automatic abundance of knowledge. Reliable results require verification appropriate to the object and intended use. Value here includes credibility within knowledge communities, authorization within institutions, and consequence-bearing within relationships and life, alongside exchange value in labor markets. AI can cheapen output without automatically conferring legitimacy on these values.

The pyramid runs through candidate generation $\to$ representational confirmation $\to$ inferential confirmation $\to$ confirmation for action $\to$ system integration $\to$ long-term consequence-bearing. Generation asks whether something can be expressed; representational confirmation whether the object exists and sources are reliable; inferential confirmation whether proofs, code, calculations, and causal chains hold; confirmation for action whether the result can enter a real environment and errors can be stopped, reversed, and traced; integration whether organizations, platforms, hospitals, roads, factories, and institutions can receive it; long-term bearing whether it withstands time, scale, anomalies, misuse, and intergenerational effects. Intelligent systems can verify, sometimes more consistently than people in particular stages; that externalizes part of verification without automatically completing its legitimacy. Intelligence can generate and verify judgments without automatically authorizing their entry into reality.

Unfolding the chain reveals different rates of migration. Earlier stages automate more readily when inputs and outputs admit clear description; later stages move slowly because their criteria emerge through time, and someone must determine who holds those criteria and who bears mistakes. Research combines hard formal stages with weighty contact with objects; the formal side changes first because the other side’s criteria lie outside the system, rather than merely because it is more complex. This distinction turns the inquiry toward two ends: search within rules and contact with real objects.

\subsection{Clocks and Steam Engines: Disciplined Time, Liberated Muscle}

\subhead{Clocks Disciplined Time First}

Before steam engines, mechanical clocks had already externalized something: time rather than muscle. Work under natural rhythms followed sunrise and sunset, local conditions, daylight, and seasons, leaving substantial control of pace to people. Clock towers and pocket watches divided time into uniform, measurable units; factory whistles turned those units into discipline, making punctuality virtuous, lateness culpable, and timed comparisons of efficiency more pervasive. This externalization produced no material object yet rearranged lives: alongside coal and iron, industrial order rested on prescribed time, taking control of rhythm rather than bodily strength.

Steam engines changed energy rather than symbols. Human and animal muscle ceased to be the main sources of power. Strength, endurance, speed, and direct work once sustained many social positions; steam power relocated force into machines, fuel, railways, factories, cities, and capital. Society reorganized around machine power as the body lost its central place in doing work. Old crafts lost weight and old labor acquired new discipline, yet people remained. Value moved from muscle toward control, organization, maintenance, dispatch, and responsibility. Greater power raises the stakes of accidents and the importance of standards, repair, training, coordination, insurance, and accountability. The Industrial Revolution changed the value of bodily work and pushed human positions toward designing, managing, coordinating, and answering for machine systems, beyond simply freeing people from labor \cite{landes1969unbound}. Clocks and steam engines together moved people from doing work to controlling it, shifting value from overcoming physical resistance toward managing complex systems. Control is more abstract than direct work, requiring coordination of machines, timetables, and strangers, and is therefore harder for one technical upgrade to erase. These externalizations left visible, measurable carriers in the external world, making displaced positions easier to locate anew. Once machines absorb rules, symbols, and formal exploration, the direction becomes less immediately visible.

\subsection{Externalized Form and Action}

\subhead{Externalizing Formal Exploration}

Research faces its own repositioning, with mathematics and theory at the sharpest edge. Three layers differ: symbol generation expresses forms, formal exploration creates structures within rules, and verification connects those structures to rules, communities, or real objects. Writing proofs, proposing constructions, and searching for algorithms once themselves attested to intensive training; these interfaces are now loosening too. In Olympiad geometry, AlphaGeometry combines neural generation with symbolic deduction: the neural model proposes auxiliary constructions, the symbolic engine reasons and checks, and the system synthesizes large numbers of geometric theorems and proofs without human demonstrations \cite{trinh2024alphageometry}. Reliable proof combines formal generation with rule-based confirmation, beyond text resembling a proof.

A stronger signal appeared in 2026, when an OpenAI model produced a counterexample overturning a central conjectural direction associated with Erdős’s 1946 planar unit-distance problem; Alon, Bloom, Gowers, Litt, Sawin, Shankar, Tsimerman, Wang, and Wood then supplied a short, digested, human-verified account and reflections on it \cite{openai2026unitdistancedisproof,alon2026remarks}. This unsettles a hard interface of formal intellectual labor; it neither settles the entire unit-distance problem in a sentence nor removes the mathematical community. A model can propose a construction that changes the picture, while mathematicians still check, compress, explain, name, and integrate it into theory before it becomes mathematical knowledge.

AlphaEvolve externalizes formal exploration in another way. It combines model generation, code modification, automated evaluation, and evolutionary search so that candidate algorithms improve through feedback, beyond merely writing a proof. Its white paper reports useful results in mathematics, computation, and infrastructure optimization; a concrete case is a procedure multiplying 4$\times$4 complex matrices with 48 scalar multiplications, improving a longstanding result in that particular setting \cite{novikov2025alphaevolve}. The case demonstrates accelerated generation and screening in formalizable, evaluable, iterative search spaces, rather than a completed solution to algorithm discovery. Human value moves toward judging problems, objectives, verification standards, and admission into a knowledge community: what merits searching, whether the evaluator is sound or overfit, and whether results are interpretable, provable, transferable, and theoretically usable. This remains formal because the evaluator can be coded; when an object must supply the evaluation, migration takes another form.

\subhead{Construction and Confirmation at the Frontier}

Together, the cases raise a larger question: how hard a problem can externalized formal exploration reach? The Riemann hypothesis, Birch and Swinnerton-Dyer conjecture, and Navier–Stokes existence and smoothness problem have special standing because their criteria concentrate on logical conditions: after specifying a proposition and framework, a proof or counterexample must meet those conditions, beyond any industry convention; the statement and its correspondence to the proof still require examination. An external system making substantive progress there reaches the hardest line examined throughout this book.

The medium-response spectrum frames this as impedance matching: mathematics and experimental science absorb the same input of intelligence differently. Some mathematical work has relatively low impedance: with clear rules and a correctly formalized candidate, independent machine checking becomes possible, though accurate translation of informal statements into a verifier remains work; experiments often require more expensive contact with objects, since the object itself supplies the test and cannot be replaced by a formal substitute. This helps explain why formal exploration loosens there first and why that progress cannot simply be extrapolated.

A related image appears in Terence Tao’s 2026 discussion, located further inside knowledge production than Chapter 3’s comparison. There, mismatch lay between model output and an external medium—atoms, life, or organizations; here both source and load lie within knowledge production, as generation and digestion. He separates mathematical work into generation, verification, and digestion: understanding a result, placing it in context, and explaining it. In his account, all three were historically difficult, and digestion arose naturally as a by-product, while communities rewarded generation and verification. Accelerated generation separates their rates: generation moves fastest, formalization speeds some verification, and digestion does not accelerate equally. He calls this an impedance mismatch, describing mathematics moving from proof scarcity to proof abundance before its culture and infrastructure have adapted \cite{tao2026aiviews}. The separation first appears as a ratio of capacities. Let $g>0$ be new candidates per unit time and $d$ the capacity for digestion on the same basis; define capacity coverage as
\begin{equation}
\begin{split}
\rho&=\min\!\left\{1,\frac{d}{g}\right\},\\
\left.\frac{\mathrm{d}\rho}{\mathrm{d}t}\right|_{0<d/g<1}&<0
\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
\frac{\dot g}{g}>\frac{\dot d}{d}
\end{split}
\label{eq:digestion-share}
\end{equation}
Both $g$ and $d$ are measured in candidates per unit time, making $\rho$ dimensionless. For $0<d<g$, coverage falls exactly when generation’s relative growth exceeds digestion’s; for $d\ge g$, coverage is capped at 1. The ratio compares current capacity with incoming load; the share actually digested also depends on backlogs, selection order, and differences among candidates. If generation contracts from months to a day while writing accelerates only slightly, the capacities diverge. Figure\ref{fig:proof-abundance} sketches this change in load.

Counterexamples and search-based improvements change knowledge differently. A counterexample supplies an object violating a proposition; search improves candidates under an explicit evaluator. AlphaEvolve’s matrix multiplication belongs to the latter. Checkable objects provide automated search with feedback, but construction and verification costs vary by problem. Usable knowledge still needs precise statements, independent checks, and understanding of scope.

The Jacobian conjecture and Navier–Stokes problem offer two cases requiring examination of concrete constructions. Proposed in 1939, the Jacobian conjecture asks whether polynomial maps satisfying the relevant Jacobian condition are invertible; in July 2026, Levent Alpöge announced a three-dimensional counterexample and credited its discovery to Claude Fable \cite{alpoge2026jacobian}. Subsequent exposition returned the polynomial construction to its algebraic-geometric setting, explaining why the counterexample works \cite{tao2026jacobiandigestion}. Different participants can discover, check, and explain, with separate costs for each. The three-dimensional counterexample also refutes higher-dimensional versions; the two-dimensional case remains unresolved by this work.

Navier–Stokes existence and smoothness is a Millennium Prize Problem. On September 8, 2026, OpenAI released a proof manuscript and Lean formalization for finite-time singularity formation in three-dimensional flow under smooth external forcing, claiming the official counterexample statements C and D; the unforced versions must be distinguished \cite{openai2026navierstokes}. The work combines candidate construction, analytical reasoning, and machine checking. Its mathematical standing requires examination of hypotheses, proof content, independent checks, and community scrutiny.

Proportions of zeta zeros satisfying the Riemann hypothesis are partial theorems progressing toward the full proposition \cite{anthropic2026riemann,lamzouri2026}. The Birch and Swinnerton-Dyer conjecture concerns a general relationship between elliptic-curve arithmetic and its $L$-function. Partial proofs, general proofs, and counterexamples demand different objects and arguments. A construction may shorten verification while being exceptionally hard to find; whichever advance comes first needs explanation through the particular problem and method.

Checking a result differs from tracing its discovery. A counterexample can admit independent computation while its search history remains incompletely disclosed; analytical proofs and formal certificates each depend on their statements, rules, and implementations. Disputes around contributions and data use during the Navier–Stokes release extend the questions to provenance, confidentiality, and credit. Reports record different participants’ accounts \cite{axios2026mathcredit,techcrunch2026buckmaster,venturebeat2026codexdata}; resolving them requires relevant records rather than correctness checks alone.

A further detail matters: the sequence began with a rumor that was not subsequently substantiated. According to OpenAI’s release, hearing that two Millennium Problems had been solved prompted evaluation across the then-open problems before the effort concentrated on Navier–Stokes. The rumor remained unconfirmed, yet the work it triggered produced a result. The signal-to-noise ratio of public information thus becomes a variable in the research process. The release reports roughly 300 billion output tokens across the attempts within days, including about 130 billion for Navier–Stokes \cite{openai2026navierstokes}. Both verification priorities and the choice of what to verify are affected.

Together these cases suggest a testable claim: external systems can both supply answers and turn a direction from presumed correct into something demanding reexamination. That act has long belonged to science; systems can now perform part of it faster. They can add knowledge and change verification priorities. The earlier separation remains: raising a checking priority can be fast, while turning checked results into usable knowledge moves less quickly; the difference remains an unsettled balance.

\subhead{When the Old Evaluation System Fails}

Once formal exploration is partly externalized, pressure first reaches academia’s apparatus for selecting knowledge. In this book’s vocabulary, it generates credentials. Peer review, journal hierarchies, citations, academic ranks, and tenure offer different evidence of training, work, and credibility; part of that credibility rests on actual processes: reviewing and replication take time, and conclusions enter shared knowledge through later understanding and use.

Increased generation presses both ends of the chain. At the output end, submissions, candidate proofs, and experimental proposals can grow rapidly while human review remains time-constrained, with tools changing that constraint only stage by stage; at the selection end, the implicit premise that one person cannot quickly produce so much good work is weakening. Acceptance rates, signal-to-noise ratios, and review loads can all come under pressure, while adjustment remains tied to human work rhythms. This is structural beyond individual scholarly ethics: a system using scarce output to establish qualification loses discriminatory power when output ceases to be scarce.

The old arrangement kept $\rho$ in Equation\eqref{eq:digestion-share} from becoming conspicuous by binding generation and digestion in one work: solving a problem required explaining it clearly enough to publish. Once that bond loosens, falling $\rho$ bears directly on review. Tao describes priority drifting from journal publication dates to preprint timestamps and then to social-media races over who first prompted an AI, rewarding omitted verification, literature review, and exposition. He proposes anchoring priority in the first public, clear explanation, whether a lecture, expository paper, or recorded talk, supplementing rather than replacing preprints and formal certificates. The journal \emph{Mathematical Discourse}, launched in 2026 to publish recorded research talks, offers an early example \cite{tao2026aiviews,tao2026discourse}. The same thought leads to a firmer norm. He divides a proof’s lifecycle into generation, verification, writing, publication, and canonicalization: becoming textbook knowledge repeatedly usable by later work. Generating and verifying a proof with AI, then declining to write, present, or submit it, leaves the result halfway through and passes completion costs to others. His proposed norm asks anyone claiming priority through a proof’s generation to try to carry it at least to publication; recognizing that the commitment cannot always be met, he also proposes a formal mechanism for offering unfinished proofs for adoption by other authors rather than leaving the handover entirely improvised \cite{tao2026aiviews}. Verification is developing a related division of labor. Palomar, a registry of Lean-formalized mathematics supported by Tao, addresses a specific consequence of abundant generation: a repository passing type checking need not prove the proposition it claims. It checks whether the code typechecks, whether it takes shortcuts such as adding axioms, and whether the formal statement semantically matches the informal claim. Lean’s comparator performs the mechanical check; large language models undertake the latter two. Palomar states that these checks remain far short of human peer review’s assessment of originality, significance, and accuracy, and explicitly disclaims being a peer-reviewed journal \cite{tao2026palomar}. Separating type checking, assumptions, and correspondence of statements lets the registry’s stages be assessed individually. When models perform intermediate checks, their grounds, review coverage, and types of omission still need recording. Formal certificates, semantic review, peer review, and accountability together form a structure of confirmation. Actual throughput and error records determine which layer becomes the bottleneck.

Comparing the two sides reveals where the questions diverge. Industry emphasizes capabilities and thresholds. At its September 3, 2026 model launch, OpenAI announced “Welcome to the AGI era”; Greg Brockman discussed whether it crossed the AGI threshold, while Jess Kinghorn reported Jensen Huang’s subsequent public claim that AGI had arrived \cite{axios2026agi,huang2026agi}. Brockman told Stratechery this was the first training run using more than 100,000 GPUs \cite{brockman2026astra}; OpenAI’s earlier safety statement designated Astra at its Critical cybersecurity capability threshold and described associated safeguards \cite{openai2026pathastra}. The professional community asks about institutions and consequences. In a September statement, Tao wrote that mathematics was rapidly approaching a path he wished to avoid; in his view, the main source of harm had shifted from unverified use before 2026 toward indiscriminate, benchmark-driven extraction. He also said that most industry insiders sharing his views had left or been marginalized, describing the Navier–Stokes episode as a vivid instance of a race to create extremely powerful autonomous systems without regard to social value \cite{tao2026statement}.

The accounts first need separating: which scale does each use? One emphasizes capability thresholds, the other how capabilities enter the world and at whose cost; they may also disagree substantively about goals, authority, and social value. The earlier chapters’ accounting returns: a capability ceiling can be announced on its own, but costs must land somewhere; divergent narratives can report the numerator and denominator rather than necessarily indicating a lie.

Reforming evaluation requires comparing different credentials. Independent replication exposes some errors at additional experimental and labor cost; actual use provides long-term feedback but can put errors into consequential chains first; credit, records, and accountability help trace decisions. Each answers a different question, requiring institutions to combine evidence while preventing a few organizations from monopolizing access.

The preceding material adds a note to the third route. Commitment and adoption mechanisms, and priority for the first clear explanation, reconnect credentials to responsibility: claimants answer for a result’s later life rather than its birth alone. Tao places this within a larger judgment. In 2026 he described a crisis of mathematical values and practices rather than reasoning, saying the community had only months to restate what being a mathematician meant, or let technology companies and financial incentives answer for it \cite{tao2026icm,tao2026nature}. The point gathers the earlier arguments: abundant generation forces institutions to ask which stages cannot be skipped with generation; one continuing task is taking responsibility for subsequent use, revision, and correction.

The three routes remain incomplete and compatible. Can the new arrangement merely add stronger tools to the old one? Part of the old arrangement’s discriminatory power came precisely from scarce output. If producing a credential accelerates, does it retain the same connection to the training, understanding, or responsibility it was meant to establish? Institutions need to determine which processes still support reliable credentials. Answers may differ by field; this book’s criteria offer a starting point for further discussion.

\subhead{Externalization in Experiments and Code}

Research’s other half works with objects: bringing candidates to samples and instruments, and code into actual systems. Experimental research carries another layer of weight beyond formal exploration. It includes experimental design, sample preparation, instrument operation, observation, error handling, replication, and failed attempts, alongside reading, coding, and proposing hypotheses. The AI Scientist-v2 reports autonomous hypothesis generation, experimental design and execution, analysis, visualization, and paper writing, with one entirely AI-generated paper reaching an ICLR workshop acceptance threshold \cite{yamada2025aiscientistv2}. It moves formal stages from hypothesis to manuscript into an agentic workflow; contact with experimental objects, community judgment, and long-term validation remain separate questions. Research value therefore moves beyond completing a paper pipeline toward problem significance, object contact, variable selection, measurement credibility, interpretation of failure, ethical boundaries, and responsibility for long-term verification.

Virtual Lab offers a stronger example closer to life science. It organizes LLM agents into a virtual laboratory, with an LLM principal investigator coordinating scientist agents to design nanobodies against SARS-CoV-2 variants under high-level human feedback \cite{swanson2025virtuallab}. The case externalizes experimental design, candidate screening, and interdisciplinary discussion, while still requiring protein models, experiments, measurement, and human judgment, rather than establishing independent AI biology. Science is no purely digital closed loop. Candidates proliferate in model space, but scientific results must pass through objects, instruments, errors, replication, and a community.

Code sits between symbols and reality. It resembles text but executes, calls interfaces, writes to systems, and changes workflows. GPT-4.1 reportedly completed 54.6\% of tasks on SWE-bench Verified; GPT-5-Codex further targets agentic coding, trained through reinforcement learning on real coding tasks and iterating through test execution until tests pass \cite{openai2025gpt41,openai2025gpt5codex}. Code generation, patch proposals, test repair, and repository navigation are being externalized. Software engineering’s value nevertheless extends beyond writing code. Its weight lies in requirements, architectural boundaries, dependency management, security review, test coverage, deployment responsibility, and maintenance. Faster generation makes confirmation more consequential, while easier patches can accumulate system debt. Value moves from producing a passage of code toward keeping it reliable within a system over time. Much confirmation still occurs inside software systems; moving further into physical environments extends externalization from symbolic operations to bodily action.

\subhead{Externalizing Action and Biological Intervention}

Some consequences of action and biological processes resist rollback, changing this layer of externalization. Automated experimental operations chiefly test hypotheses; embodied intelligence pushes beyond that purpose. Intelligence begins acting directly on roads, in factories, hospitals, homes, and public spaces. RT-2 jointly trains vision-language models with robot trajectories, translating internet-scale semantic knowledge into action tokens for robot control \cite{zitkovich2023rt2}. Gemini Robotics and GR00T N1 connect vision-language-action models and humanoid foundation models with robot trajectories, human video, and synthetic data, attempting to transfer general digital capabilities into physical agents \cite{geminirobotics2025,nvidia2025gr00t}. Benchmarks such as RoboCasa365 show why speech alone cannot establish general action. Its 365 everyday kitchen tasks, 2,500 environments, over 600 hours of human demonstrations, and over 1,600 hours of synthetic demonstrations show how action must be grounded in scenarios, tasks, data, and evaluation \cite{nasiriany2026robocasa365}. Real machines encounter contact, wear, delay, occlusion, slipping, failed grasps, instability, damage, downtime, other bodies, and changing scenes. Evolution encapsulates much bodily complexity in form, reflexes, and habits; machines do not automatically inherit that amortization, so stronger action capabilities require verification, maintenance, shutdown, tracing, and accountability. Human value in embodied intelligence includes discretion over action alongside verification of knowledge. Autonomous driving needs arrangements for edge cases, liability, takeover, road rules, insurance, and acceptable public risk beyond a smooth demonstration; surgical robots need someone to take over, record, explain, and bear losses when failure occurs, beyond executing a movement. Action is an event of admission into a chain of consequences rather than output simply extended. Machines can act, but consequences cannot hang unassigned. Registration, logs, audits, shutdown authority, and insurance give consequences an operational destination; their contribution may not appear in the speed of a single movement, yet they help make action possible.

Large models lighten symbolic output, reasoning models and scientific agents externalize formal exploration, and embodied intelligence externalizes action; intelligence applied to life reaches deeper, helping define bodies, disease, normality, risk, and life paths rather than merely speaking, calculating, or acting for us. AlphaFold 3 extends structure prediction from individual proteins to complexes involving proteins, nucleic acids, small molecules, ions, and modified residues \cite{abramson2024alphafold3}. AI drug discovery, protein design, genetic risk scores, and multimodal medical models intensify candidate generation, screening, classification, and risk prediction within biological processes \cite{fritzsche2023ethical}. These systems first move biological classifications, screening, risks, and optimization objectives into model space, rather than simply making life lighter. Molecular prediction makes candidates easier to produce, risk scoring classifies future disease probabilities, and multimodal medical models combine symptoms, images, genes, records, and lifestyles into judgments. What counts as health? What counts as normal? Which differences should remain? Which suffering can be removed? Which risks must not be transferred? Who may choose futures for people not yet born? Who may define a better human being? Once life enters design space, value concerns which people, suffering, differences, and risks are allowed to exist, beyond whether people remain useful.

The deepest danger is classifications written into futures: people labeled high-risk or low-value in advance, marked for treatment, screening, optimization, or exclusion. Intelligence can propose definitions without independently authorizing them. Institutional classifications change who counts as patient, risk, or defect, and who must undergo treatment, screening, or optimization. Even intelligence far beyond experts in epidemiology, genomics, neuroscience, and risk prediction would move the question rather than end it: who authorizes standards to govern classification, treatment, insurance, education, reproduction, and care, and who bears their lasting mistakes? If intelligent systems permeate authorization itself, patient experience, public deliberation, legal procedures, and long-term testing become still more consequential; otherwise a better human being can become merely a self-reinforcing technical classification. Externalization now concerns authority as well as capabilities, and value migration institutions as well as individuals.

\subsection{Externalized Capabilities, Migrating Value}

\subhead{The Social Conditions of Migration}

Memory, copying, timekeeping, and rule execution have repeatedly been externalized, lowering operating costs and changing the value of training, occupations, and interpretation. Difficulties may move toward calibration, organization, and distribution, or later technologies may lower them too. Human positions rearrange with these relations. Assessment requires separating needed work, recipients of gains, and costs left uncounted.

Distribution remains: who receives the new positions, and who decides? From writing to intelligence runs a deep historical line: people repeatedly externalize parts of their capability, lightening an old ability and retreating toward a deeper position. People do not thereby lose value, but can no longer demonstrate it through the old position.

High-viscosity domains do not inherently belong to humans. Verification can become a platform service, admission a capital asset, responsibility a contract, and definitional authority a possession of expert systems and institutions. Human value migrates because symbols, forms, actions, and biological interventions need interfaces for questions, appeals, refusal, and consequence-bearing when entering reality, rather than because people automatically hold a higher position. If a few platforms, institutions, or algorithmic systems monopolize those interfaces, people need not rise; they can instead become objects classified, scored, and adjusted. Value migration is a social struggle over verification, admission, accountability, and definition, rather than a gentle rising curve.

Most people cannot complete this migration through individual effort alone. Writing did not turn every keeper of memory into an interpreter, printing every scribe into an academic or publisher, or steam power every craftsperson into an engineer or manager. The age of intelligence is similar. Displaced clerks do not automatically become verification experts, nor pressured workers decision-makers. New positions can also lie in local knowledge, situated judgment, care, user feedback, rights to refuse and appeal, and public oversight. Beyond training a few elite decision-makers, more people need channels to express lived experience, reject mistaken objectives, and participate in allocating consequences. Otherwise, migration can become an upward path for a minority and functional weightlessness for the rest.

Failed migration includes a mismatch in time: new positions do not appear exactly when old ones disappear, leaving displaced people to bear the interval. Labor-market research distinguishes displacement from complementarity: automation compresses standardizable tasks while raising productivity in work alongside machines, with simultaneous effects falling on different people \cite{autor2015why}. U.S. manufacturing employment peaked around 19.6 million in 1979 and fell to roughly 11.5 million around 2010, while total national employment grew across the broader period \cite{bls2024employment}. Aggregate narratives can erase this separation of totals and distribution. Imagine a worker facing substitution after forty: acquiring a new, valuable skill may take years, with transitional losses borne now and some gains appearing only in the next generation.

Losing a position is not the only failure. Migration can also fail through an excessively smooth environment: systems generate, screen, recommend, act, and console, leaving judgment, refusal, waiting, and consequence-bearing less room for practice. Chapter 5’s stagnation and local optima describe the system side: refusal loses its object, and the system settles into comfort. Judgment needs testing, desire time to unfold, and boundaries usable refusal; without external consequences, systems can fit existing preferences ever more closely. People need room to fail, negate, reconsider, and redefine goals, rather than pain itself. Without that room, environments keep adjusting people instead of subjecthood developing.

People supply differentiated responses with history, intention, relationships, and consequence-bearing, beyond disturbances, feedback, or preferences. Systems can convert choices into data, feedback into parameters, and behavior into optimization signals without exhausting their meaning. Injury, memory, refusal, reconsideration, and consequence-bearing make subjects real openings onto the world, beyond further optimization signals. People are where meaning and consequences still occur, rather than merely inferior inputs or data fuel.
