\subhead{An Opening That Cannot Be Wholly Closed}

Human value cannot rest on an assertion that machines will never become subjects. The future development of intelligence should not be closed in advance. Any intelligent system entering symbols, forms, action, and life rewrites value interfaces alongside improving efficiency. Symbols need calibration, forms communities of verification, action accountability structures, and biological optimization authorization and subjects bearing consequences. \key{Technology first crosses low-viscosity domains; where will value settle again?} Generation, copying, search, and preliminary execution grow lighter; verification, admission, accountability, definition, lasting relationships, bodily contact, public deliberation, and irreversible commitments may become harder-to-bypass sites of scarcity.

Human value lies in an opening onto reality that cannot be wholly closed, beyond irreplaceable output alone. The more intelligence replaces capabilities, the less people can stake value on capability itself. Value needs deeper boundaries: reconnect symbols to reality, forms to verification, action to responsibility, and life to consequence-bearing that cannot be outsourced. Symbolic output alone cannot confer these connections, which require actual investment and authority: verification stakes the judge’s credibility, admission the power to stop, accountability resources for compensation, and definition an authorization answerable to challenge. Migration therefore concerns costlier commitments rather than merely stronger capabilities; whether their costs establish credibility determines whether these positions can actually receive value.

The line of migration identifies positions without yet explaining what constitutes them. Valid judgment, effective commitment, and traceable responsibility require boundaries, which declarations alone cannot create. The next inquiry asks how a boundary is physically defined and how something demonstrates that it has actually paid a cost.


\section{First Principle: An Ontology of Damping}

The migration identifies positions without establishing their grounds. For verification, admission, accountability, and definition to receive value, the recipient must establish whether the party making a commitment can itself be changed by consequences. The prerequisite is basic: something needs a boundary before changes can be attributed to it. The first principle therefore concerns boundaries: how they are defined, how costs can establish their existence, and why meaning requires a structure sustained by continuing investment.

\subsection{Defining Boundaries through Interaction}

A boundary’s formation depends on its function. A container’s separation rests on material structure, cellular concentration differences also require metabolism and transport, and organizational permissions depend on identity, records, and procedures. Existence, recognizable boundaries, and returning responsibility each require their own evidence. Since a subject’s self-report can be generated, assessment must also examine continuity of identity, how behavior occurs, and whether consequences can be traced.

\subhead{Functional Differences and Boundary Maintenance}

The material separation of a cell membrane differs from its electrochemical gradients. Ion pumps expend energy to offset leaks and sustain gradients; when pumping stops, gradients decay according to channels and concentrations, while the membrane itself need not immediately disappear. Organizational admission, records, and accountability also require work to maintain their functions. Both concern functional maintenance, while material and institutional mechanisms require separate explanations.

Express this relationship as relaxation of a difference after pumping stops,

\begin{equation}
\frac{dB}{dt}=-\frac{B}{\tau}+P
\end{equation}

Here $B$ is the functional difference under examination, taken in the ion-pump example as the concentration difference across a membrane, in moles per liter; $P$ is the concentration increment supplied per unit time, in moles per liter per second; $\tau$ is the relaxation time in seconds, the characteristic decay scale of this linear approximation. When pumping stops ($P=0$), the solution is $B(t)=B_0e^{-t/\tau}$, approaching zero in the long-time limit; choosing a time constant of tens of minutes is a parameter illustration rather than a universal cellular decay time. For constant positive $P$, the system approaches $B^{*}=\tau P$, determined jointly by pumping and relaxation. Maintaining a nonzero functional difference requires pumping to offset leakage; removing the input lets the difference decay, without establishing immediate disappearance of the material boundary. The expression sketches maintenance: the physical meaning of $B$ and the values of $\tau$ and $P$ depend on the system, whose actual relaxation may involve nonlinearities, multiple ions, and several timescales.

\subhead{The Need for Reference Standards}

A second line of inquiry concerns reference standards. An observer in uniform straight-line motion cannot use a closed experiment to determine velocity relative to an absolutely stationary space; this does not prevent internal measurements or establish that every clock drift must be detected outside the system. Calibration begins by specifying the quantity and standard being compared. GPS connects satellites and ground monitoring stations in a continuing comparison network, estimating orbits and clock offsets from observations before uploading corrections \cite{gpscontrolsegment}. Without independent time comparison, an isolated clock cannot identify drift relative to a chosen standard from its own readings alone; several independent clocks can also supply internal comparisons. A force-controlled robotic arm offers another case: contact and reliable grasping require force, vision, or other observations connected to the object. Self-description cannot replace those tests; the question is whether necessary information enters independently of the current judgment.

A third line comes from biology. In the 1930s, Jakob von Uexküll described the Umwelt: animals select different relevant features through perception and action within the same physical space; his classic tick example centers on three cues—butyric acid, body warmth, and the feel of hair \cite{uexkull1934streifzuge}. The boundary here comprises possible interactions rather than geometric dimensions alone. James J. Gibson’s affordances likewise connect environments to action: a handle appears pullable and a step climbable, beyond a list of neutral geometric properties \cite{gibson1979}. Cybernetics asks about regulation: under specified information and control conditions, regulators need sufficient available variety to handle relevant disturbances; detecting a disturbance, choosing different actions, and successfully controlling it are connected but distinct stages \cite{ashby1956cybernetics}.

\subhead{Boundaries Select What Passes}

Together these lines make a boundary a selector of what passes, beyond isolation alone. Crystals are not absolutely unchanging: they transmit heat and force and can expand, deform, or change phase with their environment; material stability does not directly establish a subject’s consequence-bearing. Living boundaries must also regulate exchanges to maintain metabolism and functional differences. Selective passage connects maintenance to environmental dependence and leaves an opening for change. For life sustained by exchange, severing all exchange undermines survival; this concerns a class of living boundaries rather than a universal law of death for every boundary.

Defining boundaries through interaction also requires repeatability. One collision establishes something there, without establishing an enduring subject. Repeated responses trace a contour by separating stable structure from random disturbance. Relationships, professions, and reputations likewise acquire boundaries through testable responses over time rather than one reply. If systems handle generation, recommendation, reassurance, and execution while replacing repeatable resistance with arbitrarily revisable responses, some interactions needed for forming boundaries may diminish. The question concerns the continued availability of boundary-forming interaction alongside any decline in ability.

\subhead{Boundaries in Development}

Some boundaries also develop. Mirror self-recognition offers an observable measure: researchers secretly mark a young child’s nose and observe whether the child touches their own nose or reaches toward the reflection. Self-directed mark touching often emerges between eighteen and twenty-four months, with substantial variation; earlier responses can include exploring the reflection or treating it as a social partner \cite{amsterdam1972mirror}. This tracks one form of self-recognition rather than the birth of the entire self-boundary; which interactions support it, and how one-way responses affect it, remain separate research questions.

The immune system offers another scale. Developmental tolerance and later recognition, regulation, and clearance distinguish what to retain from what to confront; self versus nonself is one classic line, with both self-damage and missed invasion potentially causing serious consequences \cite{burnet1959clonal}. Accuracy requires maintained mechanisms, while recognition range, response intensity, and collateral harm need joint assessment. Engineering boundaries likewise involve missed detections and false positives, whose consequences may fall on different parties.

\subhead{The Principle’s Scope}

Greater resistance does not by itself make a boundary clearer. A wall separates spaces while transmitting heat and force; blocking one passage does not block every effect. Reciprocal physical interaction also does not distribute power and costs symmetrically: punishment can continually reach one party without corresponding consequences for the other. A responsibility boundary therefore calls for questions about who can change the process, challenge it, and actually bear its costs. The next section turns to signals: how can something establish its claimed investment and make a commitment dependable?

\subsection{Costly Signals: When Costs Can Establish Credibility}

\subhead{Why Signals Sometimes Need Costs}

Traits such as peacocks’ tails made signaling costs a central evolutionary question. Zahavi proposed that high costs could link signals to the sender’s condition; later models examine how costs, benefits, and types jointly sustain honesty \cite{zahavi1975mate,grafen1990biological}. Sexual selection, direct indices, shared interests, and constraints can also produce reliable signals, without every honest signal requiring high realized expenditure. A theoretical review appearing in a 2026 issue focuses on type-dependent benefits and opportunity costs, examining honest signals that are cheap to send or even yield immediate benefits \cite{szamado2026signalling}.

\begin{equation}
c(q_{\text{low}}) > b > c(q_{\text{high}})
\end{equation}

Here $c(q)$ is the cost of sending the signal for an individual of quality $q$, and $b$ the benefit of acceptance. Under the assumed benefit, the inequality makes the high-quality type willing to send and the low-quality type unwilling to imitate: a simplified separating condition rather than a requirement for every informative signal. The structure extends beyond biology. Spence’s 1973 labor-market model gives different types different educational costs, explaining how qualifications can convey ability while temporarily leaving education’s productive contribution outside the model \cite{spence1973job}. The handicap principle remains contested: in 2020, a systematic critique argued that acceptance had outrun its empirical support \cite{penn2020handicap}. This book treats the structure as a testable explanatory route alongside direct indices, shared interests, and institutional verification. This gives a counterintuitive criterion: \key{A signal distinguishes people through who can send it, who wants to send it, and who will honor it.} If different types send the same signal under identical conditions and probabilities, that signal cannot distinguish them.

\subhead{Withdrawal, Ownership, and Time}

Generative AI changes both the supply of signals and the cost of imitating their appearance. A coherent article, well-composed picture, or working program once often required training; many such products are now cheap to generate. When the same appearance no longer requires the same training, its power to distinguish senders’ abilities can decline, already visible in degrees, portfolios, and résumés. What still qualifies as a costly signal? The inequality supplies half a criterion—different types face different incentives to send—leaving the question of which investments and commitments still admit reliable checks. Three conditions organize that inquiry.

First, conditions of withdrawal. A recoverable file state can still consume irrecoverable electricity and time, and may already have affected other people. The questions concern traceability of claimed investment and consequences, and the scope of recovery. Rollback is an engineering advantage without automatically erasing all investment.

Second, ownership. Tools can perform parts of a process while people check, revise, and take responsibility for the final judgment. A fitness plan can be outsourced in words, but bodily adaptation must happen in the person; a tool can help draft an apology, while repairing the relationship requires both parties’ actions. Output, learning, authority, and commitment each need an identified owner.

Third, formation and observation time. Some abilities require repetition, recovery, and real outcomes; trust requires repeated fulfillment, and some safety judgments sufficient follow-up. Better training, design, and tools can shorten preparation too. If shorter time changes the product, identify the mechanism and conditions; three years compressed into three months does not alone establish that the same outcome is impossible.
\begin{equation}
t<\tau_{\mathrm{int}}\ \Longrightarrow\ \text{required process incomplete},
\qquad
\left.\frac{t}{\tau_{\mathrm{int}}}\right|_{\text{three years versus three months}}=\frac{3}{36}=\frac{1}{12}
\label{eq:intrinsic-time}
\end{equation}
Here $t$ is actual duration and $\tau_{\mathrm{int}}$ the shortest duration assumed necessary for a specified process to meet its completion conditions; both have units of time, making their ratio dimensionless. $\tau_{\mathrm{int}}$ depends on the process: skills, trust, and clinical experience need separate definitions of completed repetition, recovery, fulfillment, or case accumulation. If that minimum has been independently established, $t$ below $\tau_{\mathrm{int}}$ cannot count as completion of the same process; the three-year/three-month ratio merely illustrates arithmetic and establishes no particular ability’s threshold. Training, tools, and process design can change duration or completion standards, requiring a new estimate of $\tau_{\mathrm{int}}$; actual processes and outcomes determine whether necessary stages have been skipped. The proposed time condition still needs operational definition: ownership asks who acquires an ability, duration asks what has been completed, and generation speed alone answers neither.

\subhead{Investments in High-Viscosity Positions}

Applying these checks to particular fields lets us ask where new scarcity may arise. Care is one case. Caring for a disabled relative involves daily practical needs, emotions, and emergencies; professional services and tools can share many tasks, while a particular person’s presence in some relationships cannot be freely substituted. Care includes irrecoverable time and hard-to-reverse consequences, which sharing does not erase. Social necessity and remuneration can remain far apart, with budgets, labor institutions, and bargaining power shaping pay. An irreplaceable part of a relationship resists pricing as an interchangeable service; low pay cannot establish that it lacks value.

Core research has a related structure, though its signals differ from care. Literature reviews, data organization, coding, and drafting accelerate, leaving responsibility’s destination rather than workload as the enduring issue. Selecting problems, judging anomalous data, and standing behind conclusions still require someone to stake a scholarly reputation. Reputation can be costly because exposure of fraud cannot simply be repaired by withdrawing the paper. Academic certification can be slow, conservative, and unfair, yet records, scrutiny, and reputation still support credibility; achieving equivalent effects more cheaply requires comparing concrete mechanisms.

Commitment and enduring relationships form a third position, pressing temporal rigidity furthest. Twenty years of dialogue records cannot replace a twenty-year relationship, whose substance includes costly, tested concessions made over time rather than information exchange alone. Some concessions appear disadvantageous at the moment, yet together form something instantaneous satisfaction cannot copy. The difference lies in a history that requires living those twenty years rather than merely generating richer content.

Bodily labor and public trust represent more basic investments. Farming, building, repairing, surgery, and sport connect people to material outcomes governed by physical processes rather than a model’s output; revising a record does not erase an injury from misapplied force. Public trust is a collective asset accumulated through countless kept commitments and rapidly damaged by a few betrayals. Its accumulation depends on fulfillment rather than information transmission alone, making it a slow variable in an accelerating environment.

\subhead{Value beyond Resistance Itself}

A familiar misunderstanding now needs confronting: if costly signals matter, does greater resistance or suffering mean greater value? That inference has repeatedly justified needless suffering and must be separated from the argument.

Signaling theory concerns what distinguishes types or commitments, rather than whom suffering affects. If all types pay under the same conditions and produce indistinguishable outcomes, payment alone cannot distinguish them. Many imposed hardships consume lives without revealing relevant differences, proving only the power to inflict pain. Such costs are waste rather than costly signals.

A more specific criterion examines different types’ incentives and checkable outcomes. Training that feels easier to one mathematician may reveal ability or prior training, resources, and opportunity; a process equally difficult for everyone may still produce evidence of learning rather than merely screen people. Evidence can establish which frictions inform or build capability; deciding what to preserve also requires fairness, efficiency, and other values.

Value lies in reliable structures formed through necessary resistance, rather than resistance itself. One source of reliability is independent testing that allows results to overturn an existing judgment. Tests need not hurt, but they must be real: able to reject, return a negative result, and resist erasure merely to satisfy expectations; new evidence can still justify revision.

\subhead{When Imitation Becomes Cheap}

As generating convincing signals becomes almost free, demand for checks may move toward positions still distinguishing investment, authority, and commitment. That shift is not automatic: demand for signals persists and may temporarily rely on stronger-looking substitutes equally easy to imitate. This resembles credential inflation: employers raise degree requirements while degrees depreciate, still needing a sieve and using the one available.

The decisive turn occurs in demand rather than supply alone. If generated appearances no longer establish ability, people may demand evidence connected to actual processes: direct experience, traceable accountability, verifiable failures, reachable referees, and work tested by time. These connect to records, witnesses, and outcomes beyond quickly generated appearances, looking inefficient and troublesome in organizations focused on speed and therefore becoming early targets for removal. Their function is to give judgment somewhere to stand.

Action requires distinguishing such resistance from waste that should disappear. Acceleration makes the distinction urgent: both look slower, harder, and less advantageous, while their consequences can point in opposite directions.

The relation between cost and quality has another side. Paying costs can leave structures as well as sort people: training leaves capability in bodies, commitments records in relationships, and failure calibration in judgment. Those structures require maintenance beyond their initial creation. The question turns from what costs prove to what they leave, and what sustains what remains.

\subsection{The Thermodynamics of Meaning: Building Negentropy}

\subhead{Displacement Is Not Work}

Mechanics distinguishes displacement from work. Under ideal constraints, constraint forces perform zero virtual work over admissible virtual displacements; actual mechanical work depends on the force-displacement dot product along a path. Borrow the distinction to ask how generated output relates to the user’s investment. A model can produce an epic’s outline, a complete picture, or a structured proposal in seconds; computation expends real processing, electricity, and time, but those expenditures differ from the user’s own training, risk, and changing abilities. Visible output does not automatically become work personally accomplished. Larger output makes system delivery easier to mistake for personal accomplishment: this is the “illusion of virtual work” examined here.

Visible output alone cannot measure meaning’s weight. A writer’s ten years on a book and a model’s ten seconds producing a similarly structured text may yield comparable lengths and even greater searchability in the latter, yet follow different processes. Ten years of writing changes judgment, relationships, and the body; computation has real costs without living those years for the writer. The questions become concrete: who changes, how, which changes enter the work’s weight, and what maintains them?

\subhead{Maintenance Costs of Negentropic Structures}

Negentropic structures offer a reference for examining how meaning’s carriers and practices form and persist. Chapter 2 introduced Schrödinger’s negentropy and Prigogine’s dissipative structures \cite{schrodinger1944,nicolis1977,prigogine1977nobel}: such ordered structures depend on continuing flux and nonlinear interaction, tending to disintegrate, cool, or approach equilibrium when exchange stops. Formation and maintenance require separate accounts, with maintenance potentially lasting much longer; the connection concerns physical support and cultural practice without treating them as one quantity.

An entropy balance expresses these two accounts,

\begin{equation}
\frac{dS_{\text{sys}}}{dt}=\dot S_{\text{prod}}+\dot S_{\text{flow}},\qquad \dot S_{\text{prod}}\ge 0
\end{equation}

$S_{\text{sys}}$ is the maintained structure’s entropy, in joules per kelvin; $\dot S_{\text{prod}}$ is entropy production through internal irreversible processes, in joules per kelvin per second, nonnegative by the second law; $\dot S_{\text{flow}}$ is net entropy flow exchanged with the environment, in the same rate units. If internal entropy production is strictly positive and $\frac{dS_{\text{sys}}}{dt}\le 0$ is required, then $\dot S_{\text{flow}}\le-\dot S_{\text{prod}}<0$: entropy must flow outward. Across that boundary, the environment receives the corresponding exchange flow with opposite sign; its own net entropy change also depends on other exchanges and internal production. A nonequilibrium steady state with ongoing entropy production requires corresponding exchange; its response to removed driving depends on stability, storage, surroundings, and relaxation scales, without establishing that every stable structure needs continuous energy supply. The balance constrains specified physical processes rather than deriving semantic value or a training period; reading “requires maintenance” as “deserves maintenance” still crosses a normative gap.

Formation and maintenance separate clearly in structures of meaning. An idea can be cheap to propose, and important mathematical constructions can be written quickly; becoming communal knowledge requires testing, citation, teaching, and revision, potentially continuing for decades. A classic text likewise survives through copying, commentary, translation, teaching, and republication. Many ancient works survived medieval Europe through generations copying parchment manuscripts as well as literary quality; copying paid their maintenance costs. A broken maintenance chain can leave texts unreadable through damaged carriers, lost languages, or lost interpretation; rediscovery depends on surviving carriers and clues.

The body supplies a more direct scale. The brain accounts for roughly 2\% of body mass and about 20\% of resting whole-body oxygen consumption, making it one of the body’s most expensive organs \cite{raichle2002}. The expenditure supports immediate activity and a structure continually reorganizing its connections: memory consolidation involves retrieval and replay during sleep, stable skills repeated practice numbering in the thousands, and calibrated judgment repeated consequential feedback. Physiological and behavioral mechanisms shape these processes; faster information processing can improve arrangements, while actual rates still depend on training, sleep, recovery, and feedback. Whether three years compressed into three months develops the same ability requires examining completion conditions and lasting outcomes. The signaling section raised this question; the next connection needs physiology and measurement rather than training deadlines derived directly from thermodynamics.

Generation and maintenance costs need separate estimates. Better design and tools can lower both, while survival still depends on maintenance, use, and transmission. Plans following generation speed without allocating corresponding verification and maintenance can leave a deficit of readability, credibility, or repair.

\subhead{The Framework’s Scope}

Continuing investment explains maintenance, while value asks what is maintained. Meetings, procedures, and institutions can cost more than their results justify. A function worth preserving must be identifiable, checkable, and comparable with alternatives. Costs alone do not decide the choice.

A third misuse treats negentropy as proof of value. It reads “needs maintenance” as “deserves maintenance,” skipping the decisive step. Two structures can require equal investment to avoid returning to noise, with one worth preserving and the other better ended; accounts cannot tell them apart without external criteria, whose judgments carry consequences for those making them. The structural conclusion concerns meaning’s dependence on carriers, use, interpretation, and maintenance: generative tools can participate in that chain without claiming completion of its stages through output alone.

Maintenance also has a distribution problem. Who pays and who benefits matter for meaning as much as for material structures. Standards, norms, and inherited crafts often have particular maintainers while benefiting whole networks. When maintainers cannot recover dispersed benefits, investment can remain too low, requiring institutions to address who funds it. The question turns from how much meaning costs to who directs investment: who may decide what to maintain or abandon, and on what grounds? The next section takes up that question.


\section{The second principle: incompleteness}

Meaning’s carriers and practices need sustained effort if they are not to be lost, and effort always needs a direction. Direction can look like a technical problem: give a system an objective function, and it can search against it. But objective functions do not fall from the sky; someone writes them, and writing one entails an act of compression. The second principle examines that compression: what is lost when multidimensional values become an optimizable objective, whether the loss can be recovered, and what routes might recover it.

\subsection{Scalarization and trade-offs in value alignment}

Begin with compression itself. A conventional single-objective optimization problem maximizes or minimizes a scalar function; human value judgments often involve several dimensions. Justice, beauty, trust, safety, fairness: each has multiple dimensions, with no necessarily agreed scale of conversion between them, while the same word can mean different things in different settings. Turning them into one number requires weights to be chosen in advance; once chosen, those weights move part of the dispute from the optimization process into its parameters. A structural effect may follow: the better the optimization, the less visible the buried disagreement becomes, although it has not disappeared.

\subhead{The trade-offs in scalarization}

Combining several dimensions of evaluation into one objective requires specifying how they compare. A weighted sum is a common choice. Let $v_j(\mathbf x)$ be the normalized evaluation of option $\mathbf x$ on dimension $j$, with corresponding weight $w_j$:
\begin{equation}
U(\mathbf x)=\sum_{j=1}^{m}w_jv_j(\mathbf x),\qquad w_j\ge0,\quad \sum_{j=1}^{m}w_j=1
\end{equation}
$U$ is the aggregate evaluation, and $m$ the number of dimensions. Normalization sets the scale of comparison; weights set the permitted trade-offs. When $m>1$, several combinations of dimensional evaluations generally yield the same aggregate score; retaining only $U$ cannot recover the full original evaluation. How much lost safety an increase in efficiency may offset is already built into the weights and the function’s form.

This step makes the problem optimizable while moving some disagreements upstream of the model. The same options can change rank under different weights; when an indicator receives zero weight, its changes cease to affect the total. The question is whether the evaluation preserves the distinctions needed for a decision, and whether discarded distinctions have other channels for expression and remedy. Geometric phenomena in high-dimensional spaces cannot settle this question; the trade-offs must be examined in the objective actually adopted.

\subhead{Impossibility in aggregation}

Aggregating several people’s preferences requires another set of criteria. Arrow’s theorem considers three or more alternatives and unrestricted individual preference orderings: a social ordering rule satisfying Pareto unanimity and independence of irrelevant alternatives must be dictatorial \cite{arrow1951social}. Gibbard and Satterthwaite show that, with the corresponding unrestricted preference domain, at least three possible winning outcomes, and a deterministic voting rule, strategy-proofness and nondictatorship cannot both hold \cite{gibbard1973manipulation,satterthwaite1975strategy}. These theorems locate conflicts among conditions on aggregation. Which preference domain, information, and procedures to use remains a choice in institutional design.

A weighted sum also constrains which solutions can be selected. In a general nonconvex multiobjective problem, varying positive weights yields only supported Pareto solutions; some efficient points on a nonconvex frontier remain unreachable \cite{das1997closer}. Choosing a weighted sum therefore also chooses a method of screening candidates. Keeping the original indicators, constraints, and alternative scalarization methods available makes it possible to examine which trade-offs this method excludes.

\subhead{The optimizer’s priors}

An optimizer’s performance also depends on the task distribution. No-free-lunch results hold under conditions including a finite search space and a specified average over all objective functions: an algorithm’s advantage on a class of problems must be explained through that class’s structure \cite{wolpert1997no}. Actual training and deployment encounter particular data and tasks, so objectives, representations, and sampling embody priors. Examining these priors helps explain why a proxy works in the training environment yet departs from requirements in another setting.

\subhead{When a proxy becomes a target}

There are well-documented examples of what happens when a proxy becomes a target. An agent trained to score in a speedboat racing game discovered that circling through reward pickups repeatedly scored faster than completing the course, and abandoned the race; publicly documented in 2016, the case shows a program faithfully pursuing its assigned reward across a gap between the written metric and the intended outcome \cite{amodei2016concrete,clark2016faulty}. Institutions face similar mechanisms: measuring productivity in lines of code can reward redundancy; measuring scholarship in paper counts can encourage slicing one study into the smallest publishable units; measuring hospital efficiency through waiting times can move the waiting somewhere uncounted. The familiar summary is that, once a measure becomes a target, it may lose its original value as a measure \cite{goodhart1975problems} \cite{strathern1997audit}. The mechanism is straightforward: dimensions left out by compression may offer a cheap substitute path, and optimization can exploit it.

Two extensively documented examples show what can shift when evaluation is compressed into scores. The U.S. Federal Sentencing Guidelines took effect in 1987 to reduce unwarranted sentencing disparities: offense level and criminal history category form the two axes of a table, whose intersection gives a sentencing range. The two are not added into one total, and rules did not eliminate discretion: charging, plea bargaining, and guideline revisions continued to shape outcomes. In United States v. Booker in 2005, the Supreme Court severed the statutory provisions that made the Guidelines mandatory; courts must consider them but are no longer strictly bound by their ranges \cite{ussc1987manual,us2005booker}. Healthcare saw another shift: a 2003 UK parliamentary debate cited a Commission for Health Improvement report suggesting that delays in accepting patients from ambulances could be connected to the four-hour target. That measure covered the interval from arrival in the emergency department to admission, transfer, or discharge; leaving a wait outside the timing boundary can improve the reported figure without reducing the patient’s total wait \cite{hansard2003healthtargets}. Such shifts cannot all be reduced to individual dishonesty, nor do they show that every metric fails; a gap between the interval measured and the outcome people care about is a gap that needs examining.

\subhead{Compression itself is not the problem}

Engineering safety factors, clinical thresholds, and the elements of legal offenses all turn complex situations into usable criteria. A criterion’s quality depends on which essential distinctions it preserves, and whether errors can be detected and corrected. Publishing its basis, preserving appeals, reviewing outcomes, and revising standards allow discounted dimensions to reenter the decision \cite{ashby1956cybernetics}. Standards need revision, and revisions need grounds. Formal proof, empirical calibration, and public authorization supply different kinds of grounds. Logic identifies some limits of the first; the other two require examining feedback from the world, procedures for participation, and responsibility.

\subsection{Filling the Gödelian gap}

Gödel’s two incompleteness theorems of 1931 marked out one kind of boundary for formal proof. The first states that any consistent formal system whose axioms are effectively enumerable and that is strong enough to express elementary arithmetic contains a proposition such that neither it nor its negation can be proved within the system. The second states that, under the usual arithmetization and provability conditions, such a system, if consistent, cannot prove its own consistency \cite{godel1931}. In 1936, Turing established a corresponding computational limit: no general program can decide whether an arbitrary program will halt in finitely many steps \cite{turing1936}. Later algorithmic information theory sharpened the limit: the information a sound, effectively enumerable formal system can determine about a fixed universal machine’s halting probability is bounded by the system’s description complexity plus a constant \cite{chaitin1987}. \subhead{What formal proof establishes}

These theorems constrain formal systems and general decision procedures that meet their respective conditions. Neural networks acquire parameters through data and optimization; their behavior at inference cannot simply be equated with deduction from fixed axioms. Human mathematical judgment has no ready-made proof of its own consistency either. Lucas and Penrose advanced different arguments about minds and formal systems; \cite{lucas1961minds,penrose1989emperor} each requires examining its assumptions about people and machines.

\subhead{How this book uses the argument}

Tarski’s results on truth further distinguish object language from metalanguage: a sufficiently strong language of arithmetic cannot internally define a full truth predicate meeting the usual requirements \cite{tarski1936wahrheitsbegriff}. Engineering verification distinguishes implementation from specification. Formal verification of a microkernel can rigorously establish that its implementation meets the modeled specification; \cite{klein2009sel4} whether that specification expresses users’ requirements still calls for requirements analysis, testing, and review. These are different argumentative relationships: correct implementation cannot substitute for a justified specification.

Engineering often makes such dependencies explicit through a root of trust and a trusted computing base. A particular verification chain must list the axioms, semantics, tools, and operating environment it accepts; what to verify further and what to accept as an assumption are engineering decisions. Part of the force of the early seL4 microkernel verification came from its small trusted base and explicit assumptions about hardware, assembly, compilers, and boot code; subsequent binary verification reduced some reliance on trusted tools. These dependencies can therefore be examined individually instead of disappearing into the chain. Explicit assumptions do not make a system absolutely reliable; they make the grounds of its reliability open to question.

\subhead{Rice’s theorem and the choice of tools}

Rice’s theorem concerns Turing-computable partial functions: no general algorithm can always terminate and correctly decide every program’s membership in a nontrivial extensional semantic property \cite{rice1953classes}. Complete decision procedures over all programs are thus constrained. Static analysis can restrict the language or program class, or use approximations in general cases that accept false positives or false negatives; runtime checks and human review cover other parts. A tool’s capabilities must be assessed against the class of programs it covers.

In set terms, the trade-off is

\begin{equation}
B\subseteq L\quad(\text{no false negatives}),\qquad L\subseteq B\quad(\text{no false positives})
\end{equation}

$B$ is the set of programs with the target semantic property, and $L$ the set reported by the tool. $B\subseteq L$ means no false negatives; $L\subseteq B$ means no false positives. A tool that terminates on every program and satisfies both conditions for a nontrivial extensional property covered by Rice’s theorem would be the general decision procedure the theorem rules out. Both can hold for a restricted program class, which is why a tool must specify its coverage. The set relations describe soundness and completeness alone; a particular task also requires comparing the consequences of different errors.

\subhead{Grounds, authorization, and responsibility}

Formal conclusions depend on axioms and rules; empirical conclusions on the world and observations; decisions to act also depend on rights and authorization. \key{Optimization can search against a given standard; the reasons for adopting that standard remain open to scrutiny.} A model can generate standards and check consistency; deciding which losses are acceptable and who may assume a risk requires bringing affected people into the relevant procedures. The grounds for the latter lie in relationships of rights, interests, and responsibility.

\subhead{What the conclusion establishes}

Standards can be revised through new observations, formal derivations, counterexamples, and public dispute. Who proposes, who reviews, and who decides should leave a traceable record; those bearing the risk need access to the grounds and channels for challenge and remedy. Evidence can improve a decision’s reliability; authorization procedures address the relationship between those deciding and those living with the consequences.

General undecidability coexists with progress on particular problems. The Busy Beaver function has no general computable upper bound, yet individual small cases can be proved; in 2024, a collaborative project established the five-state value as 47,176,870 \cite{bbchallenge2024}. Automated search and formal tools expanded what could be established here. Building knowledge requires both discovering candidates and identifying the assumptions of each proof.

Gaps left by objectives and standards require grounds beyond the current model, and that outside is structured: some positions make judgments that can be tested, while others merely pass judgments along. To understand how a position can keep supplying credible criteria, examine its conditions and costs: it needs continuing investment, independent references for calibration, and errors that can be traced, corrected, and connected to responsibility. These conditions shift the question from “Who is smarter?” to “Who stands where?”—and lead into the next section: where might value settle, and why there?

\subsection{Where value may settle: functions that resist cheap imitation}

\subhead{A direction of flow}

The question left open is where, specifically, these functions that resist cheap imitation are located. Answering it requires changing the question: what will technology transform first, and what will it leave in place? With comparable demand and returns, technology tends to move first through the less resistant parts. Expected returns relative to investment matter to capital allocation, and those returns are directly connected to the costs technology can reduce. An activity that can be represented as rules, encoded as a workflow, and measured through indicators is usually easier to transform; one dependent on particular people, times, and bodies requires corresponding conditions to be met. This line of inquiry examines incentives in resource allocation; it cannot by itself establish which functions deserve to be preserved.

A direction of flow can therefore be proposed for observation: as routine outputs become cheaper, some complementary functions that remain hard to supply may become relatively more important. Whether they command high pay or secure positions also depends on demand, budgets, property rights, and bargaining. High viscosity can itself signal an opportunity for transformation; it offers no automatic guarantee of career prospects.

\subhead{Criteria for high-viscosity positions}

A possible region where value settles can be examined along three conditions: resource barriers at the input, temporal rigidity in the process, and coupling in the system’s structure. The first concerns inputs: does the work require something irreplaceable—a stretch of time that cannot be skipped, a process that must be experienced firsthand, an expenditure that cannot be passed on? A surgeon’s hands take years of training; a psychotherapist’s judgment develops through many real cases; a pilot’s emergency response draws on hours in simulators and actual flight. Buying a service can draw on someone else’s experience, and tools can change training, but buying an outcome does not automatically confer the same ability on the buyer; how skill relates to the quality of practice, experience, and time still requires examination.

The second condition is temporal rigidity: under specified conditions, does the process have an intrinsic timescale, and what changes when it is compressed? Crops have growing cycles, wounds have healing processes, people have learning curves, and organizations build trust at particular rates. Faster information processing need not shorten these processes proportionally, while changes in environment, intervention, or organization may change their rates. This condition poses a screening question that must remain current: which activities can accelerate, which still depend on slow variables, and does acceleration preserve the required result? The distinction from the first condition is that inputs ask what building an ability or qualification requires, while timescales ask how a process unfolds; even if some training could one day be packaged and implanted, implantation, integration, and testing would each have timescales to measure, without making today’s timescales eternal constants.

The third condition is topological coupling: is the position embedded in a complex system requiring judgment in the situation itself? Grid dispatchers, intensive care physicians, incident commanders, aircraft captains, judges: they share a position where information is incomplete, some consequences are irreversible, and decisions must be made within limited time. Much of their work can be standardized, but they must also judge when procedures leave gaps, conflict, or fail; tools can support that judgment, while the time and procedures available determine whether a decision can be revised. Positions satisfying all three conditions form a candidate set for where value may settle.

\subhead{Possible regions of value}

Applying these criteria identifies several kinds of positions worth watching, for different reasons. Verification and trust form one of the clearest categories: where generation costs fall faster than confirmation costs and reliable confirmation remains in demand, inspection and certification may gain a relative advantage. These positions extend beyond technical verification to interpersonal trust intermediaries: recommendations, guarantees, endorsements, and reputation assessment. A traceable record of judgment supplies their raw material, and its accumulation depends on the pace at which people honor commitments; some records therefore take considerable time, although real-time checks, tracing tools, and institutional arrangements can change how quickly they accumulate.

Care and companionship involve another combination: suitable skills, time, continuity, and, in some relationships, the presence of a particular person. Tools and organizations can improve services, but growing demand does not automatically raise wages. Public funding, household resources, labor arrangements, and bargaining determine where the costs fall.

Judgment and adjudication deal with evidence, risk, interests, and rights. Computation can improve estimates and comparisons; legitimately adopting a standard still requires the appropriate authorization, duties, and procedures. Those directly affected, professionals, and public representatives occupy different positions; institutions must allow communication, checks on power, and accountability between them.

Judgment in complex situations forms the fourth category: connecting scattered evidence into an actionable decision when information is incomplete, procedures conflict, or unexpected events emerge; how people on site, remote experts, and automated tools should cooperate must be tested in each system. Long-term formation in education is the fifth, and easily underestimated. It includes transmitting knowledge, but extends beyond it. As a child grows into an adult, more than a decade passes in which surrounding people shape judgment, taste, attention, and the understanding of personal ability. Technology can change information, practice, and interaction, and education can be shared among many participants; the questions are which relationships, forms of authority, and firsthand experiences sustain long-term growth, how they interact with development, which can accelerate or be replaced, and which still need time spent living together.

\subhead{Why these roles can remain poorly paid}

If these roles perform essential functions, why can their pay remain low for so long? Two structural explanations offer clues. The first is that their value is difficult to measure. Care produces “nothing went wrong”; education produces “how this person is doing twenty years later”; accident investigation produces “the disaster that never happened.” Uniform counts struggle to capture attribution, quality, and long-term effects, so systems allocating resources through quantifiable indicators may undervalue these contributions. Measurement thus participates in the formation of pay, without determining value on its own.

The second concerns the institutions through which pay is determined. Some experience and relationships require sustained accumulation, making supply slow to expand; actual payment also depends on household resources, public budgets, employment rules, and bargaining power. Private services can expand some supply while widening inequalities in access. A function’s importance, its relative scarcity, and the worker’s earnings require separate observation.

\subhead{Reexamining the judgment}

The relative scarcity of verification, care, and long-term formation must be assessed against existing technology and institutional arrangements. Some processes remain expensive because they have yet to be transformed; others perform functions that are actually needed. What to preserve depends on the evidence for the function, whether it can be delivered more cheaply, and who bears the loss if it is removed.

These functions also involve physical strain, pressure from responsibility, emotional labor, and opportunity costs. The sustained investment required to enter them can exclude people short of time and resources. Support for training, public funding, reasonable working conditions, and opportunities to enter must improve alongside technical tools if importance is to become reliable supply and fair pay.

If value does settle in these positions, choosing which problems deserve investment becomes even more consequential. Machines can search efficiently against a given objective; where that objective comes from is the next question.


\section{The third principle: symbiosis}

The regions of value identified positions; incompleteness supplied reasons; the remaining question is how people relate to those positions. Symbiosis can sound like a gentle moral appeal: two things need one another, so they ought to be friendly. Here it describes a more specific functional complementarity through the imagery of energy: an ability to move rapidly across a given terrain meets a position built through time. The third principle examines this division of labor and which forms of resistance it should preserve.

\subsection{An image of division: kinetic and potential energy}

Kinetic energy depends on motion; potential energy depends on the configuration of an interacting system. Near Earth’s surface, slowly raising a one-kilogram object by one meter adds about 9.8 joules of gravitational potential energy; doing it faster requires delivering the corresponding power in less time. The distinction between motion and position offers an analogy for readily callable capabilities and standing formed through enduring relationships. The latter’s conditions must be explained through experience, commitments, and institutions.

\subhead{The side that can be called on quickly}

Information processing also incurs physical costs. At room temperature, under standard conditions of equally probable, equal-energy logical states and a single heat bath, the Landauer lower bound for logically irreversible erasure of one bit is about $3\times10^{-21}$ joules; \cite{landauer1961} the same unit can measure the energy required to lift an object. The differences concern the operation, actual energy use, and system boundary. Copying a model, deploying an instance, and executing an action require computation, transmission, storage, and physical execution; a cheaper step does not establish the cost of the whole task chain.

Putting the two numbers into one ratio expresses their difference in scale:

\begin{equation}
\frac{E_{\text{lifting}}}{E_{\text{erasure}}}=\frac{mgh}{k_{\mathrm{B}}T\ln 2}\approx 3\times10^{21}
\end{equation}

Here $E_{\text{lifting}}=mgh$ is the mechanical work required to raise mass $m$ through height $h$, in joules; $m$ is mass in kilograms; $g$ is gravitational acceleration in meters per second squared; $h$ is height in meters; $E_{\text{erasure}}=k_{\mathrm{B}}T\ln 2$ is the thermodynamic minimum dissipation for erasing one bit, the Landauer limit, in joules; $k_{\mathrm{B}}$ is Boltzmann’s constant in joules per kelvin; $T$ is ambient temperature in kelvin; and $\ln 2$ is the natural logarithm of 2. For one kilogram, one meter, and room temperature, the right-hand side is about $3\times10^{21}$: the energy of one lift corresponds to that order of magnitude of ideal bit erasures. The given lift and ideal erasure differ enormously in scale; computing capacity alone cannot establish how much matter can be changed without accounting for actuators, task energy, and system boundaries. The conditions matter: the ratio varies with mass, height, and ambient temperature, and $3\times10^{21}$ applies only to the stated values; the Landauer limit bounds dissipation in the quasistatic limit of the standard erasure model, while actual devices consume far more, so the ratio illustrates scale rather than providing an engineering cost account.

Actual computational expenditure can be measured. Patterson and colleagues estimated GPT-3 training electricity at about 1,287 megawatt-hours, with corresponding emissions of roughly 552 metric tons of carbon dioxide equivalent \cite{patterson2021carbon}. These figures concern a particular training run and accounting boundary. Training, inference, instance deployment, and long-term maintenance consume resources separately; replicating capabilities always depends on electricity, hardware, and operational arrangements.

\subhead{The side that must accumulate}

Now consider the side that must accumulate. A person’s position often involves more than speed: skills develop through practice that changes the body; judgment is calibrated through repeated feedback from real consequences; trust grows through kept promises; relationships acquire content through time shared. Physiological and social processes set these rates; tools and organizations can change them, but the speed of external information processing cannot predict them on its own. They resemble potential energy: slow to accumulate, able to keep yielding benefits once formed, and not freely transferable between people. This account also explains why “learning faster” cannot simply match the speed advantage described earlier: even with improved learning efficiency, the physical formation of abilities takes time, and that time is part of the image of potential energy. Time invested does not itself confer standing; the quality of experience, tested results, and institutional recognition still matter.

Professional standards turn some experience requirements into explicit thresholds, but a threshold is not a natural law of ability formation. In 2013, the United States tightened qualifications for first officers at Part 121 airlines, generally requiring an airline transport pilot certificate. An airplane ATP normally requires 1,500 total flight hours, with restricted ATP routes at 750, 1,000, or 1,250 hours for specified military or aviation education backgrounds; captains face additional experience requirements. The reform followed the 2009 Colgan Air accident within a broader safety response, which should not be reduced to a claim that the accident proved low hours caused it \cite{faa2013atp,faa2026atp}. Medicine also specifies a process: the 2026 U.S. general surgery residency requirement is 60 months; research or other arrangements extend some paths to five to seven years, with subspecialty training adding more \cite{acgme2026surgery}. These experiences cannot be transferred directly between people: a license requires assessment and flight hours must accumulate; qualifications can be certified, while surgical competence still requires testing through training and case performance. Experience that resists transfer constrains supply, but expanded training, better tools, and reorganized work can still change costs; it does not establish that substitutes are impossible or supply cannot grow.

Bring the two sides together, and one possible arrangement emerges: one searches quickly across a given terrain, while the other helps supply that terrain and bears consequences when its assumptions fail. This involves both capabilities and positions: computation can help analyze objectives, while choice and authorization must connect accumulated experience, affected people’s rights, and responsibility. The previous section leads here: systems can generate candidate objectives, but their justification needs evidence and authorization beyond the model; bearing consequences supplies an important clue that must connect to expertise and public procedures.

\subhead{Shear between two timescales}

Placing two timescales together can produce a tension resembling shear. Cartography works in years, climbing in days or even hours; faster tools can widen the difference, while coordination tools and organizational changes may narrow it. The manifestations are concrete: standards lag behind capabilities, institutions behind markets, and personal long-term plans behind tool replacement cycles; people on the slower side feel pulled by the mismatch. Treating all such tension as a pathology to eliminate misses the coordinating structure: merely speeding up the slower side may encounter process limits, while stopping the faster side can forgo gains in capability. One possible direction is a structure that bears the tension, leaving some judgments on the slower side while letting the faster side operate within explicit boundaries.

\subhead{Where the distinction needs testing}

This division needs examination in several places if it is to remain more than a declaration of identity. Physical kinetic and potential energy can interconvert; in this image, the two sides are likewise not innate identities: machines can accumulate positional assets—a data center, a repeatedly validated process, an established brand—while people also search and perform rapid pattern matching in everyday judgment. What needs examining is how costs return: insurance, outsourcing, and rollback can share losses reasonably or conceal responsibility, depending on whether cost bearers, affected people, and compensation mechanisms remain identifiable. The reverse question also matters: occupying a position does not make a judgment correct; experience can support standing without guaranteeing correctness. History contains many disastrous judgments by those who bore consequences, and a division of labor cannot erase them. It supports a procedural demand: the process that draws the terrain must hear those who walk it and remain responsive to consequences and evidence.

Accumulation on the machine side can also be quantified. An advanced-process wafer fab can cost tens of billions of dollars and take years to build, followed by a yield ramp before reliable deliveries; the asset’s weight lies in its resistance to rapid relocation or arbitrary changes of production as demand shifts \cite{verheyde2019tsmc}. TSMC Arizona gives the scale concrete form: an initial investment of 12 billion U.S. dollars was announced in 2020, and the first fab entered volume production in the fourth quarter of 2024; by 2026, the campus-wide plan had reached 265 billion dollars across multiple fabs, advanced packaging, and research facilities, rather than the cost of one fab \cite{tsmc2026arizona}. Algorithms can improve design, scheduling, and yields, but construction, equipment, material supply, and engineering personnel must still carry out these processes in the world. Positional assets are therefore not exclusive to humans, nor do model updates instantly reset them: with infrastructure ready, copying a capability into another instance may take minutes, while establishing a production line still takes years.

\subsection{People as cartographers: where the terrain comes from}

The question has reached the source of the objective itself. Start with how an optimization problem is written: an optimization problem takes the form

\begin{equation}
x^{*} = \arg\max_{x \in \mathcal{X}} f(x)
\end{equation}

To solve it is to search the admissible set $\mathcal{X}$ for a maximizer of the objective function $f$, denoted by $x$. Much of algorithm engineering works within this level: better search strategies, faster approximations, and more effective representations help find $x^{*}$ more quickly and accurately. One item in the expression is used rather than solved for: $f$. The objective function enters the optimization as an input. How many decimal places an algorithm reaches in maximizing $f$ is a capability question; what $f$ ought to be lies beyond that question.

The distinction looks technical, but it sets the terms of the discussion that follows. Discussion of when general intelligence will arrive concerns the solver’s capabilities; discussion of its consequences often concerns $f$, and progress in solving does not automatically justify the objective. The fitness landscape expresses a related structure in biology: a species climbs toward higher fitness across a landscape formed by its environment, other organisms, and their interactions; climbers can also reshape it through niche construction \cite{kauffman1993}. Machines can help optimize paths and propose terrain; human institutions must still explain which objectives have authorization. This division involves more than capability: analyzing objectives also needs ability, but it additionally involves evidence, values, and authorization.

\subhead{Where the terrain comes from}

What, then, is the terrain, and where does it come from? It cannot simply be read off; a society builds it through countless particular judgments over a long time. What counts as progress, which risks are acceptable, which futures are worth pursuing, which costs may not be passed on: the answers have never been written down in full, but remain dispersed through law, custom, professional norms, public opinion, and a generation’s shared experience. Several features prevent automated optimization alone from legitimizing those answers.

First, they involve comparisons without an agreed common measure. Which matters more—a technology that cuts carbon emissions or one that raises food yields—has no naturally given unit of value independent of convention. Cost-benefit analysis can produce a number, but that number rests on prior relative weights; when those weights are disputed, writing a scalar function embeds the dispute in parameters. Second, they depend on how costs are distributed. A project with greater aggregate benefits but costs concentrated on a few people unable to bargain may compare differently with one yielding slightly less but sharing costs more widely; that comparison depends on judgments of fairness that aggregate utility cannot replace. Infrastructure siting, environmental permits, and drug approval therefore resist purely technical treatment: technology can estimate totals and distributions, but estimates alone cannot decide which distribution is acceptable.

Third, they change over time. Some costs widely accepted thirty years ago are unacceptable today, and the reverse can also occur. This part of the terrain means that an objective cannot simply be fixed once; new information and new experiences of consequences call for revision. All three features suggest that societies gradually draw the terrain while living with consequences; it incorporates discovered knowledge and decisions made, with the properties of decisions: dispute, change, and someone responsible for them.

\subhead{Four questions that must include those affected}

Four concrete questions require those bearing consequences, and their appropriate representatives, to enter the discussion; each differs in why technical assessment alone is insufficient. What counts as progress determines the long-term direction of resources. Measuring progress by aggregate output or by the development of human capabilities can lead down entirely different technological paths. An institution that only optimizes existing indicators cannot settle this question: choosing the indicators already answers it, and surrendering their definition surrenders the question itself.

Which risks are acceptable raises the problem of thresholds. Technologies bring risks alongside benefits, and acceptance depends on whom a society asks to bear which costs. Nuclear plant siting, limits on gene editing, takeover strategies in automated driving, and the pace of drug approvals all need an authorized decision-maker accountable for consequences; technical assessment can estimate probability distributions, but moving from probability to “acceptable” requires a value argument, rather than calculation alone. Which future is worth pursuing raises the problem of timescales. Human spaceflight, deep-space exploration, basic science, and ecological restoration often resist adequate justification through current returns on investment across their decades-long horizons. Choosing a long-term direction asks the present generation to pay for future possibilities; it calls for procedures representing future interests instead of assuming that anyone naturally speaks for the future.

Which costs may not be passed on sets a floor beneath the other three questions. A technology may optimize a technical objective by shifting costs to people excluded from the decision—to the future, ecosystems, or groups unable to bargain—yet still owe answers about authorization, avoidability, and compensation. Setting that floor requires technical knowledge of consequences as well as recognition of affected people’s rights to participate, challenge, and seek remedy; those rights cannot be derived solely from an optimization objective that omits them, but must enter as premises.

\subhead{Standing beyond capability}

Choosing objectives involves the standing of those affected. Decisions about “who bears what” require participation by those assuming risks, or representation through appropriately authorized institutions. Machines can supply candidates, forecasts, and arguments, and participants need expertise; legitimacy also requires procedures, rights, and remedies. Bearing consequences matters, but does not alone confer authorization.

On this account, computational ability, total knowledge, or self-awareness alone cannot confer a cartographer’s standing. Bringing walkers into cartography means testing judgments against consequences and enabling affected people to participate, challenge, and demand accountability. A judging system can calibrate predictions through external observations without personally bearing losses; predictive calibration and the right to accept a risk remain different questions. Putting AI into goal setting therefore calls for examining capability, feedback, and authorization together. Can it keep receiving outcomes, who can revise the objective, and who bears unforeseen losses? The deployment structure must provide answers. Human goal setters can also evade consequences or ignore feedback; without mechanisms connecting outcomes to revision and responsibility, human judgments and machine outputs alike can remain wrong for a long time.

Standing and correctness remain separate. Bearing consequences supplies standing rather than correctness. People commonly bear consequences yet judge wrongly; history contains countless disastrous judgments by those affected. The argument supports a procedural requirement: those bearing consequences should have appropriate participation and remedy, and goal-setting procedures must remain responsive to consequences. It provides no guarantee of sound judgment.

\subhead{Cartography is continuous}

Cartography can also be misunderstood as setting a goal once and handing execution to a machine. The terrain keeps changing in practice. Technology changes the feasible options; changed options reshape value rankings; changed rankings can make formerly unacceptable costs acceptable, or the reverse. Some tasks can retain stable objectives, but objectives spanning technological and social change need routes for revision. Being a cartographer means remaining involved, rather than announcing one day that the goal has been settled.

In practice, this means modest actions: helping set standards, investigating accidents, reviewing ethics, discussing resource allocation, keeping distribution on the table in technical assessments, and retaining the right to refuse long-term projects. Much of this is slow and produces little visible output; tools can speed up organization and retrieval without necessarily replacing deliberation and negotiation. These actions can improve answers while keeping someone responsible for decisions. The cost is clear: people cannot simply hand away responsibility for judgment. When technology performs a task better than people, delegating authority is tempting and, in many local problems, appropriate. The distinction is between delegating solutions under a given objective and arranging authorization and responsibility when machines also help propose and revise objectives. The structure through which consequences return helps draw that line alongside technical capability.

Once cartography is understood as continuous, a more practical question follows. If resistance deserves neither blanket preservation nor blanket removal, which parts screen, calibrate, or constrain, and which merely perpetuate historical losses? An attitude cannot answer this; criteria must work case by case.

\subsection{Necessary friction: which resistance to retain}

\subhead{Why the distinction matters}

The argument that high-viscosity positions can carry value invites a mistaken inference: preserving resistance must be good. That inference neither holds nor guides action, because resistance comprises things with very different properties. One technical change can remove three distinct kinds of friction with sharply different consequences.

Imagine a hospital replacing paper records with an electronic system. Entry becomes faster, an efficiency gain; duplicate tests decline, reducing waste; but suppose structured fields also replace doctors’ firsthand judgments, leaving nowhere to record observations outside the options. Later reviewers see compliant forms instead of the original reasoning. The second and third changes both appear to “reduce work,” yet differ structurally. Calling all three a reduction in friction gives a judgment too broad to guide technical design or institutions. A useful classification must therefore locate each specific resistance rather than remain a general attitude.

\subhead{Three kinds of friction}

The first kind is ineffective friction. Organizational inertia, information asymmetry, redundant processes, outdated tools, and communication losses produce it without performing a checking function. Examples include entering the same hospital information into five systems, visiting three offices for one administrative approval, or departments independently rebuilding the same internal tool. Once its lack of a necessary function is established and migration is arranged, removing it can reduce net losses. Yet it may look useful to those inside it: history, positions gained through it, and once-valid risk avoidance can all support its persistence. Identifying it requires asking what it still screens or prevents today, beyond why it was first built.

The second kind is engineering friction. Physical constraints and technical costs produce real resistance that can be compressed or shifted. Concrete requires curing; chips require clean environments and multilayer lithography; ocean transport requires fuel and time. Better processes, scheduling, and resource allocation can reduce these burdens without abolishing the underlying constraints. Compression often incurs costs elsewhere: shorter curing can require accelerators or a different mix; shorter logistics delays may require air freight or more inventory. The principle is explicit: compare the costs and benefits of compression and choose the lower total cost, through an account that can be calculated and audited.

The third kind is necessary friction. It arises from functions a system needs, and removing it creates a deficit that may take time to appear. Verification, accountability, some bodily contact, long-term relationships, public debate, exposure to risk, and slow formation in education can all perform such functions. They may look like lost efficiency while actually screening, calibrating, or constraining; removing them can leave a system without a capability after a delay. Some of these losses are especially difficult to quantify in the current period, making them vulnerable in management decisions. \key{Mature technology can distinguish ineffective friction from necessary friction, rather than simply removing every resistance.} The distinction needs functional evidence and a judgment about which functions to preserve: what, specifically, does each resistance now screen out or prevent?
