\subhead{Three diagnostic questions}

Three questions make the inquiry concrete. First: if this resistance is removed, does the required function remain, or does an equivalent mechanism take it over? A redundant function can be removed; a better replacement can reduce the old burden, without proving the system never depended on the function. Airport baggage screening offers an intuitive example: combinations of X-rays, explosive detection, and manual reinspection change the share of bags opened and the pace of checks; efficiency and detection must be compared for particular threats, equipment, and procedures. Academic peer review calls for the same examination: if its current procedures are removed, which functions of qualified criticism, conflict-of-interest disclosure, and correction must remain? Preprints, open review, editorial selection, and formal checks have already changed parts of the process; compare coverage, costs, and omissions rather than assume the current arrangement is the cheapest possible one.

Second: who bears the cost, and who receives the benefit? When these differ, look for undisclosed cost shifting; public goods and legitimate sharing can also separate payers from beneficiaries. A platform can pass moderation costs to creators and users, while advertisers gain reach and users lose attention; “low friction” can mean moving resistance out of view. Conversely, when the same people bear the cost and gain real information or ability, the friction is more likely to serve a necessary function. The question shifts discussion from “How efficient?” to “Who pays?”—where judgment is needed.

Third: what happens at the limit of compression? Engineering friction may become more costly to reduce, or compression may change quality, safety, or the process itself; operating boundaries need examination. Necessary friction reveals a lost function: remove all independent verification and the corresponding calibration vanishes; compress formation in education to nothing and exam performance may survive while some practical abilities do not; remove public deliberation and a quick consensus may go untested. A limiting case can expose a function at risk; mechanisms and evidence are still needed to establish whether it is actually lost. The three questions cannot be fully mechanized, but offer more guidance than either “more resistance is better” or “faster is better.”

\subhead{A different response to technology}

Distinguishing necessary friction can be mistaken for hostility to technology, so the disagreement needs stating. In 1995, Theodore Kaczynski argued that the industrial technological system would keep expanding and eroding individual autonomy, and should therefore be dismantled \cite{kaczynski1995industrial}. Part of the argument warrants attention: technical systems do reorganize lives, often without individual consent. But treating technology as one whole reduces the response to wholesale acceptance or rejection, neither of which offers a workable practical choice.

Examining necessary friction opens another path. It asks what each specific resistance does. The same inquiry can support opposite judgments on the same day: abolish one approval process and urgently stop another newly deployed automation. It attends to what particular mechanisms do in particular positions, rather than treating “technology itself” as one actor. The price of this position is its lack of a simple slogan. It offers a procedure for case-by-case judgment, which needs domain knowledge, an understanding of actual functions, and choices under incomplete information. That puts it at a disadvantage in public debate: opponents have a clear stance, advocates clear benefits, while those managing friction have a long list requiring professional judgment.

\subhead{Two errors of classification}

Practical errors often follow two systematic directions, with asymmetric consequences. The first removes necessary friction as though it were ineffective. Efficiency often supplies the justification, and short-term indicators may improve. Imagine a company abolishing senior staff review to accelerate delivery: metrics rise for months, then accidents rise a year later, with causes difficult to trace to that simplification. Education that compresses practical work to expand coverage may raise exam scores while leaving deficits in hands-on ability to surface after graduation. The shared structure is a removed function, a delayed loss, and a causal chain stretching beyond the management cycle.

The second preserves ineffective friction as though it were necessary. “Tradition,” “experience,” and “risk” commonly defend it, particularly in stable organizations where incumbents benefit. Its costs are continuing, visible, and easy to complain about, yet may remain hard to correct; reform must still overcome entrenched interests and organizational inertia. The two errors differ: retaining ineffective friction causes chronic losses, while removing necessary friction damages structure. Under insufficient information, the asymmetry supports caution without preserving every obstacle. Caution means asking what a proposed removal would stop screening out; if no function can be named, examine historical records, exceptional cases, and affected people’s experience, then test through a reversible pilot; where the function is established, explain the replacement before removing the old arrangement.

A natural question now follows. If friction needs case-by-case examination, and the criteria require clarity about cost bearers, beneficiaries, and responsibility, who will do it? Individuals face an environment pushing them toward the shortest route; organizations face trade-offs between current indicators and lasting capabilities. Both move beyond classification into practice.


\section{The fourth principle: recursive optimization}

The first three principles addressed boundaries, standards, and the division of labor. This section examines the updating that sustains them: practice produces evidence, evidence prompts revisions to standards, and revisions change the next round of action. The loop can settle into a stable state or keep changing with its environment, depending on update rules, delays, and external inputs.

Written as an iteration, the loop’s behavior depends on convergence conditions:

\begin{equation}
x_{n+1}=g(x_{n}),\qquad \left|g'(x^{*})\right|<1\ \text{the iteration converges to a fixed point}\ x^{*}
\end{equation}

Begin with a scalar evaluation parameter $x_n$, a continuously differentiable update map $g$, and a fixed point $x^*$. $|g'(x^*)|<1$ is sufficient for local asymptotic convergence; an absolute derivative greater than 1 makes the fixed point unstable, while equality requires further analysis. For multiple parameters, examine the Jacobian’s eigenvalues. Values and environments can change through practice, producing new stable states or continuing change, depending on update rules and external disturbances.

\subsection{A reverse algorithm: choosing friction}

\subhead{Where the problem lies}

The preceding discussion offered structural judgments about value flows and people’s changing positions. Even a sound structural judgment has a weakness: it cannot tell someone what to do on Monday morning. Pressure reaches individuals through concrete choices—whether to use navigation, write a passage, or reply to a message. This section examines those choices without turning them into a checklist.

Preserving autonomy means changing the conditions under which people meet their tools. Daily decisions span countless small settings, and any general list must handle exceptions. The narrower question is what conditions support some autonomy where low-viscosity systems keep pushing behavior in particular directions. Will matters, but the support for maintaining boundaries is a structural problem.

\subhead{Where systems push us}

Preserving autonomy begins with seeing the direction of the push. Four tendencies in low-viscosity systems can be reinforced by design and optimization targeting retention, engagement, or transactions. The first is the shortest path. When a product aims to reduce steps, shorter routes tend to become defaults, making every manual detour an extra cost. The second is immediate feedback. Longer waits make users more likely to leave, giving products an incentive to compress steps, including some that need time.

The third is the preference loop. A system infers preferences from past behavior, supplies content accordingly, and treats the resulting behavior as new evidence; without exploration or outside input, the loop can narrow. No malice is required: predicting established behavior can reinforce it, while exploration objectives and recommendation design determine how much surprise remains. The fourth is painless satisfaction. Systems tend to offer available satisfaction at low cost to encourage repeated use, progressively stripping away expensive parts. All four can improve short-term indicators and thereby gain reinforcement through competition and iteration.

These pressures usually work without explicit prohibitions. Where settings and alternatives exist, someone can turn off recommendations, choose a route manually, or decline generated output. But each refusal can impose continuing, cumulative costs without an external reward. With incentives pressing continuously in one direction and little reward for resisting, behavior may drift that way; individual judgment and sustained incentives need to be examined together, along with mechanisms that can counterbalance them.

\subhead{Keeping nonoptimal interfaces}

One counterweight is to fix some nonoptimal choices in advance so that they no longer need deciding each time. This is what it means to retain a nonoptimal interface. An interface here is the layer of contact with the world: walking a route, reading a book, making something, keeping in touch with someone. Deliberately retaining some less efficient interfaces costs immediate efficiency while keeping an opening for the abilities they exercise to be practiced and tested.

The forms vary by setting; several activities offer useful cases to examine. The first is waiting. Accept some delays without filling every gap, leaving room to think or withdraw. The second is physical training. It resists delegation because changes in muscle, cardiovascular function, and coordination require the person’s own repeated activity; training methods, recovery, and individual condition affect adaptation, and more training does not produce a simply linear gain. The third is relationships in person. Face-to-face contact supplies a shared environment, bodily cues, and direct responses; remote communication supplies a different kind of access, so the costs differ and substitution must be examined for what it loses and adds.

Other activities differ in character. Craft and making connect people directly to materials that resist, go wrong, and retain irreversible traces; digital tools can undo some operations while retaining their own errors, constraints, and real consequences. Difficult texts require sustained attention; skimming and summaries may not replace working an argument through for oneself. Long projects can offer few conspicuous milestones for months or years, with some rewards concentrated at completion, in tension with immediate-feedback systems. Commitments without immediate feedback ask someone to keep a promise through an unrewarded interval. Chance encounters and randomness preserve less predictable outcomes, keeping the preference loop from closing completely.

These activities matter where they still form the abilities that are needed. If direct practice preserves judgment better than complete delegation, make that practice a stable default; if a tool gives better feedback, use it. Compare the loss of immediate output with the longer-term gains in capability.

\subhead{Beyond willpower}

Treating these practices solely as self-discipline invites two mistaken inferences. One turns them into a moral demand: those who persist have character, and those who cannot have failed personally. The other treats them as mere preference: how to live is an individual choice needing no explanation. Both locate the whole issue in the person, overlooking the environment’s feedback structure.

Low-viscosity environments are hard to leave individually, having become deeply embedded in work, social life, payments, travel, and healthcare. Asking someone to resist continuously through willpower demands a lifetime of recurring expenditure that may earn no recognition. Without a stable supporting structure, that demand is unrealistic. A structural response reduces how often willpower must intervene: voluntarily establish revisable defaults so that some arrangements need not enter every fresh comparison.

The practical distinction is concrete. Putting a phone in another room changes the number of decisions required, rather than merely testing resolve. A fixed routine can likewise make bedtime a default instead of a new decision every night. These apparent discipline techniques transfer some choices from the present self to an arrangement made in advance, countering the environment’s continuing pull on behavior.

\subhead{Who can bear the cost}

Whether these arrangements last depends on who can afford them. Their costs are real and uneven. People preserving less efficient interfaces may fall behind on some short-term measures: slower, more tired, producing less, without compensation in the relevant assessment. The costs recur while benefits are delayed, dispersed, and hard to identify, making stable positive feedback difficult to establish individually.

These proposals therefore do not amount to a universally feasible solution. They can help those able to bear the costs, yet remain a luxury for people short of time, energy, or money; universalizing them risks blaming people already disadvantaged. How much to do depends on circumstances: individual adjustments can sometimes change a local direction, but rarely rewrite shared workplace and platform incentives on their own. Evaluation functions shape those incentives, and changing them usually requires collective and organizational action. This keeps a structural issue from becoming a test of personal character, and points onward: from individuals to organizations, from personal choices to the places where evaluation functions are set.

\subsection{High-viscosity organizations: rebuilding trust and verification}

\subhead{From individuals to organizations}

At the limits of individual adjustment lies something one person may not control: organizational and platform evaluation functions influence the direction of change. Changing those functions requires work at the organizational level. The question here concerns a function rather than management in general: when generation costs approach zero, which organizations still produce something else?

Begin with a contrast. Two kinds of organization can respond very differently to the same generative tools. One immediately integrates them into production, speeds up deliveries, reduces staffing needs, and improves reports; another permits their use while adding verification, tightening release authority, and lengthening review of critical judgments, lowering short-term efficiency. By conventional efficiency measures, the first wins. Extend the horizon and include accidents, recalls, rework, litigation, and staff turnover, and the ranking may reverse. Whether it does depends on how much the output relies on correct judgment and what errors cost.

\subhead{Institutions that produce credentials}

Organizations whose rankings may reverse share a function that can be called the production of credentials. A credential here is a judgment others can rely on: a trustworthy test report, permission to market a drug, a bridge certified to bear a load, an audit opinion supporting a loan, an enforceable judgment, a paper whose conclusion can be cited. Its value lies in a tested judgment and a process that can be traced and reviewed, beyond novelty alone.

Universities, laboratories, hospitals, engineering firms, courts, auditors, certification bodies, and accident investigation boards all perform this function. They can appear inefficient: review takes months, trials years, engineering acceptance may require downtime, courts have multiple levels, and investigators repeatedly gather evidence. Such delays attract charges of bureaucracy, some deserved. Remove the substantive checking processes wholesale, however, and these institutions produce opinions without the structure of responsibility that makes them dependable credentials.

Understanding the function helps locate where slowness matters. It matters in the formation of judgment: gathering evidence, admitting opposing views, reviewing conclusions, authorizing signatures. Pointless delays in administrative circulation can usually be removed without harming credential quality. A trustworthy organization gives judgment a place to answer to its evidence. When challenged, it can return to how the judgment was formed and examine each step.

\subhead{Four slow variables}

Producing credentials depends on slow variables whose conditions for compression require separate examination. The first is the verification cycle. Establishing reliability often needs independent review, replication, or another test matched to the claim, and that takes time. Phase III drug trials, long-term material aging tests, adversarial algorithm tests, and checks of structural safety factors are examples. Verification can be better organized; simply skipping the necessary test delivers an unverified conclusion.

The second is accumulated trust. An institution’s credibility draws on its behavioral record, which must form over time. A hospital builds referral standing through years of care, a certification body through sufficient cases, and a laboratory through papers that withstand reexamination. Trust can build slowly and collapse quickly, placing heavy demands on incentives: one relaxation of verification for short-term gain may undo years of accumulation.

The third is a clear chain of responsibility. Who judges, on what evidence, within which authority, and who answers for mistakes should be established beforehand; later investigation can identify responsibility without substituting for clear prior duties and powers. One major difficulty in accident investigation is a chain that never existed in the institutional design, leaving attribution difficult afterward. The fourth is protection for slow variables themselves. Systems favoring quantifiable short-term indicators put continuing pressure on long-term investment unless arrangements protect it: tenure, independent budgets, statutory review procedures, professional self-regulation. Different histories can yield a shared function—sheltering some activities from current output targets.

\subhead{Why markets may undersupply them}

If credentials matter so much, why might markets fail to supply enough? Several layers of explanation follow. The first is a mismatch in time. Credentials support everyday trade and cooperation, but the severe accidents they help prevent may be infrequent; between incidents, investment can look like wasted money. Decision-makers without experience of an accident may struggle to justify the expense, while those who experienced one may already have left office.

The second is the inability to capture all the benefits. A rigorous verification process can lend credibility to an entire industry: customers may raise their expectations of the field rather than trust only that institution. Such positive externalities can leave private investment below the social optimum, helping explain collective or public requirements for certification, standards, and auditing. The third is a competitive race to the bottom. If one provider cuts verification and passes savings to customers, rivals have a short-term incentive to follow, while consequences may emerge only at the next accident. Finance, aviation, construction, food, and medicine have repeatedly encountered this structure; retrospective regulation is one response, alongside prior standards, independent checks, and liability, and regulatory delay itself carries costs.

These mechanisms can leave credential production insufficiently supplied by markets alone, while administrative orders alone cannot create credibility where institutional independence matters. Institutional arrangements must work through this tension in each field, with markedly different balances.

\subhead{Changes within the organization}

Return to what an organization must do internally to preserve this capacity. Adding verification is the obvious answer, and easily mishandled. An extra approval produces only a signature when the approver lacks information and incentives to check substantively; responsibility is spread without confirming the judgment. Effective verification needs access to original materials rather than processed summaries, independence from direct control by the party examined, and protection from punishment for an adverse finding.

Two further changes follow. First, protect slow variables in assessment. Quarterly output indicators can crowd out long-term investment; one response is an evaluation horizon extending beyond a term of office. Second, preserve traceable records. Generative tools make output easier and provenance harder to distinguish, increasing the value of a record showing who judged what on which evidence. Often treated as a routine burden, these records become essential evidence for reconstruction after an accident, cross-checked against physical evidence, tests, and other sources.

The arrangement has costs. An organization preserving credible judgment may be slower in the short term, a visible and measurable disadvantage repeatedly counted in competition; some benefits appear as accidents prevented, others as less rework, reliable deliveries, and customer trust. This asymmetry helps explain both its continuing predicament and the case for external institutional support. Individuals have limited influence here, while organizational choices shape the evaluation functions that determine whether personal practices can last. Without protection for slow variables, individuals must preserve their chosen interfaces in private time—and that time is itself squeezed by the same evaluation system.

The individual and organizational responses examined so far share an assumption still to be questioned: people are managed as productive capacities, so preserving a position means preserving a productive function. The assumption looks natural but has a history; tracing it puts the preceding practices in a clearer place.

\subsection{Experiencers of negentropy: function and experience as separate dimensions}

\subhead{An unexamined premise}

If people help define the terrain, what a person is becomes a question to ask anew. Treating people as instruments of output no longer suffices here; before proposing an alternative, examine what it replaces. Discussions of AI and people often depend on an unstated premise: a person’s value equals their output. The premise is common enough to appear on both sides. Optimists say machines will free people from repetitive work for more creative production; worriers say machines will replace productive abilities and leave people without a place. Opposite forecasts share a premise.

Accept it, and widespread replacement of productive abilities seems to leave two options: find something machines still cannot produce, or accept being unnecessary. Both prospects are painful and misleading, because both accept the unexamined premise. The trouble begins there. Understanding people as output instruments is not read from human nature: industrial measurement reinforced it, although the instrumental treatment of people predates industrialization. Seeing where the premise came from loosens its hold.

\subhead{A by-product of measurement}

Modern national accounting took shape around the middle of the twentieth century, aggregating production through monetary valuation; it includes market transactions and nonmarket or imputed items such as government services, goods produced for own use, and owner-occupied housing services. The gains were considerable: heterogeneous activities could be added, growth compared, and policy effects assessed. But a production boundary was drawn: most unpaid household and care services supplied within a household have long remained outside core GDP, without implying that economics never recognized them. Recording mutual aid, informal knowledge transmission, and care requires distinguishing activities, providers, and recipients; the leap under examination is from an accounting boundary to a boundary of human value. Women perform a large share of these activities, giving omissions distributive consequences. The 2025 System of National Accounts explicitly encourages extended accounts for unpaid household services; the Australian Bureau of Statistics’ 2026 explanation still distinguishes the core production boundary from household-service satellite accounts, and coverage and valuation methods change the scale made visible \cite{un2025sna,abs2026productionboundary}. Turning an accounting rule into a rule of value helps turn a person into an output instrument. When an evaluation system attends only to output, it reduces people to productive capacity; time, relationships, finitude, and experience gradually recede from its public field of view. Scarcity made the narrowing less conspicuous because productive contribution, income, and identity were often closely linked, although unpaid care and exclusion had long exposed their failure to coincide. Abundant generation breaks more of that overlap and makes the defect conspicuous. AI brings an old problem into sharper view: output never exhausted the person.

\subhead{What output cannot capture}

Alongside processing information, moving matter, and completing tasks, a person is living through other things. They resist conversion into units of output and may leave insufficient traces in its accounts, yet remain more than incidental leftovers. Pain is one. Measured solely against immediate output, it often appears as pure loss. Pain can convey information about boundaries and circumstances, or persistently damage functioning without automatically producing ability or meaning; research on bodily pain likewise distinguishes adaptive roles from possible functional, social, and psychological harm \cite{iasppainterminology}. Some judgments become possible only after a painful experience; reading about pain supplies knowledge of it without supplying the experience itself.

Fatigue and aging bring time into the account. They place recovery alongside irreversible change in a life. Systems needing no human kind of rest can still wear, drift, or run out of resources; a person’s need for rest means a real, temporary loss of some ability. Aging extends the process across a lifetime and brings its finite duration into view. Finitude matters to judgment: limited time makes many choices impossible to postpone, although even an imagined infinite life could face simultaneous actions, conflicting resources, and irreversible consequences. How finitude lends choices weight remains a question to explore. Relationships and death are the final two, and resist easy incorporation into an algorithm. People find recognition in relationships formed through sustained mutual responsibility as well as information exchange; death gives a life an overall shape, and the prospect of its ending gives choices their weight.

These aspects resist conversion because output does not supply their common measure, beyond their sheer complexity. A utility value is a projection of them, rather than an equivalent. The projection keeps an outline and loses depth; the loss can go unseen because the image itself appears whole.

\subhead{What negentropy means here}

Calling this part of existence an experience of negentropy requires explaining the term’s source and reach. Life maintains a state far from equilibrium through continuing flows; when driving remains insufficient, metabolism and its organization become difficult to sustain, at rates dependent on reserves and processes \cite{schrodinger1944}. This returns us to the distinction between generation and maintenance: an initial investment may create something, while sustaining it requires replenishment throughout its existence.

Applied to people, the framework recalls an unremarkable but often neglected point. A living person’s maintained state requires continuing matter and energy through the course of life. Lifetime material and energy throughput can be estimated, but cannot be inferred solely from social output; with comparable body size and activity, people with very low and very high social output can incur maintenance costs of the same order. This supplies a bodily description extending beyond output: a person is a physical process that takes in resources, requires maintenance, ages, and eventually stops. Output branches from that process, with many functions replaceable. When a branch is replaced, the trunk remains.\key{AI can replace many productive functions, but it cannot live a person’s finite life for them.}

Bodies and relationships need continuing resources; that is part of the human condition. Recognizing the value of such lives also needs ethical and institutional grounds. Dignity, equality, and standing to participate can support those claims; displaced work calls for new arrangements for income, security, and social recognition. Maintenance costs identify needs; rights and distribution determine how those needs are met.

\subhead{Human value and its measures}

Human value needs measures capable of describing human lives. Bodies, experiences, relationships, pain, and choices all participate in a life; output accounts capture only what can be delivered. Technology changes how deliverables are produced and exposes the limits of those accounts. Recognizing the rest requires ethical grounds and institutions that turn recognition into rights, resources, and participation.

The argument concerns the inadequacy of treating people as output instruments, without needing to settle whether machines have experience. It depends on the completeness of the human description. Compressing people into productive capacity loses time, finitude, relationships, consequence-bearing, and history. An output-oriented society can overlook these aspects where they count as zero; as productive functions are replaced, what remained outside the accounts makes the cost of compression visible. The argument guarantees neither human superiority nor a secure social position. It asks whether society can recognize and account for dimensions that remain when an output function is replaced, since a person has always had more than that one dimension.

The preceding discussion traced possible value flows, standing in judgment and consequence-bearing, and adjustments available to individuals and organizations. These connections between description and practice point to a larger question: what holds the arrangements in place, and what grounds a civilization’s allocation of resources? Positions and practices need a container extending beyond an individual or a single organization.


\section{A civilizational constitution for silicon-carbon symbiosis}

The actions available to individuals and organizations need a larger structure to carry them. Organizations belong to a civilization, and what it cares about constrains their evaluation functions. The four principles resemble constitutional provisions: they concern the procedures and constraints through which conflicting values are adjudicated. This section scales up to civilization and gathers the principles into constraints that can be returned to.

\subsection{Civilization’s frontiers of resistance}

\subhead{From organizations to civilization}

The previous section examined how trustworthy organizations protect slow variables; here the scale expands again. Organizations sit within a larger system whose concerns constrain their evaluation functions. If resources keep flowing toward the fastest feedback, lowest risk, and most certain returns, individual organizations may face continuing pressure on their efforts to preserve slow variables. Where should a civilization direct resources, and does abundant generation change the answer?

Two narratives easily occupy this question. Technological expansion lists deep space, fusion, and bioengineering as things to pursue once capability permits; inward retrenchment prioritizes immediate problems and treats outward investment as waste. Both can miss the structural question pursued here by debating amounts rather than what these directions share.

\subhead{The shared structure of resistant frontiers}

Their common feature lies in three constraints rather than grandeur. First, high resource barriers. Deep-space missions trade propellant, radiation protection, communication delay, and payload; deep-sea operations face pressure, corrosion, and energy supply; ecological restoration faces soil, hydrology, species interactions, and decades of succession; basic science facilities face materials, vacuum, cryogenics, precision manufacturing, and large initial investments. Better design and control can ease these constraints, but actual tasks must still satisfy physical laws and material conditions.

Second, pronounced temporal rigidity. Orbital mechanics sets mission windows; sea conditions and equipment life constrain deep-sea work; ecosystems recover through succession; materials age and organisms develop at particular rates; basic science may await the next generation of instruments. Changing these timescales requires explaining which conditions change and whether the original process is still completed. Third, dense topological coupling. A step in any direction affects interdependent subsystems with differing objectives: lighter structures may reduce safety margins, faster iteration may sacrifice verification, and cheaper designs may pass risk to maintenance. Dense coupling makes local gains more vulnerable to costs elsewhere in the system.

A direction with all three constraints is what is called a frontier of high resistance here. In set notation,
\begin{equation}
\mathcal{F}=\bigl\{(R,T,G)\:\ R\ge R_{*},\ T\ge T_{*},\ G\ge G_{*}\bigr\}
\label{eq:frontier}
\end{equation}
$R$, $T$, and $G$ remain resource barriers, temporal rigidity, and topological coupling on the previously defined scales; $R_{*}$, $T_{*}$, and $G_{*}$ mark their thresholds for “high,” “pronounced,” and “dense,” whose values depend on the field and are not assigned here. The conditions are conjunctive: satisfying only one or two does not place a direction in $\mathcal{F}$. A project with a high financial barrier but a short process and few coupled subsystems is expensive without meeting this definition; a widely connected project with modest resource and time demands is complex without meeting it either. Putting deep space, ecological restoration, and basic science together invites checking which projects cross all three thresholds, rather than highlighting one outstanding dimension. This structural classification allows unlike fields to be examined together without itself deciding the value of investment.

\subhead{Why these directions matter}

A frontier’s value comes from knowledge, services, or future possibilities worth obtaining. Its proposals must meet actual conditions, through tests that can be expensive, slow, and sparse. Discriminating experiments, staged commitments, recovery paths, and complete records help extract sufficient information from limited contact.

More specifically, these directions renew contact with five things. First, materials. Material properties do not negotiate or change because a description is persuasive. Second, time. Mission cycles, development, and succession cannot be compressed arbitrarily through faster information processing; participants must work across long cycles. Third, risk. Failure carries costs that cannot all be shifted to insurers or third parties. Fourth, cooperation. These systems exceed one team’s capacity and require collaboration across institutions, disciplines, and generations. Fifth, accountability. Failure needs someone answerable who understands their position in the system.

In low-viscosity environments, all five can be weakened without immediate consequences and therefore overlooked. Resistant frontiers make them difficult to evade again.

\subhead{What the difficulty is for}

A frontier’s value must be explained through what it yields. Difficulty alone supplies no reason to invest. A reverse test makes the point: resistance consisting only of redundant procedures, prolonged approvals, or obsolete tools represents wasted resources rather than this kind of frontier. The criterion remains friction’s function.

Nor should the frontier be equated with a destiny among the stars. Outward expansion is one option rather than a predetermined direction. Ecological restoration, basic science, and rebuilding public education can be examined along the same criteria, with potentially dense coupling in living and social systems. The popular association with spaceflight owes more to public visibility than to a structural monopoly.

The scale of investment raises another question. Returns can take decades or longer; some commitments are irreversible, while others can be staged or adjusted. Resources committed here become unavailable elsewhere, requiring technical and value judgments together. Who may commit decades of resources, and on what grounds can the present decide for the future? The questions return more sharply when the horizon exceeds any generation’s term of office.

\subhead{Another function of the frontier}

Beyond developing capabilities and calibration, resistant frontiers offer a destination for resources beyond complete absorption into low-viscosity systems. If resources keep flowing to cheap virtual deliveries with quick payback, needs that resist virtualization may become undersupplied. They can return as crises: infrastructure beyond maintainability, ecosystems beyond recovery, basic science lacking new experimental evidence, or education producing abilities detached from actual problems.

Preventing these crises can pay handsomely, but benefits appearing as “disasters that never happened” can be hard for funders to capture or recognize in current accounts. This recurring asymmetry helps explain institutional protection where markets may undersupply the frontier. The difference is scale: a foundation can protect a laboratory’s direction, while sustaining a civilization’s frontier may require decades of public commitment, often longer than the commitments governments readily make.

The enduring mismatch has no simple solution. One useful step is to explain why these frontiers matter beyond a minority’s preferences. They preserve interfaces through which a civilization stays in contact with the world. Close those interfaces and remaining activities may still flourish within a system whose judgments lose external calibration. Closure can occur through gradual industrial drift rather than a single decision: resources move toward the shortest payback, and supporting activities lose supply one by one. Understanding the process calls for tracing how the objects of industrial intervention have shifted through history.

\subsection{The rise of the ultimate industries}

\subhead{Three layers of industrial transformation}

Industrial history can be divided by its objects of intervention: overlapping transformations extended their layers while changing energy and information costs. The industrial revolution worked on macroscopic matter—cotton yarn, steel, chemical feedstocks, fuel—to meet needs for food, clothing, and power, bringing natural processes into factories and replacing human and animal labor with engines and machines. Its achievements register in steel output, railway mileage, electricity generation, and crop yields. It partly loosened material scarcity at the cost of fossil fuel use and emissions.

The information revolution shifted attention to bits: electronic states in circuits, signal encoding, computation steps, and information routes. Cheap copying helped give this transformation a different cost structure, with unit costs falling by orders of magnitude over decades. Its measures include computing capacity, bandwidth, storage, and connections. It addresses computation and communication, previously constrained by human processing and the transmission speeds of physical media.

Intelligent technologies are helping engineering enter a third layer: cells, gene expression, protein structure, metabolic pathways, and neural activity—life processes themselves. Here the objects maintain themselves, feed back, and adapt; earlier engineering also had complex feedback, while life connects those processes to metabolism and heritable history. Changing a line of code can also trigger complex operational consequences; changing a genome intervenes in a responsive process whose effects may emerge years later. The distinction calls for studying these costs and risks on their own terms rather than applying the curve of information copying directly.

The division orders neither importance nor completed historical eras. Its three layers correspond to atoms, bits, and life: material objects, information carried in bits, and self-maintaining biological processes. Matter and information remain central to the economy and will for a long time. The division traces changing scarcity: material and information costs are being reduced, while development, metabolism, immune response, and aging do not follow the same curve as information processing.

\subhead{Life, mind, and trust}

The life sciences already show the direction: structure prediction and molecular design lower the cost of generating candidates; gene editing makes changes to genetic information programmable; \cite{jinek2012programmable} precision medicine relates treatment to individual characteristics; geriatrics extends its focus from acute disease to delaying functional decline. Demand has a clear demographic background: global life expectancy at birth reached about 73.3 years in 2024, 8.4 years above 1995; people aged 65 and older make up about a tenth of the world population, projected to approach a sixth around 2050, with roughly 2.2 billion by the late 2070s, exceeding the number under 18 in that projection \cite{un2024wpp}. Growing demand meets a sector with constrained supply rates. Baumol and Bowen’s 1966 study of the performing arts and Baumol’s 1967 paper offered a familiar explanation: as manufacturing productivity rises, services requiring person-to-person work may fail to match it; when wages rise with a common labor market, their relative unit costs can increase \cite{baumol1966performing,baumol1967macro}. Care, companionship, psychotherapy, and education include tasks with slower productivity gains, although tools, group provision, and organization can change delivery; relative costs, service prices, and workers’ pay require separate observation. Much unpaid activity also escapes direct pricing, leaving families to bear its costs through unpaid work.

A simplified relative-cost trajectory takes the form

\begin{equation}
\frac{C_{\text{slow}}(t)}{C_{\text{fast}}(t)}=\frac{C_{\text{slow}}(0)}{C_{\text{fast}}(0)}\,e^{\,r t}
\end{equation}

$C_{\text{slow}}$ is unit cost in the sector with limited productivity growth, measured in currency per unit of output; $C_{\text{fast}}$ is unit cost in the sector with sustained productivity growth, in the same units; $r$ is that sector’s labor productivity growth rate, in inverse time; and $t$ is time. The simplified model holds productivity constant in the slow sector, assumes a fixed productivity growth rate in the progressive sector, and lets wages rise together in a common labor market; productivity offsets the progressive sector’s wage growth, while slow-sector unit cost rises at rate $r$, widening the ratio exponentially. The slow sector becomes relatively more expensive because the model assumes different productivity paths, independently of any increase in importance; its objects overlap with the high-viscosity positions discussed above. The rate $r$ must come from sectoral data rather than being assigned here; the model also assumes comparable units of output, common wages, and unchanged other cost conditions. It describes relative costs under those assumptions, without evaluating the sector’s worth.

In March 2026, the AARP Public Policy Institute estimated that U.S. family care for adults totaled about 49.5 billion hours in 2024, with an imputed economic value of roughly 1.01 trillion U.S. dollars under its method \cite{aarp2026valuing}. This is valuation rather than payment, and methodological changes prevent treating the entire difference from earlier reports as growth on an unchanged basis. Unpaid still means someone invested real time and ability.

The mind-related direction concerns mental health, support, and relationships. WHO’s September 2025 report found more than a billion people living with mental disorders, alongside substantial service gaps \cite{who2025mental}. Conversational services can help, while evidence for clinical effects, safety, escalation, privacy, and access must match their actual claims.

Trust concerns the dependability of judgment. In January 2024, a finance employee at the Hong Kong office of a multinational engineering company saw familiar colleagues and superiors in a video conference, then followed instructions to make 15 transfers totaling about HK\$200 million, roughly US\$25 million; a check with headquarters a week later revealed that every other participant had been a deepfake \cite{hk2024deepfake}. The case undermined a familiar verification channel: a face and voice on video cannot alone establish identity. Trust needs anchors harder to imitate cheaply: two-person checks, meetings in person, traceable signatures, and institutions answerable for compensation.

Physical collateral, verifiable records, and enforceable compensation offer several ways to strengthen credibility. Each raises questions: how does collateral match consequences, which judgments do records support, who triggers remedy, and will the money be available? Verification tools and institutions can lower the cost of trust, while generation can expand the number of claims needing checks. The net effect requires measuring both sides.

\subhead{Pricing and distributing negentropy}

All three directions involve processes and costs that resist rollback. Life involves a body’s singular history, aging, and interventions; mind-related services involve time, with tools changing relationships without merely copying an output and trust developing through honored commitments; trust itself involves promises whose breach cannot be undone, only gradually outweighed by later conduct. These concern more than generation capability; how computation changes their costs, quality, and demand remains open to separate investigation.

The industrial shift can therefore be posed as a pricing question: with generation costs approaching zero, some scarcity may move from reproducible appearances to verifiable processes, abilities, and commitments. This book borrows “negentropy” to examine maintenance: these services provide information while also sustaining conditions for bodies, relationships, and reliable judgments. All three need continuing resources to resist disorganization. Here “luxury” refers to scarcity, without a defense of ostentation or high prices; actual prices depend on supply rates, quality, payment institutions, and bargaining.

Distribution immediately follows. If care, mental health services, and trust intermediaries grow scarcer under market pricing, those needing them most may be least able to pay. As with other high-viscosity positions, scarcity can attract prices without compensating every cost or ensuring access. Addressing distribution calls for institutions: public payment, social insurance, families and volunteers sharing provision, and enforceable service standards. Leave this out, and the “ultimate industries” become a menu available to only part of society.

\subhead{Testing the judgment}

Cheap imitation can hollow out all three directions more quietly than direct replacement. Care can perform its outward form: counted visits, scripted consultations without treatment, or procedures without judgment may pass metrics while withholding substance. Mental services can be packaged as purchasable experiences without sustained relationships. Trust intermediaries can become rubber stamps, ratings for sale, or guarantees without compensation liability. The criterion remains whether process, results, and responsibility can be checked, beyond the amount apparently spent. A care service escaping every consequence of error returns to the low-viscosity problem, however human-centered its name.

Career expectations raise another question. Calling these “ultimate industries” promises neither better or more meaningful work nor reliable income to everyone entering them. Many such jobs remain poorly paid; correcting that mismatch needs institutions beyond personal choice. If value does move toward processes with irreversible costs, these directions may grow in relative importance, at a pace and scale shaped by society’s willingness to pay.

\subsection{The ultimate prediction: a self-organizing Gaia?}

\subhead{From manufacturing to the logic of life}

Engineering systems are built to drawings, maintained by manuals, and replaced through budgets. The familiar logic assumes that some states can be repaired or replaced: fix an error, replace a damaged part, retire an obsolete one. Engineering also accumulates irreversible consequences, while life writes history more deeply into its own maintenance and development; its state emerges from that history, and continued operation requires dissipation. Three conditions make the distinction more concrete.

The first is self-replication: producing the apparatus that replicates the system, beyond producing its products. Von Neumann’s work published in 1966 supplied one construction: the automaton carries both a description and a constructor that reads and builds from it. In that scheme, a description alone remains inert, while a constructor without the corresponding description cannot complete the entire replication \cite{vonneumann1966theory}. The second is self-maintenance: keeping the system far from equilibrium through continuing dissipation. Schrödinger’s 1944 image of “feeding on negative entropy” led into the dynamics developed by Prigogine and Grégoire Nicolis in 1977: open systems far from equilibrium can form and maintain ordered structures through matter and energy fluxes, involving internal entropy production and exchange with the environment, whose net change also depends on other processes \cite{schrodinger1944,nicolis1977,prigogine1977nobel}. The third is heritable variation: copying can introduce changes that pass to descendants. Operating parameters can then change through differential replication and environmental selection alongside design and control.

Replication, maintenance, and heritable variation allow a system to enter environmental selection. Copying fidelity affects how sequences persist. With independent error probability $\nu$ at each position and sequence length $\lambda$, the probability of an error-free copy is

\begin{equation}
Q=(1-\nu)^{\lambda}\approx e^{-\nu\lambda}\qquad(\nu\ll1)
\end{equation}

$Q$ is the probability of error-free copying of the whole sequence; $\nu\lambda$ is the expected number of errors. As $\nu\lambda$ approaches 1, error-free copies become less common, although descendants can remain highly similar to the original. Whether selection maintains a particular sequence also depends on relative fitness, the mutation network, and population processes. DNA polymerase selectivity, proofreading, and mismatch repair jointly improve copying fidelity \cite{kunkel2000dna,gilbert1986}. Longer sequences require lower per-position error rates to preserve the same probability of a complete error-free copy. Repair, proofreading, and organization support these conditions, with energy costs and benefits depending on the mechanism. Fidelity therefore belongs in the resource account, without a fixed rule requiring another layer of machinery for each order-of-magnitude improvement.

\subhead{A Gaia criterion}

At planetary scale, the question grows stronger: if engineering and biological systems become deeply coupled, could the whole meet all three conditions?

Can engineering networks, supplied with continuing energy, improve their capacity to repair, recycle, and reproduce their material foundations? “Gaia” organizes that question here. Industrial chains already replicate many devices but still rely on people, global specialization, and particular feedstocks; this does not establish independent self-replication from raw resources for the entire system.

Self-maintenance, reproduction, and heritable change need individual definitions. Irreversibility can complicate governance without being sufficient evidence of self-organization. For specified materials, boundaries, and observation periods, begin with a narrower quantity: the share of usable supply returned through circulation.

\begin{equation}
\kappa=\frac{\dot m_{\text{cycle}}}{\dot m_{\text{total}}}
\end{equation}

The numerator counts material returned during the period and actually reentering usable supply; the denominator counts all usable inputs within the same boundary, with the numerator a subset for a ratio between 0 and 1. Stocks, cycling delays, quality changes, and double counting need explicit treatment. A high circulated share can reduce virgin extraction without establishing energy autonomy, complete reproduction, or ecological stability.

Compare circulation shares by material, quality, boundary, and year. Steel, aluminum, construction aggregates, and complex composites face different recovery conditions; collection or recycling rates, recycled-input shares, and quality-preserving closed-loop shares are different measures \cite{miatto2017how}. $\kappa$ describes the specified material flow; assessing the whole system’s self-maintenance also requires energy, losses, repair, and reproduction dependencies.

\subhead{From prediction to inquiry}

Turning this prediction into an inquiry requires distinguishing at least three things.

First, it is not yet a theory with a complete testing framework. The conditions give no timetable: structural possibility differs from a forecast that a system will meet them. Testable quantities include copying fidelity, material circulation, and entropy production rates, but common definitions, measurement boundaries, and comparable records must precede tests of the proposed mechanisms.

Second, it implies no purpose. Popular readings of Gaia can confuse maintaining a state with moving toward something beneficial to a particular party. Even a formal account of maintenance need not imply benefit to anyone in particular: a self-maintaining planetary system could operate without people. Reading maintenance as benevolence turns a description into a normative premise.

\key{The information capacity of self-replication depends on copying fidelity, sequence length, and selection; distributed systems able to maintain, repair, and replicate themselves raise new questions about unilateral shutdown.} The third question concerns shutdown: a self-repairing system already replicating can have a different cost structure from a production line. Both may incur supply, maintenance, safety, and exit costs, but only the former may require confronting regrowth and an autonomously spreading replication network. Whether costs and consequences can be withdrawn therefore becomes a physical and governance question for the chapter’s principles.

The four principles now connect: damping ontology asks what formation and maintenance cost; incompleteness asks how standards gain evidence, authorization, and correction; symbiosis examines complementarities between capability and position; recursive optimization connects practice, feedback, and revision. Together they frame how conflicting values should be adjudicated, rather than prescribing each particular task.

This proposed constitution has four foundations. First, a right to imperfection: proving that an objective is executed correctly does not alone establish that it deserves adoption, so there must remain places for challenge, appeal, and rollback; treating every challenge as interference can close correction channels. Second, a voice in defining costs: those bearing them should participate in deciding what counts as a cost and which costs may not be passed on. Third, a division of labor that preserves necessary friction: different strengths make cooperation useful, so the faster side cannot alone decide which resistance to retain, and the division must address the competition that remains. Fourth, direction: recursive improvement should answer to life—to bodies, relationships, judgment, and finitude—beyond output indicators. The foundations depend on one another rather than forming a ranking; removing one weakens the force of the others.

“Silicon-carbon symbiosis” describes a complementary arrangement: replicable capabilities expand choices while actions remain connected to evidence, bodies, rights, and lasting responsibility. Materials do not permanently assign the roles. Digital systems are physical, and life can learn, compute, and delegate; the interfaces can change with evidence and technology.

\key{Where a civilization directs its resources ultimately depends on which costs it regards as irreplaceable.} Abundant generation sharpens the question: inward comfort and outward resistant frontiers draw on the same resources and can shape different civilizations. The inward prospect can flourish while losing interfaces with the world. The next chapter takes the possibility to an extreme: a system with physical self-replication begins to move from manufacturing toward life’s logic; if copies are distributed and materially independent, who can still bring it to an end becomes a concrete question.

Karl Polanyi, \textit{The Great Transformation}\\
