A “lock” names a high constraint for the current task under the chosen scale. Whether it can ease requires examining substitute resources, process changes, and structural reorganization. Regions locate the inquiry; evidence selects the response.

With all coordinates low, the low-viscosity region generally encounters fewer of these three obstacles. Expansion still depends on demand, reliability, and organization; a region is not a growth forecast.

A single lock directs attention to its dominant constraint and possible substitution, process changes, or reduced dependencies. Compare a detour’s feasibility and costs with direct transformation.

Double locks require examining both constraints and their interactions. An improvement may lower both together; feasible routes, investment, and verification shape the pace. A level-surface slope describes cost combinations only within its specified model.

A triple lock calls for scrutiny of resources, time, and structure. Staged investment, task redefinition, or infrastructure changes may alter the combination. Feasibility depends on the project’s feasible set rather than three scores alone.

Ratings and regions express different resolutions of one classification. Ratings retain three levels; a region keeps one cell, trading internal distinctions for a more stable boundary. Objects near the midpoint can still switch regions after a small rating change. That can reflect incomplete evidence, real transition, or criteria needing improvement; claims that a technology is “beginning to get stuck” or “not yet stuck” must return to their evidence and criteria.

Rate first, then locate the region, identifying the position and constraints needing priority checks. The next scale applies the regions to concrete technologies.

\subhead{Comparison: joint gains and cross-dimensional trade-offs}

Some relative comparisons need no numerical weights. For states $a$ and $b$, write coordinate differences $\Delta R=R_{a}-R_{b}$, $\Delta T$, and $\Delta G$; taking logarithms of the exponential form gives

\begin{equation}
\ln\frac{\eta_{a}}{\eta_{b}}
=\alpha\,\Delta R+\beta\,\Delta T+\gamma\,\Delta G
\end{equation}

With shared references and scales and positive weights, if all three constraints in $a$ are no greater than in $b$, and at least one is lower, the model gives $\eta_a<\eta_b$. This is dominance. Opposing changes generally need bounds on weight ratios and magnitudes, beyond weight rankings and signs alone. A 0–5 ordinal scale needs a meaningful quantitative scale before entering the exponential model.

\subhead{Direction: start with derivative signs}

Under the same-direction conditions below, a trend can be inferred from derivative signs. Differentiating with respect to time gives

\begin{equation}
\operatorname{sgn}\!\left(\frac{d\ln\eta}{dt}\right)
=\operatorname{sgn}\!\left(\alpha\dot{R}+\beta\dot{T}+\gamma\dot{G}\right)
\end{equation}

Positive weights and coordinates moving in the same direction determine the model’s cost direction. Opposing directions need weighted magnitudes. Time-varying coefficients add $\dot\alpha R+\dot\beta T+\dot\gamma G$ and a changing-baseline term. Cheaper generation and stable verification time must be measured at their own stages, not inferred from constraint names.

\subhead{Fuzzy, open, revisable}

Qualitative use needs public criteria, recorded uncertainty, and revision through evidence.

It is fuzzy. Criteria rather than precise measurement define the categories, so an object can fit adjacent descriptions. With insufficient evidence, that ambiguity can be more faithful than an unsupported exact number.

Criteria and weights need to answer to new evidence. Later outcomes may require new ratings, normalization, coefficients, or recognition of a mechanism missing from the three dimensions. Revise to the extent the evidence warrants and keep the corresponding record.

Judgments can be updated. A mistaken rating calls for reviewing nearby categories, regional conclusions, and dependent inferences; quantitative parameters can also be reestimated. The chain affected by the error sets the scope of revision. Every judgment should remain traceable to evidence.

\subhead{What remains to measure}

Qualitative use alone cannot quantify differences in magnitude, duration, or threshold location. The earlier $r\theta$, Deborah numbers, and threshold conditions need variables and values for particular objects; the book supplies conditional structures while cross-domain thresholds remain to be measured and tested.

Qualitative and quantitative analysis differ in questions as well as precision: direction, category, and ordering on one side; amount, duration, and threshold crossing on the other. Treating the former as an unsupported numerical approximation can give an apparent conclusion without a test. Lack of numbers is equally no reason to surrender conditional qualitative judgments that evidence can support.


\section{Decomposing technologies and measuring viscosity}

A scale should unpack “this technology is stuck” into examinable judgments: the task, stage, resources, feedback time, affected dependencies, and evidence. Begin with a constraint profile; a calibrated quantitative model can then estimate overall costs.

\subsection{Decomposition: independently examinable units}

A unit needs an examinable output and reasonably consistent internal timescales. Combining millisecond computation with years of follow-up hides constraints in an average. A span of timescales can help identify where to split:
\begin{equation}
\frac{\max_j\tau_j}{\min_j\tau_j}\leq\Lambda.
\label{eq:scale-lambda}
\end{equation}
$\tau_j$ is a subprocess’s characteristic time and $\Lambda$ a published decomposition threshold. $\Lambda$ near 10 offers a starting point; further splitting should identify distinct mechanisms rather than follow an order-of-magnitude boundary mechanically.

There are two kinds of unit. Chain units directly produce results for the next stage: making cells, conducting tests, delivering software. Interface units connect external systems: airworthiness certification, procurement access, airspace coordination, service acceptance. Technology, organization, and institutions can speed both kinds, with each component examined separately.

\subsection{Rating: ordinal judgments before quantitative scales}

Table \ref{tab:scale-anchors} provides illustrative anchors from zero to five. Levels order constraints within a coordinate; specify task criteria and supporting evidence before applying them.

\begin{table}[ht]
\centering
\caption{Ordinal anchors for the three coordinates}
\label{tab:scale-anchors}
{\small
\begin{tabularx}{\textwidth}{@{}lXXX@{}}
\toprule
Level&Resource barriers $R$&Temporal rigidity $T$&Topological coupling $G$\\
\midrule
0 &Small marginal inputs within existing capacity&Effectively immediate for the task&Local change, few dependencies\\
1 &Standard equipment and routine supply suffice&Shorter than the main operating cycle&Known, relatively standardized interfaces\\
2 &Specialized equipment or materials needed&A substantial share of operating time&Several interfaces need adaptation\\
3 &Significant capital, supply, or infrastructure investment&Spans a major planning or construction cycle&Coordination across teams or suppliers\\
4 &Scarce critical inputs or major capacity expansion&Long observation, renewal, or institutional process&Interacting organizations, standards, or jurisdictions\\
5 &Severe constraints within the specified boundary&Much longer than the current decision window&Extensive dependencies that resist isolation\\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}}
\end{table}

Level zero still consumes energy and materials; level five does not automatically mean impossible. Conservation laws constrain a task without proving every design has reached its limit. The categories need not be equally spaced: one time level does not automatically mean tenfold, and two resource levels cannot be read as a cost multiplier.

Suitable data may support a separate continuous scale. For example, explicitly defining
\begin{equation}
T=\log_{10}(\tau/\tau_0),
\qquad
\tau_{k+1}/\tau_k=10
\label{eq:scale-decade}
\end{equation}
makes level differences correspond to orders of magnitude in time. The reference $\tau_0$ is specified rather than generated by the ordinal table. Resources likewise need calibration against consistently measured quantities.

Report uncertainty through adjacent categories, confidence intervals, or missing evidence. If only the boundary between levels $k$ and $k+1$ remains unresolved, record
\begin{equation}
R_i\in\{k,k+1\},
\label{eq:scale-fuzzy}
\end{equation}
and state the evidence needed to resolve the difference. A decimal cannot substitute for it.

A clearly defined dependency-closure size $d_i$ can support a count-based classification:
\begin{equation}
G_i=\min\!\left\{5,\left\lfloor\log_{10}(1+d_i)\right\rfloor\right\}.
\label{eq:scale-G-def}
\end{equation}
Graph reachability, causal influence, synchronized modifications, and administrative coordination are four different relations. Specify which defines the closure. Counts also leave connection strength, critical nodes, and failure propagation to examine.

\subsection{Aggregation: quantities before ratings}

Resource quantities can be added with consistent units and boundaries:
\begin{equation}
P_{\text{total}}=\sum_i P_i.
\label{eq:scale-R-agg}
\end{equation}
Electricity, materials, labor hours, and money need separate accounts; combining unlike units requires explicit conversion. A weighted average of resource ratings supplies a descriptive index under the chosen rule, without recovering total resource demand.

Time follows task structure. Strictly serial durations add; simultaneously started tasks all required for completion take their maximum; a dependency graph follows its critical path:
\begin{equation}
t_{\text{serial}}=\sum_i t_i,
\qquad
t_{\text{completion}}=\max_{p\in\mathcal P}\sum_{i\in p}t_i.
\label{eq:scale-T-agg}
\end{equation}
$\mathcal P$ is the set of admissible dependency paths. Resource contention, rework, and different start times require corresponding scheduling models. The slowest workstation can limit steady throughput, which differs from the first product’s full-chain lead time.

Amdahl’s relation illustrates acceleration of the parallelizable part:
\begin{equation}
S(n)=\frac{1}{s+(1-s)/n}\longrightarrow\frac1s,\qquad s\in(0,1].
\label{eq:scale-amdahl}
\end{equation}
Workload is fixed, $s$ cannot be parallelized, the remainder parallelizes ideally, and additional overheads are initially omitted \cite{amdahl1967validity}. New algorithms or task arrangements can change $s$; the bound belongs to the stated decomposition.

For coupling, first report the dependency graph and its distribution: closures, shared dependencies, critical nodes, isolatable boundaries, and substitute paths. An average rating can be defined as
\begin{equation}
\bar G=\frac1N\sum_iG_i,
\label{eq:scale-G-agg}
\end{equation}
while retaining the distribution and critical nodes. An average can hide a few decisive dependencies.

The familiar giant-component criterion
\begin{equation}
\frac{\langle k^2\rangle}{\langle k\rangle}>2
\label{eq:scale-molloy}
\end{equation}
comes from asymptotic random-graph models under their regularity conditions \cite{molloy1995critical}. It cannot directly decide the behavior of an actual dependency graph with directions, weights, clustering, and institutional relations. Connectivity also does not imply that every node must change simultaneously.

Only after definition, normalization, and calibration should continuous variables enter a quantitative model:
\begin{equation}
\ln\frac{\eta}{\eta_0}=\alpha R+\beta T+\gamma G.
\label{eq:scale-eta}
\end{equation}
List ordinal profiles separately from fitted variables. With parameters, compare predictions and out-of-sample results; without them, report constraints, dominance, and unresolved trade-offs.

If time uses the logarithmic scale in Equation \eqref{eq:scale-decade}, its relation to the Deborah number is
\begin{equation}
\ln\mathrm{De}=(\ln10)T-\ln\frac{\tau_{\text{driving}}}{\tau_0}.
\label{eq:scale-de}
\end{equation}
This identity follows from the scale’s definition. Changing the window changes the ratio without automatically changing adjustment capacity.


\begin{figure}[ht]
\centering
\includegraphics[width=\textwidth]{assets/critical-path.pdf}
\caption{A precedes parallel tasks B and D; C waits for both. Total duration is $2+\max(5,3)+2=9$, rather than the sum 12 or the longest individual task 5. The critical path is A–B–C.}
\label{fig:mechanism-critical-path}
\end{figure}
\subsection{Priorities: large contributions and feasible improvements}

With known weights and comparable scales, the largest model contribution is
\begin{equation}
c^\ast\in\operatorname*{arg\,max}_{c\in\{R,T,G\}}\alpha_c c,
\qquad(\alpha_R,\alpha_T,\alpha_G)=(\alpha,\beta,\gamma).
\label{eq:scale-dominant}
\end{equation}
Unknown weights prevent the largest ordinal coordinate from establishing overall dominance. Even the largest contribution may not deserve first investment; feasible improvement, cost, risk, and interactions matter.

For small, independent changes with roughly constant marginal costs, let reducing coordinate $c$ by one unit cost $\mu_c>0$; then
\begin{equation}
\frac{\alpha_c}{\mu_c}
\label{eq:scale-yield}
\end{equation}
This compares the model’s log-cost reduction per unit of expenditure. It is not absolute net benefit and does not cover cross-dimensional interactions, finite budgets, thresholds, or risks. Finite projects still need comparison as complete alternatives.

\begin{table}[ht]
\centering
\caption{From constraint profiles to intervention choices}
\label{tab:scale-classes}
{\small
\begin{tabularx}{\textwidth}{@{}p{3.0cm}XX@{}}
\toprule
Situation&Evidence needed&Actions to compare\\
\midrule
Main constraint can be eased cheaply&Extent of improvement and full costs&Invest directly; check downstream effects\\
Improvement substantially raises other costs&Interactions, cost bearers, and risks&Compare net effects and distribution; redesign interfaces\\
Current constraint is hard to change, but a substitute path exists&Alternative tasks, routes, and outcome criteria&Detour, stage, or narrow scope\\
Several constraints are high&All feasible paths and input conditions&Reorganize; retain necessary waiting and tests\\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}}
\end{table}

\subsection{Example 1: nine units in low-altitude services}

Begin by splitting a low-altitude project into the nine units of Table \ref{tab:scale-lh}. The table lists conditions to establish; ratings depend on aircraft type, region, operating scope, and evidence.

\begin{table}[ht]
\centering
\caption{Low-altitude services: units, constraints, and evidence}
\label{tab:scale-lh}
{\small
\begin{tabularx}{\textwidth}{@{}p{3.2cm}XX@{}}
\toprule
Unit&What to examine&Evidence to obtain\\
\midrule
Cell manufacturing&Chemistry, supply, yield, and capacity&Specifications, supply, and production records\\
Pack integration and thermal management&System mass, heat rejection, fault isolation&Pack tests under mission conditions\\
Airframe and rotors&Materials, structure, manufacturing, and life&Tests, processes, and maintenance basis\\
Flight controls and avionics&Functions, latency, failures, and versions&Requirements, tests, and certification records\\
Takeoff and landing facilities&Sites, electricity, connections, and backups&Construction conditions, access, and planning\\
Operations and maintenance&Schedules, spares, repairs, and recovery&Operating design and measured support costs\\
Airworthiness certification&Design compliance and verification scope&Documents for the jurisdiction, type, and stage\\
Airspace and routes&Operating boundaries, separation, and emergencies&Applicable rules and actual permissions\\
Service acceptance&Prices, noise, reliability, and rights&Surveys and operating feedback for the population concerned\\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}}
\end{table}

Certification consumes people, equipment, tests, and facilities; coordination and trust also need material carriers and continuing work. An output consisting of permission does not make resources zero. Acceptance requires a defined population and conditions, rather than an assumed ten-year cycle used to predict deployment.

Draw the nine units as a dependency graph, separate parallel tasks from necessary waits, and calculate the critical path. Battery improvements may change payload, diversion margins, economics, and certification evidence together; software can also reduce testing burdens. The project’s actual path determines what controls entry into service.

If approval remains critical, shortening an off-path process may leave first operation unchanged while lowering costs or improving later throughput. Separating those outcomes locates the gain.

\subsection{Example 2: comparing five project types}

\begin{table}[ht]
\centering
\caption{Questions for five kinds of project}
\label{tab:scale-five}
{\small
\begin{tabularx}{\textwidth}{@{}p{3.1cm}XX@{}}
\toprule
Project&Resources and time&Dependencies and confirmation\\
\midrule
Large-model inference services&Existing capacity, full request cost, and expansion&Which downstream actions outputs trigger\\
Advanced-process manufacturing&Equipment, steps, yields, and delivery cycles&Changes needing suppliers and verification together\\
Low-altitude services&Mission energy, backups, and facilities&Evidence for the aircraft, airspace, and operation\\
Gene-editing therapies&Delivery, manufacturing, observation, and follow-up&Cell populations, clinical endpoints, eligible patients\\
Cement and steel decarbonization&Processes, energy, feedstocks, and replacement cycles&Sites, power, transport, product standards, and demand\\

\end{tabularx}}
\end{table}

Projects in one category can have different technologies and responsibility structures. Gene-editing therapy is not synonymous with germline editing, and decarbonization is not one uniformly mature process. Fix the object before rating and comparison; sector names merely begin the search.

The scale should bring disagreement back to evidence: which condition changed in which unit, on what basis, and which implications need recalculation? Then a broad judgment becomes a reviewable map of constraints.


\section{Three response models and routes to testing}

Throughput limits, demand absorption, and adaptive feedback can produce different response shapes. This section proposes three models and corresponding data definitions. Mechanisms and observations select a form for the task; the media classification offers clues.

One digital-service case approaches a usage plateau with relatively stable demand and distribution. Attention, budgets, supply, and product fit can shape that plateau. Measure unit generation costs separately from usage; rapidly expanding candidates do not automatically become used outputs.

One form for that trajectory is

\begin{equation}
Y_{\text{bits}}(t)=Y_{\infty}\left(1-e^{-t/\tau_{\text{approach}}}\right)
\end{equation}

$Y_{\text{bits}}$ is usage or effective processing rate for the service, $Y_\infty$ its plateau on the same measure, and $\tau_{\text{approach}}$ the time constant. With initial value zero, it first rises approximately linearly, then approaches the plateau with an exponentially shrinking gap. Estimate the plateau and approach from data; changing supply or demand may require new parameters or a new form.

Fixed equipment, space, and energy supply can bound physical output per unit time. Additional inputs may yield diminishing returns near capacity, while equipment, processes, or network expansion change the bound. Compare design, manufacturing, construction, and maintenance separately to locate AI’s actual improvements.

Two features can be expressed as conditions:

\begin{equation}
0\le Y_{\text{atoms}}(I)\le \Phi_{\max},\qquad \frac{\partial^{2}Y_{\text{atoms}}}{\partial I^{2}}\le0\quad(\text{saturation approximation})
\end{equation}

$Y_{\text{atoms}}$ is physical output rate, $\Phi_{\max}$ maximum sustainable output under the given facilities, in the same units, and $I$ consistently measured input. The first condition supplies a capacity bound; the second adds a concavity approximation in the saturation region. Stepwise expansion, learning, and complementary inputs can violate concavity, calling for forms matched to observation.

Energy comparisons likewise need a fixed task. Erasing a bit, breaking a chemical bond, and lifting a macroscopic object choose different operation units; their absolute energies cannot determine sectoral growth rates. Count required operations, actual dissipation, equipment capacity, and useful output across a complete task, then compare gains from design and execution.

Adaptive feedback can change dose–effect relationships. One testable case has mean benefit approaching a plateau beyond some intensity while outcome dispersion keeps increasing. Continued improvement, declining effects, and delayed responses are also possible. Record intensity, duration, group differences, and follow-up together to identify the feedback.

The proposed test is

\begin{equation}
\left.\frac{d\langle Y_{\text{life}}\rangle}{dP}\right|_{P>P_{c}}\approx0,\qquad \left.\frac{d\,\mathrm{Var}(Y_{\text{life}})}{dP}\right|_{P>P_{c}}>0
\end{equation}

$Y_{\text{life}}$ is the selected outcome, $P$ intervention intensity in fixed units, and $P_c$ an estimated turning point. Means and variances retain their respective units. The two conditions jointly describe a plateau with growing dispersion; other feedback shapes need different functions. Keep population, observation duration, and repeated measurements in the comparison.

The examples use time, input, and intervention intensity as different predictors, so their plotted slopes cannot be directly compared. To compare one technology across stages, first align task, inputs, and outcome definitions, then control process time and environment separately. The shapes follow mechanism assumptions; matched comparisons must establish whether actual domains differ accordingly.

The proposed classification and those independently examinable conditions have different roles. Each curve states its own criterion; a contradictory observation requires revising that curve without automatically rejecting the other two, while shared mechanisms or data dependencies require examining how far the result extends.

A technology usually crosses several stages with interacting outcomes. Total output need not linearly add the three curves. Begin with stable task boundaries, recording design, execution, verification, and maintenance times and costs separately; use controls, staged deployment, or comparable projects to investigate mechanisms. Explain overall effects after evidence supports the stage relationships.


\section{Epistemic boundaries}

Evaluation has three levels: whether constraint categories identify mechanisms, whether quantitative models explain and distinguish observations, and whether normative claims offer public reasons. Each needs its own evidence and corresponding revision.

First, classification organizes questions; calibrated quantitative models make particular predictions. Predictions need fixed tasks, variables, baselines, and parameters, followed by out-of-sample testing. Region names and uncalibrated formulas can identify constraints to examine, without determining deployment years, growth rates, or thresholds.

Second, physical forms need explicit mechanism mappings in sociotechnical analysis. A thickening analogy needs an account of how intervention rates induce compensation or structural change; a Deborah analogy needs measured response and input timescales. Supported mappings supply explanation; unsupported ones call for a different form. Similar vocabulary cannot replace that examination.

Third, categories and functional forms need separate tests. Compare log-linear, interaction, threshold, and other candidate forms on independent data; test whether media categories add mechanism explanation and out-of-sample discrimination. Repeatedly redefining variables to obtain a fit calls the definitions into question. Similar curves across media require examination of mechanisms and task scales; shape alone neither confirms nor refutes the whole framework.

Fourth, constraints explain conditions affecting transition costs; value arguments explain why results, rights, and responsibilities deserve protection. This book argues for affected people’s participation, evidence retained for judgments, and accountability for decisions. Those claims need public ethical reasons, procedures, and distributional arrangements; physical lower bounds cannot choose for them.

Chapter 7 uses these distinctions to argue for choosing, sharing, and bearing viscosity. In a concrete decision, establish feasible paths and cost distributions, compare interests and rights, then assign authority and responsibility. Data support feasibility judgments, normative reasons support trade-offs, and implementation records keep both open to testing.
